en: *Beishan lu*, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shenqing of Huayi Monastery in Zizhou;
annotated by the Śramaṇa Huibao of Caoxuan Pavilion in Western Shu.

1. The Beginning of Heaven and Earth (I). Section One: The Beginning of Heaven and Earth. This clarifies the sequence of the emergence of phenomena when heaven and earth first opened up. Ai Ru is "Ru" who exerts himself for a glorious reputation; "Ai" signifies growth. 2. The Birth of the First Sage. 3. The Arising of the Dharma Canon. 4. The Accordance of the Ultimate and the Conventional. 5. The Unification of the Hegemon and the King. 6. The Culmination of Transformation. 7. Discourse on the Patriarchs and Masters. 8. The Questions of the Monk Guest. 9. Questions on Mourning Rites. 10. Critique of Heterodox Doctrines. 11. Compendium of Names and Principles. 12. Verification of Karmic Retribution. 13. Discourse on the Principles of Karma. 14. Conduct of the Abbot. 15. Heterodox Studies. 16. External Faiths. 1. The Beginning of Heaven and Earth (I). Section One: The Beginning of Heaven and Earth. This clarifies the sequence of the emergence of phenomena when heaven and earth first opened up. Ai Ru is "Ru" who exerts himself for a glorious reputation; "Ai" signifies growth.
When one is old yet possesses the Way, such a person is esteemed by the world and called "Ai" (elderly).
This refers to those who are resolute in their intent and exalted in their conduct, distancing themselves from worldly heterodoxy and embodying the style of high antiquity;
these are the scholars of the mountains and valleys.
It is not something favored by ordinary people;
it is vigorous and striking,
as well as restful and beautiful.
"The multitude of scholars approached him to admire his teaching. "Multitude" refers to the great assembly.
"Approached" means to draw near.
It describes how the multitude of scholars, drawn by the sage's vast knowledge and excellent reputation, came to study under him.
This critique of the world’s teachings and the path of instruction is something that those who delight in learning and dwell in it may admire.
That I, a mere youth, might offer my respects regarding the origins of the universe is but the modesty of this humble person.
Some may doubt this.
"Universe" refers to heaven and earth;
"quanyu" refers to the very beginning.
He said, "I harbor doubts regarding the matter of the initial opening and creation of heaven and earth;
I have prostrated twice to express what is within my breast.

Airo (Ricci) replied, "How rich indeed is this question! 'Rich' means vast and magnificent. I know that heaven and earth were like the *mingxing*—a state of vastness and boundlessness, a form where all was yet undifferentiated. 'Dandan' (旦旦) means constant clarity and understanding."
As for the saying, "The three celestial bodies shine brightly," [the Master said,] "Stay; let me speak to you. "Stay" means to sit down.

Because he had risen to pose a question, [the Master] ordered him to sit again and showed him this: "In the *I Ching*, there is the Great Ultimate (*taiji*), which gives birth to the two polarities (*liangyi*). The *Gouming jue* states: [as follows].
The *Yi* has five "Greats" (*tai*).
First is the Great *Yi*, when the forms and appearances have not yet been differentiated.
Second is the Great Beginning (*taichu*), when the primal qi (*yuanqi*) begins to sprout.
Third is Tai-shi (Great Beginning), the initial stage of form.
Fourth is Tai-su (Great Purity), where form undergoes transformation and possesses substance.
Fifth is Tai-ji (Great Ultimate), where form and substance are fully complete.
From the Great Ultimate (Taiji) arose Heaven and Earth, the two polarities of clarity and turbidity. In the very beginning, before any signs appeared,
all was vast and expansive, surging and surging, boundless and undifferentiated.
Clarity and turbidity share a single principle.
"Chun-hun" (混沌) is without form; "hong" (澒) is a term for vast water (the character is pronounced *hú kǒng*).
"Jue" means "that which.
The *Huainanzi* says:
"Before heaven and earth had taken form, there was vast emptiness, expansive and surging, cavernous and overflowing."
All these refer to what is called the state before forms and images have been differentiated.

"Chun-hun" (chaotic unity) is the appearance of that which has not yet opened or become manifest. It is the state where the primal qi is vast and obscure, the sprouting of the source of all beginnings; "dai" (nearly/at the point of) refers to the very moment of this initial emergence.
It is also a support;
it is the qi of the vast, nebulous primordial unity.
In the writings of Zhuangzi, it is said that Pangu was born within it.
For eighteen thousand years, heaven and earth were not yet divided,
remaining like a hen’s egg; only then did the signs of the clear and the turbid begin to manifest.
These are called the Two Polarities.
The clear qi becomes Heaven;
the turbid qi becomes Earth.
Harmony constitutes humanity;
these are the Three Powers.
Thereafter, Pangu was born within them.
He has governed for eighteen thousand years since the opening of heaven and earth. Daily,
the heavens have increased by one zhang in height,
and the earth has increased by one zhang in thickness.
The day of Pangu was one zhang in length;
his head reached the extreme east.
The feet reach the extreme west;
the left hand reaches the extreme south;
the right hand reaches the extreme north.
Opening the eyes constitutes dawn;
closing the eyes constitutes night;
calling out constitutes summer heat.
Inhaling constitutes cold;
exhaling forms wind and clouds.
The sound produced becomes thunder and lightning as heaven and earth open up.
The heavens were ten zhang high,
and the earth was ten zhang thick;
Pangu’s four limbs were exceedingly vast.
"Ultimate" means reaching the limit.
"Dawn" means clarity.
Thus do the four seasons proceed.
All things are born therein.

As for the vastness of the eight horizons and the nine enclosures, how could anything be more numerous than they? The eight horizons consist of the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate corners.
The Nine Enclosures encompass the nine provinces.
Furthermore, regarding the three sovereigns and five cycles of honor at the center of the eight directions—who among them is prior?

The three sovereigns are Fuxi, Shennong, and Huangdi; the five cycles are metal, wood, water, fire, and earth. Fuxi had the cycle of wood, Shennong the cycle of fire, and Huangdi the cycle of earth. Jintian had the cycle of metal and Zhuanxu the cycle of water. By means of the mutual generation of the Five Elements, the succession of mandates for a hundred generations can be known. This was the time of ancient antiquity.
They roasted millet and split piglets; they used hollowed-out vessels for wine and scooped-up earth for drinking;
they used bundles of grass as drumsticks and earthen mounds as drums—these were all methods of burning.
In ancient times, there were no cauldrons or steamers;
they selected rice and sliced meat, placing them upon heated stones to eat.
They used dirty vessels, hollowing out the ground to serve as wine jars.
*Póu* (pronounced *bù hóu*):
to scoop up with the hands. *Kuài*:
pronounced like *kuì*.
The *pou* was a drumstick;
they used clods of earth as drumsticks. In winter they dwelt in earthen caves; in summer they dwelt in nests built on high;
in the cold they piled up earth, and in the heat they gathered firewood and lived atop it. They had not yet mastered the transformation of fire for cooking, and thus they ate raw food.
The fruits of plants and trees,
the flesh of birds and beasts,
and the drinking of their blood.
In the *Wenxuan*, "ru" (茹) refers to chewing and eating. When there were as yet no silk or hemp, people wore feathers and skins;
this was the era of high antiquity. Later, the sages arose and acted [to change this].

Thereafter, they cultivated the benefits of cremation and refined their practices. They cast metal and molded clay to forge and fire vessels for use. They constructed terraces, pavilions, palaces, and chambers with doors and windows.

They used roasting and burning by applying things to the fire; they used cauldrons for boiling and cooking; and they used skewers for grilling over the flames to produce sweet wine, curdled milk, fermented spirits, and brewed liquors.
*Tuo* (酪) refers to fermented vinegar;
*sù* (酢) is pronounced as *cuò*;
*zài* (酨) is pronounced as *zài*.
Some versions omit this sentence: "They processed the silk and hemp to produce cloth and fabric,
using them to sustain life and provide for the dead, and to serve the spirits."
From antiquity until the present,
the number of years and generations is beyond reckoning.
Following Fuxi, [the succession continued].
For more than four million years, they underwent transformations and perfected their resources,
serving as rulers and ministers.

"To act for the people" (*weiren weimin*): "people" (*min*) is a term denoting those who are inferior and lowly. "Harm and benefit" (*hairy xingwang*) refers to harm and loss, as well as prosperity and ruin. Former scholars recorded this—*zhi* meaning to record—and later scholars inherited it.
Thus, the discourse has become vast and tumultuous.
It cannot be fully discussed in a single day; "exhausted" (dàn) means to have reached the limit.

The above constitutes the account of the opening and closing of heaven and earth as narrated by the Jesuit missionary (Ài Rú). This "rustic of the northern mountains by the banks of the Fú River" has long since turned his back on the splendors of civilization and departed from worldly customs. "Rustic" (yěfū) is used here as a mark of humility.
Shen Qing, whose courtesy name was Lingyu,
was surnamed Zhang and was a native of Changming County in Mianzhou.
The three brothers left the household life;
the Master was the second-born,
yet he alone was exceptionally outstanding.
Venerable Fayun of Kaiyuan Monastery in Mianzhou was his teacher.
He passed away at the end of the Jianzhong era at Huayi Monastery in Zizhou.
He composed the *Fahua xuanyan* (Mysterious Annotations on the Lotus Sūtra) in ten fascicles.
The *Shishi nianzhi* (Chronicle of the Śākya Clan) in thirty fascicles;
the *Lüshu ya jue* (Essential Decisions on the Vinaya Commentary) in ten fascicles;
and the *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) in ten fascicles.
The two assemblies’ initial rules of conduct, as well as the *Shixin*, *Chengguan*,
and commentaries on treatises such as the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, totaling over one hundred fascicles, were still based on ancient traditions, and his knowledge was not yet extensive.
To lead oneself by means of the Way until one reaches the goal is precisely what constitutes an obstacle.
Thus, when I was first studying, I joined the ranks of the local village school; such is the nature of village learning.
As the *Book of Rites* says:
The village had its *shu* (academy), and the district had its *xiang* (school). Hearing the Confucian teachings and taking delight in them, they exclaimed:
"How magnificent are the words of the Confucian!"
When he subsequently turned his vocation toward the Śākya school,
he entered its depths for the first time;
he was as terrified as if crossing the Milky Way, yet he remained resolute and unwearied in his pursuit.
This is a change of meaning.
"Yá" (涯), "shǐ" (始), "pàn" (畔), and "àn" (岸) all refer to the edge or boundary. As Zhuangzi said:
It was a source of alarm and terror, as vast and boundless as the Milky Way.

He felt weary, dissatisfied, and resentful, lamenting that he had not heard of this earlier; he exclaimed, "How can it be? There is a sage from Gandhāra—Gandhāra being the same as Tianzhu (India)—who has heard of this long ago."
The Sage is the Buddha. It is said that when the previous kalpa had already been destroyed and heaven and earth were already empty,
from emptiness they were formed once again.
This kalpa has just begun; the world undergoes the four periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, each lasting twenty kalpas.
From a human lifespan of ten years, it increases by one year every hundred years until it reaches eighty-four thousand years.
When the lifespan decreases by one year per century until it reaches ten years, this is called one kalpa.
Such periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness together constitute eighty kalpas,
which then cycle again from the beginning.
At that time, there was a slight breeze in space;
the wind gradually grew more violent,
dwelling beneath this world-system.
This is indeed the fierce and violent wind-circle;
this is precisely it. The *Lishi apitan lun* (Abhidharmakośa-śāstra on the Establishment of the World) states:
Twenty kalpas after the world was empty, it was about to be formed;
then the Vairambha winds blew upon it, creating the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala) which rests at the very bottom,
nine hundred and sixty million yojanas in thickness.
It is twelve billion three hundred and forty-five yojanas in extent. Great clouds rise into the sky and rain down as thick as axles,
accumulating upon that wind-circle to form the water-circle.
The uppermost layer of the water wheel solidifies into gold,
like the film that forms on the surface of milk as it cools;
this constitutes the Golden Wheel, located one hundred and sixty million yojanas beneath the earth.
It is composed of pure gold;
above that, for eighty thousand [yojanas],
it is formed from a mixture of the seven elements— gold, silver, copper, iron, and so forth.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"The water wheel solidifies, like milk congealing when cold. Once these three wheels have been formed..."
Rain falls from the sky, pouring down upon the Golden Wheel;
it is both vast and deep, with raindrops as large as axle-trees,
falling without ceasing day or night.
It was like a river pouring forth for countless thousands of years,
with the water reaching a thickness of two hundred and forty million yojanas.
It is twelve billion three hundred forty-five *yojanas* in width, and thirty-six billion one thousand three hundred fifty *yojanas* in circumference; the wind strikes this water.
The pure and the turbid differ in substance.
To form the Brahma-world and the celestial abodes of the air-dwellers, there is a wind named "Upholder" (*saṃdhāraṇa*) which blows and causes the world-system to be formed.
Furthermore, there is a wind named "Circular Riser" (*parimaṇḍala-utthāna*) which forms the two continents of the East and the West.
Furthermore, there is a wind named Lute-Arisen that forms the Southern Continent;
there is another wind named Four-Sides-Four-Corners that forms the Northern Continent;
and first, the Brahma-world is formed.
Due to past causes and conditions, the abode of the Brahmā King was as large as one four-continent world system (*cāturdvīpaka*).
At that time, the Brahmā King was born there, and his sons were also born.
The six heavens of the desire realm are like awakening from a dream;
suddenly they recall past events.
At that time, the devas gather in groups, filling the air as they travel about on inspection.
They all spoke thus:
"In the past, there were Mount Sumeru, the city of Sudarśana, the garden of Duṣkīrti, and so forth;
we all remember these as having been made of precious gems."
They serve as mountains and seas;
they serve as lands;
they serve as palaces and chambers.
The various objects are intermingled like wind forming a mountain that ascends in successive stages;
the mountain then has a summit.
If the wind arises, it may do so either directly or obliquely.
Whether mountain ranges are level or towering, and whether the great earth has plains,
depressions, rocky caves, or perforated holes—
all these arise from the differing forces of the wind.
This is the stage of differentiation (*vibhaṅga*). As the realms become established through the intermingling of beings,
those among the gods of the upper realms who die are reborn below.
His body emits flying light;
his feet seem to ride upon the clouds;
he neither drinks nor eats.
For countless years, there were devas who, having relinquished their retribution, took birth therein.
Furthermore, there were devas and humans whose lives ended and who were born in the four continents to receive human birth.
At that time, these people took joy and pleasure as their food.
Abiding in bliss, they dwell in the transformation body born of mind;
naturally luminous, they abide in peace and happiness,
traveling through the air.
At that time, the sun and moon had not yet appeared in the world;
the constellations did not yet exist,
and day and night were not distinguished.

At that time, there was no distinction of age, nor were there men, women, parents, surnames, or personal names. When the essence of the earth became like honey and the pores of the ground grew sweet, when forest creepers exuded fragrant scents and the fragrant rice began to flourish, the great ocean rose and fell in succession.
Where the water recedes at the source of the riverbed,
there is fertile ground from which a great, sweet, and delicious flavor emerges.
Growing and covering the ground,
it is endowed with desirable color, fragrance, texture, and flavor, like fine honey.
Furthermore, there is a layer of earth.
Everyone ate them; when the surface of the earth was exhausted, they next ate forest creepers.
When the forest creepers were exhausted, there appeared naturally growing non-glutinous rice.
When these four— the fragrances, scents, and foods— pervade and are consumed by them, calamity befalls their bodies;
their physical forms become solid and heavy,
and their radiance vanishes.
From this point on, the sun, moon, and stars became visible. At that time,
there was a person who smelled the fragrant scent of the earth's fertility and gave rise to a mind of desire and attachment.
He pinched off a large morsel,
smelled it, and tasted it;
he knew it was sweet and delicious.
Others followed their example; this was entirely because the essence of the earth had caused their bodies to become somewhat firm and heavy,
such that they could no longer fly.
The radiance of their bodies vanished;
once that light had disappeared,
the world was plunged into darkness.

Thereupon days and months were produced, and the stars and constellations appeared; thus the methods for cleansing impurities and guiding the vital breath (*qi*) were established, whereby the Way of Humanity was perfected. "Cleansing" (*jiān*) means to remove;
it also means clarity.
There are matters of great and small impurity;
there are matters of male and female desire that guide the vital breath.
Once resentment and stinginess have sprouted, [the afflictions arise].
Sensual desire arises;
there are fathers and sons, as well as anger and resentment,
and stinginess and greed.
From the existence of craving and stinginess, greed subsequently arises;
when one is encroached upon by others,
anger follows from this.
Their countenances are ugly and their merit and virtue are meager;
they have lost their supernormal powers, yet among them there still exist rulers and ministers.
The wilds were delineated and the states divided;
thus the various kingdoms arose.
We demarcated our borders and established our hamlets.
Wealth and resources flourish therein.
To restrain depravity and punish offenses, penal laws are established; "restraining" here refers to providing a defensive barrier.
These are the laws for warding off calamities;
all of these constitute the foundation of establishing a state.
From this point on, there are lands divided into provinces within Jambudvīpa.
It is named after the Jambū tree.
This extends from a single Jambudvīpa to ten billion Jambudvīpas;
from these four continents to ten billion sets of four continents, the offerings and sustenance in Pūrvavideha are superior.
In the western continent of Aparagoyānī, one uses cattle as currency for trade.
In the northern continent of Uttarakuru, the people are upright and virtuous in heart.
These four continents constitute the world.
"Distance from the Great Iron Encircling Mountains" means reaching as far as them;
this is because they encircle [the world].
All were formed at the same time.
It is the realm of a single Great Sage; this great trichiliocosm is entirely the domain of the Buddha-king’s transformative influence.
As for the gradual decrease in the lifespan of human beings:
The lifespan decreased until it reached ten years;
having decreased, it increased again,
reaching eighty thousand years.
When the human lifespan is twenty thousand years, there is an Iron Wheel-turning King;
when it is forty thousand years, there is a Copper Wheel-turning King;
and when it is sixty thousand years, there is a Silver Wheel-turning King.
Eighty thousand years later, there will be a Golden-Wheel King who unifies Jambudvīpa in this manner,
extending even to two, three, or four continents; then there will be an Iron-Wheel King who unifies the entire world.
Copper governs two worlds;
silver, three worlds;
and gold governs four worlds.
Now, this is the ninth period of decline within the Bhadrakalpa; it is during this ninth kalpa of decline that the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa appear.
The remaining eleven kalpas may be understood accordingly.
At the end of one such period of decline,
there will be thirty years of famine and twenty years of pestilence.
When the lifespan reaches ten years, the calamity of weapons occurs;
this constitutes the minor triad of calamities. When it decreases further to thirty years, there is the calamity of famine for seven years, seven months, and seven days.
Due to the arising of violent winds that blow upon those regions,
the seasons will lose their proper measure and grain will fail to ripen.
When they reach twenty years of age, there will be the calamity of pestilence.
Due to the harm inflicted upon people by malevolent spirits and deities on the seventh day of the seventh month,
when they reach the age of ten, there will be the calamity of weapons,
and they will kill one another.
They were armed only with swords and staves for seven days and seven nights.
When the kalpa had thus come to an end, the world was about to be destroyed.
The various devas transformed their bodies to resemble rhinoceroses;
day and night, three times a day, they proclaimed this edict: "To cultivate the concentration of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*) is the most sublime bliss."
After his life ended, he was reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Seven days later, when the sun-disk arose in the sky, the great earth and Mount Sumeru all burst into flames;
simultaneously, they blazed intensely, and by that heat, the waters of the water-wheel below were drawn up like clarified butter until everything was completely exhausted.
The fire calamity reaches as far as the Nine Heavens—the six heavens of the Desire Realm together with the three heavens of the First Dhyāna.
The whirlwind calamity sweeps through the Third Dhyāna; "whirlwind" refers to the wind named *Sūciloma*, which utterly devastates all.
The wind calamity reaches as far as the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
As for water, it flows surgingly therein; "tāng" (湯) is pronounced "shāng" (傷), describing the appearance of flowing water.
Because the calamity of water reaches up to the second dhyāna, it is said that "in the interval" [between them].
There are seven cycles of calamities by fire followed by one cycle of calamity by water;
then seven cycles of calamities by water followed by one cycle of calamity by wind.
When all transformations have ceased,
the emptiness of self-destruction remains for twenty kalpas;
during nineteen of these kalpas, sentient beings are destroyed.
One kalpa is the period of the destruction of the insentient world.
From this point, it remains empty for twenty kalpas.
Once this emptiness has been established:
Furthermore, this marks the beginning of a subsequent kalpa: after being empty for twenty kalpas, it undergoes formation for another twenty kalpas;
once formed, it remains for another twenty kalpas.
As the Sūtra says:
The periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness each last twenty kalpas;
these together constitute one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*), as elucidated in such scriptures as the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*.
Now, nothing is more venerable or profound than the sublime loftiness of heaven and earth.
This is profound and generous.
In terms of duration, nothing surpasses the span of past and present.
How magnificent! The Great Sage knew the beginning of heaven and earth.
He knows the end of heaven and earth;
he knows the height of heaven;
he knows the thickness of the earth.
To know the brilliance of the three celestial bodies— the sun, moon, and stars—
is to understand their luminosity.
To know the cycles of time and years is to comprehend kalpas.
One knows the passing of the past and the coming of the present.
Regarding the power of vision, nothing surpasses the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); through it, a śrāvaka perceives a thousandfold world-system.
Pratyekabuddhas see two thousand worlds;
Bodhisattvas see three thousand worlds;
Buddhas see a great trichiliocosm.
In terms of hearing, nothing is superior to the divine ear, which hears as much as the divine eye perceives.
In terms of recollection, nothing is superior to the supernormal knowledge of past lives,
which remembers events from immeasurable kalpas ago.
There is no one who possesses such penetrating discernment yet fails to encompass all under heaven. Therefore,
there is nothing that the protective canopy does not reach and nothing that the sun and moon do not illuminate— not even the Summit of Existence or the Avīci Hell.
It is that which frost and dew do not cause to fall, nor do the four seasons alter;
it is that which neither boat nor carriage can carry, yet is naturally obtained—
equal to the realms of all Buddhas.
If one can comprehend it within the mind and eyes— where the eyes perceive it and the mind masters it—
how much more so for a mere snail’s horn in a single district! Formerly, Wei Qi and Lord Tian conspired and made a pact.
Marquis Tian turned his back on him.
Wei Ying was enraged and intended to attack him.
Hearing of this, Master Hui went to see Dai Ren.
Dai Ren was a worthy man of Liang who said:
"Do you know what is called the 'snail's horn'?
Now, on the left side of this snail's horn, there is a state called Chushi (the Touching One)."
To the right of the tip of a snail's horn, there was a state called Man.
At that time, it fought over territory with [the other state],
and tens of thousands lay dead upon the ground.
They pursued the defeated for fifteen days before returning.
The ruler said, "Alas! Those words were empty.
[Zhuangzi] replied, "I beg to make them real for Your Majesty. Does that which exists in the four directions, above, and below have an end?"
He said, "It is infinite.
He said, "To know how to roam in the infinite and return to the realm of thorough penetration is called 'coming and going.
It is like a single mustard seed upon Mount Tai."
It is like a single hair attached to the body of a horse;
what need is there to contend over it?
I pity those who are born within this [world].
"Are you a *hèjī*— a tiny insect on the surface of vinegar?
Or are you a *huìgú*— also known as a *xiānggú* or a *lóugú*?"
He is known as the Stone Mouse.
How could he possibly know the vast expanse of the universe or the long duration of kalpas?
He merely places his trust in the Sage and laments that he himself is as obscure and insignificant as a minute creature.
How can one know the vastness and distance of heaven and earth?
One simply believes with sincerity what the Sage has taught.
Indeed, years accumulated constitute a "billion" (億).
How can one hundred million years not constitute an eon (*kalpa*)?
By piling up earth to form the boundaries of a state,
how can those boundaries not constitute a world-system (*lokadhātu*)?
Tang asked Geng, saying,
"Are there limits to the eight directions, above and below?
Geng replied:
"Beyond the infinite there is yet another infinite," as stated in the *Zhuangzi*.
[The questioner] asks: "Is the world finite?
The answer says: "The world in the ten directions is infinite."
Beyond this world there is yet another world.
This differs slightly from the account in the *Liezi*.
Ran You asked Zhongni, saying:
"Is it possible to know what existed before heaven and earth?
Zhongni said, "The past was just like the present. Ran Qiu likely meant that he was asking about the time prior to the creation of the world.
The answer states: "Heaven and earth are destroyed and then re-formed; they decline and then rise again.
From this we know that the ancient and former sage-kings, as well as the earlier scholars, were not without knowledge;
it was simply that they remained silent while manifesting their realization.
Now, one who ascends Mount Meng finds Lu to be small; Mount Meng lies to the east of the city of Lu.
One who ascends Mount Tai finds the whole world to be small.
How much more so for one who stands higher than Mount Tai? Mount Tai is the Eastern Peak; ascending it, one can gaze upon the entire world.
One knows that the world is not large;
how much more so for that which is higher than it!
Thus, the four seas and the nine provinces are like a hair-tip attached to the body of a horse.
Truly, this is not in vain.
In antiquity, the Yellow Emperor, of the lineage Di Hong, was once sleeping during the day when he dreamed of traveling to the land of Huaxu; there was indeed a country named Huaxu.
It lies west of Yanzhou and north of Taizhou.
One does not know how many tens of thousands of *li* it is from Qi;
yet it is the center of Qi.
Indeed, it is beyond the reach of boats, carts, or human strength.
In that land, there are no teachers or elders;
people are spontaneously wise.
There is no death from evil, nor untimely demise.
One does not know one's kin,
nor does one know external things.
Therefore, there is neither love nor hatred;
one does not know how to turn away in opposition,
nor does one know how to incline toward compliance.
Therefore, there was neither profit nor harm;
there was nothing at all for which they felt attachment or regret,
and nothing at all from which they felt fear or dread— all of this was the result of the transformative influence of the customs of the land of Huaxu.
When the Yellow Emperor awoke from his sleep,
he was serene and felt as though he had attained something; having wandered as a spirit within his dream,
upon waking he felt as if he possessed some realization.
I have examined and reflected upon that land;
it is like the world beneath Mount Uttarakuru, namely the continent of Uttarakuru.
The *Lokaprajñapti-abhidharma* states:
In that country there are no teachers or preceptors;
they naturally obtain clothing and food.
Their lifespan is fixed at one thousand years, and women do not marry others.
The woman also did not marry a husband;
if she felt desire,
she would gaze intently at her.
If a woman sees a man looking at her, as soon as they go to another place, the *mañjuṣa* tree will immediately cover them;
thus, their amorous act is accomplished.
If it does not cover them, [the rite fails].
Knowing them to be their own kin, they did not dare to harm them.
When a child was born, they would not nurse it but instead place it on a crossroads;
passersby would insert their fingers into its mouth and suckle it.
After seven days, he became a full human being;
free from both hatred and affection, he was transformed spontaneously.
His spirit was clear as he examined his dream.
This seems to correspond to the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru).
It lies beyond the Nine Enclosures (navāvaraṇa) among the human Nine Continents (nava-jambudvīpa),
situated within the Encircling Ocean (sāgara) in the midst of the great sea to the north of Mount Sumeru.
This was not something known by Feitian, Lao Limu, or Taishan Ji; all three were ministers of the Yellow Emperor.
The Lord of Dihong unified his mind and disciplined his body, seeking the way to nourish the self and regulate the affairs of things.
Therefore, it is where the spirits roam;
were it not for the Northern Continent, it would not have been as in my dream.
Thus, when I speak of "lesser sages" in my teaching, I refer to those of the intermediate Small Vehicle.
In each preceding and succeeding kalpa, there are eighty thousand [aeons].
Regarding the two thousandfold world-systems seen and heard: with the divine eye, one perceives the events within two thousandfold world-systems;
with the divine ear, one hears the sounds within two thousandfold world-systems, and so forth.
The sages of the middle stage are able to know the three thousandfold world; this refers to the Bodhisattva vehicle.
As for the Great Awakening, it is "already complete" (ji); "complete" means exhaustive.
There is nothing they do not know and nothing they do not see.
The sun, moon, and stars are arrayed within the central void; this "arraying in brilliance" refers to the central void, which is the realm of space.
The sun and moon have no arising or perishing; they eternally abide in the heavens.
It merely revolves through the four worlds;
because Mount Sumeru obstructs it, there is darkness and light.
The stars neither wane nor wax.
In one day and night, the sun and moon illuminate the four great continents; they shine continuously upon two continents at a time.
For instance, when the sun first rises over the southern continent, it is midday on the eastern continent, dusk on the northern continent, and midnight on the western continent.
When it is midday in Jambudvīpa, it is dusk in Pūrvavideha, midnight in Uttarakuru, and sunrise in Aparagoyānī.
When it is sunset in Jambudvīpa, it is midnight in Pūrvavideha, midday in Aparagoyānī, and dawn in Uttarakuru.
The other continents follow this pattern.
North and south are distinguished by cold and heat: in summer, the sun is near the north and the moon is near the south;
in winter, the moon is near the north and the sun is near the south.
The spring and autumn are states of equilibrium.

Sustained by the power of the wind, they neither remain stationary nor fall; all are carried and rotated by the whirlwind (suvilola-vāyu), which supports them within space so that they do not descend.
Below the midpoint of Mount Sumeru,
there dwell various devas;
the lengths of their nights and days vary accordingly.

Is this not similar to the division of time into the opening and closing of day and night as found in this region? This is what is explained in the treatises of the West, such as the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Tattvasiddhi*.
"Divisions" refers to the divisions of spring and autumn.
At the winter and summer solstices and at the commencement of spring (lìchūn), it is called "opening";
at the commencement of autumn (lìdōng), it is called "closing.
The sun [traverses] fifty-one yojanas [per day].
The moon is fifty yojanas in diameter;
the largest stars are one yojana;
the smallest are one krośa in diameter.
Some say it is a *yojana*;
this is translated as "the distance a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) should travel in one day," which is either thirty or forty *li*.
*Krośa*. This is translated as "the distance of one cow's bellow," which is two *li*.
In the Hīnayāna, one *yojana* is sixteen *li*.
It signifies "minute" or "small. Below [the ground], it refers to the common use of fire-jewels and water-jewels.
The fire-jewel is the sun;
the water-jewel is the moon.
As for the year of the fall of stars like rain in Lu—this refers to the fifth day of the fourth month in the seventh year of Duke Zhuang of Lu, when it rained as if with stars.
Regarding the falling of five stones at the capital of Song, the *Zuozhuan* states:
"In the first month of the sixth year of Duke Xi of Lu,
five stones fell at Song."
It is generally said that these were all falling stars;
they appeared suddenly as auspicious anomalies.
Confucian accounts include those found in the *Dongnanhai zhi wai* (On the Regions Beyond the Southeastern Sea) and the *Huainanzi*’s *Jiesheng fu* (Rhapsody on Examining the Sages), among others.
Within the Great Wilderness, between the Sweet Springs, lies the land of Xihé.
There was a woman named Xihé who gave birth to the ten suns and constantly bathed them in the Sweet Springs.
In the age of Yao, ten suns rose simultaneously.
He commanded Yi—an ancient title for an archer—to shoot them;
nine birds were slain upon the ground, as were the crows within the suns.
In the sprouting of supreme virtue,
the sun and moon are as if joined like two jade disks,
and the five planets are as if strung together like beads; the five planets correspond to the five seasons of the year.
Mars; Venus; and Jupiter.
This is stability.
When there is a ruler of supreme virtue,
the sun and moon are as if joined like two jade disks.
The multitude of stars move from east to west.
While the sun and moon move contrary to the heavens toward the east, the multitude of stars follow the celestial sphere in its rightward rotation,
thus moving from east to west.
The sun and moon move against the turning of the heavens,
proceeding from west to east.
Fuxi, also known as Taohao, drew the eight trigrams.
They communicated with the divine spirits and established writing as a substitute for knotted cords.
Nüwa repaired the heavens and established the ultimate standard;
Gonggong and Zhuanxu vied with one another to become emperors.
Gonggong’s head struck Mount Buzhou;
the celestial pillar broke and the terrestrial moorings snapped.
Consequently, the heavens tilted toward the northwest, where the sun, moon, and stars followed.
The earth does not fill the southeast; there, the waters of the hundred rivers converge. All the hundred rivers flow toward the direction of Xun (the southeast).
Yang Zhu said: "The affairs of the Great Antiquity have perished; who can record them? 'Record' (zhì) means to document."
As for their erasure, there is no record or trace remaining.
Whether the deeds of the Three Sovereigns ever existed or have perished is uncertain.
The deeds of the Five Emperors are as if waking or as if dreaming;
the deeds of the Three Kings are likewise.
Whether hidden or manifest, they are not necessarily complete.
Now, as for Yangzi’s "discrimination" (bian), which means distinguishing;
from what then shall I verify [the truth]? "Verification" (zhi) means to confirm with faith.
Zhongni said: "The Five Emperors employed simplicity;
the Three Kings employed ritual."
Regarding what is distant, it is known solely through verbal expression;
regarding what is near, once the practice of the Dharma and its regulations have already passed,
it can likewise only be known through verbal expression.
The distinction between the void and the substantial has no fixed essence; whether the Three Kings of antiquity adhered to their laws and measures correctly or not is a matter of debate.
China takes that which is most sublime in the world as its standard.
Nothing has ever been greater than Mount Kunlun. Regarding Mount Kunlun,
according to the *Shanhai jing* (Classic of Mountains and Seas),
it is the source from which the River Water flows forth.
According to the *Hanshu*, Zhang Qian searched for it but could not find it.
Above, there are five-colored mists;
below, there are waves of five colors.
Neither great men nor divine immortals can go there or come from there.
Thus, when the Yellow Emperor ascended it, he looked south and turned back; and when King Mu feasted with the Queen Mother of the West at the Jade Pond, that Jade Pond was located on Mount Kunlun.
King Mu of Zhou held a banquet here with the Queen Mother.
The Queen Mother wore a royal cap and had a tiger’s tail and tusked fangs; she was the presiding spirit of pestilence among men.
Descending from there, how majestic! She exhausted the power of creation—this is Mount Kunlun.
Among the Śākyas, Mount Sumeru is particularly renowned for its greatness.
Rising eighty thousand yojanas above the surface of the ocean, its height and breadth are equal, and it is composed of the four precious substances; thus it is sublime.
"Maòu" means length and breadth.
Its four sides are composed of four treasures:
gold on the east, and lapis lazuli on the south.
The west is made of silver;
the north is made of crystal (*sphāṭika*).
Beneath these, there are tiered levels on all four sides.
That supreme realm contains the palaces of the Four Great Heavenly Kings;
below them are the three heavens of Dṛḍhaśiras, Mālādhara, and Nityapramudita.
It serves as the outer vassal state of Śakra and acts as a bulwark against the Asuras.
Its summit is eighty thousand [yojanas] in circumference, and its upper surface is eighty thousand yojanas wide.
"Its levelness is like that of a whetstone;
its road is like fine silk. A *zhǐ* (whetstone) is a grinding stone;
*huàng* (silk) refers to fine cotton.
The realm where Śakra resides is eight *yojanas* on each side;

the gods from these directions attend upon him in the central palace, and thus it is called the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*). On each of the four sides of Mount Sumeru, there are likewise eight heavens.
Within it is the Sudharmā Hall,
the residence of Śakra,
where all the devas pay him court.
There are thirty-three heavens,
all of which are subsumed within the single Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
These are located upon the various mountains in the midst of the ocean.
The *Taudiju* (Many-Earth) Heaven is the capital city of the Four Heavenly Kings;
thus, it is like Fangzhang and Penglai, which dwell in the midst of the ocean borne upon the back of a giant turtle. Its inhabitants are long-lived and possess beautiful countenances.
Luminous jade and purple-green hues form its chambers and pavilions;
it is a place where those devoted to the Way of the Immortals gather for their celestial excursions.
I pray that you will provide wings for it so that it may find rest therein;
may Śakra, Lord of Devas, serve as its limbs and guardians,
providing both solemnity and protection.
He presides over all those devas,
illuminating the lands below,
and governs from his thousand-wheeled palace.
The net was strung with pearls,
shimmering between them and manifesting what was revealed therein.
Therefore, the merits and demerits, deaths and births, long and short lifespans, and the timing of auspicious and inauspicious events for the masses cannot be seen within the pearl;
yet all matters concerning merit and demerit are clearly visible within the net of pearls of Śakra. For this reason:

Those above who have committed offenses, Heaven holds them accountable for their punishment; thus it is said that Heaven brings their transgressions to an end. As for the offenses of the common people below, Heaven delegates the punishment to them.
Heaven gave birth to the myriad people and established rulers to oversee and protect them; for those who are good, blessings are likewise bestowed.
Yet the gentleman says that fortune and misfortune are manifest in the mandate of Heaven;
he speaks of their being simply held within the heart of the Sovereign (Di).
Furthermore, it is said:
"Good fortune and misfortune do not err; 'to err' means to be excessive or confused, for it signifies that the Way of Qian is correct.
Thus, Shennong and Houji, who were the ancestors of the Zhou people, both sowed the various grains to encourage the people, acting as Heaven’s provision for their sustenance."

Gao Yao was the official in charge of judicial affairs during the time of Yao. As for the "Fu Xing" (Punishments of Fu), King Mu of Zhou appointed Lü Ji, the Marquis of Qi, as Minister of Justice and charged him with codifying the five punishments;
hence it is called the "Lü Xing" (Lü’s Punishments).
Later, Lü Hou became Fu Hou;
thus it is called the "Punishments of Fu.
It was an office that administered on behalf of Heaven the system of punishments.
Tang Cheng and King Fa of Zhou: Tang Cheng attacked Jie, and King Wu attacked Zhou;
these were acts of replacing Heaven’s punishment.
Fu Yue was the minister of Gaozong of Yin, and Shao Bo was the Grand Protector of Zhou; these were acts of replacing Heaven’s governance.
Should one enjoy the five blessings, they are as follows:
first, longevity; second, wealth.
On the third day, there is health and tranquility;
on the fourth day, one finds delight in virtue;
on the fifth day, one reaches a full span of life. As for the application of the six extremes: on the first day, there is misfortune, a premature death, and an untimely end.
On the second day there is illness;
on the third day, sorrow;
on the fourth day, poverty.
The fifth day is evil;
the sixth day is weak. Were it not for a sage, none could perceive the patterns of the constant principles (*yilun*). "Xun" means ordinary;
"lun" refers to ethical relations. This is the Great Brahma’s minister, Śakra.
Śakra rules over the Four Heavenly Kings;
the Four Heavenly Kings rule over the host of deities;
and these, in turn, rule over the various sovereigns.
The Book says:
"I venture to use a dark sacrificial bull;
I venture to announce clearly to the Divine Sovereign of High Heaven."
I venture to suggest that this might be none other than Mahābrahmā.
If it were not he, then since the azure heavens are neither fragrant nor foul, who else could be the true sovereign?

If it is not Mahābrahmā, who then is it? When performing the rites at the Round Mound (Yuánqīu), the Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven at the Round Mound; this is a "classical sacrifice" (*lèi*) to the Great Sovereign of Heaven (*Háotiān Shàngdì*), wherein he partakes of the spirits of the five directions, such as Lingwīyǎng and the others.
In the east is Lingyang;
in the south, Chibinwu;
in the west, Baitraoju.
In the north, there is the Radiance of the Leaves;
in the center, it contains the pivot and axis, revering the sun, moon, stars, and constellations.
These may be the affairs of the Great Brahma King, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
In all cases, when the five qi, the five suburban altars, and the five emperors ascend the altar,
the five deities are enshrined for the sacrificial banquet, and the hundred spirits are offered sacrifices in attendance.
Or perhaps it was the Four Heavenly Kings or Śakra.
However, the practices of later generations generally follow the ancient classics.
In antiquity, the world was vast, simple, and grand.

In ancient times, when heaven and earth were in a state of great wilderness and pure simplicity, things were merely abbreviated; each region was established according to the territory it occupied and the destiny of its vital energy (*qi*). Each occupied domain attained sovereignty by riding upon the movements of the five elements' *qi*, and thus the rites and classics were fashioned.
They invoked the spirits and deities, fashioning ritual classics based on ancient precedents.
They invoked Heaven, Earth, and the spirits and deities, and presented offerings of sacrificial animals.
Although their names differ, the underlying principles may well correspond mysteriously.
Therefore, in the Western Regions, there are no altars; they construct mounds of earth for altars and clear away soil for sacrificial pits.
These are the places for offering sacrifices and reporting to Heaven and Earth, and therein are temples dedicated to Heaven.
This is a case of mutual influence between the Central Kingdom and the foreign lands.
Formerly, Zhao Jianzi enjoyed the music of the Celestial Court;
the *Shiji* records that when Zhao Jianzi was ill, he lost consciousness.
After seven days he awoke and said,
"The abode of my Lord was most delightful;
I roamed with the hundred spirits in the Heaven of the Balance."
The extensive music of nine performances and the myriad dances were unlike the music of the Three Dynasties;
its sounds moved the heart. Duke Mu of Qin received the gift of the Chūnshǒu (Quail Head) fief; Duke Mu of Qin dreamed that Heaven bestowed upon him a golden tablet.
The region of Chūnshǒu (Crane’s Head) is the astrological domain of the state of Qín.
Chūnshǒu refers to the constellation of the Vermilion Bird (Zhūniǎo) in the southern quarter;
among the lunar mansions, Guǐ and Liù constitute Chūnshǒu.
The constellations Yi and Zhen constitute the Tail of the Bird (Chunwei). Herein, the spirit communes with Heaven;
while the soul departs, the physical form remains. Though the heights and depths are far apart, [they are nonetheless connected].
"His response was indeed close to the truth: 'Heaven is high and earth is low.

'Kong' (甚) means 'extreme'; 'er' (邇) means 'near. When Shengsheng made his plea with disheveled hair, Huxian, while traveling along the way, saw Shengsheng and had him drive the chariot, saying: 'Yi Wu has treated me with discourtesy; I have petitioned the Supreme Deity on his behalf.'"
Regarding the states of Jin and Qin,
later events indeed accorded with his words.
"The Lord on High" refers to Heaven.
These are all matters concerning the Jin dynasty. Liu Yue requested a fine jade;
Liu Yue was the crown prince of Liu Chong.
He dreamed that he entered the kingdom of Huaxu.
He lived for seven days; Heaven surely granted him spiritual insight, showing that death does not mean the end of consciousness.
"Shu" (孰) refers to "who"; "jue" (厥) refers to "his. As for the common people below, who among them can be truly sincere and trustworthy? "Shu" (孰) means "who," and "jue" (厥) means "his."
This is indeed possible.
If there were no such spiritual response, how could the common people believe it? From this point upward, beyond the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods...
All are said to dwell in emptiness;
it is impossible to go there without having attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
There are twenty-six such abodes in total, beginning from the Yāma Heaven and ending with the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana.
In total, there are twenty-six heavens, layered like clouds upon clouds.

Their lifespans are doubled at each level, ranging from five hundred years up to eighty thousand kalpas in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). Occasionally, there are also minor clouds.
Should there be even a subtle form,
it is encompassed within the three realms;
this clarifies their categories.
They are encompassed by the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) to distinguish their respective categories;
"total" (*tongzong*) means to unify and summarize them.
This is what is meant by "clear illumination.
Although the subtle and minute enumerations are numerous,
they do not, in total, transcend the three realms.
The twenty-eight celestial mansions encompass them;
the four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, and transformation—are used to signify that all are fully subsumed. The *Huntian Yi* (浑天仪) states:
"Heaven is like a chicken's egg."
The earth is like the yolk within an egg; it is like the yolk in the center of a chicken's egg.
The earth is within heaven; it dwells inside heaven.
Heaven is vast and the earth is small.
There is water both inside and outside.
Heaven and earth each stand upon clouds, floating as they are supported by the water; the earth lies on the exterior of the water.
There are those who float it upon clouds;
yet there are those who keep it within the waters,
and others who place it within the heavens.

Beyond the heavens there is water, which is supported by floating clouds. One who asks with good intent might say that this is established as a means of verification; yet, according to Pangu, it was divided to form the foundation of the thick earth.
Upon what, then, can it rely?
Beyond that *Huntian* (the浑天 sphere), who else could support it?

Yet the scholars of this single school are so harmonious—what thoughts and reflections do they have? "Harmonious" (*yongyong*) describes a state of stagnation, yet through it, the matter may be attained.

where he saw *qióngzhú* bamboo staffs."
