It flows eastward to the sea;

this is one source of Lake Anavatapta. The present Yellow River is what issues from Lake Anavatapta. This lake lies north of Central India, passing beyond the Seven Black Mountains and reaching the northern side of the Great Snowy Mountains (Himālaya) and the southern side of Mount Gandhamādana, situated between these two mountains. It extends as far as that limit.
The north side of the mountain is called the "Shade" (Yin),
meaning it is constricted and confined;
the river flows between the two mountains within a gorge, measuring fifty yojanas in width.
The four sides are formed by banks of the four precious substances.
From each of the four sides flows forth a great river: from the golden elephant-mouth on the eastern side flows the celestial Sindhu River;
from the silver ox-mouth on the southern side flows the celestial Sītā River.
The Anavatapta Lake flows westward to produce the Vakṣu River;

it also flows north from the crystal lion’s mouth, each entering the oceans of the four directions. As for the river that flows eastward, it branches off from the Pamir Mountains and proceeds underground.
The numinous branches of the Fusang tree rise toward the Great Radiance;
this may perhaps be the Jambū tree.
Its largest specimens span a hundred yojanas.
Its fruit was edible during the time of the Buddha.
There was an arhat who obtained one; he stretched out his skin over his arm until it reached the seed of the fruit, and having divided it, he bestowed it upon the great assembly.
Its color is like that of overripe mulberries, and it abounds in the southernmost extremity of this continent.
As for the vastness of the *kūṇa* and the *páng*, they are of the same order as the *makara* fish and the *garuḍa*, as described in the "Xiaoyao" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.
There was a *kūn* fish that transformed into a *péng* bird;
it flew facing south, spreading its wings so they hung from the heavens.
This may perhaps correspond to the *makara* fish, the *garuḍa*, and others mentioned in the sūtras.
The garuḍa is the king of the golden-winged birds (suparṇas).
King Chu did not recognize the "floating fruit" (ping-shi), and when King Zhao crossed the river, he saw an object as large as a peck-measure (dou).
Red as the sun,
it touched the king’s boat;
none recognized it.
He sent an envoy to inquire of Confucius, who said, "This is the *ping-shi* fruit; it may be eaten.
Its appearance is due to the presence of virtue. Later, the Zang family ordered a sacrifice at the *yuan-ju*, whereupon the *yuan-ju*—a sea bird—appeared.
While flying, it encountered a wind and consequently landed at the East Gate of Lu.
Although Zang Wenzhong was a Grand Officer, he did not recognize [the bird] and ordered his attendants to sacrifice to it.
Confucius said, "This is the *yuanju* bird;
its size is larger than that of a donkey. Had it not encountered the Sage Confucius, [it would have remained unknown].
This is because those two things are described as "huī-guǐ" (恢詭). "Huī" means vast; "guǐ" means strange.

Thus, from the regions of Xia to those of Jin, from the lands of Yan to those of Yue, and from within the passes to beyond the passes—in their speech, the objects are the same while the names differ. "Fang" refers to the four directions.
Xia refers to the Central Xia;
Yan is in the north;
Yue is in the south.
Names and designations differ according to language; how much more so in foreign lands—how could they possibly be identical? "Shun" (矧) means "moreover," and "wei" (韙) means "correct" or "right.
At the base of Mount Sumeru lies the Great Ocean, formed by the waters of eight virtues, which is singularly pure.
Second, coolness;
third, softness;
fourth, lightness.
Fifth, it has a fivefold fragrance.
Sixth, it does not have an unpleasant odor.
Seventh, drinking it does not harm the throat.

The eighth is that its capacity, which does not damage the belly, is as deep and vast as Mount Sumeru; Mount Sumeru enters the water by eighty-four thousand [yojanas], and the ocean is likewise eighty-four thousand [yojanas] deep, with the ocean encircling the mountain.
Following along the outer edge of the ocean is the Yugandhara Mountain, which encircles the sea like a rim.
Its height and thickness are half those of Mount Sumeru; this mountain resembles a chariot wheel surrounding Mount Sumeru.
They are called the Seven Golden Mountains:
the first is named Yugandhara,
and the second is named Īṣādhara.
The third is named Kāṣṭhavāha;
the fourth is named Sudarśana;
the fifth is named Aśvakarṇa.
The sixth is called Elephant Trunk;
the seventh is called Fish Beak.
Emerging forty-two thousand yojanas above the water, it is level with the sun and moon.
The remaining mountains and seas surround it in between;
having descended and become narrower in succession, they are each half the size of the preceding one. Outside the seventh mountain lies the salt sea known as the Yugaṃdhara Sea.
The Īṣādhāra Ocean, the Khaḷuṅka Ocean,
and the Sudarśana Ocean.
The Horse-Ear Sea, the Vinata Sea,
and the Niminda Sea;
it is also said:
First, the salt sea;
second, the milk sea;
third, the curd sea.
Fourth, the ocean of clarified butter;
fifth, the ocean of honey-water;
sixth, the ocean of auspiciousness.
The seven seas of wine and the four great continents face the four sides of Mount Sumeru, each situated on one side of the salt sea.
This is called a single small world, or a single set of four continents. A thousand such small worlds is termed a small chiliocosm, consisting of a thousand sets of four continents.
One thousand heavens of the six classes of desire gods and one thousand Brahma worlds constitute a small chiliocosm.
One thousand times a small chiliocosm is called a medium chiliocosm, consisting of one thousand small chiliocosms.
One thousand second dhyānas are called a medium chiliocosm;
one thousand times a medium chiliocosm is a great trichiliocosm, which consists of one thousand medium chiliocosms.
One thousand third dhyānas [constitute a great trichiliocosm].
This is called a great trichiliocosm; thus one knows that heaven and earth are infinite.
As the myriad things flow and take form, who can say what lies beyond the six realms?
Whether clad in Confucian robes or black monastic garb, each pursues their own excellence and superiority. There was the Master Wusheng (Mr. Who-Is-Busy-with-the-Mysterious).
He expounded upon Confucian learning and possessed a rich collection of Daoist texts, saying:
Since then, I have offered my evaluation:
as for the vastness and profundity of the Śākya tradition,
I have nothing with which to compare or deliberate upon it.
Although they are but the dregs of the sages,
all have obtained from them the lees of grain, the dregs of wine, and the sediment of oil;
though these are all the remnants and fragments of the sages, they are nonetheless sweet, sour, rich, or fatty.
To be emaciated—whom would it not be called strange?

Thus, the distant kalpas cannot be calculated by Li Shou, though Li Shou was a master of calculation in antiquity; the radiance of the sun cannot be pursued to its end by Kuafu, though the sun is the "Shao Ling" (the brilliant spirit).

Kuafu pursued the sun but could not catch it; parched with thirst, he drank from the Yellow River until it was exhausted, and when he cast down his staff, it transformed into the Deng Forest. That realm of the sun is Zhuai, and that lair of the moon is Xuanyu.
Indeed, the four seas have their distinct boundaries:
to the east lies the realm of the sun;
to the south, Zhuya.

The Western Moon Cave and the Northern Mysterious Mound—along with the Hunyi, Xintian, Qionglong, and Xuanye—are names found in ancient histories and astronomical treatises; they are but fragments of the single mass of the cosmos that has passed through the process of transformation.
In ancient times, the sages of the Central Kingdom—such as Boyang and Nifu—knew the future and stored away the past;
they examined the past and knew the future;
they exhausted the mysteries of the spirit and understood transformation.
One must examine the beginning and seek the end.
If it were not the right time, the Way would not manifest in vain; thus the Sage knew that there was a Buddha in the Western lands.
Because it was not yet the proper time, he did not wish to practice that Way; instead, he temporarily cultivated the classics of Bo Yi and followed the traces of the Great Yu.
He established the Three Bonds and the Five Constants as a provisional measure.
This refers to the compilation of the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) and other texts,
which clarify the affairs of the nine provinces regarding the regulation of waters and mountains throughout the various states of the Central Realm;
this is what is meant by "unifying the world under one system."
As for those such as the Pi-fu, Diao-ti, Zuo-ren, and Qiong-fa— the Ti-e tribes—

these belong to the categories of the Four Barbarians who are held in contempt by the transformative influence of the King’s virtue. Yet they have come to take refuge [in the Dharma] and presented precious tributes.

If there were those who came [to seek it], I would have recorded it; otherwise, I would have ceased. Since I have ceased, I do not record it—how much more so for the vast wilderness of the great chiliocosm, so immense and boundless that it remains omitted from these volumes, as I did not wish to elaborate further on its description.
The Sage was cautious regarding uncertainty.

Regarding matters that he has not yet scrutinized, he does not wish to record them; he uses this as a pretext to dismiss our school as being "extravagant" (*dan*), meaning empty, grandiose, and boastful.
Such people are those who compete for worldly fame. Now, extravagance has long been loathed by Heaven.
How could one possibly travel throughout the world?

I truly fear that if one strikes against the elm and sycamore trees, one will be laughed at for being so far removed from the Southern Ocean. The *chiran* (small gull) cannot fly beyond the elm and sycamore; seeing this, it laughs at the Great Peng, which flies ninety thousand *li* in a single bound.
*Yú* and *fáng* are the names of two types of trees.
Since "qiāng" (a spear) is the convergence of seven "liáng" (good), one seeks by measuring the mind of the Sage;
thus, out of ten thousand calculations, perhaps one succeeds, and out of ten thousand anxieties, perhaps one gains. One seeks by confining the mind within its own boundaries.
"Then regarding even one thing, he is incapable;
'incapable' means unable.
That is, he is unable to accomplish even a single matter.
This is indeed a case of being obstructed by stagnation!

As for the affairs of the two nations, the Maṇi and the Chumaṇi, they are like what was previously explained regarding the space on the tip of a snail's horn. To hear that the dwarves of the Jiao-jiao tribe possess bodies only a foot tall is truly astonishing and quite real.
"Hai" expresses alarm.
The people of Jiao-jiao are one foot five inches tall;

the people of Zhu-ru are three feet tall. When the people of Jiao-jiao and Zhu-ru hear that the Fang-feng, the Shou-pi, and the tall Di Qiao are as long as the people of this land—namely, three zhang—they are struck with awe.
The Jiao and Zhu-ru are small men whose bones could fill a carriage;
their throats were like halberds and their chests were like mortars—these were all large men.
When the state of Wu defeated Tushan, it captured the "carriage-filling" bones.
Question: Your Master said, "During the time of Yu, the Lord of Fangfeng arrived late and was executed;
these are his bones."
The long-dictators (Changdi) Qiaoru of the Xiuqiao state attacked Lu, and Shusun Dechen struck him in the throat with a halberd and killed him;
his terror was like that of the Maoniu demons. As for Pengzu being wounded by the child Yingzi, it was Pengzu [who was at fault].
The Great Officer of Yin was surnamed Cen and named Keng.
His courtesy name was Changru.
He lived for eight hundred years.
Those under twenty years of age are classified as "long-yang" (premature deaths).
Those from fifteen years of age down to twelve are classified as middle *yang*;
those above seven years of age are classified as lower *yang*. Yet they did not realize that these were the *yang* children of their maternal grandmother.

The serpent was haughty in its zigzagging movements—*chūyú* (鉏鋙) meaning a state of unevenness—as it slithered; the *kūí* (夔), with its limping and leaping—*dīngchào* (跉踔)—was haughty toward the serpent, for it was one-legged and hobbled.
Although the serpent’s gait is crooked and uneven, it still excels the wind in that it moves despite having no form.
Although the kui has but one leg and is lame, it still excels the serpent which is entirely without feet. Thus, those who rely on what is small do not recognize what is great.
Those who rely on what is near do not realize the distance;
those who rely on what is few do not realize the multitude.
How could it be otherwise?
2. The Arising of the Sage (I). Part Two: The Arising of the Sage. His covenant with the Unconditioned is profound; his benevolence is lofty and possesses manifest form.
His virtue eclipses all other merits, and his transformative influence pervades the myriad practices.
He is thus titled "Sage.
The *I Ching* states: "The sage unites his virtue with Heaven and Earth.
This precisely refers to the event of the descent of the Holy Lord Śākyamuni. It was on the eighth day of the second month in the spring of the twenty-fourth year of King Zhou, the year of Jia-yin.
The Great Sage was born in Kāpi, during the reign of the fourth sovereign of the Ji Zhou dynasty, King Zhao,
whose name was Xia;
he was the son of King Kang.
He reigned for fifty-one years.
In his twenty-fourth year, in the year of Jiayin (434 CE), on the eighth day of the fourth month,
the Buddha was born beneath an Ashoka tree in the Nandana Garden of Kapilavastu.
This refers to the land of India within the city of King Śuddhodana. He spread his virtuous teachings throughout the five regions of India;
this was unknown to the people of Zhou. These five regions of India consist of the east, south, west, north, and the center.
All are called "devas" (heavenly beings).
They are originally descendants of Brahmā.
"Fu-bu" (敷布) means to spread out or extend.
The transformation took place in the Western Land;
the people of Zhou did not know of it. Initially, the rivers and springs overflowed and the earth shook violently;
auspicious vapors drifted through the air, piercing upward through the Taiwei constellation.
Pervading the western direction with a bluish-red hue, though the people of Zhou did not understand it,
on the morning of the eighth day of the fourth month, they suddenly saw the earth tremble and springs overflow;
looking toward the west, they beheld rainbow-like light and other such phenomena.
The auspicious omen ascended to the Purple Microcosm (Ziwěi), where King Wén asked the Grand Astrologer Sū Yóu, "What kind of auspicious sign is this?
King Zhāo, having beheld an unfathomable auspicious manifestation in the west, questioned Sū Yóu.
The Grand Astrologer, who divined the celestial phenomena, said:
"There is a Great Sage."
He was born in the Western Regions.
The King asked,
"How is it in the world?"
He replied, "At that time there was nothing else.

A thousand years later, his voice and teachings will reach this land; the Grand Historian shall then use ancient books to divinely know that a Great Sage has descended and been born in a western country."
The King, suspecting that [the teaching] belonged to that land, asked how matters stood in the world.
He was answered that it would be only after a thousand years that the sound of its instruction would reach here.
Thus, from the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty until the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, there has been no other [teaching].
Calculating this, it has been one thousand nine hundred and sixty years; the King therefore engraved this upon a stone at the Southern Suburb to commemorate the event.
This account appears in the *Zhou shu yiji* (Record of Anomalies from the Book of Zhou). Formerly, Gao Li questioned a person from Qi regarding this matter.
Furthermore, the Dharma Master Fashang also used this same passage to inform the people of Qi that the matter of the Buddha’s birth had not yet reached the people of Goryeo;

the eminent monk Fashang likewise cited this text in his response to them. Indeed, King Zhao inherited the glorious legacy of Kings Wen, Wu, Cheng, and Kang; Kings Wen and Wu spread their virtue and established the foundation of the state.
Kings Cheng and Kang praised the inheritance of the imperial mandate;

this continued down to King Zhao, during whose reign punishments were laid aside and the state was well-governed. "Laid aside" (chou-ze) means they ceased their application. Had he been able to rectify his thoughts through non-action and carefully align himself with the Way, [the result would have been even greater].
Yet he merely observed these auspicious omens with his eyes, failing to seek them out with his mind.
This was likely because there is a fixed destiny for such responses of merit to arrive; although King Zhao beheld these rare wonders, he was unable to seek out and inquire after the Sage.
Yet when he went on an inspection tour to the south, visiting the region of Chu, his boat became stuck in the Han River and he drowned.
This was surely because for a sage, the convergence of conditions occurs only at its appointed time. Long ago, when the world was first formed, there were those who beheld a thousand flowers.
This signifies that in the present Bhadrakalpa, one thousand Buddhas shall appear. Long ago, at the beginning of this kalpa, a thousand lotuses emerged from the ocean;
this was seen as a sign that one thousand Buddhas would arise in the world. Now, we are in the ninth aeon of decline (kṣayakalpa).
Human lifespan decreases from sixty thousand years down to one hundred.
During this present ninth kalpa, when human life spans sixty thousand years, the Buddha Krakucchanda appeared in the world.
When the human lifespan was forty thousand years, Krakucchanda Buddha appeared in the world;
when it was twenty thousand years, Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world;

and when the human lifespan was one hundred years, Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world. As for the other Buddhas, nine hundred and ninety-six of them appeared during other periods of decrease (*apacaya-kalpa*). The Great Sage, having inherited the position of the crown prince following Kāśyapa Buddha, knew in his own mind that he would descend from the Tuṣita Palace to take birth in a royal household.
His light pervades ten billion worlds,
and those who follow him are deities of great majesty and virtue.
Having reached the zenith and nadir of heaven and earth,
at this time when the lunar mansion of Ghosts (Ārdrā) was in conjunction,
he sat beneath a *pāla* tree in the Vairambhya Garden.
"Born from the right side" means "to reach.
"Contentment" (Zizu) is Tuṣita.
*Vilana* is translated here as "Maidservant-Protector" (Bishou).
The *pāla* tree is the same as the *aśoka* tree.
"Right" signifies conformity.
That it grew from his flank marks its distinction from the ordinary. In antiquity, when the pivot of the rainbow responded to his birth, it manifested his mandate for a transformative age.
Therefore, the Great Sage likewise took a white elephant as an auspicious omen.
Zhuanxu, Gaosun, and others were all born when rainbow light encircled the Pivot Star (Polaris);
thus they are titled "Sovereigns of an Era."

The Buddha likewise manifested his auspicious sign through the white elephant of the solar disc. In antiquity, one with eight-colored pupils and double vision ascended to the position of the Great Sovereign; "ascended" (zhé) means to rise, and "Great" (yuán) means vast.
The Sovereign is the ruler.
Yao had eyebrows of eight colors and double pupils; thus, even the Great Sage manifested the thirty-two marks to ascend the steps.
In the state there was an ancient immortal, whom the ancient immortal called Ayetou Qi.
Or it is said that Asita spoke to the king, saying:
"Alas, the Prince possesses extraordinary marks;
if he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning King."
He left the household life to achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
Observing that his marks and signs were so brilliantly manifest, it was impossible for him to remain a householder;
"brilliantly manifest" means they were clearly visible through the marks and signs of a prince.
"I fear he will not remain at home to become a Wheel-Turning King;
it is more likely he will leave the household life and achieve the Way.

When King Śuddhodana heard this, his heart was filled with distress—this "daodan" (忉怛) refers to a state of bitter grief and sorrow—as he realized that the true heir to the kingdom would not be found in him.
"Then my clan would surely perish; it is just as you have said, sir.

If the Crown Prince does not remain at home to become a Wheel-Turning King, I fear our clan will have no successor and will be extinguished. The common people will have no one to protect them, and our descendants will become mere guests in this land."
Where does that state reside? It resides in preservation.
When a state is lost, its descendants become the successors of the two royal houses and are then called "state guests"; yet even while contemplating security, they cut away their own hearts.
Appointing tutors and mentors to provide instruction,
and practicing archery and charioteering to manifest their skills;
the prince rode a sheep-drawn carriage to the school hall.
The teaching regarding conduct in the three stages refers to the heir apparent entering school and yielding his place according to age with the people of the state. First,
because his father is still living, he yields so that he may come to know the way of father and son.
Because the two lords were present, he yielded so that they might know the righteousness between ruler and subject;
because the three elders were present, he yielded so that they might know the propriety between elder and younger.
Thereupon, teachers and friends were selected to instruct the Crown Prince in the sixty-four scripts and other arts; thus he rode upon elephants and drew the bowstring.
Whether galloping in pursuit or competing in races,
whether preparing objects or achieving great feats,
there was none who did not take the lead for all under heaven; thus he contemplated how to bring peace and security.
If one settles them within the family, it is appropriate to prune away their inclination toward ascetic practice.
One should establish teachers and guardians to provide instruction in the Way of both civil and martial arts,
while casting aside such games as elephant-throwing, archery, drum-beating, and wrestling.
Having prepared all things and perfected the ritual functions, none could equal him;
thereupon he further examined the palace of the Minor Yang.
They summon the long-haired maidens of the realm;
their garments are dark blue, yellow, vermilion, and white,
flowing and shimmering in profusion— this is the perfection of the ritual.
"Man" means long.
A beautiful woman is long and slender.
Thus says Liezi.
"E-mao" and "Mi-man" refer to exquisite beauty.
Once the palace had been established for the Crown Prince,
he issued a summons to seek out beautiful women.
This refers to his taking Yaśodharā, the daughter of King Suprabuddha, and others as wives;
they were adorned in garments of dark blue and yellow,
their forms graceful and elegant, and their deportment and movements refined— like the resonance of stones being struck together.
Striking the zither, beating the flutes, and playing stone music refers to the *qing*.
This is what is meant by delighting them with music; they merely strive for pleasure and amusement, indulging in grand banquets until their intoxication subsides, thereby dissipating their thoughts.
Those of dull faculties and limited hearing and sight may find their natures temporarily stilled;
"stilled" (po) implies a state of detachment, yet at the beginning of the year, fragrance arises—referring to the eighth day of the second month—when the conditions for spiritual resonance arrive.

The spirits and deities conspired, saying that the Son of Heaven from the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa) was arriving; the night had not yet ended, for "ai" signifies both the end of the day and the middle of the night. Grieving, he held his gall and lungs in his breast, wearying even the ladies of the court.
He urged on a white horse to soar through the void.
He went to Green Mountain to cut his hair, whereupon the Prince leaped over the city walls.
Thus he prayed to become a Buddha, one whose body is eternally blissful and who transforms all under heaven through his realization.
Alas! Human deliberation is obscured by the deliberations of spirits;
the deliberations of spirits are obscured by the deliberations of Heaven. "Obscured" means as if in darkness.
Human deliberation refers to consultation among the multitude.
Although humans possess schemes, they are unable to employ them because they contemplate the schemes of the divine in darkness. Human schemes follow desire;
the schemes of Heaven follow the Way.
Even ghosts are not the enemy of man, let alone those who rely on Heaven. Therefore, the gatekeeper is diligent in guarding his door; the *hūn* (gatekeeper) is what is meant by "gatekeeper.

The *qié hú shì* (official in charge of water clocks) is diligent in observing the time; according to the *Zhou Lǐ*, the *qié hú shì* oversees the water-drops and clepsydra. As for the palace guards, the lowering of armor, and the prohibition of military forces—these belong to the category of the *xuán xuán* (the four-sided musical ensemble), the raising of banners, and the performance of music. Those people are so preoccupied with their own confusion that they have no leisure for anything else.
How could one possibly apply diligent effort to one's duties?
Therefore, the nature of sentient beings,
though said to be innate, [is not fixed].
His merit lies in benefiting all things, yet he cannot act according to the nature of Heaven; for the way of father and son is the very nature of Heaven.
Although the Buddha manifests through an apparitional body, his fundamental purpose is to save all beings.
The practice of saving sentient beings must rely upon the perfection of the Way;
yet the perfection of the Way cannot reside within desire.

Therefore, he could not help but carry out the deeds of his fundamental intent. His father, the King, waited for his return, but the palace was dim and lacked luster—“dim” meaning dark—as he gazed toward those mountain forests, departing forever with serene composure.

Weeping with tears streaming down his face, he issued an edict for five members of his paternal clan and five from the maternal clan of his uncle to go and seek him; these ten individuals, including Jue-lun and the others, were all kinsmen of the Crown Prince.

He was sent into the mountains to seek out and accompany him, observing the changes in temperature and following his movements and stillness so as not to obstruct the Prince’s desires—“obstruct” meaning to oppose or contravene. After six years had passed, he repeatedly examined and awakened to the truth.
A life of emaciation and hunger does not constitute merit;
rather, it is by filling the belly with rich food that one becomes a vessel for the ultimate Way and a great carrier of the daily meal.
Thus, he consumed hemp and wheat to subdue the non-Buddhists.
He then said, "I possess a dharma that the world does not know:
all sentient beings subsist upon food.
Thereupon, he accepted six pecks and four sheng of milk gruel and consumed it.
Thus he attained the Way. On this very month, on this very day, and during this very night—when the night was how deep?—the Milky Way had already shifted and all movement had ceased;
there, he sat upon the Vajrāsana.
Like a coiled dragon,
he quelled great calamities;
ten thousand virtues came to court him.
How majestic are the great merits of this vast eon! Thus,
within the interval of a mere arrow-shot, on the eighth day of the twelfth month, having partaken of the milk gruel,
he bathed in the Nairañjanā River.
He entered meditative concentration upon the Vajrāsana, demonstrating that the various afflictions of the three realms and nine stages were severed;
through thirty-four moments of mind, he attained perfect enlightenment. Indeed, the celestial cycle is vast and luminous.
The earth is as much as a handful of soil;
a mountain is as much as a single fistful of stone;
the ocean is as much as a single spoonful of water—yet their brilliant and radiant light remains manifest.
Heaven is formed by the accumulation of minute particles;
Earth is formed by the accumulation of handfuls of soil;
Mountains are formed by the accumulation of stones.
"The ocean is formed by the accumulation of spoonfuls of water.
This is from the "Zhongyong" (Doctrine of the Mean). Thus, through accumulation it becomes great and can serve a great purpose.
The Great Being (Mahāsattva), having cultivated great practices in the past, has raised up all that is good without omission.
Because, through the vows of Samantabhadra, one universally enters all the practices and vows of Samantabhadra as described in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
on this occasion, his body sits pervasively within all places of practice.
Those of small wisdom perceive it as sixteen feet tall;
the Great Being perceives it as vast and remote.
This vastness and remoteness encompass the very substance of the retribution-body (*vipākakāya*).
The sixteen-foot [form] is dedicated solely to the manifested body;
it is like looking at the Way of Heaven through a window, or seeing its extent through a crack.
Although he attained equal and perfect enlightenment with a sixteen-foot body on the Vajra Seat at the side of Gayā, [it was merely for the sake of those of inferior capacity].
True measure knows no equality;
it does not belong to the three realms—how tragic!
The ocean of suffering swirls in confusion.
The torrential floods swirl and eddy;
who would first touch the banks and wait for a crossing?
I shall surely ferry them across by means of the Way. Who is "who"? It refers to the people.
"Yi" means the shore.
"Ai" means to wait for.
"Ji" means to ferry across.
It is a means of crossing over.
Who shall be the first to reach the shore and seek to cross the ocean of suffering?
I shall deliver them; for this reason.
He wandered about, hesitating in all directions, for twenty-one days;
he then set out on foot in the morning and arrived at the Deer Park.
The Deer Park (Mṛgadāva) was a grove manifested by former Buddhas in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
In the past, there was a king who possessed a thousand deer and was about to slaughter them all.
At that time, the Tathāgata and Devadatta were both kings of the deer.
Each leading five hundred [attendants],
they then informed the king, saying:
"We request that one deer be provided for our sustenance each day."
When it was the turn for another to provide the offering, that person was pregnant;
the Deer King then went in her stead.
The King was moved by his benevolence and compassion.
He then released all the deer and gave this grove as a gift to them;
thus it was named the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva). Now, five men were gained here at this site, namely the group of five (Pañcavaggiya).
First was Kauṇḍinya; second, Daśabala-Kāśyapa;
third, Aśvajit (also known as Mañjuśrī); and fourth, Bhadrika.
Fifth is Mahānāma, who accords with his past deeds.
This likely refers to the three turnings of the subtle words, namely the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The path of no-more-learning;
the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma—these were realized only before those of great capacity; as for others, I know nothing of them, save that they have nearly reached it.

Do not do so. Although it is said that the Four Noble Truths were first expounded, there were differences in the manner of realization and entry during those intervals; at that time, the earth deities raised their voices.
The hundred deities were all in harmony;

[this influence] ascended to pervade the Nine Heavens—meaning that the three heavens of the First Dhyāna together with the Nine Heavens possess the faculty of auditory consciousness—and descended to encompass the Yellow Carriage, which refers to the earth.
The *Huainanzi* states:
"The terrain is like a carriage, with its flow spreading to the eight directions.
Heaven and man share in mutual celebration."
The sun and moon shine with constancy;
there are none who do not leap for joy,
and none who do not clap their hands and shout.
The multitude of spirits were joyous, mutually delighting in one another; "joyous" (xi xi) signifies harmony. "Mutually" (xu) means together.
The myriad sages delighted in promoting [the Way], taking the Great Enlightenment as their Dharma-King.
This was during the time of King Mu.
From a country at the western extremity, a transformed person came;
he entered fire and water,
and pierced through metal and stone.
They returned to the mountains and rivers and moved the cities and towns;
riding upon the void, they did not fall.
In reality, touch is not obstructed;
its myriad transformations are inexhaustible. During the time of King Zhou Mu, a transformed person already came to visit.
It was simply because the responsive resonance of sentient beings had not yet been aroused.
Since he could transform the forms of things and alter the thoughts of men,
being able both to manifest supernatural powers and to transform the mental dispositions of people, King Mu revered him as if he were a deity.
He served him as if he were his sovereign.
His transformative influence on people was boundless.
He visited the King and traveled with him.
The King grasped the sleeve of the transformed man;
they leaped upward and stopped halfway through the heavens. There, he paid his respects and made his request.
Having reached the palace of the transformed man, they proceeded further.
Framed with gold and silver,
draped with pearls and jade,
it rises above the clouds and rain.
Yet they did not know what lay beneath them; from afar,
it appeared like a mass of gathering clouds,
and the King himself took it to be his dwelling place.
For thousands of years, they did not think of their king’s residence within his transformed realm;
they did not think of returning to that land to transform others and once again visit the king to travel together.
As for the place to which they returned:
Looking upward, one could not see the sun or moon;
looking downward, one could not see the rivers or seas.
The radiance of its light shone everywhere.
His vision was blurred so that he could not see, and the sounds from all directions were so chaotic that his ears could not hear;
this was because the conjured man had been traveling with King Mu into the pure lands of various Buddhas. The King requested the conjured man to return.
A conjured person moved him;
the king felt as if he had fallen into emptiness.
Upon awakening, he realized that his seat was still in the very same place as before.
The king asked where he had come from.
His attendants said, "The king was silently contemplating. The attendants saw that the king was sitting in silence.
The king and the transformed person then traveled in a divine manner through the Pure Land; however, after three months, the king could no longer see him.
He questioned the transformed person again, and the transformed person replied:
I have been roaming with the King in spirit;
how could my physical form have moved? Moreover, what difference is there between the place where I previously resided and the King’s palace?
"The places we have traveled to in the past—
how are they any different from the King's own park?
The King was greatly pleased.

I humbly reflect that the one I have encountered is indeed the Buddha. Although the Tathāgata was in the world when his voice and teachings had not yet reached this land, the Buddha did indeed come here;
it was simply that I failed to realize he was the Buddha.
How lamentable! How could one obtain it?
The "Junchen" says:
"Ordinary people, when they have not yet seen a sage, feel as if they cannot bear not seeing him."
"Having already met the Sage, yet one is still unable to follow the Sage"—
this is precisely what is meant here. These are the words from the *Book of Zhou*,
and the Master Kong’s commentary states:
Ordinary people have a beginning but no end;
they have not yet seen the Path and thus cannot see it,
and even when they have seen the Noble Path, they are unable to utilize it.
This is why there has been no success.
Now, King Mu beheld the Sage yet was unable to seek and pursue sagehood;
how truly a pity! The shade cast by that Bodhi tree is dense and profound.
The Vajrāsana (Diamond Throne), which is immovable, is located fourteen or fifteen *li* to the southwest of Mount Gayā in the kingdom of Magadha;
it is the Pippala tree. Its trunk is yellowish-white, and its branches and leaves are lush green.
It does not wither in winter or summer;
its luster remains fresh and unchanged.
It stands several hundred feet high.
The Vajrāsana is situated beneath it;
it is the place where the Bodhisattva realized sainthood,
and is also called the Bodhimaṇḍa.
The great earth shook,
yet [the seat] alone did not tilt or sway; the tree served as the symbol of the seat,
and by occupying that seat, one was shaded by its tree.
"The trees are worthy of being neither pruned nor felled" reflects their beauty;
"the seat shall not be worn away nor collapse" reflects its solidity—all these are from the poems of Shao Bo. When the Way of the Sage is perfected, his virtue becomes weighty throughout the world.

Since nothing else besides this can withstand [the test of time], it is fitting to preserve these ancient objects to manifest the sacred traces. Thus, the former kings of foreign lands carved stone into images, establishing markers to the north and south so that future generations might behold their enduring legacy. "Carved" (䤿) means engraved.
Beneath the Bodhi tree at the Vajrāsana, two great stone bodhisattvas were carved.

It is said that in a future age when the Buddha-dharma declines and the bodhisattvas have vanished from the earth, the mark left by Master Xuanzang’s departure will reach their chests. Laozi was born on the fourteenth day of the ninth month in the third year of King Ding of the Zhou dynasty; he was born in the village of Curén in Lài Township, Chén County, the state of Chǔ.
His surname was Li;
his given name was Er;
his courtesy name was Boyang.

The posthumous title "Dān" (聃) was given to him; Zhongni was born in the state of Lu during the reign of Duke Xiang. Zhongni was born in the winter of the twenty-first year of Duke Xiang’s reign in the city of Pingxiang in the state of Lu. Laozi silently recognized the capacity for benevolence in him.
Zhongni (Confucius) inquired about the rites from Boyang (Laozi).
In the *Qingjing Faxing jing* (Sutra on the Practice of the Pure and Quiescent Dharma), Mahākāśyapa is identified as Laozi.
He identifies the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī with Confucius.
The *Xi sheng jing* states that the Way-Scriptures were taught by my Master as he traveled and transformed beings in India, skillfully entering into *nirvāṇa*;
this is precisely Laozi’s silent realization of the Buddha, the path of guarding the feminine and preserving weakness.
This is the instruction to "dare not take precedence over the world.
It is here that the virtue of the Master Lao is perfected.
As the *Shi* says:
"Nothing surpasses non-contention"—this is found in the teachings of Laozi. "Nothing surpasses contention"—this refers to the *Qingmiao* (Pure Temple) section of the *Mao Shi*.
"Contention" here means military strength. This poem praises King Wu for his achievement in defeating Zhou.
This is a fierce undertaking. One must be able to strengthen one’s meritorious achievements.
As it is said in the *Laozi*: "Though possessing the Way and Virtue, he does not take precedence over the world. And as the *Fuzi* says:
The teacher of Laozi was named Śākyamuni Fúlǎng, styled Yuánda;
he was the younger brother of Fú Jiān and served as the Governor of Qīngzhōu.
He was captured and brought back by Xie Xuan.
Later, during the Jin dynasty, he was slandered and killed by Wang Guobao.
Possessing wisdom and discernment, he excelled at distinguishing flavors and authored several treatises titled *Fuzi* (The Master Fu); these may perhaps be a pursuit of the teachings of Laozi.
Formerly, Pi, the Grand Chancellor of Shang—that is, Bo Pi, the Grand Chancellor of Wu—questioned Confucius, saying:
"Master, are you a sage? He replied:
"I, Qiu, am merely one of broad knowledge and strong memory; I am not a sage."
The three sage-kings were Xia Yu Wenming,
Tang Wang Lü, and Zhou King Fa.
Regarding the Three Kings, it is said that the Three Kings were skilled in employing wisdom and valor;
whether they were sages is not something Confucius knows.
As for the Five Emperors—Shao Hao, Zhuanxu, Gaosun, Yao, and Shun—are they the sages? It is said that the Five Emperors were skilled in employing benevolence and trustworthiness.
"Sageship is not something I, Qiu, can fully know.
As for the Three Sovereigns—Fuxi, Shennong, and Huangdi—are they not sages? It is said that the Three Sovereigns were adept at employing the principles of governance according to the times."
"The Sage is not something I know," [the Master] said.
The Grand Minister was greatly startled and asked, "In that case, who then is the Sage? [The Master] replied, "One should say that all those of antiquity were not Sages."
It was for this reason that the Grand Minister was greatly startled. The Master, with a slight movement, adjusted his countenance and replied:
"In the west there is a sage who brings order without governing and inspires confidence without speaking."
Without transforming others, one acts spontaneously; without the use of weapons or penal laws, all within the dharma-realm submit naturally.
Is this not to achieve order without governance?
Without relying on a formal proclamation or oath, the dragons and devas all surround him;
is this not because he inspires confidence through his very silence? Even those with dull consciousness place their faith and orientation in him, and all creatures know where to turn for refuge.

"Could it be that [the Buddha] acts spontaneously without transformation? Vast and boundless, no one is able to name him. This was how Zhongni, through his wisdom, knew that there was a Buddha in the West;
thus he answered the Grand Chancellor. One thereby knows that the Way of the Confucians is as luminous and pervasive as the sun in the sky.
That he was able to be so humble and modest demonstrates that the influence of the Buddhist master has permeated deeply. Thus,
the three teachings are mysteriously unified and the fundamental human relations are brought into harmony.
Yet the Dharma pervades many regions,
and the scriptures emerge from many gateways;
the Buddhist school takes cause and effect as its foundation.
Laozi took the way of emptiness and non-being as his standard;
Zhongni (Confucius) took ritual and music as his.
Proceeding from the shallow to reach the profound.
Those of humble origin become eminent;
each serves as a vessel suited to the needs of the time,
complementing one another to form a harmony of excellence.

It is like the heavens and earth and the four seasons: they do not cease to be spring because of the *móu* (barley) or the *jǐ* (sweet herb), nor do they cease to be autumn because of the *líng* (water chestnut) or the *tiáo* (reed).
The *móu* is a type of great wheat; the *jǐ* is a sweet vegetable; and the *líng* and *tiáo* belong to the category of grasses. Thus, the gradual arrival of the Confucian teaching is like this.
Tang of Yin changed the prayers.
Confucius fished without using a net; King Jie was without the Way, so [Confucius] set out his net and prayed, saying:
[The net is for catching fish, not people].
All those who come from the heavens, the earth, and the four quarters shall enter this net of mine.
King Tang of Yin removed three sides of it;
he opened only one side and changed his prayer, saying: [The rest of the text follows].
I request that you, who bear my command, cast this net for me.
As the *Analects* says:
"The Master fishes but does not net."
"However, by using but a single hook to catch them, those killed are not many.
These are all passages from the gradualist teachings of Confucianism regarding non-killing; they represent the ultimate [teaching] within the Lao school."
First is benevolence;
second is frugality;
third is not daring to take precedence over the world—these are what the Daoist teachings call the Three Treasures. They represent the ultimate pinnacle of the Buddhist teachings.

From birds and beasts to grass and soil, all that deviates from the norm is subject to punishment; such is the warning in the legal statutes. If there are those who employ the teachings of Śākyamuni, they shall cause people to dwell in the state where outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*).
If there are those who employ the teachings of Laozi...
It causes the people to reach a state of profound harmony.
If there were one who employed the teachings of Confucius,
it would cause the people to ascend to benevolence and longevity.
For this reason, the Great Sage was born during the reign of a flourishing monarch in the era of King Zhao of Zhou; at that time, among the people of the five regions,
there were lords of territories consisting of a thousand chariots and lords of territories of a hundred chariots.
Those who have ascended to the level of sage-wisdom include the lords of fiefdoms of a thousand chariots and those of a hundred chariots—
referring here to the vassals of King Śuddhodana.

In the era of the Buddha’s birth, all nations had realized the fruits of enlightenment and were uniformly sagely; the two teachings arose in an age of decline, when the Great Way faltered amidst decay.
It was during the reign of the twelfth sovereign of the Zhou dynasty, King You, that he favored Bao Si.
He lost control of the empire.
King Ping moved the capital to Luoyi;
the feudal lords usurped the right to wage war, and the rites and music fell into ruin.
This was called the period of the Decline of the Zhou; thus, the Sage Laozi submerged his dragon-like virtue and remained hidden beneath the pillars.
A purple vapor floated over the Pass as he journeyed beyond the Flowing Sands. As the Archivist beneath the pillars of Zhou, Laozi perceived that the virtue of the Zhou was faltering and declining.
He then departed through the pass for the Wilderness of Liusha,
where he expounded the two chapters on the Way and its Power (*Dao De*) for Yin Xi, the Magistrate of the Pass. Confucius followed the legacy of Yao and Shun and took Wen and Wu as his model.
Having returned to Lu from his self-defense, he compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals;
moved by their spiritual resonance,
he turned back his sleeves to wipe his face.
To claim that my Way has reached its end is not their true intent. Confucius returned to Lu from Wei in the eleventh year of Duke Ai’s reign;
in the fourteenth year, while hunting in the west, he captured a *qilin*, and thereupon he compiled the *Spring and Autumn Annals*. Yet it was Guanzhu Yin who truly understood his Way.
Yan Hui was the one who understood the Way of the Confucians;
the hundred kings were those who practiced the two teachings;
and Laozi became a transcendent immortal.
Zhongni (Confucius) served as the "Plain King" (a sovereign without a realm).
His sagely deliberations are vast and expansive, coextensive with Heaven and Earth and without end.

At times, there have been those who view him with resentment, saying: "This is merely a matter of feigned guest and host; if one does not disparage these two teachings [Buddhism and Daoism], it is already excessive. Why then praise his virtue? Why indeed? What does this mean?

One can indeed instruct them; how could it be said that they have an excess of virtue? This is because one does not recognize the contradiction. Once there was a man selling both spears and shields who boasted of their respective merits.
Speaking of the shield, he said that no spear could pierce it.
To speak of the spear, it is capable of piercing ten shields;
some even say, "Sell me your spear so that I may pierce your shield.
How could they remain without words? In my sutras, I take these two sages as the pinnacle of transformation, yet now you disparage them, identifying one as Kāśyapa and the other as Laozi.
If the Child of Confucius (Routong) is indeed Zhongni, how could he have contravened its meaning?
On the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mu’s reign, the year of Renshen, the Great Sage manifested his parinirvāṇa.
On this day, black clouds rose from all four directions,
and a great wind shook the earth.
From the west, twelve white rainbows appeared.
It extended from south to north,
burning continuously through the night without extinguishing.
The King questioned the court astrologer, Hutu.
Huduō said, "A Great Sage has passed away in the West;
this is merely a sign of decline."
At first, King Mu heard that there was a sage in the west.

Furthermore, he repeatedly beheld radiant vapors—"repeatedly" meaning frequently—and he feared this was not something appropriate for the Way of Zhou; he worried that the sage might come to invade the ancestral tombs of the state. He then commanded Lü Hou to convene the feudal lords at Tushan—Tushan being located in Kuaiji within the astrological domain of Wu-Yue—and Lü Hou, whose personal name was Lü Ji, did so to prepare for such an upheaval. When the [sage] arrived, [Lü Hou]...

There is nothing here that does not provide great enlightenment and instruction; now, hearing that the Sage of the West has entered parinirvāṇa, I am filled with joy beyond measure. In the past, the Great Sage entrusted his charge to the Great Tortoise Lord, the Dharma-treasury Great Tortoise Lord, whose clan name was Mahākāśyapa.

Having received the Tathāgata’s final charge, he completed his duties and proceeded to the Bodhimanda of the Twin Śāla Trees—located by the river of Kuśinagara—where, at the end of his life, he lay upon a bed of the seven precious gems.
Lying with his head to the north,
amidst the silence of the still night,
the moon of the Samyaksaṃbuddha vanished behind the mountain of Great Parinirvāṇa— the Buddha’s body being likened to the moon.
When he entered parinirvāṇa, the mountains were likened to his passing and all living beings wailed in lamentation;
the springs were choked and the peaks collapsed,
as if malevolent stars had suddenly fallen from the sky.
The rivers flow backward;
Ānanda’s mind sinks into an ocean of sorrow,
while Rāhula contemplates only impermanence.
The *śaikṣas* and *aśaikṣas* departed with sorrowful hearts.
The devas exclaimed, "Alas!
This Sāla grove"—in the language of India, *sāla*.
This is called "firm and solid," meaning it does not wither even through winter. Four pairs, or eight branches, form two trees;
their drooping branches hang down to cover [the ground].
The leaves fall away until they are as pure white as the color of a white crane;
for this reason, it is called the Crane Tree (*hakuju*).
Its sturdy leaves hold the frost and do not wither even through winter.
Therefore, it is called the Forest of Firmness (Sāla-vana).
Initially, when the Great Sage was about to return to the state of non-action, before his final extinction, he departed from Vaiśālī and proceeded to the bank of the southern river.
Stepping upon a large square stone,
he looked toward Ānanda and said,
"This is my final view of the Vajrāsana and the city of Rājagṛha."
This is the trace left behind. The country of Vaiśālī lies seven hundred *li* south of the Ganges River, within the borders of Central India;
it was there that the sages and saints held their council.
This is precisely the country of Vaiyālī, and thus there are now the Buddha’s twin footprints upon the stone.
It is one chi and eight cun (one chi being ten cun) in length and one-third of that in width, measuring six cun.
On its lower part are the marks of a thousand-spoked wheel, the *svastika* on the tips of the fingers, floral patterns, and designs of vases and fish.
The light shines brilliantly even now; upon the stone, these characters remain visible. Since ancient times, heterodox followers have attempted to destroy them, yet they have always been restored.
Herein the Sage left his traces to manifest his teaching.
The teachings remain and their traces have not perished;
when those who behold them weep at their enduring presence, it is because the longing for eternal contemplation persists.
The second month of the Zhou calendar is our twelfth month; in the Zhou court, the eleventh month—the month of Zi—is established as the beginning of the year.

Thus, the twelfth month of today is actually the second month of the Zhou calendar; the fifteenth day is the final day (the *huì*) of the month in the Western lands. In the Western countries, within a single month of thirty days—
The first fifteen days are designated as the white fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*),
and the latter fifteen days as the black fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*).
The first day of the month is the new moon (*pratipad*) of the white fortnight, and the fifteenth day is the last day of the white fortnight (*amāvāsyā*).

The sixteenth day marks the beginning of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), and the final day of that month is the new moon (amāvāsī). Each of those twelve months is called by the name of its presiding constellation; the first month is Kṛttikā.
The second month is Vaiśākha;
the third month is Jyeṣṭha;
the fourth month is Āṣāḍha.
In the fifth month is Śravaṇa;
in the sixth month, Prauṣṭhapada;
in the seventh month, Āśvayuja.
The eighth month is Kārttika;
the ninth month is Āśvina;
the tenth month is Bhādrapada.
The eleventh month is Mṛgaśīrṣa;
the twelfth month is Puṣya. The beginning of the lunar mansion marks the first day of the month (śukla-pratipad), and the end of the lunar mansion marks the last day of the month (amāvāsī).
Therefore, the sixteenth day corresponds to the first day of the lunar month (*pratipad*).
Combined with the preceding fifteen days, they constitute the fifteen days of the waxing moon; the subsequent fifteen days form the waning moon.

The first half of the month is called "dark" (*kṛṣṇa*) or "death," referring to the period from the beginning of the month when the dark shadow gradually diminishes. The latter half of the month is called "bright" (*śukla*) or "arising," referring to the time starting from the sixteenth day when the moonlight reaches its full splendor. Thus, the twelve months are divided into three seasons.

From the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month is the period of heat, which refers to the summer season; from the sixteenth day thereafter to the fifteenth day of the ninth month is the period of rain.
From the sixteenth day of this month until the fifteenth day of the first month constitutes the cold season;
the winds of coolness and heat correspond somewhat to these astronomical calculations.
In antiquity, the calendars of the Three Dynasties each had their own points of adoption and rejection.
The Xia Hou clan honored black and established the month of Yin as the first month of the year; this was Xia Yu, whose surname was Shi.
His name was Wenming, and he received the auspicious omen of the dark jade tablet bestowed by Heaven.
The month of Yin was established as the first month of the military cycle and designated as the "Human Rectitude" (Ren Zheng).
For sacrifices, banners, and clothing, black was the preferred color.

The dawn is taken as the beginning of the month. The people of Yin honored white and established the second month (the ox) as their first month. The founder of the Yin dynasty was surnamed Zi and named Lü;
his courtesy name was Tianyi.
He received the auspicious omen of a white wolf holding a hook in its mouth.
They take the month of Jiànchǒu as the beginning of the year,
designating it the "Earth-Primacy" (Dìzhèng).
For sacrifices, banners, and clothing, they all honor the color white.

The first day of the lunar month (*shuo*) was determined at the fifth watch of the night. The people of Zhou venerated red and established the eleventh month (*zi*) as the beginning of the year; Zhou was of the Ji clan.
His name was Fa, and he received the auspicious omen of a fire descending upon Mount Wangwu.
The month of Jianzi (the eleventh lunar month) was established as the beginning of the year and designated as the "Heavenly Prime" (Tiānzhèng).
For sacrifices, banners, and clothing, red was the preferred color.
The first day of the new moon (shuò) was set at midnight, and thus the Great Sage’s birthday fell within the year.
Therefore, the eleventh month can be called "Zheng" (the first month).
This is different from the practice of the present age. Since the Buddha was born during the Zhou dynasty, all the months and years mentioned within the sūtras [follow that system].

All of them adopted the *zhengshuo* (the beginning of the year) of the Zhou dynasty, which differs from the current *jiantin* (commencing with the second month), the summer calendar. In this month, heaven and earth are in a state of stagnation and closure;
dragons and snakes hibernate.
The subtle Yang is secretly diffused in the springs below;
its nascent sprouts have not yet reached the soil above.
Thus, those who are born respond to the movement of the vital breaths as they arrive.

Regarding this "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*), it should be understood as a transition and departure. Master Beishan used the Zhou calendar for the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, which differs from the *nirvāṇa* observed on the fifteenth day of the second month in the current [calendar].
The "hooked sprout" refers to things at their initial birth, resembling a hook;
it signifies the process of germination. Now, one who dwells in the end yet cannot die is not a sage. A sage has no obstruction with regard to things.
In his birth, he manifested as being identical to ordinary beings;
in his extinction, he manifested as returning through transformation to the Truth.
Although he appeared to be born, there was no birth.

Although he manifests extinction, he does not truly perish; one who has died and cannot be reborn is not a sage. Since his conditions here have ended, he appears transformed in other realms, which is not the same as the minor sages who merely extinguish their physical bodies. Therefore, it is said that he constantly dwells on Vulture Peak and, in truth, has not entered parinirvāṇa. He neither dies nor is born, yet he is able to die and be born.
This is what is called a Great Sage: fundamentally not belonging to birth and death, yet manifesting as though subject to birth and death.
Truly a Great Sage indeed, he presides over the myriad categories of existence within the six realms of the universe.
Not yet having abandoned the conditioned,
nor yet having become indolent regarding the unconditioned,
one is born again and again.
There has never been a limit to this;
yet when a sage arises in response to it,
how could there be any limit to his presiding over his office?
"To relinquish" means to abandon;
"lazy" means indolent.
The Buddha is the sovereign of all classes of beings.
Because he has not yet abandoned the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), he manifests signs;
because he does not remain indolent or weary regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), his transformation ends in returning to quiescence.

Since his conditions are exhausted here while he continues to transform in other realms, there is no one who reaches a final end. For this reason, the Great Sage is born into a world where birth is possible.
The world that can be extinguished is extinguished;
arising and ceasing reside in things and certainly do not reside in oneself. This demonstrates the mutual arising and ceasing of phenomena.
The original reality is fundamentally non-existent;
therefore it is said: "While the multitude perceive the kalpa-ending conflagration, my land remains peaceful and secure.
Its birth on the eighth day symbolizes the initial blossoming that proceeds toward fullness. Four months later is the Buddha’s birth, which corresponds to the present second month.
When things reach their full splendor,
the eighth day represents the moon gradually becoming full; that it "perishes" on the fifteenth day illustrates its transition from fullness to waning,
as the fifteenth day marks the ultimate peak of the moon's roundness.
Fearing that sentient beings might give rise to the view of permanence,
he manifested the waning of the moon after its sixteen phases;
for when it is full, its flowers flourish.
When it wanes, it harms what is full; because it gradually becomes full from the eighth day onward, its flourishing increases.
Because it gradually wanes after the fifteenth day, it harms what is full. This is measured by the days.
Therefore, one perceives only the conditioned nature of arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, those who are born during the day and pass away during the night are likewise subject to this.
Birth signifies manifestation while death signifies obscurity;
this is the evidence of diligence in the morning and indolence in the evening. That the Buddha was born by day and entered nirvana at night is because birth represents clarity and illumination.
Death is darkness. Furthermore, life dwells in the dawn and must necessarily involve the toil of exertion;
death dwells in the evening and is thus the principle of leisure and repose. Alas! The bustling throng of living beings is as if in a dream.

Some perceive the Buddha as being born or passing away, as being near or distant, as having a body that eternally exists, or as being fundamentally unborn; thus, according to what each realizes through their own mind, there are different perceptions.
Although these manifested forms are manifold, [the reality remains one].
The Dharma-body is fundamentally without birth or extinction; it is like being in the same room yet having different dreams.
Those who dream do not know the dreams of others.
It is only after attaining great awakening that one knows what others have dreamed. Thus it is stated in the sacred teachings.
The Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month;
he descended from the Tuṣita Heaven on the fifteenth day of the seventh month;
and he left the city over the wall on the eighth day of the second month.
He attained enlightenment on the eighth day of the twelfth month and entered parinirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the second month. Furthermore,
there is the sacred teaching [to this effect].
He was born on the eighth day of the second month;
he left the city on the eighth day of the second month;
and he entered parinirvāṇa on the eighth day of the second month.
Furthermore, there are those who maintain that he was born on the eighth day of the second month,
left the city on the eighth day of the twelfth month,
and attained enlightenment on the eighth day of the tenth month.
He entered parinirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month;

the records of the various schools differ, like people having different dreams within the same room. Indeed, where there are distinct divisions, one cannot reconcile their differences, and where there is commonality, one cannot separate their variations. As for those who maintain that he was born on the eighth day of the fourth month of this year:
According to the Xia calendar system, he was born on the eighth day of the second month;
according to the Zhou calendar system, he is the present-day Master Beishan, also on the eighth day of the second month.
Both traditions agree on the eighth day of the second month.
This is a calculation devised by a specific sect of the Hinayana in India. Some take the tenth year of King Zhuang as the time of the Buddha’s birth;
however, this is based on the *Lüshi* (Spring and Autumn Annals) while arbitrarily twisting the meaning of the scriptures.
However, this excessive tendency toward forced interpretation is characteristic of Fei Changfang;
he took the tenth year of King Zhuang of Zhou to be the fourth year of Duke Zhuang of Lu,
[claiming it was the time] when the fixed stars were no longer visible.
"The falling of stars like rain was the occasion of the Buddha's birth.
This is merely a baseless and arbitrary interpretation based on the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
The Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao, the fourth sovereign of the Zhou dynasty.
King Zhuang was the fifteenth sovereign.
Furthermore, at that time, the fixed stars were no longer visible.
This was the fifth day of the fourth month,
which was the day when, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva converted five hundred rishis on the Snowy Mountains and returned to his own country.
The radiance [of the Buddha] eclipsed the fixed stars so that they were no longer visible. There are those who take the fifteenth day of the third month as the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
this is the teaching of the Tāmraparṇīya school of the Western Regions.
The others were not so. When the Sage Laozi was being condoled by Qin Yi,
if he were to return to Zhou, Zhuangzi says that Qin Yi entered to offer his condolences.
When Laozi departed after his third summons, Zhongni dreamt that he was placing his staff between the two pillars.
Zhongni said, "The Xia dynasty buried its dead between the eastern pillars;
the people of Zhou bury theirs between the western pillars."
"The people of Yin stood between the two pillars.
I am a descendant of those people of Yin;
shall I not perish? Thus he passed away. He looked down upon the myriad transformations and saw that all end alike."
Celestial wisdom emerges from the cosmos;
death is coextensive with the cosmos.
Is this its reality, or is it its expedient manifestation?
The Real (zhen) is the image of the Sage;
the Expedient (quan) is the Sage himself.
Without the Real, there is no Expedient.
Thus, one perceives the mind that arises and ceases. The universe is heaven and earth.
If human wisdom transcends heaven and earth, yet birth and death remain identical to those of heaven, earth, and the myriad things.
One asks whether this is the ultimate truth or a provisional means.
If it is the ultimate truth, then the image is praised as being the Sage himself.
If it is a provisional transformation, it nonetheless may be considered the Sage.
Apart from this, if one does not rely on both the Real and the Expedient,
there is no way to penetrate the mind of birth and death.
*Beishan lu*, Scroll One.
*Beishan lu*, Scroll II, Section 3:

*The Flourishing of the Dharma Canon* (2). *The Flourishing of the Dharma Canon*, Part III. This chapter clarifies the origins of the establishment of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras throughout the Tathāgata’s lifetime of teaching.

At the Bodhi tree, beneath the Vajra-seat in the city of Gayā, the Buddha subdued the Māras by the power of his wisdom after attaining enlightenment, thereby bringing tranquility and purity to all under heaven. When the Buddha first attained the Way... [he] subdued the Māras.
Thereafter, the Dharma-realm was serene and still.
He remained in the world to establish the teachings for forty-nine years, attaining enlightenment at thirty and preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings for those forty-nine years.
He entered parinirvāṇa at the age of seventy-nine. The Tripiṭaka consists of the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma:
the Sūtra is the Sūtrapiṭaka; the Vinaya is the Vinayapiṭaka; and the Abhidharma is the Mātṛkāpiṭaka.

The five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, the four truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the six perfections constitute the five vehicles: the five precepts constitute the vehicle of humans;
the ten wholesome actions constitute the vehicle of devas;
and the four truths constitute the vehicle of the śrāvakas.
The twelvefold dependent origination constitutes the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas;
the six pāramitās constitute the vehicle of the bodhisattvas. These are governed by the twelve divisions of the scriptures:
first, the sūtras; second, the geyas.
Third, the prediction;
fourth, the repeated teaching;
fifth, the spontaneous utterance.
Sixth, dependent origination;
seventh, parables;
eighth, past events.
Ninth, the Jātaka;
tenth, the Vaipulya;
eleventh, the Adbhutadharma.

The twelve treatises on doctrine are also called the twelve divisions of the teaching. When these are opened up, they constitute the four categories of Sūtra, Vinaya, Abhidharma, and Mantra; though the teaching began with a single sound, it perfectly accords with the minds of all beings.
It is called "Amṛta" (Nectar).
It is also called the "Poisonous Drum," for when it accords with the illness [of the listener], it removes their feverish affliction and is thus called Amṛta;

when it does not accord with the illness, it gives rise to affliction and is thus called the Poisonous Drum. Since the Supreme Sage had passed away, these subtle words were nearly extinguished. The Supreme Sage is the Tathāgata. Mahākāśyapa then urgently summoned a thousand companions who were Arhats.
I have composed this preface to establish the definitive interpretation, so that its essential meaning may never fall into ruin.
It was begun at the first assembly in the royal capital and completed in the Stone Chamber.

Therefore, the Southern School takes emptiness, the provisional, and the middle as the three contemplations: it holds that contemplating the emptiness of the *parikalpita* (imagined) afflictions reveals the true principle, which is the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

To contemplate the ultimate truth as the merging of the conventional and the real is the contemplation of the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*). In the Northern School, the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) constitute the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
