Quieting all movement within the state where no traces remain—vast and expansive, this is truly the level road for entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality; it encompasses all phenomena and brings them into the single point of ultimate intent.
Quieting the multitude of thoughts, one dissolves all physical traces;
regarding whatever is encountered, there is clarity and no obstruction.
Neither grasping at the internal nor the external, the intermediate is fundamentally non-existent.

This is precisely entering the gate of non-duality. Why? Because "the True" is defined as reaching the ultimate and relinquishing all emotions, while "the Conventional" is defined as arising from the subtle and engaging with movement;
it is not necessarily by creating a state of the ultimate limit that one attains it.
That which accords with it is called the "True" (zhen);
that which involves the characteristics of conditioned existence is called the "Conventional" (su).

How could one have expected this? "True" (zhen) refers to the emptiness of nature (xingkong), meaning the principle of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva). "Conventional" (su) refers to provisional existence, meaning the illusory existence of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva). This existence of provisional existence is called "semblance-existence," for the dharmas are fundamentally non-existent.
Existence arises by depending on conditions; when conditions depart, it is non-existent.

This existence that is like an illusion and emptiness that is its nature is called "true emptiness. Because within true nature, the hundred negations and four marks are clearly seen as unattainable, the awakened one establishes the real within the conventional; this reality that contradicts the conventional is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The conventional is precisely the conditioned, for these two dharmas are distinct. To unify the conventional and the ultimate in non-duality:
the ultimate is principle, while the conventional is phenomena.
There are no phenomena that do not arise from principle;
there is no principle that is not manifested through phenomena.
Without the conventional, the ultimate cannot be spoken of.
One must not discuss matters from the standpoint of irrationality.
Because it is neither identical with nor separate from [phenomena], it is called non-duality (*advaya*). When the Middle Way is clearly illuminated, there is a profound realization;
never has there been a single thing that accords with the emotional mind.
In this way, where would the principle of simplicity not be manifest?
Where would the enterprise of the long-term and vast not be complete? The *Xici* says:
"That which is easy is easy to know."
When concise, it is easy to follow.
When easy to understand, there is affinity;
when easy to follow, there is achievement.
To accord with the nature of all things and to penetrate the wills of the world, one can achieve enduring and magnificent merit.
Though *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas may seem distant, the Dharmakāya is without exterior; herein lies the realization. *Asaṃkhyeya* here means "immeasurable."
From the initial arousal of the mind at the first stage of the ten faiths up to the end of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) is called the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.

From the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) up to the end of the seventh stage is called the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*. From the eighth stage up to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is called the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.
Is it not far removed that one can only attain Buddhahood after these three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*?
Nevertheless, the principle of the Dharma-body is fundamentally interpenetrating and harmonious.
Although delusion and awakening differ, neither is obtained from without; therefore, the myriad phenomena speak of their reality, taking emptiness as their nature.
Every verdant bamboo shoot is entirely suchness.

The lush yellow flowers are none other than *prajñā*; they are distinguished as provisional, yet they rely upon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Since the provisional is itself the characteristic of true emptiness, once empty, the provisional and the real are of one substance;
thus, no duality between the two limits can be attained.
If it were not the Middle Way, how could emptiness be the nature and the provisional be the characteristic?
The characteristic does not depart from the nature.
Nature is not separate from its characteristics;
therefore, it is called "one substance.
"Two limits" refers to the two extremes.
Because neither of the two extremes can be attained, one accords with the Middle Way. Thus, when observing the arising of an image, it possesses no inherent self-nature;
it arises depending upon various conditions.
Since it depends on conditions, the image is fundamentally non-existent. The nature of all phenomena is likewise fundamentally devoid of self-nature.
They arise through the conjunction of conditions and cease when conditions disperse.
As for mental phenomena, there are four conditions.
Form-dharmas depend on two conditions;

since they cannot arise by themselves, they are without intrinsic substance and are rooted in emptiness. They are provisional existences whose image takes emptiness as its basis, and emptiness is contained within the image.
One waits for the elephant to manifest.
Since manifestation resides in the elephant, emptiness becomes the elephant;
there is no emptiness outside of the elephant. The emptiness of non-action contains the forms of conditioned existence.
This demonstrates that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) must necessarily rely upon the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Since the conditioned can manifest the unconditioned, it is that which manifests; it is like the moon in water, which is seen when conditions coincide.
How could one say it is empty?
The form is empty and non-existent;
who can say it exists? The moon is originally in the sky, yet its reflection flows in the water.

Who says that the water is empty and that there was originally no moon? Since it is merely a reflection appearing in the flowing current, who can say it exists? Thus, the Sage’s wondrous embodiment lies between existence and non-existence, enabling the functioning of both existence and non-existence.
This is called the ultimate. Therefore, the Sage has clearly realized its essence and function, as Qingbian said:
"The conditioned is like an illusion or a transformation;
the unconditioned is like a flower in the sky. The *Tattvasaṃgraha* (Pal-zhen lun) says: "Conditioned phenomena are just like illusions and transformations."
Because they are fundamentally non-existent, unconditioned dharmas are like flowers in the sky;
for they certainly do not arise. Indeed, illusory phenomena exist only as provisional designations.
This is because that which exists adapts to the non-existent; the rabbit’s horn is fundamentally non-existent, yet a magician makes it appear as if existent by means of a handkerchief.
Apart from the handkerchief, there is absolutely no rabbit’s horn.
Conditioned phenomena exist only as provisional designations dependent upon a multitude of causes and conditions;
apart from these causes and conditions, the provisional phenomenon has no fundamental reality.
Thus, one uses existence to reach non-existence, for empty flowers are originally non-existent.
It is because that which is non-existent appears as if it were existent;
though non-existent, it seems to exist.
It is profoundly still at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); true nature is fundamentally non-existent and does not arise, being like flowers in the sky.
Because there is that which acts as the basis for conditioned existence, there is what appears to exist; yet this appearance of existence is fundamentally non-existent.
This is precisely the profound and tranquil true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), where existence is immediately non-existence.

Returning once more to non-existence: if one regards that which exists as a dharma of provisional existence, then when conditions disperse and return to the source, it is fundamentally nothing at all. To illustrate this principle through two metaphors, the Dharma has no fixed location; these are the two metaphors.
The dharma of illusion is used as a metaphor for the conditioned nature of true reality;
the metaphor of flowers in the sky is used for the unconditioned nature of true reality.
However, those who are merely skilled in words grasp its periphery but do not grasp its essence.
The student of the good mind knows its ultimate limit but does not know its phenomenal forms; things arise with forms,
and only after there are forms do numerical categories exist.
"Jiāo" (徼) means the border;
"jí" (極) means the end.
Those who merely follow the literal text—
Although one may have attained a minor path along the remote frontiers,
one has not grasped the total number of its ultimate destinations.
Thus it is with those who transmit the mind-seal.
Although one may attain the wondrous gateway of the ultimate, one still does not know the signs and omens of its origin. To cling to both extremes without ceasing—this is the source of affliction.
One such error is to become attached to existence by following the literal words of texts.
First, some reject all phenomenal characteristics and cling to emptiness;
each adheres to the edge of one shore.
How could they reach the path of the Middle Way? Thus, those who stagnate in existence erroneously equate it with permanence.
Those who sink into emptiness fall into the view of annihilation, while those who cling to existence grasp at all phenomena as being permanent—
such as the non-Buddhists who calculate the four types of eternalism,
or the followers of the Lesser Vehicle who calculate that "all exists."
Those who cling to emptiness are like the non-Buddhists who propound the seven theories of annihilation and so forth.
Furthermore, within our own school, there are those who negate all phenomena as being entirely empty; such views are more akin to nihilism than they are to the confusion of permanence.
If there were permanence, there would be dharmas to be cultivated;
if there were annihilation, there would be no good that would not be abandoned.
To abandon [the good] is to fall into false views.
If one practices, one gradually approaches the true Way; however, because some dismiss both *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* as being entirely empty, it is said that it would be better to cling to existence.

Just as Mount Sumeru cannot be dismissed as empty while a mustard seed remains, there are those today who are fixated on the path of clinging to existence and taking emptiness as the ultimate gateway—such as those who preach Chan in recent times and remain stuck in the way of clinging to existence.
If one then takes emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in its entirety as the ultimate path, let me ask:

is this emptiness something that can be grasped, or is it something that cannot be grasped? What would be the error in either case? If there were an emptiness that could be grasped, then emptiness would itself become existence. Since emptiness could then be grasped, would it not follow that it is existence? Thus, to grasp at the vast, formless emptiness with a mind of dogmatic attachment merely results in the extinction of that very emptiness; how does this have anything to do with the principle of cultivating practice and realizing one's nature?

If emptiness cannot be grasped, it is discarded along with existence; yet if existence also cannot be grasped, how does it differ from emptiness? Since it is discarded along with existence, it must likewise persist along with existence. If existence cannot be grasped, then emptiness persists.
If one dismisses both existence and emptiness, they likewise cannot be grasped.
What prevents one from maintaining both existence and emptiness, rather than maintaining the path of emptiness alone?
Indeed, one is able to both dismiss and maintain both.
When one is free from all attachments, abiding in the state where appearance is empty yet existence is not non-existent;

when merging with the truth, both existence and non-existence are extinguished—this is what is called the right contemplation of the Mahāsattva and the profound illumination of the *dharmadhātu*. Because one is detached from duality and does not grasp at appearances, this is named "abiding in consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). As Nāgārjuna said:
It is like someone traveling to a foreign land who stays at an inn—
an inn being a guest house— and the innkeeper serves him a meal of delicacies.
Just as the food is being cleared away— that is, removed and put aside— the guest rises and takes his leave, saying:
"How could such a thing exist? he thought, seeing that the man had asked about the food upon finding it delicious.
The host replied, "It is because my country has sauce.
He withdrew and said to himself:
If even when sauce is combined with other flavors it still reaches [the palate], how much more so when it is used alone for flavor!
This serves to proclaim the host’s kindness; "proclaim" means to make manifest.
This means he clearly remembered the words of his master; for this reason,
while at the house of the sauce-seller— where "yin" refers to darkness and "yu" means to sell—
he indulged his own greedy desires and stayed in an uninhabited room.
To eat until one is satiated and then eat to the point of repletion is excessive; by overindulging in saltiness, one dies of thirst.

Likewise, those who take partial emptiness (*ekānta-śūnyatā*) as the Way will ultimately be harmed by that very emptiness. It becomes a harm because one is stuck and lacks penetration. As the *Madhyamaka* says:
If a person sees emptiness, they are not transformed by the Buddhas, for there is the warning against the fear of clinging to the view of annihilationism.
A sutra states:
"The bhikṣu Vijñātagati heard the Bodhisattva Nandika say that lust, anger, and ignorance are the Path; he also heard the Bodhisattva Nandika say that lust, anger, and ignorance constitute the Path."
Statements such as "first one is drawn by the hook of desire and later led into the Buddha's wisdom" are unbalanced in their reasoning;
from this, anger and pride arise.
One who contemplates the benefits of future lives gives rise to the faculty of joy.
Even if one is forced to accept [this teaching] without hesitation and does not yet understand it, it will ultimately serve as a virtuous cause for future lives.
"Hesitation" refers to resentment; however, those with wrong views today mistakenly grasp its literal phrasing and treat it as a mere nominal characteristic (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).
To regard all things as empty and yet commit evil without shame—where "shame" (zuo) refers to a sense of moral remorse—is to fail to grasp the meaning of the teaching on emptiness.
Upon hearing the words of emptiness, they immediately dismiss names and characteristics as being entirely void, showing no sense of shame; how could this possibly capture the intent of the sutras?
However, the Book says:
"The Sovereign establishes the Supreme Ultimate (ji) and gathers people to that Supreme Ultimate;
he returns them to that Supreme Ultimate. The "Supreme" (huang) is great, and the "Ultimate" (ji) is the Mean. In establishing any undertaking, one must employ the Way of Great Centrality.
This differs slightly from the text of the *Shangshu*; it is the Way of Great Centrality (*dazhong*).
No one but a Sage can approximate its practice. The Way of Great Centrality refers to the Nine Categories (*jiuchou*).
First is the Five Elements;
second is the reverent application of the Five Matters;
third is the agricultural application of the Eight Administrations.
The fourth is: "To employ the five cycles in coordination.
The fifth is: "To establish the Imperial Standard in its application.
The sixth is: "To govern by means of the three virtues."
Seventh is: "To clarify the use of inquiry when in doubt.
Eighth is: "To reflect upon the use of the various omens.
Ninth is: "To enjoy the use of the five blessings and to employ the use of the six extremes."
These nine refer to sages, gentlemen, and sovereigns. The *Li* says:
"The Doctrine of the Mean is the ultimate. This is the sixteenth chapter of the *Liji*, titled "Zhongyong. "Yong" means constant.
To employ the Mean as the Constant Way:
thus, the Imperial Ultimate (Huangji) is the center of the center among the myriad transformations.

The Mean (Zhongyong) is likewise the center of the center among the myriad transformations. What are called the "myriad things" each possess a Way within them, which constitutes the nature of supreme virtue.
It is the form and appearance of all things, the sovereign of all transformations, and the true master of yin and yang. As the Sage Laozi said:
"Thirty spokes converge upon a single hub."
"When there is nothingness, there is the utility of the chariot"—this is from Chapter Eleven of the *Laozi Daodejing*.
"The thirty spokes" represent the many;
"the single hub" represents the few.
This means that by means of a few, one encompasses the many.
This illustrates the principle of using the substantiality of the carriage’s frame and sides to facilitate its insubstantial function. It is like molding clay to create vessels.
When it is non-existent, there is the utility of the vessel;
when it is molded and harmonized, it is clay. By blending the clay, one makes earthenware vessels.

This is because there is the function of containing things within the space of emptiness; thus, "being" serves as the vessel, like conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), while "non-being" serves as the function, like the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) which manifests by relying upon conditioned phenomena. Non-being is the center; the center is used as a metaphor for the Ultimate Way (*paramārtha-mārga*), and the center demonstrates oneness.
Therefore it is said:
"Heaven attains unity and becomes clear;
Earth attains unity and becomes tranquil. This is from Chapter Thirty-nine of the *Laozi*.
Because things obtain the functioning of the Dao, heaven is clear and earth is tranquil;
when this functioning is lost, reality is forfeited. The *I Ching* says:
"The Spirit has no fixed location and the Changes have no substance. (From the *Xici*).

The Divine (*shen*) is the unfathomable interplay of Yin and Yang; the *Yi* (the Book of Changes) signifies that which follows wherever change leads. It cannot be elucidated through a single perspective or a fixed form.
Furthermore, it says: "One Yin and one Yang are called the Dao. The Dao is a designation for that which is quiescent and without corporeal substance.
Although yin and yang differ, there is not one that does not await the other:
when in yin, it is through non-yin that yin gives birth;
when in yang, it is through non-yang that yang brings completion.
Therefore it is said that there is one yin and one yang; however, as the depths of immersion vary, the explanations regarding the three methods differ. As the *Lunyu* states:
"If it is deep, one must wade through it."
"If shallow, wade through.
The *Erya* states:
"To cross water in one's clothes is called *li* (wading)."
If it is shallow, one enters with the robes intact;
if it is shallow, one lifts up the robes.
This lifting of the robes is a metaphor for the varying depths of practice and contemplation on the Path. Indeed, one who maintains the Great Mean within...
When virtue and instruction are practiced abroad,
heaven and earth are harmonious and peaceful,
and ghosts and spirits lose their power.
Therefore, Daoting and Hexu were both sovereigns who presided over the governance of antiquity;
they attained the art of the "center within the circle" and integrated the myriad transformations through non-action (*wuwei*). They did not personally favor their own kin.
He did not treat his son as his own;

he transformed others through non-action. Formerly, in the temple of Duke Huan of Lu, there was a vessel of inclination belonging to Zhongzi, the son of Lady Zhongzi and younger brother of Duke Yin—the son of Duke Hui of Lu. This vessel was shaped like a small earthenware jar.
When used to hold water,
it tilts when empty;
"tilt" means to lean.
When it is half-filled, it stands upright; when full, it overturns.
This is a metaphor for maintaining the centrality and rectitude, demonstrating to others the outward manifestation of centrality and rectitude.
Now, that which is central is upright;
being upright, it is empty yet full, harmonizing with the proper measure,
standing aloof and uniquely established.
It begins with the eye and culminates in response to the mind;
it is profound and reliable— truly established by those who plant it.
It causes one to first behold it with the eyes and ultimately realize it with the mind;
it is profound yet credible. As the Book says:
"Firmness without cruelty;
simplicity without arrogance" is from the "Canon of Shun.
When firmness loses its way, it enters into cruelty.
"Simple and free from loss; entering with mildness yet maintaining severity;
majestic without being fierce"—these are the words of the *Analects*.
"Mildness" means warmth and gentleness.
Furthermore, it is stern;
yet though stern, it is not violent. These are all sages and gentlemen who weigh the principles of things with a balance.
The mind merges with phenomena,
yet it does not lose its central balance. Although the above points are elucidated in non-Buddhist classics,
they all adopt the meaning of the "Middle Way" (zhongyong).

The intention of Master Beishan is to point out that those who study emptiness and study existence should attain the wisdom of the Middle Way. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, a great being contemplates both form and emptiness, like the disciple of a butcher.
This is as stated in the text of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
This is entirely identical in meaning to the passage in the *Zhuangzi*. According to Master Zhuang, when Cook Ding was dismembering an ox for Lord Wen Hui, his eyes saw no whole ox.
Cook Ding was dismembering the ox for Lord Wen Hui.
That which the hands touch,
that upon which the shoulders lean,
and that which the feet tread upon.
Wherever the knees were stuck,
there was a "hu" sound; as he applied the blade,
there was a "hua" sound— none failed to accord with the musical notes, matching the rhythm of a dance performed upon soft wood.
This was the very meeting point of the "Foreword to the Classic of the Center.
He encountered [the ox] with his spirit rather than viewing it with his eyes;
with a single blade, over nineteen years, he had dissected several thousand oxen.
The blade was as if newly emerged from its whetstone;
for while the joints have spaces, the blade has no thickness.
"By inserting that which has no thickness into that which has space,
there will surely be ample room for the free movement of the blade.
This is indeed Zhuangzi’s allegorical expression used to illustrate the Way.
This is because one takes up the principle of utility without obstruction.
Why is this so? As for the substance of an ox, it has horns and a dewlap—the dewlap being the fleshy protuberance on its neck—and there is nothing between its joints.
When a blade of no thickness enters a body with interstices,
how could it not pass through with ample ease?
What cow is there that could resist it?
The butcher Zhao was proficient in his craft; before he had even begun to dismember the ox, there was nothing he saw that was not an ox.
After three years, however—
"I have never seen a whole ox," he said, for he meets it with his spirit.
This is how the disciple of the butcher-teacher clarifies the difficulty. It is like the difference between a skilled cook and a butcher who hacks at the carcass:

one changes his knife every year because he cuts through bone; the other changes his knife monthly because he cuts through joints; while the master changes his knife only once in nineteen years because he follows the natural grain of the flesh.
The butcher who changes his knife every month is merely one who carves;

he differs from the butcher whose knife remains intact after nineteen years. Therefore, one who penetrates the essence is not obstructed by substantial objects; for one who has attained the Way, things cannot hinder him—thus even Mount Sumeru can be contained within a mustard seed.
To entrust the vast expanse to a mere hair’s breadth is indeed as easy as casting it into the great ocean; such is the intent of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, as the Sage Laozi said:
"The rhinoceros has nowhere to thrust its horn."
The tiger has nowhere to plant its claws;
the soldier has no place to admit his blade. This is because he does not seek to harm things, as he possesses no harmful intent.
Thus, there is no place for him to cast his horns, plant his claws, or admit his blade. So said Master Zhuang.
"Even when a great flood reaches the heavens, one is not drowned"—a "great flood" refers to the sea.
"Reaches" (*ji*) means to level with.

In the *Xiaoyao* chapter it says: "In a great drought, metal and stone melt and the earthen mountains wither, yet one is not heated"; thus, one does not alter their fundamental nature due to cold or heat.

One does not allow worldly things to rob one of their integrity. When Zhongni saw the Elder of Lüliang swimming across a torrent thirty *zhen* deep—where one *zhen* equals seven feet—he relied solely on his loyalty and good faith.
Relying on the way of loyalty and good faith,
they do not fear perilous obstacles; is this not because they all embrace the principle of the Great Mean and harmonize the natures of all things?
And yet, they are able to reach such a state.
Therefore, they tread upon water, rush into fire,
encounter blades, and walk upon peril.
The body can move with lightness;
the ears can hear through all things;
the eyes can see through all things.
It is precisely because the mind is empty. As Laozi said:
"Empty the mind, fill the belly.
Because the mind is empty, one does not oppose the myriad things; one engages with them without the distinction of self and other. Thus, the myriad things also accord with me in a profound manner.
The vast and pervasive nature is in harmony with all things;
one who seeks them with an empty mind will encounter them in profound resonance. Furthermore, water and fire are among the most harmful of things; water can drown and submerge.
Fire can burn and consume;

these are all harms inherent in things. Yet scales grow in springs, and fish and dragons depend on water to live; beasts are born from fire, such as the fire-rat and the fire-tortoise, both of which are born within the flames—how could they possibly rely on techniques to ward off water or fire?
However, their natures accord with dryness and moisture,
and their vital energies correspond to cold and heat;
therefore, they coexist without contradicting one another.
They give rise to one another without harming each other;

when they are sincere, they are complete. Since they do not injure one another, it is evident that water and fire can sustain all things; how much more so for those who possess the Way, whose virtue is fully realized within the myriad species!
Therefore, the Great Being trains with this mind;
he designates it as "dhyāna.
Dhyāna means "meditative concentration" (靜慮); in the Sanskrit language, it is *samādhi*.
This is called *dhyāna* (静虑).

This meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can still and quiet the mental deliberations; because external objects are insufficient to shift one's sentiments, it is termed "concentration" (*ding*). In Sanskrit, it is called *samādhi*.
This means "right concentration. "Concentration" (*ding*) signifies single-mindedness.
Those who claim that the physical body is itself the Buddha, thereby discarding images and occupying the seat of the Great Sage, are truly foolish, perverse, and cruel.
It would be like the followers of Vajra-dhyāna who would even test their sincerity with water and fire.
How could one possibly obtain such great fortune and escape harm? If one were cast into water or fire, how could one avoid injury?
Those below are deluded by his wandering words and do not attend to his actual conduct.
To rely on the blind in seeking a straight path is already difficult; it is like the case of the blind leading the blind. Now, for one who practices the Way, there are three aspects:
the knowing mind, the practicing mind, and the directing mind.
Having examined all these matters thoroughly, one then speaks of the destination reached.
"Knowing the mind" means comprehending the distinction between the true and the false;
"practicing the mind" means extinguishing attachment and aversion.
The "power over the mind" refers to transforming that defiled or pure mind; when the mind is pure, the world is pure, and so forth.
Now, those who have only recently begun their studies wish to have some semblance of understanding, yet they remain deficient regarding other matters.
Why seek to deceive oneself? Among the Chan masters of today, there are many who,
claiming to have attained realization themselves,
go so far as to mislead and deceive others.
Since there are many who hold deluded views, such as those of the Mountain Fruit or Vajra Chan, Great Compassion is inexhaustible;
thus, the fragrant food is inexhaustible.
Great Wisdom is unimpeded.
The abbot is not obstructed; like Vimalakīrti, his great compassion is inexhaustible.
The fragrant food he partakes of is never depleted, and the wisdom-practices he cultivates are unimpeded.
Even what the current Abbot has experienced does not constitute an obstruction. As the sutra says,
"When one attains Buddhahood,
one will be endowed with the thirty-two marks," it is only upon reaching such a state as described in the *Lotus Sutra* that one can be said to have reached ultimate exhaustion [of all defilements].
Mount Heng and Mount Tiantai are where the Great Master Si resided at Nanyue and where the Great Master Zhizhe resided at Tiantai. The single mind and threefold contemplation are called Mahāprajñā.
The Mahā-dharmakāya is the Mahā-nirvāṇa. First,
one enters emptiness from the conventional.
First, by observing that form is emptiness, one manifests the Dharmakāya; second, by entering from emptiness into the conventional, one observes that emptiness is form, thereby manifesting Prajñā;
third, emptiness and the conventional are equal.

This means that because form and emptiness are non-different, this is nirvana. Having established the three virtues of the perfect *ī* (the syllable *i*), these three dharmas above mutually require one another to be accomplished;
they are called the "Three Virtues."
It is also called the "Circular *i*.
This refers to the three dots of the letter *i* in the Sanskrit script, which are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara; it was indeed obtained from Nāgārjuna.
Huikai of Jiaxiang Temple in Kuaiji was a monk who practiced both the provisional and the ultimate, thereby perfecting both compassion and wisdom.
His learning encompassed both internal and external teachings, and he was proficient in the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
He left traces such as the Brahmajāla Sūtra and the Nirvāṇa Sūtra;
because of his great compassion, he delighted in delivering sentient beings,
and because of his great wisdom, he delighted in severing [afflictions] and realizing [enlightenment].

They are mutually dependent like the two feet of a person; this was indeed obtained from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, and it is the essential principle for attaining true nature (*dharmatā*). Bodhidharma directed his contemplation toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), being without thought and without deliberation.

I attained this through the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) when I arrived here during the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty. Yet, those of recent times do not realize that emptiness is not separate from the conventional;

they discard the conventional in their quest for emptiness, and thus heterodox views arise. How can it be that true emptiness is not separate from conventional existence? Therefore, one who walks in the mundane world must know that the conventional is not separate from emptiness. When engaging with phenomena, one must understand that phenomena take emptiness as their basis; only then does one comprehend the nature of what I have done, which is not called "the mundane. Though it is mundane, one is able to penetrate its true essence.
How could it be said that the conventional is not the ultimate? One who dwells in the ultimate knows that the ultimate is not separate from the conventional;

thus, they perceive that the "self" is not something that can be called non-ultimate. One who dwells in the ultimate and is able to know the ultimate through its manifestation in the conventional does not cling to the ultimate and thereby become stagnant. Therefore, the Great Sage maintains that the three realms are non-arising.
The two vehicles [of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas] take the cessation of the three realms as non-arising, whereas the Mahāyāna speaks of the ultimate truth while remaining within the conventional.

Thus, regarding the partial and the complete, the superiority and inferiority of the Small Vehicle and the Great Vehicle are distinguished here. The Mahāyāna achieves liberation through perfect penetration.
The Hīnayāna adherents are hindered by their biased attachments; as the Sūtra says:

"Though they know that the Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty, they constantly cultivate pure lands to transform all classes of beings; though they know that conditioned phenomena are empty," and so forth.
Yet, not ceasing the saving of sentient beings—this is called practicing the Middle Way.
Thus, when gold is melted or silk is embroidered, who would say they exist?
When one sits cross-legged with eyes closed in meditation, who would say they are empty? To act within existence and yet realize its nature is the way.
Who would say that one who possesses the marks of conditioned activity falls into existence?

One who penetrates non-activity—who would say that such a person falls into the emptiness of non-activity? Only one who can embody and penetrate this, practicing the non-path while universally attaining the Buddha-way.
Only when one can discuss its ultimate limit, realize that it is not the Way [of the world], and is able to harmonize with the Buddha-way, may one then discourse upon its supreme principle.

What could those who are narrow-minded and isolated say of this? How could those who are deluded regarding emptiness and attached to existence ever recognize this path? The wise Bao was cautious regarding his reputation and integrity, standing out with a resolute and solitary aloofness.
While they may gain renown for upholding the Vinaya, they are unable to empty their minds to accord with the Way;
instead, they merely cling to a narrow sense of minor precepts, remaining ignorant of the path of perfect penetration—like one who enters the water when it is cold.
When hot, they seek fire;
when thirsty, they eat salt.
Their death is truly piteous.
Aisheng served as the tutelary deity of the monastery;
although he was diligent in his conduct and profound in his sincerity,
he did not understand the way by which one attains the Dao.
Cold and heat are the constant laws of heaven and earth;

if one is so stubborn as to oppose them—stubbornness being a form of perversity—how much less could such a person harmonize their mind with the non-duality of self and others? The twentieth patriarch was named Jayata.
Upon arriving at the city of Rājagṛha,
he saw a dhūta ascetic who was performing prostrations and recitations during the six periods of the day.
He had few desires and was content;
he sat upright for long periods without reclining and took but a single meal a day.
The Venerable One addressed the assembly, saying,
"How do you perceive this dhūta practitioner?
The assembly replied:
"Inconceivable! You constantly practice the holy life.
Is this the Path? It is indeed as the Venerable One has said.
Thus he spoke.
Now this dhūta practitioner will before long fall away;
he is far removed from the Way,
for that which the mind perceives as an attainment is not called the Way.
The assembly asked,
"How do you know?
The Venerable One replied:
I do not seek the Way,
nor am I deluded; I do not perform prostrations during the six periods of the day.
Nor do I treat others with contempt.
I do not remain seated for long periods, nor am I indolent.
I do not eat only once a day,
nor do I eat mixed foods; I am not content.
He was also free from covetousness.
Upon hearing this teaching, the dhūta practitioner immediately conceived a sense of reverence.

In India, this is called the "all-pervading dhūta" (sarvatraga-dhūta), which is precisely *vāyubhakṣa* (wind-eater). Thus, one exhausts one's body in life and sinks into a state of formlessness at death.
Furthermore, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, those who uphold the precepts within the Mahāyāna are considered to have broken them from the perspective of the Hīnayāna.

If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings undergoing the results of evil karma, he may take their life upon himself to undergo the karma of killing, thereby enabling them to escape from suffering bodies and the like.

Diligence is the opposite of indolence; being addicted to minor dharmas is indolence. It is evident that faith can become an obstacle to wisdom, for by believing in inferior fruits one fails to give rise to great wisdom.
There are those who maintain that forgetting words constitutes the Way;
they are indeed quite similar to this [earlier case].
For one who does not understand words yet speaks is a speaker of delusions.
To not speak when one does not know what to say is to be cautious in speech.
To speak by receiving the words of others is to learn from the words of others. To receive the words of others, yet knowing them, refrain from speaking, is to maintain stillness in speech.
If one desires to cease from speech yet does not succeed in the mind that has ceased from speaking,
then although the resonance may subside externally,
the emotions will remain turbulent within.
Indeed, that which does not perish is the mind; though the mouth may be silenced and speech cease, if the mind still pursues fame and profit, then it is not truly a mind that has ceased speaking.
One who can realize that speech arises from things—and that as all things transform of themselves, so too does speech—will find that the speaker also transforms of itself.

To speak all day long yet remain constantly silent—this is what is meant by being truly one who has transcended speech; it is to speak while the mind remains unattached. Yet, in the sutra, Vimalakīrti does not say this.
Since the words of the aforementioned great beings have reached their conclusion, what further could be said regarding "not speaking" as the true entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality?
It is like the Master Zhuang’s *Wuwei* (Non-action), which states that he did not inform others when he traveled north.
Because such persons are unable to embody the words and immediately realize the Way, it is not taught to them; "to teach" (gào) here means to request.
Since they have attained self-attestation, there is no need for them to request instruction.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "This Dharma cannot be shown; it is the quiescent Dharma beyond words and signs. (Lotus Sutra Text).
This discourse concerns the characteristics of ultimate truth; how could it not be explained?
Therefore, *prajñā* (wisdom) and *upāya* (skillful means) are the two complements of the Perfect Teaching.
If skillful means are removed, then Prajñā shines in isolation. In Sanskrit it is called *prajñā*;
here it is translated as "wisdom.
In Sanskrit it is called *upāyakauśalya*.
This is called "expedient means" (upāya).
Expedient means and wisdom are mutually dependent in terms of essence and function.
If one were to discard the function of expedient means, [wisdom would be lost].
Thus, the essence of Prajñā constitutes solitary illumination; it is therefore the Ultimate Way (To),
which encompasses heaven and earth and contains all things.

Movement and transformation: when one attains this, entering a single atom, one is vast within the Dharma-realm; the single atom is not narrow, nor is the Dharma-realm broad. When one loses it, traversing the Dharma-realm, one becomes cramped within a single atom. For those who do not attain this Way, even the Dharma-realm is narrower than a minute speck of dust; to them, a great mountain and the tip of an autumn hair are as different as day and night.
How far apart are delusion and awakening? Like Mount Tai and a fine hair, their sizes differ;
so too do the states of delusion and awakening differ in terms of being obstructed or unobstructed.
*Beishan lu*, Volume II.
*Beishan lu*, Scroll Three, Section Five:

"The Convergence of Hegemons and Kings" (III), Part Five: "The Convergence of Hegemons and Kings. It clarifies matters such as the succession of enlightened sovereigns, the encounters of *śramaṇas* from the Western Regions and the Han lands with contemporary rulers, and the rise and fall of dynasties.

At the beginning of the kalpa, the people all lived on grain; "zheng" means the masses. "Xu" means mutually. When the fertility of the earth was exhausted, there appeared natural non-glutinous rice and fragrant rice.
It was exhausted.
The land was divided and cultivated—that is, managed.
Once people had begun to encroach upon and seize it.
Thereupon, the lands and fields were divided and each was governed separately; boundaries and districts were established, and the Great Samata, the Samatas, were appointed.

These were village chiefs who, fearing that the strong might encroach upon and seize their property, established one man as king to receive their tribute and offerings, so that he might serve as the lord of the people and be honored by all classes.
His grace flowed throughout the land.
As the double sun (the second Buddha) succeeded to the throne, his dynastic fortune continued in India; his father and grandfather succeeded one another as the lords of India, down to Śuddhodana.
In total, there were eighty-four thousand two hundred and sixty-odd kings. The *Āgama Sūtra* states:
"In the past, there was a king named Yima (Yiduo).
He had four sons born of concubines."
1. Manifesting the Eye;
2. Linking the Eye;
3. Taming the Elephant.
The four *nīla* queens were all intelligent and sagacious, possessing divine prowess and great majestic virtue.
The first lady had a son named Jīvaka.
They were stubborn, coarse, and ugly,
and were despised by all people.
The lady feared that these four sons would usurp her position.
Consequently, they slandered Wang Chang, leading to his dismissal; the King then issued an edict to his four sons, commanding each to depart from the country with all haste.
At that time, the Mallas and all the people wished to follow them into exile.
He went to dwell among the snow mountains in a grove of straight trees;
within a few years, those who turned to his virtue gathered like people at a market,
and he eventually became a powerful state.
The father longed to see him;
he summoned him, but he did not go.
The father then sighed three times, saying, "My son possesses true capability."
For this reason, his clan was named Śākya.
The Āgama Sūtras state that "Śāka grove" (śāka-vana) constitutes his family name.
Thus there arose the Śākya clan;
"Śākya" refers to the tree. After King Mahāsammata, there was a king named Mahāsudassana.
Over seven generations, they belonged to the Gautama clan. Long ago, there was a king.
His parents died early;
he ceded the kingdom to his younger brother and relinquished his position to seek the Way.
He saw a Brahmin of the Gautama clan and followed him to study the Way.
The brāhmaṇa said, "You should remove your royal robes and receive the clan name Gautama as I do;
thus you shall be known as the Bodhisattva Little Gautama. After King Urumā, there was a king named Nīla-cūḍa.
In all five generations, there was the Śākya clan. King Nīla gave birth to King Uttara;
King Uttara became the sovereign of the kingdom of Kapilavastu and gave birth to King Gopura.
King Gopāla begot King Sihahala. King Sihahala begot four sons:
the first was King Śuddhodana.
Second, King Śuklodana;
third, King Droṇodana;
fourth, King Amṛtodana.

King Śuddhodana was the father of the Buddha. Having cultivated the primary and secondary marks for a hundred kalpas, the Great Being practiced the path of the Bodhisattva through three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas until he reached the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*).
After one hundred kalpas, he cultivates the primary and secondary marks;
after one thousand kalpas, he studies majestic deportment;
and after ten thousand kalpas, he studies transformative conduct. Thereafter, when examining his future birth, none is more suitable than that of a kṣatriya or a brāhmaṇa.
The status of a Kṣatriya is one of great importance;
in Sanskrit it is called *kṣatriya*, which here means "lord of the land," referring to the royal caste. The Brahmin’s virtue is most honored; in Sanskrit, the term is correctly *brāhmaṇa*.
This is called Jingyu (Pure Chariot).
He is a descendant of the Brahmā Heaven.
This exists only in the Five Indies and is found in no other lands.
Because he serves as the teacher of kings, it is said that his virtue is honored. However, in this age of degeneration (kalpa-kaṣāya), virtue does not outweigh one’s status;
therefore, I was not born into the Brahmin caste.
Although my country lacked the Kṣatriya caste, even in their absence, my lineage has been continuous for a long time.

Nothing surpasses this: from King Samata to King Śuddhodana, there have been eighty-four thousand two hundred and sixty-six kings of the Śākya lineage. Therefore, the Great Sage was not born into the other two lineages, for they were of low and humble origin; "se" (塞) means to obstruct or suppress, as such origins would have provided grounds for public censure.
The two castes are: first, the Vaiśya, which is translated here as "sitting to trade"; they are so named because they possess much worldly wealth.
Second, the Śūdra.
It is also called Śūdra,
referring to those who engage in agriculture, government service, and scholarship. The region of the Five Indias spans over ninety thousand *li* and is bounded on three sides by the great ocean.
To the north, with its back to the Snowy Mountains,
there were eight great kingdoms, sixteen great cities, and more than seventy small kingdoms;
at that time, no Wheel-Turning King reigned over them.
Just as when there is a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) by the command of a hegemon,
all small kingdoms submit and become subject;
now that there is no longer a Wheel-Turning King, [the same applies].
To regard only the powerful as a hegemon is like the era of the Spring and Autumn Annals among the various states of China:
the Way of the King had declined, the feudal lords were constrained by Duke Huan and Duke Wen, and since the time King You was assassinated, the Zhou dynasty itself had fallen into decay.
When King Ping moved the capital east to Luoyi, the feudal lords were permitted to exercise independent authority over military expeditions.

Consequently, as in the cases of Duke Wen of Jin and Duke Huan of Qi, matters of ritual, music, and military conquest were no longer determined by a single person alone. In ancient times, the formulation of rites and music, as well as the conduct of military campaigns, was not left to the discretion of individuals.
All must come from the Son of Heaven himself;

since his arrival, these instances of corruption and abuse have not issued from anyone else. This is because Magadha is a great kingdom—here called "Not-Arriving"—and it possesses generals, brave soldiers, and strategic counsel.
The armies of neighboring enemies were all unable to reach it.
It was five thousand *li* in circumference;
there were few inhabitants within the city walls, but the surrounding districts contained many registered households.
The soil is rich and fertile, nourishing the crops;
there is fragrant rice with grains that are plump and of extraordinary flavor,
which the local people call "rice for the Great Man."
The soil is damp and low-lying;
towns and states are situated amidst marshes.
The customs are refined and the character of the people is simple and honest.
The climate is mild, situated in a corner by the sea.
King Bimbisāra was its sovereign ruler;
this name means "one of upright countenance."
King Ajātaśatru was the father [of the Buddha], ranking among the foremost of sovereigns.
The city of Rājagṛha served as the supreme assembly for the gathering of the Dharma, representing the myriad streams that flow toward their source. This is the city of Rājagṛha.
In the language of India,
it is called Kuśāgrapura; in this language,
it is translated as "City of the Tip of Kusa Grass."
It is the most excellent kusa grass.
In the kingdom of Magadha, it was formerly produced when [the Buddha] had to leave his residence due to a fire.
He then abandoned this city and departed.
Later, King Aśoka moved his residence to Pāṭaliputra;
here, only a thousand Brahmins resided. Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa served as the secret treasury of the multitude of sages.
It overlooks the appearance of the surrounding peaks;
the city of Kusumā is a mountain fortress and is situated near Rājagṛha.
Although there are five mountains, this mountain alone is preeminent;
being both high and prominent,
it symbolizes the transcendence of the two vehicles.
Because many vultures dwell there, it is named Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*). Regarding Ajātaśatru: "Shi" (思) means "to contemplate"; "Huang" (皇) means "sovereign," where "huang" signifies greatness;
"deng" (登) means "to ascend";
and "yong" (庸) means "to employ."

To ascend to greatness by acting as a ruler, yet to bring about the murder of one's father and ruin one's reputation—though he possessed merit, it was not worth recounting; he conspired with Devadatta to murder his father.
He imprisoned and killed King Bimbisāra;
furthermore, he drew his sword to pursue his mother Vaidehī and others until reaching King Aśoka,
during whose reign the dynasty flourished.
His majesty extends to the corners of the sea,
and his power is equal to the iron wheel;
yet he does not immediately attain the truth— “equal” here meaning equivalent [to the ultimate].
It is thus accomplished.
Although its force is equal to that of an iron wheel, it is not an iron wheel.

King Bimbisāra was a great-grandson [of King Mahāsammata]. Initially, according to the *Faxiang jing* (Sūtra on the Images of Dharmas), one constructs the images of the hells based on this teaching: with steep walls and deep moats, glowing molten iron flows, and people are cast into them, crushed and scorched.
Although there have been instances in antiquity of disembowelment, execution by slicing, boiling, and burning, none were as cruel as this;
in the past, King Zhou of Shang disemboweled pregnant women, sliced the legs of those crossing the river at dawn, and established the punishment of the "burning grid."
He burned and roasted the loyal and virtuous, and剖 [dissected] the hearts of sages.
If one were to compare this, it would not be considered extreme;
he admired valor and pursued evil with zeal, fully advancing his cruel nature. Beneath the Southern Mountain there was a man.
He was so cruel that he could have served as a jailer;
his parents refused when summoned, so he killed them and came here. He encountered a practitioner of the Way who transformed him through supernatural power.
Suddenly, the system was changed; previously, all offenders within the kingdom, regardless of the severity of their crimes, were collectively cast into the mire of suffering.
Later, whenever someone reached the vicinity of the prison, they would be immediately seized and executed.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa wandering through the streets begging for alms.
The prison officials seized him and brought him inside.
Terrified, the śramaṇa requested permission to perform prostrations and repentance for seven days.
Suddenly, he saw a man being led in bound, his hands and feet severed and his body torn apart.
Upon seeing this, his grief and lamentation deepened;
he cultivated the contemplation of impermanence and realized the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Although he entered the boiling cauldron, it was like a clear pond;
there was a great lotus flower that served as his seat.
When the King heard of this, he went out to observe it and deeply praised the divine protection.
Later, he killed the jailer and subsequently abolished that prison. The Venerable Upagupta further enlightened [others] through cause and effect—“enlightened” (qidi) meaning to open up;
“di” (迪) means the Way.
This was the fifth patriarch, Upagupta.
Guided by the principles of cause and effect, he redoubled his self-examination and grew fearful, reflecting deeply on how to restore what had been lost.
Thereupon, he opened the eight royal coffers and vases and erected eighty thousand sacred shrines (*caityas*). This was after the time when Kṣudraka had abandoned his prison.
The Emperor further provided kind exhortations,
extensively explaining the causes for offering the land and the Tathāgata’s prophetic prediction regarding the merit of its construction;
he then assembled the spirits and deities.
They united their efforts with one heart,
so that the eight kingdoms might share the collection of the śarīra relics.
They commanded the ghosts and spirits, and on the appointed day, there appeared daily a shadowy obscuration in the shape of a hand.

On the day the śarīra were to be lowered, at the hour of midday, the arhats extended their hands to shield the sun, and the construction was thus completed. By virtue of the merit of offering the land, the king’s rank and status became exalted, reaching even unto Arhatship.
Mahādeva expelled the worthy and holy ones,
causing the Saṃgha to split into two factions; since Mahādeva entered the palace,
he has daily received imperial favor.
On the night of the *poṣadha* ceremony, he quarreled with the Saṃgha;
King Aśoka took his side, and thus the Great Assembly was divided into two sections, the Sthaviras and the Mahāsāṃghikas. This was the first schism in the Buddha-dharma.

Although the primary evil and great treachery did not originally lie with himself, as a sovereign he lacked the foresight to prevent it and could not help but take the blame upon his own person; from this point on, the Dharma deviated from its single flavor.
"Yuǎn" means "to resent.

This was likely because the King could not determine the guilt or rectify the injustice; this was his fault. "Shēndú" (申毒) refers to the region north of Shēndú; according to the *Hànshū Yìwén* (Phonetics and Explanations of the Book of Han), "dú" (毒) is pronounced as "dù" (篤).
This is India. It is also called "Xianzheng" (賢亘),
which in the language of Tang means "Moon."
The moon has a thousand names.
Sentient beings revolve in the cycle of existence without ceasing through the long night;
the sages transform them and guide all things as the moon illuminates the night.
It is for this reason that the name of that land was established. There is the kingdom of Gandhāra, which is North India;
it is five hundred *li* from Magadha and has no frost or snow.
The people there were fond of practicing the arts and revered non-Buddhist paths.
Asaṅga and Vasubandhu were born there; its king was named Kaniṣka, who, four hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, held dominion and was possessed of propriety.
Broad in learning and able to inspire trust,
the Master Mo (Sengmo) cited the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* regarding the Bhikṣu Pārśva, saying:
"The Bhikṣu Pārśva was once born such that he never lay on his side nor rested upon a mat."
The people of that time called him the Venerable Pārśva; he refined and analyzed the categories and differences among the various schools.

Although there were kingdoms and rulers, there was no time when the Saṃgha did not exist; dwelling in faith, he practiced that faith. He compiled the *Mahāvibhāṣā* in two hundred fascicles. Though there were states and sovereigns, there was never a time without the Sangha, for they dwelt in faith and practiced their faith.
This is called not being sycophantic; to call one's eloquence "sycophancy" is to say that the ruler of a state dwells in loyalty and good faith and practices respectful trustworthiness—
this is what is meant by not being sycophantic or flattering.
At first, the king did not believe in sin and merit.
While hunting, he saw two cowherd boys standing before a stūpa;
when he questioned them, they said:
The Buddha had prophesied that there would be a king here who would collect my *śarīra*.

As the Great King’s past planting of merit now accorded with this prophecy, his faith became profound and his reverence for the Buddha-dharma deepened. Both monastics and laypeople utilized [this teaching], and its great achievement brought clarity and submission to the people of the Western lands; both clergy and laity studied this treatise. In recent times, King Śīlāditya was his equal. King Śīlāditya was the King of Magadha during the early Tang period.
In the eras of the Zhou and Qin,
the true source was distantly shrouded and the divine stream was long obstructed.
The rulers acted contrary to the Way,
and at court no men of virtue were promoted.
Laozi and Confucius met with misfortune during the eras of the Zhou and Qin dynasties.

Although Confucius and Laozi were great sages, neither was employed; Shang Yang and Li Si exercised their cruelty, both being officials of violent and harsh character who likewise did not meet their deaths with dignity. Because the followers of Śākyamuni are cautious regarding their difficulties, they do not fall into such extremes. This is why Buddhism had not yet reached [this land].
He understood the hardships of the violent Qin dynasty;
yet, transformation occurs in its own time and cannot be forced. Moreover, the Han succeeded to the decline of the Qin and seized the empire while mounted on horseback.

It was by relying on the strength of heroes that the imperial enterprise was accomplished; the High Ancestor of Han relied upon a three-foot sword to seize the empire. Thus, when merit was being deliberated, they all drew their swords and spoke in secret.

The High Ancestor was distressed by this. In the fifth year of the Han, after the battle at Gaixia, when he was about to confer fiefs for meritorious services, the various generals vied with one another to draw their swords and spoke in secret conspiracies.
The High Ancestor [dealt with] Yong Chi...
In the past, [Gaozu] had harbored a grudge against those who had shot at him;

he first bestowed titles upon them so that the various generals would know his expectations were settled. It was for this reason that Shusun Tong summoned the scholars of Lu to establish the rituals for court assemblies.
Beholding the imperial carriage,
the hundred officials were all struck with awe and trepidation;
thus he suppressed the evils of the time.

By honoring the majestic demeanor of the Ten-Thousand-Wagon Sovereign, one thereby honors the Son of Heaven while suppressing the feudal lords; thus, the Grand Emperor returned the bow to his high-great-grandfather, and the Household Steward received the imperial gift.
He proclaimed his own hegemonic achievements and bequeathed his plans to his descendants;
such was the legacy of the Emperors and Kings.

It has never been heard of that one would show reverence to a teacher by lowering their own status through ritual courtesy. Previously, during the Former Han, figures such as Shusun Tong merely codified Han rituals;

they did not demonstrate the practice of honoring the teacher and valuing the Way by humbling themselves as subjects. Now, the Yellow Emperor sought the Way from Guangcheng, and Xuanyuan (the Yellow Emperor) likewise sought the Way from Guangchengzi. King Yao followed the wind to Mount Juci, and King Yao performed the rites for the Master of Juci—both accounts appear in the *Zhuangzi*. Is this not indeed the conduct of the most exalted?
By the time the House of Han rose again,

Emperor Zhuangping— whose personal name was Zhuangping and whose posthumous title was Ming (the "Brilliant")— the second sovereign of the Later Han, received [the foreign monks] as guests at the Court of State Ceremonial (Dahonglu) and placed them under the supervision of the Minister of Rites (Dazongbo).
It was from the Western Regions that Mātanga and others arrived.

Some were stationed at the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Si), while others were presided over by the Minister of Rites (Zongbo). Thus, Zhi Qian and An Qing— Zhi Qian was a lay follower (upāsaka) from the country of Yuezhi,
whose courtesy name was Gongming.
In the late Han dynasty, Wei traveled to Luoyang,
where he studied under Zhi Liang; Liang,
in turn, had been taught by Zhi Chen.
The world proclaims that no one possesses such vast knowledge as the Three Masters.
An Qing, whose courtesy name was Shigao,
was a prince of the kingdom of Parthia (Anxi).
Yanliu Jushi yielded his position to enter the monastic order; he arrived here during the first year of the Yuanjia era of Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty.
His virtue was esteemed by the ranks of the clergy, yet he had not yet been taken as a teacher or friend by kings or lords.
Although the King of Chu maintained the ancestral sacrifices of the benevolent and sagely, [he did not honor him].
Emperor Xiaohuan of the Han dynasty promoted sacrifices involving the *huagai* canopy;

these were merely for the spirits of the various Han princes and did not yet seek those who worshipped at benevolent shrines (*rensi*) or used the *huagai*. He simply solemnized their ritual implements. Wei followed the rites of Han and recruited those with extraordinary inclinations for use.
Since I am occupied solely with the anxieties of serving the King during this era of the Three Kingdoms,
how could I find leisure for a benevolent shrine? This was Wei Cao Cao,
whose courtesy name was Mengde.
He served as Chancellor of Han;
because the House of Han was weak,
he used the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords.
However, as they were preoccupied with schemes to divide the realm, they had no leisure to honor and promote our teaching.

Although they were unable to propagate its spirit, they nonetheless did not ultimately obscure its Way. Furthermore, during the early period of the Three Kingdoms, the Tripiṭaka masters Kang Sengyi and Tan Di arrived and translated [the scriptures].
The people of Wu did not yet place much faith in it.
The Indian śramaṇa Kang Senghui first arrived in Wu and established a center for practicing the Way.
Sun Quan, whose courtesy name was Zhongmou and who resided in Jinling, considered this to be a deceptive fabrication that deviated from local customs.
"Shè ràng" (攝讓) means "to constrain and reproach.
"Ràng" (讓) means "to reprove.
It refers to constraining the śramaṇas and reproaching them, saying: "What spiritual power does the Buddha possess that you alone have changed your appearance?"
Hui said: "Although the Buddha's body has passed away,
his remaining relics, the śarīras, manifest without fixed direction."
The kings of foreign lands previously erected eighty-four thousand stupas to manifest their remaining influence.

"Kuan" means to deceive; "zhai" (pronounced *dài*) refers to deceitful speech. [The king] caused them to await the śarīra relics, strictly enforcing the rules and delaying the punishment until the twenty-first day.
As the assembly was about to perish,
the śarīra finally descended;

He arrived in the first year of Dàkāng (290 CE), starting from the era of Chìwū.
At the end of Tiānjǐ, when Sun Hào surrendered, he passed away without having celebrated the Lă sacrifice; this was in the fourth year of Chìwū, the Xiṇyǒu year.
Arriving in Wu, he reached the fourth year of the Tianji era, the gengzi year, when Sun Hao surrendered; thus he had been there for thirty-nine years. In the winter, he died in Wu.

At the beginning he rose with the state, and at the end he perished with the state—this "jin" means total destruction. he was a Xiongnu of the Mo-dun lineage from Xinzhong.

During the reigns of six emperors over forty-four years, Shi Le and Shi Hu possessed both military might and vast numbers;
they resisted violence and cultivated virtue.
They were slaughtered like grass and trees;
those among the śramaṇas who met their deaths were exceedingly numerous.
Fotucheng lamented for them, saying:
For what offense was that man’s life not spared?
Because [Fu] Le brought forth Guo Heilüe to manifest his divine wonders and provide him with military stratagems.

Fotucheng reported the matter to Shi Le.
Le summoned him with joy and questioned him;
Fotucheng knew that Le did not comprehend the profound principles.
He replied, "The Ultimate Way, though distant, can also be verified in the near term. Thereupon,
he filled his alms bowl with water, burned incense, and recited incantations over it.
In an instant, blue lotuses sprang forth.
Fu Le, moved by their divine sanctity,
bowed his head toward the wind [in salutation].
With an open mind, he accepted admonitions;
moved by compassion for those suffering in the mire and fire,
his thoughts were such that he could not even conceive of Shi Le, who had initially been a bandit alongside Wang Yang and Zhi Xiong.
He committed many acts of slaughter.

was the nephew of Shi Le.
In their martial prowess, they resist all who oppose them, leaving few of the men and women alive.

Thus we know that longevity or brevity of life depends on the Sage and not on the Lord of Fate.

This is not something that even the Lord of Fate can determine. Cheng listened to the sound of the bells while simultaneously observing the oil in his palms;
he entrusted his keen intelligence to his ears and eyes.
In reality, his empty illumination resided within his mind;
thus, what he said never failed to correspond with the facts. Whenever Fo Tucheng foresaw that Shi Hu was about to suffer defeat, he would use oil to coat his palms and manifest light.
Furthermore, Guo Jinglue used this to demonstrate it to him;
he employed the sound of a bell and focused his mind on the Prajñāpāramitā.

What has been proclaimed will surely correspond to reality. Shi Le died, and Shi Hu usurped the false title.

consequently, he personally increased his own diligent devotion toward Fotudeng and issued an edict stating:

he does not accept honors or titles,

If rank and emolument were not esteemed,
by what means could virtue be distinguished?
From this point forward...
He should be clothed in brocade and silk,
and mounted upon an ornate palanquin on the days of court assemblies.
When the Upādhyāya ascended the hall,

while the Crown Prince and various dukes supported and escorted him from the sides.
When the presiding master announces "The Great Preceptor," the entire assembly rises from their seats to manifest his honor.
He further commanded the Minister of Works, Li Nong,
to personally inquire after him morning and evening;
meanwhile, the Crown Prince and the various princes were required to pay their respects every five days.
This expresses my reverence.
When the Jin army marched out to the Huai and Fei rivers— the Huai River originates at Mount Tongbai,
and the Fei River is located in Lujiang— at that time, the capital of the Jin was Jinling.

In the monastery of Kaśmīra, offerings were constantly made.

Though he has passed away, it is as if he still exists;

This means reform. Although one may establish temples and strictly venerate the Buddha-dharma, if the penal laws are cruel and excessive, it will ultimately be of no benefit.
