Since the mandate of Heaven has not yet been altered, it is difficult to plot [a change].
The gentleman also considers that to privately protect and support his own dynasty is, in truth, to act in accordance with propriety.
Therefore, he expresses both points in a single statement.
Fu wrote in his letter: "The 'solitary man' refers to Zhou;
thus he raised a host of one million.
Fu Rong was appointed to govern the vanguard army."
When the Jin army feigned retreat and their drums had not yet sounded in formation, the Qin forces were utterly shattered.
Fu Jian had mobilized eight hundred and seventy thousand cavalry and infantry from Chang’an;
for a distance of a thousand li from front to rear, their banners and drums could be seen facing one another.
The forces extended ten thousand *li* from east to west, advancing by both land and water.
Fu Rong served as their general.
Jin’s Xie Xuan and others countered them with seventy thousand naval troops.
Wang Daozi sought assistance from the spirit of Mount Zhongshan by means of martial music.
When Shi Jian arrived at Shouchun,
he ascended the city wall and beheld him from afar.
The grasses and trees on Mount Baga all took on human forms; [Fu] Rong drew up his army in formation at the Fei River.
The Jin forces were unable to cross.
He dispatched an envoy to say to Rong:
Your Lordship has led your army deep into enemy territory and drawn up your forces along the river.
This is a strategy for a protracted siege;
do you not intend to engage in battle?
If the Master were to withdraw slightly and command the officers and soldiers to maneuver,
while I and the gentlemen rode with relaxed reins to observe them,
would that not be excellent?
Rong signaled his troops to retreat and withdraw from the formation;
the army then fled in disarray,
and he could not restrain them.
Rong galloped his horse to raid the enemy lines, but his mount fell and he was killed by the troops.
Subsequently, after the defeat at Yan-jian, Murong Chong raised an army and attacked Chang’an.

Tú Mùchuí returned to Yecheng and established the Later Yan; as for Liǎng, it was restored to Liǎng by Lǐ Gǎo, who was originally a general under Zhāng Guǐ, and later established the Western Liǎng in Dūnhuáng.
Lü Guang proclaimed himself the ruler of Later Liang in Guzang, while Qin occupied the region of Qin. Yao Chang dispatched a general to besiege Fu Jian at Mount Wujiang;
he was captured and strangled at a Buddhist temple in Xingping.

He established himself as the ruler of Later Qin. Previously, when Master Shi (Dao’an) had passed away, Yao Jian stood by his side and wailed with such profound grief that he said: "I am still not yet across [the river of suffering].
He lamented: "I am still not yet across."
"Master Dao'an has abandoned me and departed.
How could his words possibly be mistaken?
At first, Master Dao'an said to Wang Zinian:
"The ways of the world are such as these; why not go? Why indeed should you not? Nian replied, "You may go ahead;
I shall merely settle my remaining debts."
One year later, he brought harm to Yao Chang. Wang Jia,
whose courtesy name was Zinian,
was a native of Luoyang.
His physical appearance was humble and coarse, as if he were deficient;
he delighted in jesting and did not eat the five grains.
When asked about good or evil, he would respond.
The response should have been like a playful jest;
however, as the matter was excessively scrutinized, Dao’an replied: "I say."
A small debt remained unpaid,
so they could not depart together.
Subsequently, Yao Chang captured Chang’an.
He held out against Fu Deng for a very long time.
Chang asked him,
"Will Your Majesty be able to prevail?"
The answer was:
"Briefly obtained.
Chang said:
One should say that it is attained;
what abbreviation could there be?
Because one cuts it down.
After Chang died,
his son Xing then killed Deng.
Xing’s courtesy name was Zilüe.

This is precisely what Jia [Zhi] meant by "briefly grasping the essential meaning. When Fatai went to Jingzhou to pay his respects to Huan Wen, Wen—relying on the weight of his prestige and reputation—was not prompt in receiving him as a guest.
Fatai grew anxious at his hesitation.
Suddenly, he told his usher, "I am ill; withdraw at once.
On another day, Daotai arrived at Wenshui.
He did not wait for his sandals to be brought before proceeding forward. Fatai was a native of Dongxian.
In his youth, he studied together with Dao’an; although his talent and eloquence were inferior to Dao’an’s, [he was nonetheless distinguished].
Yet his physical appearance surpassed that of [An Shigao]. Once An had been captured by the Qin, his disciples each fled in different directions.
Huìyuǎn, intending initially to reach Mount Luófú near the South Sea, arrived at Xúnyáng in Jāngzhōu; there he divined a site on Mount Lú and settled to dwell there.
Having already obtained decaying soil from which springs had gushed forth, he did not seek to leave.

Huiyong and Dao’an were both disciples of [Dharma Master] Huichi; they invited him to stay at Xilin Temple on Mount Lu. Later, the Regional Inspector Huan Yi—a subject of the Eastern Jin—established Donglin Temple separately.
Previously, Tao Khun governed Guangzhou. Tao Khun,
courtesy name Shiheng,
was initially fond of learning and welcomed guests and companions.
When a guest arrived at his home, he was so poor that his mother cut her hair and sold it to provide for the hospitality.

Later, he became the Regional Commander (Dudu) of the Eight Provinces and obtained an image of King Aśoka—the very image created by King Aśoka himself—and sent it to Hanxi Temple in Wuchang (Wuchang being Ezhou). When the temple was completed, Huiyuan requested the image from afar.
He then descended from the void.

At that time, among the gentry and scholars who were disdainful of the world and longing for the seclusion of Mount Kao—such as those of the lineage of Zong Bing, Lei Cizong, Liu Yimin, Zhou Xuzhi, and Zhang Jishuo, as well as Zong Bing of Nanyang, Zhang Caimin, and Zhang Jishuo—[he appeared].
Liu Yimin of Pengcheng,
Lei Cizong of Yuzhang,
and Zhou Xuzhi of Yanmen.

Bi Yingzhi of Xincai, along with the monks Huichi and Huiyong, together established the Lotus Society. In total, over a hundred men of great name and virtue all joined and supported one another. In his youth, Huiyuan had studied alongside Huichi as a common scholar, specializing in the learning of the Six Classics.
Ritual, music, and the teachings of named institutions serve specifically as the legal standards for both the court and the common realm.
Wang Xun wrote a letter to Fan Ning; Wang Xun served as the Secretary to Huan Wen, while Fan Ning authored a commentary on the *Guliang Zhuan*. It says:
"Between Master Hui-chi and Master Hui-yuan, who was superior? 'Shu' means 'who'; 'yu' means 'superior,' that is, more excellent.
Master Fan further remarked, "Truly they were virtuous brothers; Hui-chi and Hui-yuan were indeed secular brothers. Wang Chong said: [End of quote].
To find even those who are like brothers is truly not easy;
how much less so those who are virtuous.
When Yao Xing first completed the translation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Zhilun*.
It is also called the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
It was composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna at the earnest invitation of [Emperor] Wu, who personally commissioned him from afar to write its preface.
Its exceptional esteem is thus beyond compare.
Huan Xuan campaigned against Yin Zhongkan. Huan Xuan’s courtesy name was Jingdao;
he was the son of Grand Marshal (Dasisima) Huan Wen.
He served as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Jiangzhou.
In the second year of the Yuanshuai era, Liu Yu raised an army to usurp the Jin Emperor An.
Consequently, Huan Xuan marched against Zhongkan and summoned Huiyuan to leave Mount Lu for the Tiger Brook (Huxi).
Huiyuan feigned illness.
Huida entered the mountains himself.
His attendants said:
Formerly, Yin Zhongkan was respectful toward Yuan;
[Huiyuan] wished for the Duke not to revere him,
but [Yin] said, "How can such a principle exist?"
Zhongkan was originally a dead man.
Upon seeing Huisu, he reverted to his former agreement; Huisu was the one who had spoken first.
Zhongkan had initially said he would not pay him homage, but as soon as he saw Huisu, he did so. As he left the mountain, he said to those around him:
Truly, this was something I had never seen before in my life.
Later, when Xuanyu wished to purge the ecclesiastical officials, he said:
"Mount Lu is the dwelling place of those who possess the Way and its Virtue."
This does not fall under the category of searching through records; it refers to the initial period when Emperor Cheng was still an infant and Yu Bing was assisting in the administration.
(The personal name of Emperor Cheng of Jin was Yan.)
He was the eldest son of Emperor Ming.
While Empress Dowager Yu was acting as regent and governing the court,
during the period when Zu Yue, Su Jun, and the Yu clan held exclusive power, [Huiyuan] maintained that śramaṇas should pay homage to the sovereign.
He Chong, Wang Mi, and others submitted refutations and debates,
the points of agreement and disagreement remaining unsettled. Later, Huan Xuan was at Guchu (Guchu being Dangtu County).
Formerly, the Song Emperor changed the name to Taiping Prefecture, desiring that [the monastics] pay full homage.
He sent a message to inquire about this,
to which Huiyuan replied with a letter and composed the "Five Treatises on Why Śramaṇas Do Not Pay Homage to Kings."

The memorial refuting perverse arguments, along with the treatise, is both contained in the Hongming ji (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism). Emperor An was forced by Huan Xuan to abdicate in favor of the Prince of Nanjun.
Emperor An’s posthumous name was Dezong;
he was the son of Emperor Xiaowu.
With Wang Daozi of the Kuaiji Commandery serving as Grand Tutor (Taifu) to assume the regency,
Wang Gong, the Inspector of Yanzhou, rebelled along with Huan Xuan and moved the Emperor to Xunyang.
Xuan then usurped the throne for two years.
Liu Yu executed him, and Xuan died.
The Imperial Carriage successfully reclaimed the ancient capital.
Previously, when He Wujī had urged Xie Lingyun to welcome [the Emperor], Lingyun served as a Shizhong (Attendant-in-Ordinary) but distanced himself by claiming illness and failing to go.
The Emperor’s gracious decree inquired after his well-being;
Lingyun sent a letter in thanks, to which the Emperor replied with a decree expressing his admiration and regret that he was unable to meet him in person.
He carried [the scriptures] to Jingluo.
When the people of Jingluo heard of his reputation, they flocked to him in admiration;
thus Huichi entered Shu and resided at the Rear Rock Monastery in Zheng County. During the period of the illegitimate state of Shu, Daofu, the son of Qiao Zong, [ruled].

There was an especially cruel and rebellious general who, having returned from a military campaign he had undertaken to suppress a rebellion, arrived at Gai Foding Temple in Zhongzhou County. The monks of the temple saw the man and his horse covered in blood from afar; terrified that they were warriors, they fled in all directions. [The general] took hold of them before the gate and began to wash himself.
His countenance remained serene and composed.
As his merit had reached its fulfillment,
he continued to snap his fingers and strain water without ceasing.
Fuxie emerged dripping with sweat and said to his officers,
"A great man is indeed different from the common crowd."
The gentleman said:
"Jin has lost the Central Plains;
it now lies between the states along the Yangtze River."
The gentry and officials fled the chaos of the Five Hu;
the Five Hu were: Former Zhao (Liu Yuanhai) and Later Zhao (Shi Le).
The Tuoba clan of the Later Wei,
the Fu clan of the Former Qin,
and the Yao clan of the Later Qin all migrated southward.
The state has adopted a strategy of northern expedition; furthermore,
out of admiration for their courage and valor,
it has brought forth its eminent and wise men.
Both the clergy and the laity dwell their minds beyond the external world;
like the cry of the phoenix and the flight of the crane, they regard ritual vessels and ceremonial robes as things cast aside. "Dwelling" (zhai) refers to their abode.
It is also a matter of things.
Those of noble character, beholding the decline of the world,
dwell their minds beyond material objects.
They let loose the spirit of the phoenix and crane, concealing themselves by the side of forests and springs;
indeed, they pay no heed to rites and music. Thus, Cheng, An, Lin, and Yuan composed these rhyming couplets in response.

All his words and expressions were profound and deep, possessing both systematic order and ethical significance; though they proclaimed a spirit beyond the mundane realm, they mostly contained strategic insights for statecraft.
Thus, when he first spoke of initiating an undertaking, it was necessarily regarded with great trust and weight by the world. When Lü Guang entered Kucha, he captured Kumārajīva.
He knelt his head down so that [Kumārajīva] could sit astride him on a camel, yet Kumārajīva showed no sign of resentment.

Lü Guang regarded him as a uniquely extraordinary vessel and did not dare to treat him with familiarity or contempt. Later, upon the command of Fu Jian, Lü Guang led an army to invade Kucha in search of Kumārajīva.
Having captured him, they did not treat him with great severity;
instead, they forcibly took the daughter of the King of Kucha as his wife and compelled him to ride a vicious horse at full gallop.
Kumārajīva showed no sign of anger.
Upon his return, he advised [the ruler] to move the camp; as it turned out, heavy rains caused the waters to rise.
Because of this, Yao Guang treated him with exceptional courtesy and respect. When the army returned to Liang, they heard of the defeat of the Qin.
He then usurped that territory and changed the standards of vehicles and scripts.
When Lü Guang returned from his campaign against Kucha, he brought back more than twenty thousand camels, ten thousand fine horses, and over a thousand treasures upon his arrival at Guzang.
Hearing that Fu Jian had already been defeated in battle,
he styled himself the Governor of Liangzhou;
later, he usurped the throne and established the Later Liang dynasty.
In the fourteenth year, Yao Xing dispatched generals to campaign against Liang to seek for Kumārajīva.
When Liang fell, he was brought to Guanzhong,
where scholars from all quarters gathered in great numbers at the court of Qin.
He plotted to perpetuate his lineage through a woman of noble family. Yao Xing, admiring his intelligence and brilliance, pressured him with palace women to seek his offspring;
the pure practitioner was ashamed even to hear of such matters.
Now, the tortoise of Song was auspicious and received its shell;
the man of Jing was discerning yet suffered the amputation of his foot. The Lord of Yuan in Song dreamed of a man with disheveled hair who addressed him, saying:
I said, "The messenger from Qingjiang, the fisherman Boyu, will likely obtain me.
When King Yuan summoned him and questioned him, he replied,
"I obtained a tortoise and then carved it open."
This was because when he divined seventy-two times, there was no error in his augury.
Furthermore, Bian He obtained a stone at Mount Jing;
having discerned that it contained jade, he presented it to the King of Chu.
The king did not recognize them and cut off both their feet;
it was only after the third offering that he distinguished them.
In all these cases, they underwent mutilation by means of their spiritual wisdom.
If Kumārajīva violated the precepts despite his brilliance,
was it not because there are limits to wisdom and constraints upon one's power? Therefore,
he followed the principle of "adding to increase" with the principle of "subtracting to diminish."
Do not practice it with delusion.
Emperor Xiaowen of the Wei dynasty issued an edict seeking Kumārajīva;
his courtesy name was Hongxian.
The eldest son of Emperor Wen,
he received the abdication from his father at the age of five and moved the capital to Luoyang.
He changed his surname to Yuan.
He reigned for twenty-nine years.
Benevolent and filial, he was refinedly fond of the teachings of Huang-Lao.
He was especially proficient in explaining the meanings [of the scriptures], and later he was granted a stipend for his service.

Although my teaching has been overturned and I have fallen into great deception and injustice, according to the principles of the *Chunqiu*, those who have performed meritorious deeds may have their offenses pardoned for ten generations. The *Chunqiu* states that merit can pardon the sins of ten generations. Previously, when Kumārajīva was in a foreign land, he encountered a sage.
He told him, "Be careful not to go to the eastern lands;
there will be great misfortune for you."
Sengqishi then came forward regardless;
was this not because a good minister dies for the sake of the state’s plan,
and a loyal official dies for the sake of lofty righteousness?
"A benevolent person dies having fulfilled their benevolence;

what is there to look back upon? To propagate the Great Teaching, one must not be bound by minor details. Thus he firmly upheld the Dharma-gate, and even today we receive the benefits of the flourishing of the teachings, which is due to the efforts of Kumārajīva. Therefore, when Kumārajīva died...
He burned them, yet his heart and tongue were not scorched.
When Sengdao was ten years old, he followed a teacher to receive the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra. He asked:
"How many fascicles does this sutra have?
The Master wished to test him,
so he replied, "There is only one fascicle."
The Guide said:
Since it first states, "At that time,
Akṣayamati," one knows that there must have already been events prior to that point.
The Master marveled at him; though he lived in poverty and lacked the means for firewood or fodder, he studied in the evening until his studies were completed.
Yao Xing admired his virtue and visited the monastery to pay his respects.
They returned to the palace together in the same carriage.

Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty was pleased with his virtue and established Dongshan Temple for him in Shouchun. When Liu Yu, the founder of the Song, captured the Later Qin and brought the monk Dao back to Jinling, there was the monk Tanxi during the late Eastern Jin under Emperor Xiaowu; when Emperor Fu Jian’s army arrived, Xie Xuan defeated them, and [Tanxi] subsequently went to Liaodong.
This was the beginning of the propagation [of the Dharma] in Goryeo.
Later, he returned to the Three Prefectures (Sānfǔ); the Three Prefectures refers here to Xiānyáng County.
Formerly, the First Emperor of Qin established a palace there, and the people of the Three Prefectures revered and looked up to it.
When Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty defeated Yao Hong,
he left his son Yizhen to garrison Chang’an.
Helian Chuju— Helian Bobo— pursued and defeated him.
Monastics and laypeople, young and old alike, were all caught in the slaughter.
At first, when he encountered the blades, he was not wounded;
though they bent their bodies to strike him with the swords they wore at their waists, they were unable to harm him.
He then prostrated himself in fear and apologized for his transgressions.

When Emperor Shizu of the Wei dynasty captured Helian Chang—the son of Helian Bobo—who had been defeated by the Later Wei, he received Shi with exceptional honor. Once the Dharma was extinguished, [Shi]...

The profound influence [of the Dharma] was severed and extinguished; those clad in crimson robes were nearly annihilated—"crimson" (*zhe*) referring to red garments, for the color *kāṇḍa* (red ochre) had begun to close off their forms within secluded and obstructed places.

This was not because they were subject to cruel decrees, but because they had retreated their traces into mountain valleys. Like great birds soaring into the vast void and looking down from the heights toward the horizon, they could not be caught by nets—*wei* meaning a net. Later, he realized that the Great Dharma was about to flourish.
On the first day of the first month, the Son of Heaven "treads the beginning"; this refers to the dawn of the first month.
He treads the beginning at its start and establishes the standard through the midpoint.
The accumulated surplus is returned at the end.
Those who construct the calendar take the beginning of the step as their starting point;
when the lunar nodes reach the midpoint of the seasonal energy (zhongqi), it constitutes that month’s two hundred and fifty-four days.
There remain eleven days and twenty-five *fen*.
Accumulating thirty-two days constitutes one intercalary month. "Ting" (廷) means reality; "shi" (實) means fullness;
"lü" (旅) means multitude.
This refers to the fact that on the first day of the year, the offerings presented to the court were filled with [the Emperor's] robes;
when these were carried to the national gate, it was intended as an omen of change.
When the Wei ruler heard of this, he was enraged.
He commanded his officers to hasten the execution;
yet the flesh could not admit the blade,
for as he drew his sword upon it, the wound was no more than a mere thread.
He caused [the tiger] to be cast into its cage.
The tiger retreated and lay in wait; it was you.
"Pi" (辟) means punishment.
To leave such a state of affairs as it is at its conclusion—what can be done?

I summoned him to the palace to examine in detail the causes of its rise and fall, and subsequently inquired about the principles for ensuring the longevity of the national destiny. Thereupon, he bolted the gates of heterodoxy and cleared away the obstructions on the path.
Tao Tao was moved to sorrowful realization. (Note: "Tao" is the taboo name of Emperor Taiwu of the Later Wei dynasty.
Initially, he did not believe in the Buddhist teachings and had monks buried alive and Buddha images destroyed.
Having encountered the conversion of Tan-shi, he later repented his errors.

He led a southern campaign for the Song dynasty, during which he slaughtered the innocent; he held office for twenty-nine years. Senglang of Mount Tai was a person whom neither ordinary nor sage men could fathom.
The six sovereigns of Jin, Wei, Yan, Qin, and so forth, issued imperial edicts inquiring after what they might provide by way of diplomatic gifts;
these were all the most extraordinary and rare treasures and goods of the world.
Though pearls and gems have no legs to reach others and people have no minds to seek them out, [they arrived nonetheless].
Yet, because it is summoned by virtue, there is nowhere so distant that it does not reach. The Perfected Person originally has no mind to seek pearls and jade;
the pearls and jade likewise have no shins or feet to walk.
It is simply that when the Way and its Virtue manifest their resonance, nothing remains far away that does not arrive. Thus, virtue causes one's reputation to become manifest.
Fame is made firm by virtue;
when fame and virtue correspond in reality, it endures forever.
Thus, today, the sacred traces at Jinyu Valley remain undimmed. At Shentong Temple on Mount Tai in Qizhou:
The Southern Yan ruler, Murong De, established this for the Chan Master Senglang and provided it with the inhabitants of three counties.
Its long corridors extend for more than a hundred paces.
On three occasions, when temples were being abolished and destroyed,
those who dared to violate [the Master's will] would suddenly see Lang’s own body appear and strike them with his monk’s staff until they were on the verge of death;
they would then beg for mercy as before.
There was a well;
when a woman approached it, it immediately dried up.
She burned incense and performed repentance, seeking its restoration, and it returned to its former state.
It was established four hundred years ago, and to this day, the Buddha images remain as vivid as if newly made.
The assembly has not trodden upon them; they remain solemn and intact even now. Both Xiqin and Beiliang were minor states. Xiqin was occupied by Qifu Guoren in the Hexi region.
Juqu Mengxun of Northern Liang held Guzang and looked toward the sages and worthies.
It was there that Dharmakṣema, Fajin, and Daolang translated, compiled, and authored [their works];
thus, his kingdom was no small one.
Therefore, the Book of Chu says:
"The state of Chu has nothing to regard as its treasure;
it regards only goodness as its treasure."
Were it not so, how could he have distanced himself from the five phases, abandoned the wilderness, and suddenly established a shrine to build for himself a grand enterprise in a single region?
Huiyue of the Liang dynasty had already displayed an air of maturity even before he reached the age of study.
The people of Shan sang a ballad:
"Liu the Layman has attained the subtle principle. Once he had entered the Way, [he became known as] Master Lou.
Xuande was delighted by these reports.
He appointed [the monk] Sheng as National Preceptor and issued an edict designating his former residence as Bensheng Temple.
The village where he resided was known as Zhizhe Li (Village of the Wise).
During the Northern Qi dynasty, Fashang lived at a time when Gao Huan received the abdication of the Eastern Wei and established his capital at Ye, calling it the Northern Qi.
When he was destroyed by the Later Zhou dynasty, Sengzhao had his hair tied in two tufts;
yet he stood out with a dignified presence as a vessel of virtue, dedicating himself to earnest cultivation and noble conduct.
He thoroughly investigated the profound and subtle mysteries;
people of the time regarded him as a holy śrāmaṇera,
though his physical appearance was not handsome.
A proverb says: "If a village śrāmaṇera comes to a high seat, he will encounter calamity.
Emperor Wenxuan invited him to serve as his preceptor for the precepts.
He covered his face and disheveled his hair to allow [the enemy] to tread upon him;
thus, the reverence due to one who has surrendered was fully exhausted.
He protected the Middle Kingdom by establishing ten administrative divisions.
The above constitutes the "Grand Standard" (dàtǒng). The character for "descend" (jiàng) is pronounced as gǔnì (古𮎙).
This means that one lowers the dignity of a sovereign or parent to practice the reverence due to a teacher or master. — Wenxuan.
His taboo name was Yang,
his courtesy name was Zijin,
and he was the third son of Gao Huan.
At that time, there was the chaos caused by Erzhu Rong;
everyone was distressed by the cold and hunger.
The Emperor had only been born for several months.
Suddenly, he said with a joyful expression, "I have been saved!
Upon ascending the throne, his divine prowess was preeminent;
yet by the end of his reign, his cruelty and executions were beyond description.
He passed away at the age of thirty-six. Sui Lingzang was a friend of the High Ancestor during his period of concealment;
the Sui High Ancestor’s surname was Yang and his given name was Jian.
He was born in the seventh year of the Dàtóng era of the Northern Zhou dynasty.
Purple vapors filled the courtyard of Bānruò Monastery in Fēngyǐ.
He inherited the title of Duke of Suí.
Zhou Wu was betrothed to the eldest daughter of the Emperor while he was still the Crown Prince.
Upon the demise of Emperor Xuan,
Liu Fang and others supported the Emperor as he served as Chancellor.
When the Emperor passed away, he received the abdication from the Zhou and reigned for twelve years.
Qianlong was a close friend of Yu Cang; once he had ascended the throne, he redoubled his former intimacy.
He issued an edict that the palace gatekeepers were not to forbid them entry whenever they wished to enter.
He did the same when leaving;
when sitting, they shared the same couch,
and when traveling, they shared the same carriage.
He said: "The disciple is a 'Son of Heaven' among worldly people;
the Vinaya Master is a 'Son of Heaven' among those who have left the world.
Now, I say that the words of the Emperor are excessive."

When Your Majesty speaks, it is recorded; how can one treat this with levity? Those whom Your Majesty’s attendants recommend must necessarily be recorded. The Left Scribe records words, and the Right Scribe records deeds. If one loves others without losing their sense of righteousness, then that love will extend far.
In that year, there was a severe drought; they performed the *yu* rain-praying rituals, yet it did not rain. The people were distressed, lamenting that it would not be a bountiful year.
The Emperor [said], "In listening to the spirits, one should not act as if listening to a sage."
Thereupon, he invited Fayan to the Daxing Hall;
ascending the imperial throne and facing south, Fayan transmitted the precepts,
while the Emperor commanded the ministers of state to take their seats facing north and receive them on their knees.
It did not take more than a brief morning for it to rain;
both clothing and food came from the imperial palace,
transmitted directly from the Emperor’s own hands.
He was subsequently promoted to the rank of *pingdeng* śramaṇa.
Regarding those who had committed offenses, he would first hear the testimony of both parties;
only then would he weep and administer punishment.
Mourningfully respecting the penal codes and expanding upon the compassionate punishments of Great Yu was Tan Yan.
His surname was Wang;
he was a native of Sangquan in Puzhou.
From childhood he was exceptionally intelligent. While still a śrāmaṇera,
there was a layman named Bi who showed him four characters written down.
"Squareness, roundness, motion, and stillness—let him embody these.
Yan responded with a voice that said:
"Squareness is like the city of Vaipulya."
Yuanruo Zhihui said: "When it moves, it resembles the waves of consciousness;
when it is still, it is akin to the chamber of nirvana."
Huì was struck with alarm.
Later, he composed fifteen fascicles of a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
He offered prayers before the Śarīra stupa.
The "Emitting Light" (Fàngguāng) refers to the night candle. Once, the Emperor wished to test the capacity and character of the śramaṇas;
he summoned a vast assembly of those who could whistle and chant in the palace courtyard and issued orders to his armored guards and tiger-clad attendants to maintain strict discipline.
He brandished his sword and pursued him,
but Jingtuo’s every step was as leisurely and unhurried as he retreated with measured grace.
The Emperor praised his profound and far-reaching character, commanding him to ascend the palace hall and bestowing upon him religious articles and monastic robes to honor his extraordinary nature.
The eminent monk Jingtuo constantly carried his mother while pursuing his studies; he was skilled in large-scale calligraphy.
His brush was as long as his arm, measuring three chi;
when he wrote a single character on a square-foot screen, it was not at all refined or neat.
Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty commanded him to ascend the hall and bestowed upon him a large bamboo fan three chi wide, ordering him to hold and use it immediately.
He was also granted tall wooden clogs with high soles and was permitted to wear them while leaving the palace.
The Emperor personally saw him off, saying:
"Truly, he is a paragon among monks. Observe how, during the Renshou and Kaihuang eras, the empire attained great stability.
This is also because his goodness was at its ultimate limit.
Yet, his wisdom did not plan for the long term, and his familial affection was not "zang" (proper/wholesome); "zang" here refers to goodness.
Familial affection refers to Emperor Yang, who inherited his father’s great enterprise but failed to cultivate virtuous conduct.
Deluded by the charms of women, they brought about their own ruin and downfall, ultimately causing the duration of their dynasties not to endure.
Therefore, my teaching holds that merit and wisdom constitute the two means of salvation;
if either is lacking, what more need be said? Thus, the three emperors of the Sui dynasty together ruled for thirty-eight years.
Now, those who performed the suburban sacrifice at Tang were granted ranks for their virtue and emoluments for their merit;
yet among the śramaṇas, there are those who have attained the rank and emoluments of high ministers and great officers.
In antiquity, one received a birth-name at birth and a courtesy-name upon capping;

for the deceased, there was the posthumous title (shì). Among śramaṇas, there are even those who receive posthumous titles equivalent to those of Marquises or Barons. When a son reaches twenty, he is capped and given a courtesy-name;
the courtesy-name is used to manifest his virtue.
Upon death, one’s name becomes excessive.
The people of Zhou used names to serve the spirits, and since the name would be used until the end of life, they were to be avoided thereafter;
therefore, they substituted them with posthumous titles (shì).
In ancient times, there were those who were granted purple robes and titles of "Master," but there were also those who were granted posthumous titles (*shih*).
For instance, Dinglan was granted the posthumous title Juexing—how tragic! Furthermore, the Qin people exiled Guṇabhadra to Mount Lu; *Bhadra* is translated here as "Juexian" (Awakened Virtue).
In a single day he could recite and master what it took others a month to do.
From Central India to the state of Qin,
his debates with Kumārajīva were filled with extraordinary spiritual wonders.
Accused of slandering the Sangha by Sengqie and others,
he was banished to Mount Lu,
where he translated over one hundred fascicles of scriptures.
He died at the age of seventy-one. Emperor Taiwu of the Wei dynasty summoned Tanyao to Pingcheng; Yao was born with divine and extraordinary qualities.
Later, when Tuoba Tao of the Later Wei usurped the throne at Pingcheng, Yao was on good terms with the Crown Prince, Huang.
Huang was slandered, and his father suspected Gao of complicity;
furthermore, because Cui Hao, Kou Qian, and others had slandered him to the Emperor,
the Emperor grew enraged, bound him, and put him to death.
When the light reached the monastery,
his disciples finally realized what had happened;
they then requested the corpse so that they might bury it.
Gao rose again and spoke fully of matters of fortune and misfortune before passing away.
This account appears in the *Liang shu*.
If one is not in their proper time, even sages and worthies may still suffer the cruelty of endangering their own lives.
How could it be merely a matter of weeping for the Qilin and grieving for the Feng?
Thus, although Emperor Wen of Han favored the worthy, Jia Yi was still exiled; though Emperor Wen was benevolent and sagely, [his subjects] still suffered.
Yet even the worthy and talented Jia Yi was exiled to Changsha and died there;
and although Wei Wu honored scholars, Kong Rong was put to death. Kong Rong.
His courtesy name was Wenju.
Wei Wu (Cao Cao) executed him.
Rong’s two sons were eight or nine years old.
As he was playing chess, he did not rise.
His attendants said, "Your father has been executed; why do you not rise?"
The two sons said,
"How could there be any eggs left intact beneath a overturned nest?"
Seeking them, they were both captured and died; was this not because the fate of one’s passage or obstruction is suspended upon the destiny of the times?
Once, while traveling through the vast wilderness—the wild outskirts—I encountered a fresh breeze wafting a fragrant scent.
He looked around in all directions and found several stalks of purple mushrooms at the edge of a withered thicket; however,
where the wild fire had reached, their stems and caps were damaged and incomplete.
I then plucked it to examine it—the character "plucked" being pronounced with the *hu* and *jie* rhymes—but found myself clumsy in its application.
At sunset, I placed it upon a stone and returned home.
On another day, I ascended the vermilion gate.
Beholding it within its jade casket,
draped with patterned embroidery—
how does this differ from what I previously beheld?
It is simply a matter of encountering or not encountering [the right conditions]. Alas! Among people’s relations with one another, how can there be anything that does not follow this principle?

6. Ultimate Transformation (III). Ultimate Transformation, Part Six: This clarifies that the Great Awakened One, through a mind of compassion and wisdom, carries out the ultimate transformation; the Great Sage maintains a reverent composure.
The myriad spirits act as his assistants;
his heart is set on manifesting for the benefit of others;
his merit lies in providing rectification and salvation.
He who brings light and residence to all under heaven transforms the devas and dragons as his attendants;
he is the honored teacher of Śakra and Brahmā.
He presides over the Three Realms while abiding in supreme dignity;
he governs the four modes of birth through simultaneous transformation.

At times he appears as a great minister, and at times as a human king; he manifests in the forms of high officials, minor kings, and so forth, down to the various artisans and the incense-seller who was the head of a vast kingdom.
He was named Utpala;
he was skilled in discerning all fragrances and also knew the methods for compounding all types of incense, such as those for burning, anointing, and powdered incense.
Furthermore, one knows its origin:
there is a fragrance named Elephant-Treasury (Gajagarbha) that is produced from the combat of nāgas.
If one burns a single pellet,
a great cloud of incense will arise, pervading the royal capital,
and for seven days it will rain fine fragrant rain.
The garments on their bodies and the towers they inhabit are all made of golden color.
On Mount Malaya there is sandalwood known as "ox-head incense" (*gośīrṣa*);
if one anoints the body with it, [the fragrance remains].
Even if one enters a pit of fire, the fire cannot burn them.
On the Snowy Mountains there is a fragrance named Aruṇa;
those sentient beings who smell it are freed from all defiled desires. There is a city in the south that serves as a ferryman for crossing the ocean.
Within the pavilion there was a boatman named Vaśira,
who was upon that sea.
Together with hundreds of thousands of merchants, he skillfully revealed the Dharma of the Buddha’s merits;
he delivered sentient beings from suffering and practiced asceticism at Mount Sundara in the city of Tuṣāra.
There was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Viśvāmitra who expounded all the worldly arts and crafts for others,
and was also able to subdue ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhists.

He caused Śariputra to abandon all views; meanwhile, the youth Viśvantara of the South was playing at building sandcastles with ten thousand other youths amidst the river islets of the country of Yaśas.

This youth thoroughly understands the names of all sentient beings, the names of all karmas, and the names of all truths; regarding that which is beneficial to the people, there is nothing he will not do.

Some appear dull and simple, yet they manifest simplicity; "dull" is the appearance of being dark and ignorant. Some appear discerning and sharp, yet they manifest wisdom; "discerning" is the appearance of clarity and penetration. Some appear bold and aggressive, yet they manifest courage; "bold" is the appearance of being stern and forceful. Some appear easygoing and harmonious, yet they manifest harmony; "easygoing" is the appearance of being peaceful and joyful. Thus, one cannot seek a single consistency among them.
One must not abandon one [aspect] in order to seek the other.
Therefore, there are times of inhalation and times of expansion;
times of manifestation and times of obscurity.
"Or sunken, or raised" refers to being gathered together.
"Opening up" means to spread out.
"Manifesting clearly" means to reveal.
Obscurity; a hollow depth; a lofty eminence. To gain it and yet lose it.
To follow them and yet contradict them—
how profound is their virtue, yet how changed are their traces!
How awakened is their outward manifestation, yet how distorted is their reflection!
Its resonance is lofty and its echo fills all space;
truly, its subtlety is beyond verification.
Therefore, through the True Way, one may cultivate the self.
The provisional path (upāya-mārga) can be used to govern and transform, whereas the true path (bhūta-mārga) fulfills the teaching.
Not seeking exclusive benefit for oneself is the provisional path; it is but half of the teaching.
It cannot be simultaneously governed and encompassed; the True Way may not be abandoned for even a moment.
Therefore, it remains unmixed and untainted: it does not increase in fruition, nor does it decrease in its causal basis.
It follows the constant flow without being submerged, for it gathers within the multitude without being different from them. Expedient means (*upāya*) cannot be established for long;
therefore, one abandons them to merge with the Way (*mārga*). Because expedient means are employed only temporarily, they cannot be established for long.
One must return to the eternal Way, and the True Way culminates therein. The upper instance of the character "zhōng" (culmination) signifies perfect circularity;
the lower instance of the character "zhōng" refers to the fruit of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, which is the ultimate point of completion.

The true path consists of the ten thousand practices of the six perfections, which can bring to full completion the fruits of the three great kalpas. Regarding the provisional path: the first "beginning" (shǐ) refers to the initial arousal of the bodhicitta;
the second "beginning" (shǐ) refers to the practices of the lesser sages, such as the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.

The Buddha opened this teaching of expedient means as the beginning for those first setting out on the path of entry. For example, although Devadatta committed the three heinous crimes, he ultimately received a prophecy of enlightenment.
Even the three heinous crimes have their retribution. In Sanskrit, he is called Devadatta.
This is known as Devadatta.
He was the son of King Droṇodana, the Buddha’s maternal cousin,
and was obtained through a request made to a celestial deity.
Therefore, he was constantly at enmity with the Buddha;
he struck the Buddha's foot with a stone,
wounding it and causing blood to flow from the Buddha's body.
To cause a schism in the Saṃgha and to kill a bhikṣuṇī—
these are the three immediate transgressions (ānantarya-karma).
Although he entered hell, he also received a prophecy at the assembly on Vulture Peak.
How could the retribution for the three grave offenses have been in vain? The holy prophecy clearly shows that he has returned to his original nature.
If Constantly Not Disparaging had prostrated to the fourfold assembly,
he would have truly violated the rules of propriety;
however, the kalpa of turbidity is difficult to transform.
Yet the Sage skillfully makes use of time;
entrusting his traces to manifest the rites of the *Lotus Sūtra*,
the Constantly-Not-Light Bodhisattva constantly paid homage to the fourfold assembly and thereby attained Buddhahood.
Regarding those who must be guided through skillful means according to the times:
because people of that era were largely characterized by negligence and arrogance, he transformed them by extensively practicing ritual reverence. This was King Udayana of the Western Regions.
He had been a close friend of Piṇḍola since their youth;
Piṇḍola’s family name was Bharadvāja,
and he resided on Mount Mālina.
King Aniruddha never rose when he encountered Piṇḍola.
His attendants requested that the King employ the methods of governance [to deal with him].
The King said,
"The matter is already concluded;
that which previously could not be resolved is now finished, and it requires my subsequent arrival."
On another day, when the king arrived at Piṇḍola’s dwelling,
the latter’s thought of desire did not arise;
he feared that the king might harm him and cause him to fall into hell.
He felt a desire to rise [in rank],
yet fearing it would diminish the King’s merit and cause him to lose his royal position,
he immediately restrained himself once more.
The gravity of losing his kingdom was not so great as his aversion to the improper path.
Qi rose; since he had risen, it was appropriate to follow him.
Thereupon, he stepped forward seven paces to meet the King.
The king was startled by his lack of constancy. Piṇḍola said,
"I previously foresaw that the king would lose his position."
"Now, because he intends to bring me harm, I have not been able to consider his plan.
The King asked,
"How much of my kingdom has he lost?"
He replied, "In seven days the state shall perish; it has already been seven years.
When the Northern Qi monk Chou saw that Wenxuan had no one to escort him, he escorted Wenxuan Gao Yang to Hedong.

Having reigned for ten years, Emperor Mimin died. At that time, Xie Zhen concurrently used prophecies to incite suspicion against those in black robes. There was one who slandered Emperor Wenxuan, saying:
"I saw him fail to rise when the King passed; he harbors the intent to slight you, His Majesty, and treat you, the Lord, with contempt."
Furthermore, there was a prophecy that said:

"One in black robes shall become king. Because he wore dark monastic robes, it was suspected that this referred to him. Later, when he went [to court], he was dismissed for the great offense of irreverence, just as the Imperial Carriage was traveling through the mountains.
Huidaou stood twenty li outside the mountain, standing alone by the side of the road.
The Emperor said, "In other days you were not like this toward me; now you are.
Huidaou replied:
He feared that his own blood might be impure and defile the monastic quarters.
The Emperor, inwardly awestruck, requested that he carry Huidaou back to his residence on his back.
Huidaou firmly declined this command; he did not accept the order to carry him back. As the *I Ching* says: [The hexagram indicates... (Note: The original text here appears to be truncated).
The way of the noble person is such that they may either emerge from seclusion or remain therein;
they may either maintain silence or engage in speech.
This means responding appropriately according to the times; as it is said: "When the state is in accordance with the Way, one is wise;
when the state is not in accordance with the Way, one is simple.
When there is occasion for its use, one acts."
To abandon them is to conceal them. Now, those who possess the wealth of the world and those who hold the honor of having a people must look to conduct and skill.
They are merely like the categories of chickens, dogs, oxen, and horses.

At first, people delighted in them because they were capable of knowing the proper times—chickens; because they could bark and guard—dogs; because they could travel long distances—oxen; and because they could bear heavy burdens and travel far to relieve human toil—horses. Thus, they took pleasure in them.
He never refrains from killing or eating them simply because they are capable, nor does he fail to utilize their fur or hides.
Thus, those creatures cautiously rely on his rewards while fearing that his harm might fall upon them.
How much less so for those who possess virtue and the Way?

Even such birds and beasts, though they may receive rewards and affection, are still subject to slaughter and harm—let alone extraordinary birds and strange beasts that serve as urgent necessities for the myriad households.
A "well" refers to a neighborhood well; nine families constitute a well. Should one of these ever encounter the favor of a single gentleman, [their fate would be different].
How could such a state endure?
It was the era of ultimate virtue in the high antiquity, when bird nests could be peered into and deer could be tethered; why was this so?
Because the mechanism of killing was subtle.
In later generations, people admired their high nests and distanced themselves from them; as for birds, they kept them in high nests, and as for beasts, they kept them far from humans.
This was because they feared slaughter and killing, so that none could be tamed or made familiar.
Is it not because his spiritual resonance was so profound? When Wu’s Ji Zha went on a diplomatic mission to Jin,
upon entering its borders he sighed, saying,
"How violent!"
His attendants asked for the reason,
and he said,
"I saw that the bird's nest was high."
Or perhaps it was because of their cruelty; as Confucius said:
"When nests are overturned and eggs destroyed, the phoenix does not come.
When thickets are exhausted and marshes drained, the qilin does not come."
Because they loathe its harm and detest injuring their own kind, the worthy do not assist it.
Since its power naturally inclines downward, it does not form factions or sit high and aloof; therefore, Heaven bestows blessings upon it.
People think there is no rival to fate; life and death depend on destiny, and wealth and honor reside in Heaven.

What is moved by the retribution of past deeds does not err. Now, as for those who dwell in positions of authority and power—those men of influence and strength—there are few who do not become arrogant toward others.
Those who strive to emulate others are few. "Wu" (務) means to practice;
"mu" (慕) means to admire or yearn for.
They are still superior.

Among those of high status, noble rank, and great power, there are few who do not practice this mindfulness; yet once they have practiced it, they inevitably seek to surpass others in their excellence. They look down upon those of humble lineage and meager support.
Even if one possesses wisdom and artistry, what can they do against those who hold power and status?

As for those of humble origins, dwelling in thatched huts and wattle-and-daub homes, even if their talents soar above the clouds, such men will not be taken into account; if one does not treat them with leniency, they will surely be ensnared and destroyed.
To poison them with their own crimes is a form of indulgence and pity;
yet, if one does not show such pity, one will inevitably fabricate other charges and inflict guilt and harm upon them. Therefore, the Book says:
"Families of hereditary rank rarely conform to ritual," as stated in the "Biming" chapter of the *Shangshu*.
Families that possess hereditary rank and position seldom are able to employ ritual. How much less can they be expected to govern their subordinates with ritual?
Yet among the officials, there are some who possess ambition and spirit, yet regard cruelty as a virtue.
How could they know of the grace of gentle kindness? Even if one were to encounter a tiger or a rhinoceros glaring with malice, one would still strike back with all one's might.
What expectation can there be regarding anger? "Mie-ya" (眦睚) is the appearance of being enraged;
it refers to the act of confronting or striking back.
How could one fear such anger? Formerly, Guan Fan killed Bo Yuan, whose courtesy name was Fazuo.
His original surname was Wan.
A native of Henei,
he left the household life in his youth.
His intellectual acumen was brilliant and penetrating;
he could recite ten thousand words daily.
Zhang Fu held him in high esteem.
When he wished to request permission to return to lay life,
it was not granted. Later, while debating with the Daoist Guan Fan,
Fan was defeated and subsequently slandered him to the Prince of Fu.
Fu killed him. When the various Hu tribes heard of this,
they entered Qinzhou in a rage.
He killed Fu and Fan; Yu Gong murdered Fahui.
Fahui was a man from Guanzhong who was properly possessed of disciplined conduct.
During the Jianyuan era of Emperor Kang of the Jin dynasty, he resided in Xiangyang.
He did not accept separate invitations and instead went out for alms every day.
He would always carry a rope bed with him.
Once, when he encountered rain,
he covered himself with an oil-silk cloak.
When the rain stopped, he could no longer see him.
The monk Fazhao said,
"You have gone too far."
In the past, he once injured the foot of a chicken;
the retribution for that is now approaching.
Later, he was killed by Yu Zhi-gong while serving as General Who Conquers the West. How extreme is this reckless fury and violent punishment!
It is likely because he did not flee or hide himself;
furthermore, he was not treacherous or submissive, but was sincere and trustworthy.
"Dun" (遁) means to flee or escape.
The wise person avoids the world.
If one cannot avoid the evils of the world,
then one should act with caution and speak with humility.

He provided for his own safety with defenses that encompassed his entire person, yet he brought calamity upon himself; this was because he became stagnant and attached to worldly affairs, reaching such a state.

It is simply because he was obstructed and failed to penetrate through, judging matters solely by the retribution of karma. Alternatively, it may be because when one is rich in the Way, they no longer possess a sense of self.
Therefore, they wore coarse cloth and ate simple grains;
casting off their physical forms as if discarding cast-off skins,
they certainly did not find death difficult.

How could they possibly feign such a display? Among them, there may be those whose virtue and character are solitary and lofty, who have penetrated the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, and for whom both self and object have been lost;
thus, regarding death, they have nothing to fear.

How could one who seeks life through artificial embellishment understand the true meaning of death? Such a person neither rectifies and protects the Dharma-gate nor seeks the Way to save sentient beings;
they merely pursue a hollow death in vain.

What need is there for further deliberation? There are those who die lightly out of valor, and there are those who die lightly because they have lost their sense of self. Regarding those who die out of valor:
if they are not foolish, they must be benevolent. Those who die out of valor [are either the one or the other].
Some do not fear death because of their folly;

others are brave in facing death because of their benevolence. "Folly" refers to the violent tiger [leaping] over a river—where "leaping over a river" means crossing it by wading alone—and "benevolence" refers to attaining righteousness, ascending to the Hall of Enlightenment to defend the state against calamity, and dying therein.
Thus, ascending to the Hall of Illumination, those who lose the self are sages and benevolent ones.
It is not that they intentionally provoke death;
rather, when death arrives, they do not fear it. Having awakened to the thorough understanding of life and death, why should one fear?

Only karma is to be feared. In the past, during the transition between the Wei and Zhou dynasties, who ever saw one who was unswerving in his devotion, broke the railings of the throne, and died bravely for the sake of righteousness?
[Think of] Zhu Yun of the Han period.
His courtesy name was Ziyou.
He was a native of Lu.
During the reign of Emperor Cheng.
Zhang Yu was the Imperial Teacher and held in very high esteem.
Yang Yun submitted a memorial stating:
"I pray that you grant me the 'Horse-Slaying Sword' from the Imperial Armory."
He executed one sycophantic minister to serve as a warning to the rest. The Emperor asked, "Who was it?
and replied, "Zhang Yu, Marquis of Anchang."
The Emperor was enraged that a minor official had insulted his superior while in the court, bringing disgrace upon his teachers; he ordered the Censor to escort him down from the hall.
Zhi Yun clung to the palace railing until it broke, and Xin Ji struck the ground in remonstrance, whereupon the Emperor desisted.

Since the Later Wei and Later Zhou dynasties, when has there ever been such a person? Although those like Jing Ai and Daoji sacrificed their lives in empty caves, they were merely among those who ended their lives in ditches and streams.
When Ai remonstrated with Emperor Wu of Zhou regarding the purge of the monastic community, his advice was not followed.
He entered the mountains and drew blood to inscribe [the text] upon a rock;
he hung his intestines from a tree,
extracted his heart to hold it aloft, and then passed away.
The *Analects* says:
"How can this compare to the integrity of a common man or woman who drowns themselves in a ditch?
This was after the unification of Qi and Zhongshan.
Huiyuan was indignant and lamented with such intensity that his words were as abrupt as a thunderclap; moreover, his phrasing was not conciliatory.

With his braided beard bristling like the scales of a dragon, he nearly incurred harm. When Master Huiyuan remonstrated with Emperor Zhou Wu, he nearly met with disaster because his words were deemed improper.
Later, he fled deep into the mountain forests to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
It was not until the rise of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty that he emerged; thus, the worthy were able to exercise skillful means (*upāya*), and the sages knew how to discern the opportune moment.
"Although one does not prize life, one must also not treat death lightly.
Tanyou said to Gao Yang,
"In the past, you were a rākṣasa."
He merely had him look at himself reflected in the water.
The Emperor followed his advice and beheld a multitude of rākṣasas;
he subsequently ceased eating meat.

He abolished the tethering of birds and beasts and prohibited the slaughter of sharks; he forbade the sale of pungent spices in the markets. When the states of Jin and Qi spoke of Gao Yang’s campaign against the Khitan, [the people] first bared their heads and exposed their bodies.
For a thousand *li*, he ate nothing but meat and drank only water;
his vigorous spirit became even more intense after becoming your subject.
The ancestors exposed their bodies;
they applied powder and collyrium. Camels, oxen, and horses were not equipped with saddles or bridles.
Men and women mingled together as they gathered.
Lustful and lewd, he personally witnesses such impropriety;
he dismembers women and uses their skin to make lutes.
He split open his own belly,
climbed onto the beam of the house,
and ran swiftly as if upon the ground.
The slaughter was beyond reckoning.
Judging by this, it would not be incorrect to call him a rākṣasa. When the Emperor was first in Jinyang...
The Emperor ordered men to ride camels toward the monastery to fetch the scripture cases.
When the messengers asked where they were located, Faxiang said:
He allowed the camel to lead him out of the city;
as soon as they emerged, it was as if he had been dreaming, and they arrived at a mountain.
On the slope of the mountain stood a Buddhist temple.
A group of śrāmaṇeras called out from afar,
"Gao Yang’s camel is coming!
and they then led him to see an elderly monk.
The monk said,
"If Yang were to become the Son of Heaven, how would he be? Dayu replied,
"He would be sagely and enlightened."
He asked, "What have you come for?
He replied, "To collect the scripture cases.
The monk said:
Yang resided at the temple and was indolent regarding the recitation of sutras;
it is now the East Head [Temple] located northward.
Later, the Emperor arrived at Mujing Temple at the mouth of the valley.
At that time, there was a foolish man who had offered his body;
previously he did not understand speech,
but suddenly said to the Emperor:
"I shall go after you;
that night the fool died.
The Emperor also subsequently passed away at Jinyang. There was a man of the Way on Mount Tai.
The Emperor asked him, saying,
"For how many years shall I serve as the Son of Heaven?
He replied, "Thirty years."
The Emperor said, "The tenth day of the tenth month of the tenth year—could it not be the thirtieth?
When the appointed time arrived, he indeed passed away; whether the Emperor was foolish or wise, none could fathom it.
He entrusted the administration to Yang Zunyan,
while he himself spent his days in the temple extensively building monastic structures,
sitting in meditation, worshipping the Buddha, and performing circumambulations.
Its swiftness was like the wind.
I consider this to be like Gao Yang fulfilling the black prophecy. Previously, the prophecy had stated that one in black robes would become the Son of Heaven;
it is suspected that Master Daochan is now the Monk of the Northern Mountain.
I believe that the pronunciation of Gao Yang’s given name is the same as that of "lamb" (羔羊), which means "black.
This was prior to the reign of Empress Dowager Hu during the Zhengguang era of the Wei dynasty.
Prince Xie of Qinghe marshaled his troops and adjudicated affairs within the palace.
He changed the era name to Zhengguang (Reign of Correct Light) in the first year.
Those entering the marketplace were each taxed one coin; thus, the territories under his administration were beset by many anxieties.
When King Yao Guang fell ill,
the common people in his domain followed him one after another into the Way; their numbers became so numerous and excessive that they accumulated in great abundance.
Roughly estimated, there were more than thirty thousand temples and two million monks and nuns;
this continued until the Zhou Emperor Wu conquered Qi.
Qi succeeded Wei;
the monasteries numbered four thousand five hundred,
and the assembly decreased to three million.
Wei Yuansong may have regarded the Buddha-dharma as something base and contemptible, entrusting those who incite calamity through their false severity and slander with its destruction; yet,
though it was destroyed, it shall rise again.
This accords with the principle of "renewing all under heaven.
Yuansong was a native of Xinfan County in Shu.
He left the household life at Black Water on Mount Emei.
The superior strategy consists of twenty measures:
to purge those monks who lack practice despite their wealth,
and to establish a single Great Temple called Yanping.
To provide peace for those in the four seas who are sickly and weak is a principle that is most appropriate.
Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty saw him in prison when he entered the underworld.

He himself said that his experience here was like the bliss of the third dhyāna; thus, the *Biographies of Those Who Attained the Way* (Danglin zhuan) states that this person does not abide within the three realms.
As the Sūtra says:
The *Lotus Sūtra* states that there are those who manifest the three poisons and are seen to possess the characteristics of false views; are these not the very kind of people [described therein]?
However, when a person of ultimate practice employs skillful means, they initiate such expedient actions to bring about salvation.
If one were to keep [these matters] perpetually concealed and never reveal them,
then the crafty would exploit such power to subvert the reality.
As for Yuan Song, he had not yet exhausted the arts of such power.
Song Bei was a man of transcendent talent who crossed the sea upon a wooden cup;
he concealed his name and surname,
and people of the time referred to him as "the one who crosses by cup."
This was done because he called out to him by name on that very occasion.

He is also called Du-lian, though some regions call him Du-lian-ku; in ancient times, monks were referred to as Dao-shi, A-lian, or A-shang—these are the three names by which he was known. Once, while staying overnight at an inn, he stole a golden image and departed at the break of dawn.
The host galloped after him on horseback, but he proceeded slowly and was not overtaken; "dai" means to overtake.
The galloping horse could not reach him until they arrived at Mengjin, where they crossed the river by floating cups—the Mengjin being the Yellow River—and reached the capital.
His clothing was tattered and worn;
he took no moderation in his food and drink or in his moods of joy and anger.
He carried a single *lu-chuan*—a bamboo vessel—upon his shoulder.
It was like a small basket, all made of *lu* bamboo; inside the basket was placed a wooden cup.
He once wished to go to Guabù (瓜步), a place-name for a location on the Yangtze River between the Huai and the Yangtze.
In the past, Sun Zhong cultivated melons here.
When he was on the Yangtze River, the ferryman would not row for him;
thereupon, Sun stepped upon the boatman’s head with his feet.
Gazing about and chanting verses, he crossed directly to the north bank.
Once, at a village house in Guangling (modern-day Jinling), he encountered an assembly for the Eight Precepts (Bāguānzhāi).
A grain basket had been placed in the courtyard.
When his family was about to move him away,
they found that he was so heavy that no one could lift him.
Someone who had previously peered inside saw four small children living there.
Initially, he feigned death beneath the northern cliffs of Guangling, where lotus blossoms grew around his body from the rocks.
After his burial, some saw him in Pengcheng, Xuzhou; when they opened the coffin to look for him, [he was found there].
Only his boots remained; the monks wore short-topped boots called *pūrala*. Zhuxuqi was a person from the Song dynasty who returned from Goryeo.
He lost his way on an island and there obtained a bowl used for crossing [water].

Upon his arrival, Sengdu said, "I have not seen this bowl for four thousand years. When Sengdu saw the bowl, he recognized it; [it was] the bowl used by Liang Baozhi, who consumed things contrary to the Dharma.
His hair was several inches long.
He carried a single *khakkhara* staff, hung with scissors and a mirror, or two or three pieces of silk cloth.
Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty remarked that he was feigning madness to delude the masses; this refers to Emperor Wu of the Southern Qi.
His surname was Xiao,
his given name was Qiu,
and his courtesy name was Xuanyuan.
He was the son of Daocheng.
He reigned for eleven years before passing away.
His last will and testament stated that no sacrificial animals should be used in the offerings at his imperial mausoleum.
It consisted of nothing more than cakes and rice.
He was not permitted to leave home to enter the Way, nor to build stupas or temples, nor to convert his residence into a vihāra; he remained tied to Jiankang.
Yet, Hui-zhi manifested different forms as he wandered through the marketplace.
Once, he requested minced meat from someone;
having eaten his fill and departed,
the host looked into the basin.
The fish remained as if alive; once, when Master Zhigong was eating minced raw fish before Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
the Emperor criticized and disapproved of it,
whereupon Zhigong immediately spat it into the water.
Everyone saw that the fish was as it had been before, except that its tail was damaged;
to this day, there is a "sliced-remnant fish" in Jiangling. Emperor Wu [of Liang] was notorious for his cruel punishments.

Zhi, by means of his supernatural powers, caused [the Emperor] to see Emperor Gao (Xiao Daocheng) undergoing extreme suffering beneath the earth; because of this, he abolished the harmful practice of using needles and blades.

The inscription manifests its true form;

Zhang Nu composed a song titled "On the Locust Tree," which says:

Within the vast expanse of the Great Elephant, the Dharma-realm is empty and spacious; the myriad phenomena are surging and boundless. Illuminating and truly manifesting, the numinous clarity of one's original nature constantly shines by itself. Why, then, do you, my deluded child, remain in confusion?
Even though delusion brings calamity upon oneself, the nature of original enlightenment cannot recognize this for itself;
thus, one falls headlong into the five desires and invites disaster through confusion.
This expresses the lament that ordinary, ignorant people do not awaken, while the realm of the Buddhas—where those who delight in it rarely go—is forever extended with guidance and salvation.
Ordinary people, ignorant and deluded, are unwilling to enter the path of suffering; like an overturned sack, they sink and drown in the three miserable realms.
Once one loses this human body, it cannot be regained again.
It is like a water bag that lacks the resolve of a pine or cypress;
how can it withstand the wind and frost? Without firm resolve, how can one face the manifold objects of experience?
When the winds and frosts of birth and death arrive, what preparation can one make? One remains at ease beyond the purple clouds;
with a long song, one emerges from the vast blue heavens—*Hao Cang*, which means "the Great Blue Sky.
This is the meaning of Zhang Nu’s own account.

Thus, he serenely chanted and delighted in the Way, swimming between heaven and earth. His mind was clear and empty, colorless like water; as the water is excellent, so too was his clarity and emptiness free of waves.

The myriad objects were unmoving, and the ripples of consciousness were fundamentally level. When the world is governed by superficial assistance during a time when decadent customs are overflowing and pervasive, it is appropriate to establish extraordinary conduct to transform through expedient means; the "Assistant Instructor" (Jiàozhù) thus acts like wind, rain, thunder, and lightning, bringing about a revolutionary transformation in the nature of all things. "Revolutionary transformation" (gē) means to reform.

he harbors loyalty and good faith to await being appointed.

yet there are the petty scholars of today who merely memorize fragments of texts and single characters,
only to surreptitiously steal a reputation for themselves.
Therefore, it is called "thievery. The ignorant monastics and the ignorant laity regard the Dharma as something to be stolen.

The world hailed them as sages;
they, in turn, secretly imitated their wondrous countenances and strange vestments to delude the world—a profound instance of excessive excess.

In the end, they will be base and disgraced, like the fruits of a mountain; indeed, there are many such as those of the Vajra-dhyāna. However, even among those of ultimate faith, both the genuine and the fraudulent advance together.

and subsequently praise it;

That their supreme virtue can reach such a state means that the Sangha possesses a virtue that harmonizes with Heaven and Earth;

The virtue of one who has reached the ultimate can attain such a state. This monk was esteemed for his capacity, renowned for his name, a patriarch of the teaching, and a model for the people.

He could be looked up to but not drawn near; he could be approached through his virtue and reputation, yet not through intimacy of emotion. When the Sangha possesses kindness and goodness, directing their thoughts toward all things so that they may share in joy, this is called "kindness" (maitrī).

To deliberate and act with propriety is called *shu* (forbearance); to yield and allow others to reach their goals while humbling oneself and restraining one's own desires is called *rang* (yielding). To rejoice when others excel and to ensure that affairs are prosperous and flourishing is called *qing* (celebration). Such is the way these virtues nourish all things.
