The people of Qin and Luo have never participated in such assemblies;
could it be that there was no great sage among them?
Or is the account merely an exaggeration? When the Buddha emitted light that pervaded the entire dharma-realm, [the people of those lands] were not present.
"Why is it that in the capitals of Jing and Luo there are none who have seen or heard of this?
Is it because the Great Sage’s transformation was partial, or is it because the transmitters have exaggerated and fabricated falsehoods? The host replied:
The fish hides in the depths and does not know of the water; the person stands on land and does not perceive the wind.
It is not that these things can be known but are not known, nor that they can be seen but are not seen; rather, it is because one dwells within them that one remains unaware of them.
Moreover, regarding the "fangzhu" (the concave mirror) used to draw down the moon:
were it not for the fangzhu, one might say there is no moon.
As for the fangzhu, Wang Chong’s *Lunheng* states: [text follows].
It is a water-mirror.
On the night of the midnight hour of the rat (zi) in the eleventh month,
the Prince refined stones from the five directions and cast them into the shape of basins and bowls.
"By facing the moon, one obtains water.
Gao You said: "The *yinsui* resembles a large clam."
If one polishes and rubs it thoroughly and holds it toward the moon and water, one obtains several *shí* [of liquid]; a fire lens (*yángsuǐ*) focuses the sun.
Is it because there is no sun that one would say there is no fire lens? There is a pearl that reflects the light of the sun.
If one uses mugwort and *sōng* (pine) to receive it, fire is produced;
this is called the "sun-stone" (*yángsuì*).
Furthermore, mirrors may be cast using medicinal substances such as *liúhuáng* (orpiment).
It is said that by facing the sun one produces fire,
and by facing the moon one produces water;
the circular device is called the *yangsui* (sun-catcher).
The vessel used for this is called the *fangzhu*.
When the sun and moon are constant yet the *fangzhu* suddenly fails, water and fire cannot be obtained.

This is like the Buddha’s universal manifestation: those who lack the necessary conditions may fail to see or hear him. This truly arises because spiritual transformations reside within the mind and respond externally to things.
As for that which is unchanging within the mind-only, what could it possibly attain? The three realms are mind-only;
the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only.
The mind undergoes transformation and perceives objects;
it does not arise in vain.
As the *Book of Rites* says:
When the mind is not present,
one looks but does not see;
one listens but does not hear.
One may eat yet not know its flavor.
Thus we know that in the past, faith did not reside in them because they were not accustomed to hearing or seeing such things;
likewise, in this land, people formerly lacked faith, so even when they occasionally witnessed the gates of light or the shaking of the earth, they paid it no heed.

Therefore, it is not recorded. Even if there were those who, possessing faith, attained [the truth] individually and spoke of it, people would condemn them as being deceptive and delusional. That which is absent for the multitude cannot be seen;
yet, there may be individuals with the necessary conditions who alone perceive and hear it.
Consequently, people will surely hold them accountable for their strangeness and absurdity;

how could they possibly believe them together? This has been the case as the succession of years has long passed and the bamboo slips have decayed, let alone through the vast span of successive dynasties.
The records have been lost or fallen into ruin;
how could one possibly know them all in detail? Perhaps the *Zhou Shi* (History of Zhou) knew that these were not matters of the Central Kingdom, and therefore did not record them.
This is generally the case for those who serve as historiographers.
Each records the affairs of their own country;
this is not a matter concerning the Central Kingdom.
Furthermore, the gentleman is cautious regarding doubt.
Therefore, it was not recorded. Confucius, the Sage, hesitated because [the recipient] lacked the vessel for receiving the Way;
thus he did not speak of it. This was due to his hesitation.
Confucius humbled himself, considering himself to lack the vessel for receiving the Way.
Therefore, one should not wish to say that because something is missing from the *Shiji*, it did not exist.

Consider, for instance, the pillar that supports the axis of the universe, the rainbow, the sun and moon, the rising of the moon at dusk, the pivot of the North Star, and the tail of the Northern Dipper. Long ago, when Nüwa contended with the Lord of Gonggong for the empire, [the world was in chaos].
The head of the Great Tortoise struck the mountain so that it failed to reach it, and the Celestial Pillar broke.

Furthermore, he severed the feet of the Giant Turtle to establish the Pole Star; and Nüwa, moved by the light of a rainbow piercing the sun, gave birth to Zhuanxu. During the Spring and Autumn period, clouds like red birds flew alongside the sun for three days. Moreover, Houyi requested the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West, but his wife, Chang'e, stole it and fled into the moon. These accounts appear in the *Yi lüe*.
Furthermore, when lightning circled the Polar Star (Polaris), the Yellow Emperor was born.

Moreover, it is transmitted that after his death, the spirit of Fu Sheng ascended as a star among the constellations, situated above the Tail (Wěi) mansion; thus it is said that he "rides" [the heavens] and covers and sustains all—this constitutes one point of identity.
The three luminaries are of one accord;
yet that which is not seen or recorded in the Western Regions might truly lead one to consider Chinese words as unreliable.
If that [other view] is doubted as being incorrect, then how can this [view] be correct?
If that is believed to be real, then how can this be false?
Nevertheless, according to the Six Codes of China:
Valuing simplicity and prioritizing essentials,
[the teachings] were nearly extinguished during the Qin dynasty;
thus, even now, one cannot fully hear the ancient books.
Originally, it was intended to be concise;
furthermore, having encountered the destruction by the violent Qin,
how could the events of the past be heard in their entirety, as was the case with the eras of Tang and Yu?
The *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) survives in only a few chapters— merely the five chapters beginning with the "Yao Dian" (Canon of Yao)— and as for the flourishing culture of the Shang and Zhou,
how many dozen pieces of their *Shi* (Odes) and *Song* (Eulogies) can remain?
Thus, even regarding the gravity of punishments and virtues, there are still deficiencies.
How much less could one possibly encompass that which transcends the realm of elephants?
Thus, Yao took Yi Yin as his minister,
and Shun saw his affairs flourish through his endeavors.
Even the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius do not record this.

When Kong Qiu spoke of the Way, it is found in the works of Zhuangzi; the Five Classics do not mention them appearing together. As for Zhuangzi and Lao Dan knowing the rites, this is preserved in the works of Dai Sheng and Dai De; their names are close to that of the Prince [of Dai], and the transmission of the rites is titled the *Dai Dai Li* (Greater Dai Rites).
He reached the position of Grand Tutor in Xindu.
Dai Sheng, whose courtesy name was Cijun, transmitted the Rites; this is known as the "Little Dai Liji.
He served as a *boshi* at the Shiqu debate and eventually became the Governor of Jiuyang. Had this book been reduced to ashes and embers, [the tradition would have perished].

How could they have known that the two sages had exhausted the principles of ritual and realized the Way? That it was destroyed by the cruel Qin dynasty’s burning of the books—how could this possibly have been fully understood [at that time]? The guest said:
"When Lan Teng arrived in the kingdom..."
The man pursued the black ash to question him.
Lan said, "This is the ash remaining from the conflagration at the end of a kalpa."
"Is it truly that one attains the matter itself, or is it truly the ashes of the kalpa-fire? The host replied:
"The words remain, but the person has passed away;
how can one know their mind? Although these words have been transmitted and still exist,"
That person no longer exists;
how could one know the intent of their answer or where their mind was directed? Confucius said, "The desire for sincerity is the desire for eloquence;
this is what is meant by eloquence. This is the meaning of the response given here.
However, Lan’s dialectical response may also be "upright but not credulous. "Upright" (zhēn) means rectitude;
"credulous" (liàng) means trust.
This means that while his intention is upright, his words are not necessarily held as trustworthy. Indeed, they are like things consumed by the fires of the kalpa.
The great earth is completely exhausted;
yet, as it returns once more,
how could there be any embers at the end of the kalpa-fire?
The great earth blazes with fiery radiance,
burning up to the First Dhyāna,
and then it subsides and returns to its original state.
How could there be any ashes?
Thus we know that the kalpa-fire leaves no ash behind. Formerly, Zhuang Zhou, despite the wisdom of Zhongni, did not treat even the most wicked with contempt;

thus he looked far back to Dongling to express his meaning through metaphor, for it was there that Daozhi resided. Furthermore, Lan also considered the profound mysteries of the Śākya not as something to alarm the ears, nor did he regard them as strange.
Therefore, he relied upon the metaphor of the kalpa-fire to open up his teachings, intending to startle the listeners with what seemed extraordinary.

Thus, as he was about to initiate their transformation, he employed this as a provisional means to move them; for the gentleman takes virtue and righteousness as his standard of trust. The gentleman acts with righteousness before he trusts.
"Faithfulness is close to righteousness; thus one's words can be relied upon.
If he had merely said that it was always fire, how could Manqian have refused? Manqian is Fangshuo, whose courtesy name is Xiang.
If one were to answer simply by saying that this is the eternal fire, how could that avoid the rebuke of Dongfang Shuo?
Therefore, by embracing the "non-existent" (wu) to guide toward the reality, and by setting aside the near to verify the distant, [the Buddha] sought to transform them.

For this reason, he first provisionally pointed to the non-existent to entice them; by discarding the notion of the ordinary, ever-present fire and pointing toward the distant kalpa-fire, he caused people to thirst for what was new to them.
Yet one wishes to lead them toward the good.
Now, when one hears [the teaching] with thirst, doubt arises;
once doubt has arisen, one will inevitably seek to reach the underlying principle.

When principle reaches its destination, one returns before it is far; this is reaching the reality. It is like the mechanism of a bow being drawn and the notch of the arrow being inspected, attaining it through the proper measure. "Tai Jia" (The Great Jia) is the text.
"Ji" refers to the trigger of a crossbow.
"To anticipate. Before releasing an arrow, one first gauges its mechanism so that it will surely hit the mark when released.
If one intends to transform and guide others, one must ensure they certainly attain [enlightenment]. The guest said:
The Buddha appeared among the Rong;
his teachings reached the people of the Rong,
and the Chinese culture was transformed by the Rong.
"Is this not indeed pitiful? The host replied, "It is not so."
That is not the case. Even the dwellings of the junzi (superior person) are not considered mean;
how much less so those of the sage? Thus it is said in the *Analects*.
The Master wished to go to the nine tribes of the East.
Someone said, "They are so uncivilized; how can you do that?"
Confucius said,
"When a gentleman dwells therein,
what meanness could there be?"
The gentleman honors this;
the sage dwells within it.
Thus, transformation is certainly not something base. Heaven has no partiality.
Virtue alone is what one assists.
In learning, there is no fixed teacher;
take what is good as your teacher, and take your kin as your guide.
If there is good, one follows it according to one's inclination; the goodness of the world is one and the same.
How can it be limited by boundaries or territorial divisions? One should simply take the benefit and salvation of others as one's primary concern.

How could one set boundaries by mere territorial limits? Thus, the Great Yu and King Wen were both sage-kings; yet the Great Yu emerged from the Western Qiang and was born at Shixi—which is now the route of Maozhou.
King Wen of Zhou was born in Bin, which was entirely inhabited by Rong and Qiang tribesmen; Youyu and Ri Di were his worthy ministers.
When the envoy of the Rong arrived at Qin, the Qin state was building palaces and residences.
Yu criticized it, saying:
"If it was not the work of spirits, then it must have been made by humans.
This refers to the Jinri Stele.
A person from the frontier during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han was exceptionally virtuous while residing in the Han palace.

Though he was not born within the Central Plains, [the comparison is made because] Tai Kang was a ruler of the Zhou who lived in the remote wilderness. Tai Kang, the King of Xia, was fond of hunting and excursions.
The five sons composed songs to admonish him, yet he did not return for ten months.
King You of Zhou brought about his own destruction by doting on Bao Si. Han Xue and Shen Hou were rebellious ministers; Han Xue was a slanderous scion of the Boming clan.
He succeeded Yi after Yi was extinguished;
Shen Hou extinguished King You of Zhou. Since their deaths did not occur among the four barbarian tribes, how could one judge their worthiness or baseness based merely on the borders of their states?
Now, when the Yellow Emperor ascended Mount Kunlun,
the Sage Laozi departed for the Flowing Sands. The Yellow Emperor ascended Mount Kunlun and inquired about the Way from Guangchengzi.
Laozi traveled to the Flowing Sands to seek Śākyamuni; both esteemed what they heard and admired what they shared in common.

It is only after this that they go forth; those of like sound respond to one another, and those who follow the same Way seek each other out. Now, the horses of the Hu are clad in black, and the *zao* slaves tend these horses as menial officials. Hu music includes instruments such as the *pipa*, the *qiangdi*, and others. Hu jade ornaments fill the court, and jade *cong* and *bi* discs come from foreign lands. Is it not then said that these things are vulgar? Yet they are accepted. How much more so, then, for the Dharma! How could it be considered vulgar? It is simply because people have not yet heard of it. Therefore, when the Way is spread, there is no limit to its reach. This is why we know that the Buddha’s Dharma is the ultimate truth. Furthermore, the Buddha’s teachings are vast and profound, encompassing all phenomena and penetrating the three periods of time. They are subtle and wondrous, beyond the reach of thought or speech. Even the sages of antiquity could not exhaustively describe them. Thus, when the Buddha first appeared in the world, he taught according to the capacities of beings, providing various medicines to cure their afflictions. He did not speak of the Mahayana to those of the Two Vehicles, nor did he speak of the Three Vehicles to those of the One Vehicle. Because his teachings were adapted to the circumstances, they were not uniform. Therefore, although the Buddha has long since entered parinirvāṇa, his teachings remain diverse and manifold.
