Therefore, those who aspire to the Way that transcends the mundane should adopt the outward forms that distance one from the world: the shaven head and the square-cut robe.

For those of middling or superior capacity who merely occupy these forms without desiring to exert themselves in the Way, this is simply a matter of shame; they dwell in a realm free from worldly dust.
They perform rituals that feign transcendence from the secular world,
yet they are unable to advance in virtue or cultivate their studies,
remaining instead distracted and restless in the realm of wealth and profit.
The Superior Man regards this as a cause for shame, as the Sage Confucius said.
The injunction "not daring to injure or damage [one's body]" is likely intended as a warning that such acts invite harm through transgression; here, *sheng* (眚) means "error" or "transgression."
This refers to harm and calamity. The *Classic of Filial Piety* states:
"One dares not injure or damage one's body, hair, or skin."
This is because it serves as a warning against excessive harm. As for Taibo’s shaving of his hair as the height of supreme virtue:
Yu Rang lacquered his body out of loyalty, while Taibo of Wu was the eldest son of Tai Wang of Zhou.
Because his younger brother Ji Li was virtuous and had fathered the sagely son King Wen,
Chang knew that he would certainly possess the empire.
He subsequently avoided [the world] and went to Wu,
where he cut his hair and tattooed his body;
Confucius regarded this as the height of virtue.
In the *Shiji*,
it is recorded that after Zhao Xiangzi killed Zhi Bo,
Yu Rang conceived the intent to take revenge for him.
Xiangzi knew that the people of the state had been ordered to pursue him.
Yu Rang, thereupon lacquered his body to alter his appearance and swallowed charcoal to change his voice, before entering the state.
The *Shiji* considers this to be loyalty; thus,
even severing one's hair and altering one's appearance does not constitute a lack of loyalty or filial piety, for such acts enable one to establish virtue and spread one's fame.
How could it ever have been considered filial piety to preserve one's hair and skin intact?

Consequently, throughout the ancient and modern eras of the Middle Kingdom, people have known this principle of profound benefit; they have followed and emulated it, and thus the practice of altering one's physical appearance has not been abandoned by the most eminent and virtuous.
If one preserves the crown and robes, the family and state will flourish.
Thus, although You Yuan did not wear his hair-pin or sash and Ji You of Wei was in hurried distress, both were virtuous men.
Was the virtue of these two sons caused by their hair-pins and sashes? Huan Mao did not shave his head or wear crimson garments, yet Huan Tui and Shao Zheng Mao were both unrighteous.
How can it be that [the distinction between] honor and disgrace depends on shaving the head and dyeing the skin?
Long ago, King Wu-ling of Zhao first changed his attire to that of the Hu people. King Wu-ling said to Lou Huan: [text continues]
"I wish to adopt the Hu dress.
[The King] said, "Excellent.
The ministers, however, did not desire it.
Fei Yi was attending the King,
and the King further told him:
"I wish to adopt the clothing of the Hu."
Yet I fear that future generations will criticize me; what shall I do?
Yi replied: "Your servant has heard that..."
Doubtful actions yield no merit;
doubtful conduct brings no renown.
Your Majesty has already incurred the suspicion of the common people.
In governing, one need not heed the criticisms of the world.
The ignorant are blind to accomplished facts;
the wise perceive them before they have even sprouted.
"If that is so, why should Your Majesty have any doubts?
Thereupon, he accordingly adopted the Hu costume. After the Sui and Tang dynasties, the style of dress and headgear was gradually modified.
What is esteemed lies in governance.
To establish the royal standard, recording events and words has never been subject to censure; for in governing, what is esteemed is the effective administration of the people.
He established his own royal system;
yet we do not see him being censured for wearing the clothing of the Hu.

Indeed, although Confucius was not a minister of the Yu or Xia dynasties, he took the rites and music of the Three Dynasties—Yu, Xia, and Shang—as his model. Likewise, Wu and Yue were not subordinate states of Lu or Wei.
Yet they practiced the teachings of King Wen, the Duke of Zhou, and the Master Confucius.

As for the hundred officials, penal administration, and legal codes established by the Qin and the Xin dynasty, subsequent emperors and kings for the most part followed these contemporary political systems without alteration; although both the First Emperor of Qin and Wang Mang of the Xin dynasty were without virtue.

The laws and regulations for the appointment of officials were sometimes maintained as they were and not altered; this was because the two [Han] emperors and Wang Mang had all resided within the Central Xia,
and thus they followed one another in succession.
It is not that those remote regions are excluded;
rather, it may be that the intent of Heaven in establishing rulers as shepherds has been lost. Heaven gave birth to the masses of the people and established rulers over them as their shepherds.
It is further said:
"In employing the Way of Heaven, why limit it to the barbarians or the Chinese? For wherever the sun and moon shine, all is our realm."
I practice goodness throughout the world;
who then would not consider it their own world?
Formerly, when the King of Chu lost his bow, he said, "Let a man of Chu find it."
Zhongni said, "It is a pity that it is not made great.
Why not let all people obtain it? When the King of Chu lost his bow, he said, "Let it simply not be obtained by anyone other than a person of Chu."
When Zhongni heard of this, he said:
"What a pity! Why did they not simply say, 'A man lost his bow and a man found it'?
Nowadays, all who speak refer to the Western Regions as "Hu," yet in reality, the Hu consist of more than thirty kingdoms situated south of the Pamir Mountains.
To the west of the mountain ranges lies the kingdom of Śrīvijaya, which is called the Kingdom of the Brahmins.
Nevertheless, among its inhabitants there are not a few of mixed origins;
their eyes are sunken and their noses are flat.
In this region, the lands of the Rong and Di tribes press close upon the royal domain; thus,
the land between the Yi and Luo rivers in present-day Henan is considered extremely lowly by the Hu of India.
All possess military dwellings; yet the *Wangfu Hu jing* (The Scripture of King Fu’s Conversion of the Barbarians) states:
"The Hu people are fierce and cruel, therefore they were converted into Buddhas, made to shave their heads and wear saffron robes, and forbidden from continuing their lineage. How delusory this is!
During the Spring and Autumn period,
the Red Di and White Di were raiders and enemies of the feudal states,
while the Xianyun were exceedingly fierce.
The barbarians were extremely disruptive within the central lands;
"disruptive" here means causing chaos.
This was during the Spring and Autumn period.
When the Di attacked states such as Jin and Lu, how could they have been so close yet remain unsubdued?
They were far away, beyond the Liu-sha sands at the edge of the Great Wilderness, where they were currently indulging their ferocity.
Laozi was born in the Central Kingdom during the time of King Ding.
Since you yourself have been pressed by the Rong and Di tribes, why not submit to them?

Yet you speak of going to India to subdue those barbarians. Furthermore, since ancient times, all sage-kings have brought the distant under their influence; how could there ever be such a thing as secretly plotting the extermination of a lineage and subverting the way of humanity? When distant people do not submit, one should cultivate civil virtue to bring them around.
It is further said:
"Virtue alone moves Heaven;
there is no distance too great for it to reach."
Furthermore, being neither indolent nor negligent, the four barbarian tribes came to offer their allegiance as kings;

how could this have been achieved by artificially imposing prohibitions or fabricating stern edicts? Consider carefully: even the extreme cruelty of the Three Miao and the draconian laws of Shang Yang did not surpass this [simplicity]. This was the time of Shun.
The state of Sanmiao had Lake Dongting to its left and Mount Pengshui to its right.
It lay beyond the borders of the Huangfu (Outer Regions);
for thousands of generations it had not followed the Way of the King, and the kings had repeatedly failed to execute punitive measures against it.
During the time of Duke Xiao of Qin,
the favorite minister Jing Jian introduced Shang Yang, a native of Wei;
through his severity, he assisted the state of Qin.
Later, after Duke Xiao passed away and King Hui ascended the throne,
he dispatched envoys to arrest Shangjun.
Shangjun fled to the foot of the frontier pass, intending to stay at an inn.
The guest did not know that he was the Lord Shang.
[The official] said, "According to the Lord Shang's decree, those who provide lodging for a person without verification shall be held liable.
The Lord Shang said:
Alas! How has the degeneration of the Dharma come to this?
He was subsequently torn apart and killed.
Now, the disciples of Śākyamuni are not of the lineage of the Three Miao tribes, and the Sage Laozi is not of the same sort as Shang Yang.
Why has it come to this? Yet the Sage Laozi spoke of constantly and skillfully saving all things.
"Could it truly be so? If that were the case, then one's words would contradict one's actions.
The guest replied, "To disobey my father’s command brings grief to my mother;
to disregard fear and seek out danger is improper."

Can this be called filial piety? Prince Siddhārtha desired to leave the household, but his father the King would not permit it; he further surrounded him with palace women to keep him occupied. At midnight, the Prince secretly departed and leaped over the city wall—this was a violation of his father’s command.
To cause his maternal aunt to weep with such grief that her very entrails were rent asunder was to bring sorrow upon his mother; yet,
while occupying the rank of heir apparent, he dwelt alone in the mountain valleys.
This is a matter of slight fear;
to be amidst the Snowy Mountains is to encounter peril.
Can such a person truly be called filial? He served as the preceptor to King Bimbisāra.
While dwelling among the Śākya clan,
he was treacherously harmed by Ajātaśatru and attacked by Virūḍhaka.
Since he was ultimately unable to save him,
can he truly be called benevolent?
King Bimbisāra is none other than Piṇḍola-bharadvāja.
He was residing in the city of Rājagṛha.
King Ajātaśatru imprisoned his father,
King Śreṇiya, until he died of starvation.
Even the Buddha could not save him.
Furthermore, King Virūḍhaka, the son of King Prasenajit,
was born of Queen Mṛgāvatī.
He was, in fact, the maternal nephew of the Śākya clan.
Yet, based on the words of a slave girl, he launched a military attack and slaughtered the entire Śākya lineage.
The Buddha knew that due to the karmic conditions of their past lives, none of them could save him. Devadatta was his brother from the same celestial lineage;
he was the son of King Droṇodana.
The Buddha’s younger cousin, Sunakṣatra, was of noble character;
yet in life he suffered humiliation,
and at death he encountered the depths of misery.
Can this be called righteousness? Devadatta and Sunakṣatra both fell into hell, yet they sit upon beds of precious gems and receive the prostrations of their sovereign and father;
such words are a great violation of humility.
His countenance was haughty and his bearing arrogant;
can this be called propriety? Not even ten days had passed since the bow was suspended [at his birth].
The Queen Mother has been in a state of perpetual distress;
the calamity of her boundless grief is a transgression of no small magnitude.
Can this be called "blessing," now that the Crown Prince has been born?
This is why the ritual of suspending the bow of mulberry wood and the arrows of *pang* grass was established at the gate.

In ancient times, when the Buddha was a crown prince, his mother Māyā passed away just seven days after his birth. If such were the case, where is the benefit in it? Those who wish to cause this practice to be adopted within the Middle Kingdom [should consider this].
The host said, "Regarding the discourse on love and hatred,
how can praise and disgrace be determined?"
In antiquity, there were those who blamed the Three Sovereigns and disparaged the Five Emperors;
there was Zhuangzi, who praised the man by the well in Han-yin and suppressed the reputation of Confucius.
This "Old Man of Han-yin" entered the well carrying a water jar.
He drew water to irrigate his garden.
Zigong taught him how to construct a lever-dipper.
The old man of Han-yin deeply disparaged Zhongni’s clever artifice. There was also the strong fisherman who rebuked the Three-Liu Official, Qu Yuan.
Having encountered the praise of Jin Shang,
King Huai became suspicious of him;
consequently, he was demoted to Changsha.
Walking alone by the riverbank,
he saw a fisherman and questioned him;
therefore, it is said:
"The whole world is drunk, yet I alone am sober.
The whole world is turbid, yet I alone am pure.
Fisherman, do not urge me; you cannot."

He subsequently drowned himself and died. There was one who excelled in disparaging the Qin laws while praising the New Chamber (the Xin dynasty); the laws of the First Emperor of Qin and Wang Mang were cruel and tyrannical.
Later generations saw Yang Xiong compose the "Mei Xin" (Praising the New) in one chapter.
They vilified Qin and glorified Wang Mang, judging them by their shifting allegiances;

they broke down walls and pierced through foundations, achieving nothing more than the labor of sparrows and mice. There are those who, having practiced the "feeding troughs" of the ancients, further increase these breaches and burrows to incite the clamor of right and wrong.
As for Wang Chong, Liu Zixuan, and others, they did nothing but engage in the "yellowing of the white" (critical revision). The *Book of Rites* states:
"The greatest filial piety is to revere one's parents."
The next is to avoid bringing disgrace.
The next is to be able to nourish one’s venerable parents, which means causing them to honor their ancestors.
Avoiding disgrace consists in cultivating the person and maintaining one's conduct; as for transforming the family into a state—
The world calls this the Great Transformation.
When one acts as a sage throughout the world, who would say it is small?
Thus, even those nearby lose their sense of sternness and affection, while those far away venture into the mountain forests.
Thus, he causes the people of the world to know that their father is the father of a Great Sage and their mother is the mother of a Great Sage;
once they know this, they revere them.
Having honored them and brought peace to them, the righteousness of a filial son is truly called "unfailing"; "failing" means deficiency.
This is the way of honoring one's parents.
The Odes say:
"The filial son is inexhaustible;
he is forever granted his kindred. How could one consider this unfilial?
"Then who is able to practice true filial piety?
Zengzi replied, "To provide material support is possible, but to show reverence is difficult. Even dogs and horses can be provided with material support."
Without reverence, how can one distinguish it? Reverence is possible; being at ease with it is difficult.
Being at ease with it is possible; persevering in it until the end is difficult.
Once one's parents have passed away—
He was careful in his conduct so as not to leave his parents with an ill reputation;
this may be called being able to bring one's life to a worthy end. It began at Vairambha.
At last, beneath the śāla trees,
all his virtues were extolled and there was no evil of which he could be accused.
"Reality" refers to the culmination of filial piety; how could the Great Sage not be earnest in its perfection?
Thus, when a sage acts, he does not deviate from the two luminaries of sun and moon in their alternation of dusk and dawn, nor does he deviate from the four seasons.
That which may be subject to flourishing and decay is merely a temporary transformation;
if this transformation persists for long, it deviates from the nature of things.

Vast wonders, marvels, and anomalies arise from this; even a sage cannot escape the consequences of past karma. As for those who were imprisoned, starved to death, buried in pits, or had their flesh cut by blades—these are all retributions for causes in previous lives, such as King Bimbisāra being childless.
The divination stated:
"A mountain immortal shall become your son.
Thereupon, she killed him and caused him to be reborn immediately.
Furthermore, he was born again as a white rabbit and was killed once more;
thus, he is now imprisoned and executed by King Ajātaśatru.
This is the retribution for his previous karma, arising from his past killing of the great Makara fish during his time as a member of the Śākya clan.
It is not that a sage cannot cause [the karmic result] to be temporarily averted;
it is simply that it does not constitute a permanent exhaustion of the principle of karma. As the Sūtra says:
"Even if one were to pass through a hundred kalpas..."
What has been done as karma does not perish;
when causes and conditions meet, one receives the retribution oneself. Now, the Queen has sown good deeds in accordance with the seasons of Heaven.
Bian Que was skilled in medicine because he relied upon destiny;
to contravene the timing and fate was beyond his power.
Thus, when the form departs, the shadow vanishes.
Only by eliminating karma can one’s retribution for the deceased be ended.

If one were to cause the shadow to vanish while the form remains, thereby dispatching the retribution while the karma persists, it would be nothing more than sorcery and illusion; unless the karma is purified through repentance and eliminated, the retribution will not cease.
This is identical to the deceptive and illusory claims of sorcerers;
it is like the story of [the Buddha] formerly eating horse fodder, or Maudgalyāyana requesting the "earth-flavor" (pṛthivī-rasa), or the Brahmin Aśvaka inviting the Buddha for ninety days.
They ate nothing but horse-gram.
At the beginning of the kalpa, there was "earth-flavor" (pṛthivī-rasa) that had subsided beneath the earth;
Maudgalyāyana wished to employ his supernormal powers to retrieve it.
The Tathāgata did not permit either;
he intended these as omens for future generations.
When Kapilavastu was besieged, Maudgalyāyana requested that a city be made of iron; when the Śākya clan was besieged by King Virūḍhaka, [the city] was made of lapis lazuli.
Maudgalyāyana wished to transform an iron city to protect him, but the Tathāgata did not permit it.
For karma cannot be escaped; even the Great Sages all maintain that the retribution of karma is not otherwise.
Therefore, to do what can be done and yet not do it is inhumane.
But as for not doing what cannot be done, why would that be called inhumane?
If one attains the principle, even if it involves injury, it is called righteousness;
if one loses the principle, even if it exists, it cannot be called righteousness.
Danjun disparaged Yao and Shun because he deemed them lacking in talent; thus, he disparaged them for that reason.

Yet he did not allow them to succeed to the throne. Guan and Cai were banished to Zhou; when the two uncles, Guan and Cai, spread false rumors and slandered the Duke of Zhou, the Duke of Zhou did not refrain from punishing them because they were his own flesh and blood.
He subsequently executed Guan Shu and banished Cai Shu. Zheng Zhuang Gong’s uterine younger brother, Gongsun Shou (also known as Gongsun Du), was a man who incited rebellion;
Zheng Zhuang Gong defeated him at Yan Shi. Shi Que slaughtered Shi Hou; Shi Que was the father of Shi Hou.
Thou assisted Prince Zhuyou in assassinating Duke Huan of Wei and established himself as ruler.

When asked by the Duke for advice on how to stabilize the succession, Guan Que sent him to court at Chen, where he was executed. This was because he had shown such cruelty toward his own flesh and blood.
To preserve the ancestral temple is their primary task;
they promulgate the penal laws to serve as a warning for posterity,
so that those who fail in filial piety or fraternal respect may stand in awe and be deterred.
If figures such as Devadatta or Sunakṣatra were to be pardoned for their crimes through your great personal favor,
they would then incite the whole world to commit acts of rebellion.
Therefore, he called for spit to humiliate him; after Devadatta had mastered supernatural powers,
he transformed himself into a small child and sat upon King Ajātaśatru’s lap.
King Ajātaśatru spat into his mouth,
and Devadatta accepted and ate it; therefore,
the Buddha used this humiliation of eating spittle to manifest the gravity of his suffering and to exhort him as he practiced the night-walk.
After a long time, Śunakṣatra wished to desist;
he therefore feigned being the Bakkula ghost to frighten the Buddha, intending to cause him to fall into hell so that they might share the same foul odor.
Having been rebuked, he was ashamed and remained silent. "Ge" (格) means "to restrain" or "to correct."

Although there may appear to be grounds for shame regarding one’s own flesh and bone, the principle ultimately returns to what is correct: those of the same clan share the same "odor" (blood ties), and thus none should seek to evade [punishment] through such kinship. One does not grant exemption by means of a "door of privilege. Thus, the sages administer punishment starting from those close at hand and extending outward to the distant.
One does not cultivate intimacy with the near while alienating the distant;
thus, how can the meaning of great authority be fathomed?
If, moreover, the Great Rite shares its rhythm with Heaven and Earth, [how can it be measured by petty standards?]
Virtue is as venerable as Heaven and Earth.
The Sage is one in essence with virtue.
When a ruler or a father observes the rites, they thereby honor Heaven and Earth.
To honor Heaven and Earth is to be close to the Way and its Virtue.
To be close to the Way and its Virtue is to revere the Sage.
To revere the sages is to harmonize with the rhythms of Heaven and Earth and to broaden the influence of the Way and its Virtue.
It is not that our Great Sage seeks respect by striving for superiority.
It is because rulers and fathers have come to respect themselves through moral virtue.
Once the rites and laws were made manifest, people followed them as models;
thus, their physical appearance and demeanor became distinct from those of other customs.
Thus, those who do not differ from him are treated with ritual respect;
this accords with the Way and its Virtue.
His physical appearance and demeanor do not differ from the common custom.
To cause those of different customs to pay them ritual reverence would be to turn one's back on the Way and its Virtue.
Even if those who are different are not necessarily more worthy than those who are not, [the former still do so].
It is not that one must necessarily be ignorant of difference;

yet, even a clay or stone effigy representing an image may still be worthy of veneration. If a wooden or earthen figure is carved and sculpted into an image, why would it not be venerated? Furthermore, the sons of farmers and merchants who manifest themselves in specific dress and appearance—how could they not be respected? Those from the four castes who leave the household life all share the same lineage as the Śākyas.

One does not fail to show respect because of a low-born lineage; respecting one who is unworthy is still better than showing no respect at all. One respects even an ordinary person, for such respect is superior to disrespect. To maintain the sheep while observing the rites was the constant practice of Lu.
It was required that a sheep be slaughtered to announce the month at the temple;
however, after Duke Wen, the ritual of announcing the month was no longer practiced,
and they merely sacrificed the sheep.
During the time of Duke Ai,

Zi Gong served as the Director of the Granaries and was in charge of the ancestral temple rituals, including the ceremony for the announcement of the new moon. Because the ruler did not personally attend the audience for the new moon,
[Zi Gong took over these duties].
He then wished to abolish the ritual of sacrificing the sheep.
The Master said,
"You love the sheep."
I cherish these rites.
Although you, my lord, do not personally observe the monthly inspection, the presence of the sheep still allows one to know this rite.
If the sheep were also removed, the rite would have no means of being recorded.
The present case is likewise: one buys the bones of a fine horse to attract the worthy.
Formerly, when King Zhao of Yan wished to honor men of talent, Guo Kui said, "I request that Your Majesty build a terrace with gold and hold me in high esteem."
Thus, the worthy men of the four quarters will arrive.
If Your Majesty still employs someone as unworthy as I,
how much more so those who are truly worthy?
Formerly, there was one who sought a dragon-horse but did not find it;
another obtained the head of a dead horse and presented it [to the king].
The king rewarded him with a thousand pieces of gold.
All those who heard this arrived.
Within one month, three dragon-horses were obtained.
The King was invited along with his honored ministers.
Later, several individuals such as Yue Li arrived; this is indeed the great way of human relations.

Thus, whether one shows respect to a sovereign or a father depends on oneself, whereas whether a śramaṇa accepts or refuses it depends on others. Unless one were a Great Sage, if one were to insist that a sovereign or a father must show reverence to a śramaṇa, one would surely have to sit and accept their prostrations and bows.
The *Li* says:
"When the son has put on his new cap, the mother bows. The "Meaning of Capping" (*Guanyi*) in the *Liji* says:
"Once he has been capped, he is given a courtesy name (*zi*)."
This is the way of becoming an adult.
When he is seen by his mother, she bows to him;
when he is seen by his brothers, they bow to him.
It is established that one performs bows as a matter of ritual propriety; however, those wearing armor do not bow.
In both cases, the reverence due to the sovereign and one’s parents is not lost.

How much more so for the Confucian sages who did not serve the Son of Heaven nor hold office under the feudal lords—such as Nüwa and Xu You, or the Four White-Headed Recluses—and even Māyā, who assumed a long life to serve as the mother of the Buddha.
Now that the Sage has been born,
his form is manifested once more in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
all Buddhas of the past and future have Māyā as their mother.
Having realized the Buddha-nature within birth,
he subsequently returned to his mother in heaven with abundance;
how could this not be a source of merit?
Formerly, when Xia Qi was born, his mother transformed into stone; the *Shiji* (Records of the Sovereigns and Kings) states:
"Gun took the daughter of the Ye clan, named Xiujǐ. While traveling in the mountains, she perceived a shooting star and was moved by emotion."
Furthermore, she swallowed Yi, and for three years she did not give birth.
Later, she split her back and gave birth to Yu.
Today, in Guangye County of Wenshan in Shu, there is a place named Shixi.
This was the place where Yu’s mother turned into stone.
Furthermore, Yu wished to open a passage through Mount Yüan and said to his wife, the daughter of Tushan:
When Nüwa was bringing me provisions, she heard the sound of bells and drums and came toward it.

Yu had leaped upon a rock, being able to strike the pitch of the drum; as Nüwa went to bring him food, she saw Yu in the midst of transformation and movement, and upon reaching the foot of Mount Song, he had transformed into stone.
When the mother of Qi was pregnant, she showed it to Yu, saying, "My child is stone.

Upon returning home, she broke open [her womb] and gave birth; her mother then transformed into stone. When Yi Yin was born, his mother became the Empty Mulberry Tree (*kongsang*); Yi Yin was born from the tree, and his mother subsequently transformed into the Empty Mulberry Tree. How could this not be considered an inauspicious omen?
Therefore, the two teachings directly address this life,
while the Śākya teaching generally indicates future lives;
it is like those two mothers who were transformed into mulberry trees and stones.
Where has the spirit gone?
The Holy Mother looks down from on high, grieving beneath the sun and moon;
yet in truth, human life is sustained by the blessings of fortune.
The guest said:
"As for the cruelty toward the Wei, there was execution within the inner circle of trust;
as for the confusion regarding the Zhou, it was not in accord with the dark companions. This refers to the Northern Wei Emperor Taizu, Tuoba Tao."
In the fifth year of the Taiyan era, the Dharma was suppressed.
A monk who had hidden [the scriptures] died.
This was during the reign of Yuwen Yong of the Northern Zhou.
In the second year of Jiande, Buddhism was suppressed; eminent monks were executed one after another, the world was filled with wailing, and the royal bounty was exhausted.
It seemed as though their desires would be fulfilled at first, but in the end they brought swift ruin upon themselves. Thus did the two kings initially destroy the Dharma.
"It seemed to accord with his will, yet he ultimately perished from a malignant disease. How did he come to this?
The host replied:
When baleful vapors steam forth, the five cardinal virtues are ruined;
when the wicked and depraved arise, the myriad spirits are incensed. Once the five elements have been ruined, the hundred deities are enraged.
Therefore, that which Heaven assists is that which is compliant with the Way.
That which people assist is trustworthiness. If one lacks trustworthiness and lacks compliance,
they shall be punished by both humans and devas in concert.
Can one avoid perishing? As the Book of Documents says:
"Calamities sent by Heaven may still be escaped;
calamities brought upon oneself cannot be avoided. Initially, there was Emperor Taizu and Emperor Taizong of the Wei dynasty; Taizu was Tuoba Gui.
Emperor Taizong, Tuoba Si,
was styled Emperor Ming.
He was the eldest son of Emperor Wudi, the Founder, and was deeply devoted to the teachings on causes and conditions.
The śramaṇa Faguo was pure and refined in his observance of the precepts;
he expounded and disseminated the scriptural teachings of the Dharma.
Emperor Taizu issued an edict appointing him as the Head of the Śramaṇas (Sha-men-tong).
Emperor Taizong further increased his veneration and respect,
bestowing upon him the titles of Fugu (Aid to the State), Yicheng Zi (Viscount of Yicheng), Zhongxin Hou (Marquis of Zhongxin), and Ancheng Gong (Duke of Ancheng), all of which he declined.
The Emperor visited his residence;
because the gate was too narrow to admit carriages and litters,
he issued an edict to widen it.
He died at the age of eighty.

The Emperor attended his funeral in person and posthumously conferred upon him the title of General Laoshou; these honors were all manifestations of the Emperor’s favor. When Emperor Ling of the Zhao dynasty ascended the throne as the Great Ancestor, Emperor Taizu followed and practiced this tradition from the beginning of his reign.
He would frequently invite eminent śramaṇas to engage in philosophical discourse with them.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, he carried the image through the broad streets.
The Emperor went to the palace gate and stood at the balustrade;
scattering flowers and prostrating with his forehead to the ground, he paid his respects,
yet he was already at the extreme limit of eight years of age.
He visited State Counselor Cui Hao to consult him on state affairs.
Hao spoke at length about Zhuangzi and Laozi,
asserting that they deeply undermine the Buddhist school.
The Emperor, who deeply trusted and esteemed him, sought out practitioners of esoteric arts.
Upon obtaining the Celestial Master Kou Qian,
he issued an edict for all provinces and commanderies to establish Daoist altars.
In the fifth year of the Taiyan era, the Jia-mao year,
Hui Gai rose in rebellion at Xingcheng, causing turmoil throughout Guanzhong.

After the Emperor’s western campaign against Chang’an, during the time when the Later Wei dynasty was headquartered at Pingcheng, there was a śramaṇa who grew wheat within the monastery. The Emperor’s groom was tending horses there;
when the Emperor entered the monastery to inspect his horses, he [encountered the wheat].
An official took advantage of a lapse;
the room contained property consisting of bows and arrows used for guarding the pastures,
as well as tens of thousands of items entrusted for safekeeping by the wealthy and noble.
At that time, the Emperor was twenty-four years old;
though his prime was yet in its vigor,
he had little proficiency in the study of principles.
Observing that these events corresponded with the words of Cui Hao,
he consequently issued an edict to burn and destroy scriptures and images.
Only the four temples remaining at the Imperial Residence were like those in Chang'an.
In the fifth year of the Taiping Zhenjun era,
another edict was issued.
From the princes and dukes down to the common people,
those who privately maintain śramaṇas shall be restricted to the fifteenth day of the second month.
If they do not emerge by the expiration of the period,
the śramaṇa shall die; if he remains inside,
his entire household shall be executed.
At that time, Sōkū respectfully submitted a memorial to the Crown Prince acting as Regent,
advising him that the execution of śramaṇas was excessive and cruel,
and furthermore, that it was not for the sake of the offense of the images.
Now it is appropriate to abolish its rites and close the gates of all monasteries,
so that the world shall no longer practice or venerate them.
The civil and military works, as well as the paintings, naturally fell into ruin.
The memorial was not accepted.
In the spring of the third month of this year, Crown Prince Huáng’s preceptor, the śramaṇa Xuánɡāo, and Hào were both slandered to death along with the Crown Prince. It was the seventh year.
An edict was issued to eradicate all Buddhist teachings and to piton all śramaṇas, regardless of their age.
Although Zonggong’s words were not adopted, he nevertheless delayed the proclamation of the imperial decree.
Those far and near each obtained the secret treasury and made flight and concealment their plan.
Sun Hao died within eleven years.
Emperor Wu was on his deathbed when he was murdered by the eunuch Zong Ai. During the early years of the Later Wei dynasty, the capital was at Pingcheng;
the imperial clan name was Tuoba.
Upon reaching Emperor Wen of the Han dynasty, the capital was moved to Luoyang,
and the family name was changed to Yuan.
During the Western Wei, they followed Yuwen Tai and established their capital at Chang’an.
When the Eastern Wei withdrew the palace and imperial precincts from Luoyang to establish the capital at Ye, Cui and Kou were both accompanying the imperial carriage.
Kou argued vehemently while Cui would not comply. Kou said:

"You, my lord, shall now have your years shortened and your lineage extinguished; you will ultimately face execution and be forced to urinate upon your own mouth. Emperor Gaozu of the Northern Zhou, believing that the śramaṇas corresponded to the "black prophecy," [acted accordingly].
Initially, when the founding emperor Hei Tai fled westward under the protection of the Wei,
his clothing and banners were entirely black.
Subsequently, the śramaṇas all came to wear yellow robes.
The common people of Qi were especially averse to them,
yet the people of Zhou said, "Nothing blacker than the crow"— this was to eliminate those of the Crow clan;
"Nothing blacker than the bean"— this was to eliminate those of the Dou clan.
There was Wei Yuansong, a man from Xinfan County in Shu who wore mourning clothes while in rebellion.

In his memorial on rebellion, he proposed the purging of those in yellow robes (*huángguān*). Zhang Bin and [Wei] were paired as fellow plowmen; they plowed together to cultivate the religious teachings. During the spring and autumn, two teams of five plows each were used. The Emperor of Jin personally received the talismans and registers (*fúlù*).
In the third month of spring in the year of Jichou (498 CE), the fourth year of the Tianhe era,
those who had heard of the auspicious news gathered for the Great Assembly of the Three Teachings,
numbering over two thousand people, both civil and military officials.
The collective deliberations on whether to promote or abolish [the practice] could not reach a decision.
In the fourth month of summer, an imperial edict was issued for Zhen Luan of the Office of the Inspector General to examine and collate the matter in detail.
In the fifth year, Luan submitted the *Xiaodao lun* (Treatise on Laughing at the Dao), which remains preserved in the canon.
The Emperor, considering that the Daoist teachings were being promulgated in such a corrupt and disgraceful manner, ordered them to be burned.
Dao’an then presented the *Treatise on the Two Teachings* (*Erjiao lun*),
whereupon the Emperor’s plan was largely abandoned.
In the fifth month of the summer of the third year of the Jiande era,
the scheme to mutually disparage the two teachings was implemented once again; thus,
both Buddhism and Daoism were cast aside like straw dogs (*chugou*— a "straw dog" being a dog made of straw).
The *Laozi Daodejing* regards all things as straw dogs; it would be unfitting to hear of burying images or executing people.
In the spring of the sixth year, the Zhou army defeated Qi.
[The Emperor] considered this a divine blessing for the eradication of heterodox teachings. On the nineteenth day of the first month of the sixth year of Jiande, he pacified Northern Qi.
He obtained the jade seal transmitted from the Qin dynasty;
it was four inches square,
and its inscription read:
Mandated by Heaven, he enjoyed long life and perpetual prosperity.
He obtained fifty-five prefectures and one hundred and sixty-one commanderies.
There were three hundred and eighty-five counties,
with a total of three million two thousand five hundred and twenty-eight households and thirty million two hundred and eighty-six inhabitants.
In the second month, the Master returned. In the seventh year, the era name was changed to Xuānzhèng.
That year, he did not reach the autumn sacrifice (cháng), for he passed away at Yúnyáng; "cháng" here refers to the autumn sacrifice.
In the sixth month, the Emperor passed away.
The Crown Prince Yǔn ascended the throne; on that day, Emperor Xuandi changed the era name to Xuānzhèng.
He later changed it again to Dàchéng and then to Dàxiàng.
Debauched by wine and women, he imposed a tax of one coin on every person entering the market.
He soon established his crown prince as emperor and styled himself the Emperor Tianyuan; for a greedy man prizes profit above all else.
What regard did they have for their sovereign and parents?
Like Shangchen and Kuai Kui, they showed no aversion to evil. Shangchen was the crown prince of King Cheng of Chu;
he murdered his father and yet was further bestowed with a derogatory posthumous title.
The father’s eyes did not close.
His posthumous title was changed to "Cheng" (Accomplished),
whereupon his eyes closed and he accepted the mouthfuls of food.
Kuai Kui, the crown prince of Duke Ling of Wei, desired to kill his mother, Nanzi;
failing in this, he fled. When the Duke passed away, they established Kuai Kui’s son, Zhe, on the throne.
Father and son then attacked one another in their struggle for the state, killing each other as they entered and exited the capital.
How could he avoid an evil reputation? The Tuoba killed the crown prince Yuanzi, Huang, on account of slanderous words; it was reported that he had committed lewd acts within the inner palace.
The Emperor was enraged.
Huang feared execution and plotted rebellion;
the Emperor then feigned death and sent for the Crown Prince to come.
He was placed inside an iron cage and beaten three hundred times;
he was then killed and cast among thorns.
Zong Ai, the Palace Attendant, soon thereafter murdered Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, as Yuwen had harbored suspicions and resentment toward his chief minister, the Duke of Jin, Yuwen Hu.
He served as Grand Chancellor (Taizai) and held the administration of government.
In the third month of the first year of the Jiande era, the Emperor became suspicious of and resented him.
The Emperor himself used a mallet to strike and kill him within the palace.
While the Emperor personally managed the myriad affairs of state, the other [Wu] treated his own kinsmen like sea monsters (*jingni*).

How could he possibly have been benevolent and forgiving in matters of Dao and virtue? Sea monsters are large fish that love to fight; thus, even today there is not a child three feet tall who does not clasp their hands together and sigh deeply over this matter—to clasp the palms is to speak while gesturing with the hands. One pities those two Wus for being unable to become ghosts.
"How can you be so shameless before your ancestors? Bin replied,
"Empress Ling of the Wei dynasty built a stupa."
Exhausting the wealth of billions,
it stands firm like the work of creation;
humanity truly preserves it.
If Heaven were to abandon them,
then in a single morning they would become a calamity,
their smoke and flames blazing across the nine extremities of the earth.
The steaming heat and parching flames extend to the farthest horizons;
is it possible to discern the will of Heaven?
The host replied:
Now, all things take conformity to the proper measure as their virtue;
to lose that measure is to incur calamity.
To possess virtue is to abide eternally.
If one brings about calamity, they will perish.
The House of Hu has brought about calamity;
this is because they exceeded the bounds of the Great Strength hexagram.
Is this not merely the work of human effort, rather than the agency of spirits or ghosts?
It stands a thousand feet high and consists of nine tiers.
The golden vase atop the stupa has a capacity of twenty-five hu;
it features eleven tiers of golden dew-receiving basins,
with four iron chains extending from each corner to anchor the stupa.
Golden bells hang from it, each as large as a one-bushel vessel;
on each of its four sides there are three gates,
with six windows interspersed between them.
The vermilion gates are adorned with engraved rings;
the embroidered pillars feature golden door-knobs.
In the clear autumn night, they shimmer and blaze, illuminating the void.
The resonant clanging of its bells could be heard for more than ten li;
it was vast and expansive in its expanse, with its ascending and descending terraces rising steeply and majestically.
It is the foremost dwelling in Jambudvīpa. The *Yì* says:
"In ancient times, people lived in caves and dwelt in the wilds;
later sages replaced these with houses and palaces."

"Raising the ridgepole above and placing the eaves below to await wind and rain"—this was taken from the image of Dazhuang (Great Strength). Indeed, none who violate humility or transgress propriety can achieve such strength; even when at its height, it must reach its limit.
To the south, there was a powerful neighbor.
Dividing the sun and moon between them, at that time the Empress Dowager resided in Luoyang.
In the kingdom of Jinling, there were treacherous ministers.
To seek out the maladies of the ruler refers to those such as Erzhu Rong; once the gold and jade are exhausted, the exploitation of the people also becomes bitter.
Subsequently, Erzhu took advantage of these vulnerabilities.
The bridges over the Chen, Luo, and He rivers shook, and the coffins of the scholar-officials were buried among fish and turtles. Empress Dowager did not cultivate virtuous governance;
thus, Er Zhu Rong and others submitted a memorial stating:
Now, throughout the realm, everyone says that the late Emperor was harmed by poisoned wine.
You have been entrusted with this infant whose words you have yet to hear.
Having brought the four seas under his control,
Rong led his troops across the river and reached Luoyang,
where he dispatched cavalry to seize the Empress Dowager and the young heir apparent.
They were both subsequently submerged in the river. Formerly, Zhang Li and Zhang Liang, the Secretaries of State under the Later Zhao, each erected a great stupa.
Fotudeng said to them, "Serving the Buddha consists in being pure and free from desire."
With compassion as their guiding heart,
these donors have proclaimed and upheld the Great Dharma,
yet their greed and stinginess remain unabated.
Hunting without restraint and accumulating wealth without limit—
these are the very sins one shall undergo in this present life.
What blessings and rewards could one hope for?
Yeli and the others were subsequently all executed;
thus, the human mind has no place to rest.
Therefore, by relying on the pagoda and its images to discern the underlying principles, one ought to perceive the compassionate and forgiving heart of the Sage.
If, outwardly, he suppresses the wicked and promotes the good, yet inwardly he secretly harbors cruelty and tyranny; [then this would not be the case].
This must be the concentrated fruition of karmic retribution;
it is not something that even the power of a sage could avert.
Moreover, the Great Sage cut his own flesh and smeared his skin [with medicinal herbs].
In such matters, there is no duality; the Tathāgata possesses three equalities:
first, applying sandalwood paste to the left [side] and cutting with a sharp blade on the right.
Among these three people, one neither painted nor carved [the image].
Since the Tathāgata regards the minds of these three people with equal impartiality, how can it be right to grant him only a single stūpa while withholding it from the others?
Therefore, one who practices goodness should attain the ultimate good through goodness;
it cannot be attained through what is not good.
As the Book says:
"A hen does not crow at dawn.
When a hen crows at dawn, it portends the ruin of the family.
How desolate! Empress Hu has brought about the ruin of the Yuan clan; this is the text of the "Speech at Muye."
To use the analogy of a woman governing state affairs:
it is like a hen taking the place of a cock to crow; the household will surely fall into desolation.
This illustrates that although Empress Hu took charge of the government, she sought to establish extraordinary achievements for the dynasty.
In truth, she did not establish a household; she was Lady Hu Chonghua of the Northern Wei,
the Empress Dowager Ling, the consort of Emperor Xuanwu and the mother of Emperor Xiaoming.
The Emperor was made the Crown Prince,
while the Empress Dowager governed the court on behalf of the young Emperor Xiaoming.
He was licentious in the court.
He commanded his attendants to shoot at targets, punishing those who could not hit them;
he himself shot through the eye of a needle and was greatly delighted.
A high minister committed lewd acts with Yang Baibai, who possessed both talent and beauty.
The Empress pressured him;
fearing that disaster would befall him, Baibai fled to the Liang court.
The Empress Dowager’s remembrance of him was unceasing;
she commanded a scholar to compose lyrics,
which she had the palace women sing day and night, the rhythmic chanting being most piteous and mournful.
Yuan Shun, the Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate, remonstrated against this.
After Emperor Ming passed away, the Empress Dowager assumed the regency and wrote:
"The fragrance of millet and rice is not what makes one truly fragrant."
"Virtuous brilliance is fragrant.
The *I Ching* says:
"The neighbor to the east slaughters an ox."
"It is not as good as the *yue* sacrifice of the western neighbor;
for even the ghosts and spirits respond to sincerity,
how much more so the Sage?"
There may be those who claim that wealth acquired through unrighteous means is better than succumbing to evil, and thus should not be openly condemned.
Such individuals are merely followers of the Ājīvikas, who do not value the fundamental and instead prioritize the trivial.
Now, for a śramaṇa to store up goods for trade is like a mere image;
according to the Vinaya masters, such a person is neither honored nor respected, as it is contrary to the Way.
As for those who steal wealth for the sake of food, the righteous man rejects and spits out the essence of Yuan Jingmu.
Once, when he was starving by the roadside,
Huqiu saw him and gave him food.
He then asked:
"Who are you? he asked. He replied, "I am a man from Foxiu."
Out of pity for his son's hunger, he stole his father’s rice to feed him,
saying, "I am a man of righteousness."
He refused to eat food that was not his own offspring’s, and finally, pressing both hands against the ground, he vomited it up and died.
This is recorded in the *Liezi*. The *Book of Rites* says:
Once one's parents have passed away, one must seek out the grain of a benevolent person to perform their ancestral sacrifices;
this is what is called ritual propriety (*li*).
Thus we know that wealth obtained through unrighteousness does not constitute a source of blessing.
If it were truly as you argue, it would be like a petty person attempting to justify his own inferiority within a state of unrighteousness—

just as one might reward a son for not continuing his father’s excesses by claiming that not succeeding to his father’s drunkenness is a virtue, or as a thief who breaks into a chest might claim that his theft is virtuous.
"To be able to practice benevolence and righteousness is what constitutes being worthy," said Guiguzi.
"The term 'qu' (胠) refers to opening from the side;
it means to open from the side and take things out of a chest or bag. This is not the kind of instruction found in the clear and dogmatic classics."
The guest said:
"Emperor Wu of Liang exhausted his efforts in propagating [the Dharma],
and his fame crowned the universe."

It is fitting that the celestial mandate extend its far-reaching governance and that Heaven bestow eternal life; why then do you suffer fragmentation and disintegration, with even those of the same flesh and bone turning against one another?
Is this not a failure to provide for the world’s prosperity throughout your lifetime? Thus did Xiao Yan, the Emperor Wu of Liang, receive the abdication of the Qi dynasty.
His aspirations were lofty, being devoted to Buddhism;
he maintained a vegetarian diet at the ancestral temple and personally donned Dharma robes.
He gave up his body to enter the monastery;
his ministers provided the funds to redeem him and bring him back.
This continued until Hou Jing rose in rebellion.
When the Stone City fell, he died of indignation and distress;
both Emperor Jianwen and Emperor Xiaoyuan were likewise killed. The Master said:
"The mandate of destiny rests with Heaven."
To know the subtle resides in the sage;
yet even the worthy are still dim-sighted regarding it, let alone what can be said by those of meager talent—*xiǎo* meaning small, few, and thin. As for the Great System of the Xiao clan:
Occupying the position of the Great Jewel and practicing the teachings of the Sage,
yet failing to perceive the Sage’s heart— how far removed that would be!
Now, one who wears patterned robes and carries a sharp sword,
standing behind the screen to preside over the assembly of lords—
why must he diminish himself to become a palace slave? A palace slave is a person of low station.

Furthermore, you act as a menial servant for Tongbi; if you loathe the yellow palace, then align yourself with those who humble their palaces and restrain their desires. Why not follow those of virtuous conduct and practice lofty renunciation?
Why do you tread upon the golden cord yet fail to return? Why is this so?

When Jeta Grove was demarcated with golden cords, how could it have awaited the requests of rulers and ministers? When Emperor Wu of Liang, residing in the dignity of a sovereign over ten thousand chariots, surrendered his body three times to be sold as a slave to provide for the permanent endowment of the Sangha.
The court official offered ten thousand coins with the intention of ransoming him, whereupon he returned; Yang Zhu said,
"Tang Yao feigned renunciation to enjoy blessings,
while Yi and Qi practiced true renunciation yet met with starvation."
How much more so for the Liang dynasty, which suffered the simultaneous loss of both the true and the false?
Although there was peace beyond the Yangtze for forty-five years,
its administration and penal system were deficient and neglected.
Rituals and music fell into ruin;
corvée labor was not diminished; and the widowed and the orphaned had no one to turn to for help.
The ruler initiates and the ministers harmonize;
the father initiates and the sons harmonize.
They claim that they bring about orderly governance through non-action (*wuwei*).
He engaged in grand discourses on governing the state,
which ultimately allowed Hou Jing to watch for an opening and rely on the power of Heaven to establish his own tyranny.
Having already lost his person,
he also abandons his clan;
the topmost nine (the final line) is at the beginning.
How could one avoid regret? This refers to the line "The dragon goes to excess; there will be regret" at the topmost (ninth) position of the Qian hexagram.
To occupy the extreme limit of a high position leads to regret.
To speak thus is to know advancement but not retreat,
to know preservation but not loss,
and to know gain but not what is forfeited.
In the first year of the Taicheng era, Hou Jing rebelled at Shouchun;
he subsequently crossed the Yangtze River and besieged the Tai City.
Amidst the ten failures of Emperor Chen, the援軍 (auxiliary forces) lacked any will to fight.
The capital city was subsequently besieged and captured.
Xiao Jing assumed the position of Chancellor himself.
The Emperor, overcome by grief and indignation, fell ill.
His mouth became bitter, and though he sought honey, he could not find any; he died with a gasping "he-he" sound.
At the age of eighty-six, Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty said to Guṇavarman, "I, your disciple, have always desired to observe the fasts."
"If one does not kill, yet is forced to sacrifice one's body for the sake of external things and cannot follow one's own will,
how should the Dharma Master instruct such a person? Baoma replied:
The sovereign and the commoner differ in what they cultivate.
The commoner is of humble station and inferior reputation.
If one's commands lack majesty,
and if one does not conquer oneself and subject one's person to austerity, what purpose will they serve?
A sovereign takes the four seas as his home.
When the myriad people are treated as his children,
every noble word he utters brings joy to both men and women;
when a single virtuous policy is disseminated, humanity and the spirits are brought into harmony.
Truly, punishments shall not cause untimely deaths and labor shall not exhaust strength;
thus, wind and rain will follow their seasons, and cold and warmth will correspond to their proper times.
The hundred grains flourish and multiply;
the mulberry and hemp grow luxuriantly.
Such is the maintenance of purity.
Qi is also great. If one does not kill in this manner, their virtue will likewise be manifold; purity and cleanliness constitute Qi.
Is the precept of guarding against wrongdoing truly fulfilled only after one has sacrificed half a day’s meal or saved the life of a single bird?
Only then can it be called a means for great salvation?
The Emperor struck the armrest of his throne and said,
"What the Dharma Master has spoken truly awakens the minds of men and clarifies the principles of things."
This may be called a discourse upon the interface between humans and devas.
How admirable is such a person!
Not only do they lead others forward toward the Gate of Truth, but they also cause the royal transformation to flourish.
Now, as for the relationship between equanimity (*qí*) and vigilance (*jiè*),
although it reaches its ultimate principle from the Son of Heaven down to the commoner,
their fundamental texts differ— just as the five types of filial piety are not the same. The Son of Heaven regards broad love and expansive reverence as filial piety.
The feudal lords practice filial piety by being free from arrogance and by being diligent in observing the laws.
The high ministers and great officers practice filial piety by following the laws and adhering to ritual propriety.
The scholars practice filial piety by loving their fathers as they do their sovereigns.
Among the commoners, there was one who became renowned for filial piety through the careful cultivation of his person and the support of his parents—one who knew the second by hearing the first.
Was this not Wen Di of the Song? His personal name was Yilong;
he was the third son of the High Ancestor of Song.
Upon ascending the throne, he changed the era name to Yuanjia.
He possessed both civil and martial talent and harbored the virtue of broad-mindedness and clarity.

Diligent, austere, and frugal, he occupied the throne for thirty years. Had Emperor Wu of Liang accepted the counsel of the Grand Recorder (Dalu) and had his various officials followed antiquity while being prudent regarding the end, [the dynasty] would have flourished. "Lü" (麓) refers to the Recorder;
it means that he personally managed the myriad affairs of state.
In selecting and appointing the various officials, the only difficulty lies in finding the right people.
One should follow and implement the Way of the ancient emperors, exercising reverence and caution until the very end.
This is what is meant by "in times of security, one must think of danger."
This is the way to govern without forgetting disorder: to reflect upon past words.

Yet, there may be those who fail to apply this to difficult situations. If Emperor Liang had constantly reflected upon past words, I fear he would not have faced the crisis that befell his son, Prince Geng (the future Emperor Jianwen), during the rebellion of the Hou clan.

The Emperor’s third son, Lún, was Prince of Shàolíng; Jì was the Regional Inspector of Yǐzhōu and Prince of Wǔlíng. These various princes of the imperial clan frequently engaged in literary pursuits and requested that the Emperor lecture on the classics himself.
The imperial response stated:
"You have not yet grasped the hardships of sowing and reaping;
how can you know the heavy burden borne by the world?"
The reason why mediocre rulers and young princes have repeatedly met with ruin is that they all fail to contemplate danger while in a state of security;
how much more so for those who have not yet attained security?
The lessons of the Yin dynasty are not far off; they lie in the events of previous ages.
Although my current conduct differs from that of former days, I am content merely to lecture and expound upon the teachings, showing no concern for the affairs of state.
Thus, he was no different from those others who perished through their heterodox arts; for "arts" are but paths, yet he repeatedly requested them, while the Emperor likewise repeatedly rejected him.
It was simply that he was advanced in years and his faculties were clouded.
The essence has already been exhausted.
Within the family is the son of a sycophantic father;
at court there are no officials who devote themselves to public service.
What was previously denied was later granted, proving exactly as he had said, just like the prediction that they would perish together through a different means.
This came to pass when Shi Jing incited a rebellion after the Emperor’s demise;
Jing then established Jianwen on the throne.
Xunyou went to Yongfu Province to cut off all hope of being found.
Jingxun subsequently assassinated him.
Later, when Wang Sengbian defeated Hou Jing and established Emperor Xiaoyuan, [the situation changed].
Later, when the troops of the Northern Wei arrived, the city fell and he was captured.
He composed a poem and threw himself into an earthen pit to his death.
The former four rulers of the Liang dynasty subsequently returned their states to the Chen.
Regarding the three successive rulers of the Later Liang who entered the Sui as subjects, [Wang] Bin said:
"If one person loses control of the reins of government, it already invites the retribution of Heaven;
how could the hundred artisans and officials, acting in their respective duties, be at fault for being caught up in the calamity?"
"Does this mean that the deceased must carry their thighs and lean upon their heads as they continue day after day?
The host replied,
"What kind of words are these?"
"Generally, when a ruler brings humiliation upon his ministers, they die;
how much more so when the ruler himself dies?
For those who rule over the empire, it is by employing the loyal and virtuous that they are deemed sages."
Loyalty and integrity are esteemed as virtues for the protection of the state;
thus, ministers of both civil and military rank advance with the thought of exhausting their loyalty.
Reflecting upon this with regret,
I consider that although at that time I responded to the vital energy of Jinling,
it was merely by coinciding with the fortune of the era of Yong.
The court officials did not consult on strategic calculations for the state,
and the generals did not consider how to achieve victory. Consequently,

those who merely filled their posts and consumed the people's provisions each sought to advertise themselves through literary compositions— such as Shen Yue, He Shangzhi, and Yan Yanzhan— who produced works like the *Fǎbǎoliánbì* (Linked Jades of the Dharma Treasure), the *Xíngshénmièlùn* (Treatise on the Extinction of Form and Spirit), and various responses to challenges regarding the Buddha-nature and the Two Truths.
The ruler lacks his majesty;
the ministers bring harm to their neighbors—there is no escaping this.
The marquis Hai Jing entangles himself within the gardens and parks.
"One should not take on tasks for which one is not qualified. Master Zhuang said:
"Though a cook may not attend to the kitchen, he does not lose his place."
How could the sacrificial priest overstep the boundaries of the wine-vessels and ritual trays?
Formerly, when Chen Ping did not respond regarding the grain in the granaries, Emperor Wen asked Zhou Bo:
"How much grain is there in the granaries throughout the empire? How much money is in the treasuries, and how much is the daily income and expenditure?"
Zhou Bo broke into a sweat and was unable to respond to the questions concerning the military formations.
Chen Ping said,
"Matters regarding the granaries and treasuries each have their respective officials in charge."
A Chancellor merely regulates the yin and yang; Bing Ji merely inquired about the ox’s panting.
Bing Ji, courtesy name Shaoqing, was a native of Beihai.
During the reign of Emperor Xuan of the Han dynasty, he served as Chancellor.
Seeing a panting ox, he asked how long it had been since its arrival.

[The answer was that it had arrived recently. He said, "If it is recent, then the Yin and Yang have lost their proper measure. Therefore, a king should practice non-action (*wuwei*); the Son of Heaven should simply drape his ceremonial robes and stand with hands folded, wearing the crown with its hanging tassels and yellow silk plugs."
This is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). One does not employ one's own ability regarding the conditioned, nor does one employ one's own ability regarding the unconditioned.

One does not cause the ruler to act within the unconditioned; it is because the minister cannot govern that the ruler must preside over it himself. Thus, like a fire spreading across a plain, its brilliance is such that there is no pardon. As the Book says: [text follows].
Evil is easy to spread.
It is like a fire blazing across the plains;
one cannot approach it from any direction.

"Can it be extinguished by striking it down? "The carriage's spokes have fallen out, and the body is carried away. This is the line for the second nine of the Xiaoxu hexagram. "The carriage's spokes have fallen out; the disciple carries the corpse. This is the line for the fifth six of the Shi hexagram, which says: "The disciple carries the corpse; what lamentation can avail?"
The ode says:
"Be serene and respectful in your station;
grant your favor to those who are upright and just."
"The spirits hear this; they will grant you blessings.
This is from the "Jingzhi" (Tranquil Governance) section of the Xiao Ya (Minor Odes) of the Book of Poetry.
"Er" means "you."
"Shi" (式) means "to employ.
"Gu" (穀) means "emoluments.
This refers to reverently attending to your office and administrative affairs.
Only with those who are upright can one be a peer.
The Divine hears what you do;
He bestows blessings upon you. If He does not grant them to the upright, how can one hope for grain?
The guest said:
"Kauṇḍinya wears tattered robes worth five coins;
Subhūti dwells in a flower-adorned chamber of a hundred jewels."
Both were noble ones; Kauṇḍinya is also called Kauṇḍina,
and he was one of the group of five companions.
He did not seek ornamental adornments.
After Subhūti had left the household life, he did not attain the fruits of the Path for a long time.
The Buddha asked Ānanda:
Ānanda said, "It is because the implements for precious adornment are lacking.
The Buddha ordered Ānanda to provide them.
Ānanda lacked the necessary requisites;
the Buddha ordered that they be borrowed from the royal palace and spread within the room,
whereupon he immediately attained liberation.
Having realized the fruit of Arhatship, Nanyue Huisi wore a single robe for the rest of his life on Mount Heng. The eminent monk Xuanjing changed his clothes every time dawn broke;
Xuanjing invariably donned fresh garments each day.
Regarding the practice of giving to others while remaining within one's own body, both are eminent monks.
As for the four things to be cultivated within oneself, what comes first?
The host said:
"Excellent! For one who is excellent, there is nothing that is not excellent;
for one who is not excellent, there is nothing that can be made excellent.
Thus, whether these four qualities are mastered or not depends upon oneself."
Whether it is possible or not does not depend on external things; whether one can cultivate oneself or not depends on the person.
It does not arise from external objects. Why is this? For when one is poor, one may simply cultivate one's own person.
When wealthy, one should practice extensive charity and broad salvation;
when extravagant, one should be devoted to ritual propriety;
when frugal, one should draw near to benevolence.
This is the mark of the wise and virtuous.
To fall into despondency when poor and to become arrogant when wealthy— this is the meaning of the *Daxu* hexagram.
The substance of Dàxù (Great Accumulation) lies in using it to nourish the worthy;
thus, it is decreed that the worthy shall not eat at home. This is because extravagance leads to usurpation and dissipation, while parsimony leads to narrow-mindedness.
For instance, the Jì family was parsimonious yet arrogant, while Yàn Yīng was parsimonious yet lacked the proper ritual decorum.
All these are instances of being stubborn and uncultivated, or foolish and base.
Therefore, the sages are not separated by wealth or poverty;
whether in poverty or wealth, they all abide as sages.
The worthy are not separated by luxury or frugality;
whether living in luxury or in frugality, both are considered eminent monks.
As the ancients said:
Frugality is the mark of virtue and the source of respect;
extravagance is the greatest of evils.
If one lacks virtue and frugality while harboring overflowing wickedness and indulging in extravagance, this truly constitutes the womb of calamity; how can one remain at ease without trepidation?
The *Yi* says:
"He makes his house vast;
he screens his home with thick foliage."
He peered through the door;
it was silent and empty, with no one there.
For three years he had not been seen—this signifies being shrouded by the obstruction of misfortune.
This is the line-text for the sixth (topmost) line of the *Feng* hexagram in the *Yi Jing*.
Its meaning states:
"To receive emolument without virtue is a calamity for one's person."
Within three years, one will surely suffer its calamity.
Therefore it is said that [the place] is desolate and devoid of people; however, silk, cotton, and leather are permitted by the Sage’s compassionate grace.
Now, if one practices this, it constitutes a deficiency in virtue;
if one reverses it, it accords with the Way.
This is a delusion, for to wear silk and cotton is considered a deficiency in virtue.
They consider seclusion and abandonment to be in accord with the Way, yet they fail to realize that the Tathāgata possesses both the path of opening and the path of prohibition;
this is because they cling tenaciously to worldly sentiments. Thus, there are those who devote themselves to self-inflicted austerity.
Filling their bodies with hemp and mugwort,
they made their practice lofty and serene;
this is truly admirable.
If one practices hypocrisy to purchase fame—
wearing light, fine silk and trailing delicate tassels— "purchase" means to sell oneself;
"hypocrisy" means to deceive.
Fine silk cloth is merely fine cloth;
it originally possesses no moral virtue,
yet it falsely displays the appearance of solitary integrity.
They wear garments of fine cloth and socks of coarse cloth;
what frugality is there in this? Indeed, such extravagance as this wastes wealth.
Who is the upright scholar?
Now, clothing is the outward manifestation of the mind and its conduct;
if one attains the proper decorum, one will rarely suffer disgrace and seldom commit errors.
To deviate from this principle is to open the door to depravity and invite harm.
Thus, the *Rites* state:
"When a gentleman wears the sackcloth and headband of mourning, his countenance reflects sorrow."
When wearing the ceremonial cap and robes, one has an expression of reverence;
when wearing armor and helmet, one has an expression that cannot be humiliated.
Now, when this śramaṇa dwells in the rice fields, he ought to have an expression of emptiness and stillness—the rice fields being his *kāṣāya*.
The Buddha saw a field of watered rice paddies and pointed to it, saying to Ānanda:
"My disciples shall cut and sew this into robes.
This field of watered rice paddies has the significance of 'giving birth'."
One can cultivate the field of merit through emptiness, for emptiness is the Way.

Therefore, what one serves depends upon the Way; it is not necessary to insist on skins and cotton wool while promoting felt and ramie, thereby encouraging people toward deception. If one were to focus solely on promoting ramie and hemp...
Thus, those who are deceitful strive at artificial embellishment. When the Liang dynasty’s Shen Yue [argued] that śramaṇas eat meat—
claiming that while the Lesser Vehicle permits it, the Later Teaching prohibits it—
why would the same logic not apply to the matter of silk from silkworms?
However, it was not appropriate for him merely to leave this omission unaddressed;
he therefore composed the *Jiujing cibei lun* (Treatise on Ultimate Compassion) to extensively set forth its principles.
However, I fear that Shen’s explanation is incorrect. Shen [Yue],
courtesy name Xiwen,
was a native of Wukang in Wuxing.
A displaced refugee living in poverty,
he was resolute in his aspirations and fond of learning,
studying day and night without ceasing.
His mother feared he would become exhausted and often reduced the oil and extinguished the lamps. Later,
he assisted Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty when he ascended the throne like a soaring dragon.
He was promoted through successive offices to the rank of Minister (Shangshu). Having long occupied the position of Chief Counselor (Duankui),
he aspired to serve in the Imperial Secretariat (Taishi).
The Emperor ultimately did not accept it.
He sent a letter to Xu Mian,
who then spoke of it to the Emperor on his behalf.
He merely added the performance of drumming and blowing instruments.
By nature he did not drink alcohol and had few desires.
His left eye had a double pupil.
His waist bore purple markings.
He collected twenty thousand scrolls of books and served as the Governor of Danyang and a Palace Attendant.
