one *pārājika* and two *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Three *pāyattika* offenses;
four *pratideśanīya* offenses;
five *duṣkṛta* offenses.

It is only the two karmas of body and speech that are guarded; however, the ox-cart [analogy] applies to all three aggregates of body, speech, and mind. Those who fail at the beginning and end sink among dragons and ghosts, for many who break the precepts sink among dragons and ghosts; those who fulfill them from start to finish transcend to the realms of humans and devas.
Its radiance is like that of the sun and moon;
its beauty is like that of a jeweled necklace.
Thus, it is bound with *gośīrṣa* grass; the binding with *gośīrṣa* grass is as described above.
Regarding the "Protector of the Goose":
Once, there was a bhikṣu who entered a royal palace and saw a goose swallow a pearl.
Later, when the king could not find the pearl,
he suspected that the bhikṣu had taken it and questioned him.
Fearing that the goose would be killed, the bhikṣu did not speak.
The king was about to execute the bhikṣu,
yet the bhikṣu remained silent;
the goose then disgorged the pearl.
The king, knowing it was not a question,
asked, "Why did you not speak?
The bhikṣu replied:
He said, "I fear that the geese will be killed; I would rather die than waver.
He drove the dragon down and brought the geese to safety.
His sincerity was consistent throughout, just like that of a bhikṣu.
If one goes to a dragon’s dwelling and manifests supernatural powers to drive them out, they will never fail to leave.
However, if a precept-keeper goes there and snaps their fingers three times,
the dragon will depart immediately.
The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
There was a bhikṣu who maintained the precepts;
when the time for eating arrived, he brought to mind the karmic retribution of food.
The king of the geese learned of this and commanded the geese to alight on the ground so that he might offer them food.
The bhikṣu, having understood this, did not eat, saying, "Moreover, both you and I are clad in black."
On his head he wears no crown;
on his body he wears only coarse cloth.
He alone is the one for all under heaven.
There is no preference for one over another; neither is favored nor disparaged. Why then limit oneself to selecting monks based on their seniority (*la*)?
One should instead provide abundant offerings at the incense burner for monks from the age of twenty, when they have received the full precepts (*mahāśramaṇa*).

Passing through both summer and winter is what is called "summer *la*. If one's ritual conduct and standards are not governed by discipline, how can one distinguish between the dyed robes and the plain white?
Nowadays, monks simply regard those with the highest seniority in years as superior.
While occupying the seat of seniority and receiving offerings,
he was entirely unaware of cultivating and regulating his deportment. Indeed, among the practices of the sages,
none is more esteemed than fasting and purification (*śīla-vrata*).
In the hearts of the sages,
nothing is more esteemed than compassion and frugality;
were it not for their observance of fasting and abstinence, one would surely slander the conduct of the sages.
If one is not compassionate and frugal, one violates the heart of the Sage.
When one's conduct is slanderous and contrary to the heart, the eight difficulties do not fail to come upon one; the eight difficulties approach without waiting for one to walk toward them.
First, hell; second, hungry ghosts;
third, animals.
Fourth, the northern continent;
fifth, the heaven of non-conceptualization;
sixth, those born blind, deaf, or mute.
Seventh, being wise, eloquent, and sharp-witted;
eighth, [being born] before the Buddha or after the Dharma.
These are all obstacles to the Noble Path; the five sufferings do not wait for an invitation.
Thus, they create deep enmity and grievous offenses for this life, future lives, and the spirits of the afterlife,
all because of slandering [the Dharma] with their present bodies.
This causes the consciousnesses of future generations to sink into the abyss and accumulate resentment. If one adopts the vast openness of the Great Way,
then minor practices will not harm one's virtue.
In that case, what further need would there be for the Bodhisattva Precept Sūtras? If one cannot maintain the precepts of the Hīnayāna, how could one possibly maintain the Bodhisattva precepts?
Such is the nature of the Hīnayāna precepts.

Originally flowing forth from the Mahāyāna, they nevertheless still venture to claim the substance of a tiger while calling themselves mice, or assume the form of a horse while acting as monks who cannot maintain the precepts;
thus, they further exalt the great while reviling the small.

In reality, they possess the forms of dogs and rats while falsely assuming the substance of tigers and horses; though they wish to evade responsibility through borrowed terminology, they are in fact glossing over their own crimes.
An alternative explanation states:
Dhyāna is the study of the mind.
When the mind merges with the spiritual transformation, it passes away without acting;
thus, one who would halt this swift departure must exert effort.
Its movement is like surging waves; its stillness is like the silence of a deep abyss.
One should allow it to find its own natural state and let it unfold within non-action.
Why must one sit upright and wither the body to wait for the non-existent?
For one who attains it for a hundred years is but a man.
Those who do not attain it are likewise people of a hundred-year lifespan;

how much more so for those who, though they may have arrogantly established their own sectarian paths and remain mired in the obscurity of their private chambers, cannot escape birth and death even if they should happen to master its principles.
How much more so when one’s traces transcend those of Vairocana—
how could this not be a towering eminence?
Matter and mind are in a state of chaotic unity.
Is this not a state of neglect and corruption? Even if one were to gather [truth] from actual reality, who would awaken to it?
It is far better to simply allow the body to find ease through rising, sitting, reclining, and stretching.
Zhongfan delighted in lecturing and reciting, finding great pleasure therein.
He said, "As for dhyāna, I have nothing to do with it; my mind is set on lecturing and chanting, and I find no joy in the flavor of meditation. A critic remarked: [text continues]
Vague and false; remote and perilous. "Fan" means floating;
"you" means distant.
Upon hearing a heterodox teaching for the first time,
one may mistakenly perceive its superficial and shallow slander as the profound and mysterious principles of deep contemplation.
To be entirely at odds with it is perilous.
When principle is neglected, danger arises; once one has ascended only to fall headlong, this is truly a cause for reverent remorse.
Indeed, there is nothing that the five paths cannot ensnare.
The Three Vehicles are thereby like the reins that restrain a tethered horse—*sui* being the rope for ascending a carriage.
One who attains the principle of emptiness cannot have their body constrained by the five destinies;
how then could the Three Vehicles retain control over their station?
Transcending the mundane, one emerges from the clamor and dust of the thoroughfare;
one opens the profound pivot of the gate of spiritual awakening upon the Great Road of Zhuangzi.
The pivot is the mechanism of the gate, yet nothing precedes the study of Chan (Zen) for this purpose.
Therefore, those who cultivate virtue and keep themselves aloof from depravity have never failed to dwell like a corpse and consume food like a shell-insect,
until they reach the state of non-action as their safeguard.
The *ruò* is the chick of a bird.
The man who has forgotten his mind dwells like a corpse, making no movement;
he eats like a chick, not competing for food, remaining merely in a state of placid indifference. There are those who do not follow this way.
Thus, words and thoughts are as numerous as hemp seeds;
calculations and affairs are like a flowing stream;
and the physical form is driven by the mind.
Suffering and the end of one's years approach.

One is dazed and bewildered; "sui-xu" (睢盱) means to look about with wide-open eyes. "La-cu" (剌促) and "ci-ju" (趑趄) describe the manner of a hurried, small-step walk—what leisurely dwelling could there be? As for those who call themselves practitioners of Chan today:
Unable to attain tranquility,
body and mind follow after objects as they shift and change;
from dawn until dusk, one is driven in ceaseless pursuit.
How could it be said that this pertains only to those in leisurely seclusion? Rather, dhyāna (meditative concentration) penetrates both the internal and external;
while their stages differ as small or great, dhyāna involves the mind’s aversion toward lower planes and its drawing toward higher planes, thereby subduing afflictions so that they do not arise.
One performs the six practices.
This observation encompasses what is practiced within the inner teachings and outer paths, as well as within the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;

it is not merely a matter of a single word or phrase, for each varies in depth and shallowness according to one's cultivation and realization. These include the proximate and fundamental [attainments], as well as the aspects of principle and phenomena.
The Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna treatises differ in their depth and shallowness, much like the three animals—the elephant, the horse, and the rabbit—crossing a river.
This is merely the poetic expression of the ancient sages; therein, the Hīnayāna is likened to the rabbit.
The Middle Vehicle is likened to a horse, and the Great Vehicle is likened to an elephant;
this distinguishes between their depths. Formerly, during the Jin and Song dynasties...
The Tripitaka Master from the West primarily instructed them in the Dharma of Chan;
they practiced it in silence, with profound reverence and solemnity.
He did not seek to dazzle the world,
much like Zhu Daoyou, whose power of meditative concentration was profound and far-reaching.
Gao Yan was reciting the sutras when a pack of tigers came forward to listen;
one tiger alone fell asleep.
Sengyou struck his head with a *ruyi* (wish-fulfilling gem) to make him listen,
but Guṇavarman did not rise for several days.
His disciples went to inquire after him.
He saw white lions standing upon pillars,
filling the sky and spreading everywhere,
from which blue lotus flowers grew.
Therefore, he was not dampened by the rain nor soiled by the mud.
In the Wei dynasty, there was Bhadra.
He transmitted the realization of the mind to Huiguang.
Guang possessed little power of meditative concentration;
in the end, he took the texts of the Tripiṭaka as his primary focus. His ancestral surname was Yang.
He was a native of Dingzhou.
When Xituo saw him, he marveled at his extraordinary qualities and kept him to enter the monastic life.
He was of peerless intelligence and wisdom,
and was thus known at the time as the "Holy Śrāmaṇera.
During the Southern Qi dynasty, he served as an official in the monastic administration.
Later, he served as the Sanghasthavira.
He was highly accomplished in literary composition, and his works have circulated in the world. Among those who followed him, only Sengchou attained the Way of Buddhabhadra.
The monk Chou used his *khakkhara* to subdue tigers and his *kāṣāya* to protect himself from hardships while at Mount Wangwu.
He saw two tigers fighting;
he resolved their conflict with his mendicant’s staff,
and they each departed.
During the Gao Qi dynasty, Lu Xiujing and others submitted a memorial proposing a trial of ritual methods against the monks;
they invoked blessings upon the monks' robes and alms bowls, which then soared and fluttered through the air.
Da Tongling Tanxian confronted him.
He then cast a large wooden beam into the air and placed Master Zhou’s patched robe upon it.
Thereupon, although they performed incantations and ritual methods, none could move him.
The Emperor was greatly pleased; previously, when Sengchou entered meditative absorption, he did not emerge for nine days.
Bhadra said, "From the Pamir Mountains onward, you are the foremost among those who study Chan;
you are truly such a person."
At the end of the Eastern Wei dynasty, Bodhidharma presented the Dharma of the Four Practices, which comprehensively encompasses the profound and mysterious essence. As for these four practices:
first is the practice of repaying resentment.

Second, one follows conditions: whether encountering love or hatred, one accepts them with a willing heart, for these are entirely the result of one's own past actions and involve no resentment toward others.
This is "acting in accordance with conditions."
This means being without joy or anger toward any object.
Third is the practice of seeking nothing,
which means being free from greedy desire.

Fourth is the Practice in Accordance with the Dharma (Chengfahang), which is the principle of the intrinsically pure and perfectly luminous nature. Regarding the transmission of the Dharma to Huike, the first patriarch: Huike encountered bandits who severed his arm.
He governed his mind with the Dharma,
never experiencing pain or affliction;
he would often praise the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, saying:
It is deeply lamentable that after four generations, this sutra has been transformed into mere names and appearances.
Sengcan, Daoxin, Hongren, and Huineng constitute these four generations.
Thereafter, the transmission of the mind was mostly conveyed through names and designations, continuing down to the Sixth Patriarch.
It then split into the Northern and Southern schools,
each citing the strong and disparaging the weak.
They vied with one another regarding their merits.
However, to distinguish between their relative decline and prosperity, one need only examine their words and deeds: Shenxiu was the Northern School, while Huineng possessed the divine.
Huineng is the Southern School. Generally, a stone is not lustrous unless it is jade;
a pool is not majestic unless it contains a dragon.
So it is with those who possess the Way.
The mind is vast and far-reaching;
thus, when the sounds of bells and drums are struck with fury, they manifest martiality.
Struck by sorrow, one grieves;
struck by joy, one delights.
As the mind changes, the voice follows accordingly.
There has never been one who had attained the Way and possessed the wisdom of a sage, yet spoke with the words of a fool.
In the past, I observed the Chan school of Jingzhong;
it was revered without being arrogant.
He was broad in learning yet not given to flattery;

he never followed the eccentric nor sought to startle the common world, truly a man of great wisdom who dwelt in leisurely composure. He was the Venerable Master Jin of Jingzhong Monastery in Shu, titled Chan Master Wuxiang.
He was the third crown prince of the Silla kingdom.
He entered the monastic order at Namsungsa Temple in Wonsaek-gun in his native land and arrived in the capital in the sixteenth year of the Kaiyuan era.
Later, he entered Shu and arrived at Zizhong,
where he paid his respects to Master Xian to study dhyāna-concentration.
He then settled at Jingzhong Monastery in Shu.
He entrusted the Dharma-gate to his disciple Shenhui.
Furthermore, there were Huiguang of Nanyin,
as well as An-seng, Liang-seng, and others.

All followed the teachings of Chan as their primary doctrine; they prostrated at his feet to take him as their teacher and requested instruction in these principles. Yet, those who studied remained complacent because they had not yet seen Ban Chui’s work on the curved rafters and roof-beams—Ban Chui being a master craftsman.
The *ying* are the pillars;
the *meng* and *dong* are the ridgepoles and rafters.

One does not encounter the likes of Huan Rong, yet one indulges the afflictions of one's own lungs and entrails. Huan Rong was a famous physician of antiquity from the state of Qin; if he were here today, it would simply be a matter of searching within oneself with precision.
If one considers external matters alone to be the source of one's own entanglements,
it is like heading north in a wagon while intending to reach Chu; the wagon’s yoke is bound for the north,
yet Chu lies in the south.
Nowadays, students are unable to investigate thoroughly or penetrate with clear insight;
they merely seek out words and phrases, which instead become a source of self-entanglement—
like heading north while entering the south.
In the end, they could not reach it. An alternative tradition states:
"Among those who practice dhyāna, none surpass our Master.
His dhyāna is called the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. It was transmitted from the Buddha to Mahākāśyapa."
From Bodhidharma down to our own teacher,
mind has been transmitted to mind.
Other schools cannot compare with ours. The Tripitaka Master Prajñādeśa brought ten fascicles of the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa Sūtra* and, at Guangzhou, translated them together with Fang Rong.
This was presented to the Empress Dowager;
it is what is called the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden (Yuan-dun).
All of these were masters of the Chan school, yet critics said:
A person of good fortune uses few words.
Merits are not rewarded for their own sake;
how much less could one who lacks merit yet falsely claims credit over others be considered fortunate?
The *Fofa chuan* (Biographies of the Dharma-transmitters) contains only twenty-four individuals.
The four masters following Śīlabhadra, such as Śeṇaprabha and others, are all sectarian accounts from other lineages recorded in the *Baolin zhuan*. Furthermore, the twenty-ninth name is Dharmatrāta.
It was not Bodhidharma. Among those holy sages who transmitted the Dharma,
there were occasionally śrāvakas interspersed.
Although Kāśyapa and others had turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna],
they still possessed only limited wisdom; thus, even though Kāśyapa, Ānanda, and the rest received prophecies on Vulture Peak, [their realization remained incomplete].
Since you are still but a minor sage, how could you possibly transmit the Buddha’s seal of mind?
Long ago, Śāṇakavāsin told Upagupta:
"The samādhis of the Buddha are unknown even to pratyekabuddhas."
The samādhi of a pratyekabuddha is unknown to śrāvakas;
the samādhi of the great śrāvakas is unknown to the other assembly of śrāvakas;
and even the samādhi of Ānanda is now unknown to me.
I am now in samādhi, which even you do not know;
such a samādhi shall all cease with my passing.
Furthermore, there are seventy-seven thousand Jātaka-sūtras,
ten thousand Abhidharma texts,
and eighty thousand pure Vinaya rules.
They shall likewise perish with me;
therefore, those who transmit the Dharma transmit only its words,
while those who inherit the Dharma realize the mind through the words.
This means that although one has attained the Dharma and what is called "contemplative wisdom," it is merely the transmission of words and phrases. It is like the art of wheel-making:
one may transmit the craft, but not its subtle essence. King Huan of Qi [realized this].
While the Duke was in the Hall of Books,
Lun Pian was carving wheels beneath the hall. Putting down his mallet and chisel,
he ascended the steps and asked Duke Huan:
"I venture to ask: what are the words you read, sir?
The Master replied, "The words of the sages."
He asked, "Is there perhaps a sage among us?
The Duke replied, "He has already passed away.
He said, "In that case, what is it that Your Majesty is currently reading?"
"These are but the dregs of the ancients.
Duke Huan said,
"I have been reading books."
How could a wheelwright dare to debate this?
If he has an explanation, that is the end of it;
if he has no explanation, he dies.
Lun Pian said, "I am a craftsman.
Judging from my own work of carving wheels:
if I carve too slowly, they are smooth but not firm."
If it is too hurried, one suffers and does not enter [the state of concentration]. When neither too slow nor too hurried,
it is attained by the hand and responds to the mind, such that words cannot express it.
There were several sons who survived among them;
yet, during that time, the father could not fully explain it to his son,
and the son likewise could not receive it from his father.
For this reason, at the age of seventy, he grew old while carving wheels.
The ancients and those who transmitted their teachings have passed away;
yet, such is what you, my lord, are reading.
The lute of Shi Xiang is the dregs of the ancients.
Having obtained the lute but not its numerical principles,
Zhongni was in Wei and studied the lute under Master Xiangzi.
After ten days he had made no progress.
Master Xiangzi said,
"He can now advance further."
Confucius said,
"I have practiced its application,
yet I have not mastered its underlying principles."
Yanzi said, "By practicing these calculations, one can increase [one's understanding].
Confucius said:
"I have not yet attained my ambitions," he said.
After a pause, he added,
"If one practices these ambitions, they can be further increased."
Confucius said,
"I have not yet been able to understand this man.
After a short while, he added:
What he cultivated was serene; he contemplated deeply.
Suddenly, he felt a sense of joy as his gaze rose loftily and his aspirations became far-reaching.
He said, "I have found the way to be a true man."
Dark and silent; tall and imposing.
His eyes gaze like those of a wild sheep, as he surveys the four quarters like a sovereign king—this must be King Wen! Who else could have done this?
Master Xiangzi left his seat and bowed, saying:

"The Master likely said that this is the 'Performance of King Wen. Thus, there are those who practice for a long time without success, and there are also those who realize the truth as soon as they resolve their minds."
Some may attain it through a subtle current alone;
those of exceptional talent do not realize this, for what is truly precious lies in profound resonance,
not necessarily in formal transmission.
Yet now, all these schools practice meditation;
how then can one know the Buddha?
Is meditation merely the specialty of a single school, as has been transmitted by the venerable masters of old?
Each has their own founding master. A divergent account states:
"Once Bodhidharma had been appointed as the transmitter of the Dharma, he sent two disciples to the land of Han.
They were banished by the people of Qin to Mount Lu, where they met Buddhabhadra. Consequently, together with Master Huiyuan, they produced the *Dhyāna-essentials Sūtra* (*Chanyao jing*)."
Upon hearing this, Bodhidharma was moved with profound resolve;
he then set out from the Western Regions, crossed the sea, and arrived in Liang.
However, the people of Liang did not place much faith in him.
Looking northward, he perceived the presence of the Mahāyāna;
he subsequently traveled to Wei. These accounts differ from those in the *Baolin zhuan* and the *Gaoseng zhuan*. Critics say:
To lose the propriety of one's words and to use crookedness to conceal the straight—
how can this be called wisdom?
However, as for the school of the Patriarchs,
the whole world turns toward its benevolence; thus,
the virtue of Chan naturally stands high.
Is it that one must wait for the transmission of the Dharma before beginning to establish a religious tradition? Yet,
there is a formal examination of the sequence of years.
Since the Bhikṣu Siṃha was already destined to reach the end of his life,
and Dharma was the twenty-ninth [patriarch],
he translated [the scriptures] during the Jin period.

What error has been made regarding the chronological order? When the disciples of Bodhidharma were expelled during the Jin period, eighty years had passed from the beginning of the Qin dynasty until the end of the Song.
Furthermore, the Southern Qi lasted twenty-four years; thus, more than a hundred years elapsed between them.

How could it be that the twenty-ninth patriarch lived two hundred years before the twenty-fourth? There was once a tradition concerning Lu Ban Fotu; Lu Ban’s words were spoken during the Spring and Autumn period, according to those of his time.

Buddhist stupas first appeared during the Jin and Song dynasties. Regarding the "Right Army" (Youjun) Prajñā, popular tradition claims it was personally transcribed by Wang Xizhi, the Right Army General of the Jin dynasty;

however, it is little known that the *Heart Sūtra* (Duōxīn jīng) was actually translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty. Furthermore, he [Wang Xizhi] likely knew of the existence of the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras only from the Spring and Autumn period.
If King Mu of Jin had resided [there],
these words would not have been spoken.
Another tradition says:
Dharmaruci committed six offenses.
When he was poisoned by the food prepared by Bodhiruci, the State Preceptor,
he vomited up five of them.
Upon reaching the sixth round,
he died without vomiting.
He then said to his disciples:
In the sixth generation of my lineage, our lives were as precarious as a thread suspended from above.
Thus we know that even the loftiest mountains, however steep, are brought down by crumbling soil.
Even the most sturdy of great trees is consumed by woodworms;
thus, it is said that while my ancestors may not have suffered long ago, there will be harm that ultimately brings grief to their descendants.
Bodhiruci is translated here as "Awakening Rare."
A native of Northern India,
he was thoroughly versed in the Tripitaka and had attained mastery in the dhāraṇīs.
His resolve was to propagate and expound [the teachings],
widely circulating them for all to see and hear.
Thus, in the first year of the Yongping era of Emperor Xuanwu of the Wei dynasty— the year of Jichou— he arrived in Luoyang.
He translated thirty-nine scriptures and treatises in one hundred and twenty-seven fascicles;
the manuscript copies he transcribed filled an entire room,
and he was also proficient in various miscellaneous arts.
He once sat at the mouth of a well and placed his ritual pitcher in the air; at times,
he would recite mantras over the well until it gushed forth water.
Drawing upon these principles to establish his practice,
Master Daoguang was a preeminent genius of his era; moreover,
he held the office of presiding abbot.
How could it possibly be so?
The *Baolin zhuan* contains a great many errors and discrepancies.
Later scholars should examine this matter even more carefully. A critic says:
"The depraved man encroaches upon the upright."
The correct becomes perverse;
the deluded scholar discourses on the truth,
yet the truth itself turns into delusion.
How tragic it is that within our own ranks, members of the Buddhist community have come to such an extreme,
harming one another for the sake of fame and profit!
It must be that his virtue was so exalted that he became an object of envy.

Shen used this to manifest his own intent, asserting that the high virtue of Dharmayaśas had been the cause of the jealousy harbored by Paramārtha and others; yet he failed to realize that he was merely harming himself, which was truly the height of folly.
In the past, during the Wei and Zhou dynasties, the Dharma was suppressed.

The Imperial Edict states: "The *Three Refutations* and other works by Master Gu—this refers to Master Gu Huan—falsely slandered the evils of the Śākya [Buddhist] teachings; compared to this, [the current situation] is not particularly severe.
As the poem says:
When people lack goodness,
they harbor resentment against one another from their own respective perspectives; is this not what is meant by that?

Indeed, when a capable general is executed on the basis of slanderous words, it truly gratifies the hearts of the enemy—such as the case of Bai Qi being put to death at Duyou. When high virtue is scorched by defamation, [the same result follows].
In truth, one provides material for the insults of external factions and the slanders of external kin; those who hear such slander do not cover their ears.
This, too, is a manner of encouraging slander.
As for the men of the Way in antiquity:
Tranquil and boundless,
all manner of excellence follows it;
therefore, even fierce tigers do not seize it.
A bird of prey does not seize its quarry by clawing; "seizing" means grasping with the talons.
It does not flaunt its majesty to display its valor—how much less so should a human being?
If one encounters poison through the six transgressions and knowingly consumes it,
why seek one's own destruction?
To eat without knowing [what one has consumed]—who would say such a person possesses the Way? Could he truly be called a sage?
As for Lingyang Wucheng, it is unheard of that he suffered from poisoned meat. Lingyang Wucheng! Lingyang Wucheng!
All those who possessed the Way in antiquity did not even resort to poison or harm; how could such things exist within the Empty Gate (the Buddhist tradition)?
Therefore, one who is truly skilled in the Way—
If one does not cause others to love oneself, yet causes them to sever their affection,
how much more so would one cause them to harm oneself?
This was the case with Paramārtha and Huiguang.
The transformative power of virtue was spread far and wide;
humans and devas looked up to him with utmost hope as he encouraged the worthy and assisted the good.
Together they propagated the teachings and customs, like those at the gate of Huiguang.
Among the ten men of virtue under Huiguang’s tutelage, their fame was manifold; yet now there is this sycophant.
"How would I dare slander or disparage Zhongni?
Therefore, I loathe those who are sycophantic and would cast them to the jackals and tigers.
Who would say that this constitutes an exhaustive critique?
Furthermore, "In hearing lawsuits, I am like other men;

in examining oneself, I consider it benevolence. If one cannot be resolute in practicing benevolence toward others, how can one be resolute in benevolence? For the benevolent person is fundamentally characterized by resoluteness and courage.
To decide and resolve is its essential meaning.
Now, when wicked people produce texts of slander and calumny directed not at the virtuous,
one who cannot yet discern right from wrong nevertheless believes them.
If this were so, benevolence would have no room for resolute action. Therefore,
the way of the gentleman is to measure others by reflecting upon himself.
It is simply loyalty and reciprocity. To measure others by one's own standard is what is meant by loyalty and reciprocity.

In ancient times, the lords of Yu and Rui disputed over land and were even ashamed before the Lord of Xi (the Duke of Zhou). The two states of Yu and Rui contended over a field and brought their dispute to litigation.
Year after year they could not reach a decision,
so they said to one another,
"The Chief of the West is benevolent."
"Why do you not go and consult him?
Having entered his territory, he saw farmers yielding the boundaries of their fields to one another.
The practitioner yields the path;
the court officials yield their positions, saying,
