Wearing tattered robes,
sitting beneath a tree,
he takes but one meal a day.
Possessing only the three robes,
he constantly sat and did not lie down;
he gazed upon the dead.
They did not eat meat.
All such as these, through their dhūta practices, went directly to see the Buddha.
The Buddha, perceiving their fewness of desires, praised them.
Only those who are not of few desires realize that this is the practice of *pratisaṃlayana*.
It is through us that we follow the example of Andhaka;
by following Andhaka, one may behold the Buddha. It was because Andhaka possessed few desires that he beheld the Buddha.
Those with many desires led one another toward having few desires; previously, the ninefold scriptures were preached to glorify dwelling in a city,
yet such dwelling was devoid of reality.
When one reaches the place of treasures, the Buddha’s teachings of the provisional and intermediate vehicles are called "expedient devices.
It is like a person who wishes to reach a place of treasures.
When their resolve wavered midway,
the Guide then conjured a city of nirvana in the middle of the road as a provisional destination for the treasure.
To rest for a while is merely a provisional means;
leading them further toward the precious realm,
the ninefold teachings of the Hīnayāna are identical in their verbal expression.
Their intentions are always different.
There are cases where the words diverge while the underlying meaning is harmonious, such as in the *Anusāsana-sutta* (Teaching Discourse), which states:
"A bhikṣu should not bared his shoulder."
The Great Sage has bequeathed this reprimand.
In the *Dharmapada-sūtra*,
it is said that one should bare the shoulder but not both shoulders simultaneously.
Furthermore, regarding the reprimand: "to bare" means to expose the shoulders.
When both shoulders are covered across the back, it is not "bared. Śāriputra spoke these correct words.

It appears that the point regarding what to adopt and what to reject has not yet been clarified; it is not known whether one should follow the Buddha’s words to perform offerings while baring the shoulder.
One should not bare the shoulder when acting as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*);
what is valued is the proper timing.
It is not that the "hard" and "white" can be separated; rather, taking and discarding are appropriate to the occasion, and advancing or retreating follows the exigency of the moment.
This is not like being ground without being worn away, which alone constitutes true firmness.
"Though dyed black, it remains unsullied; how could its whiteness ever be lost? Thus he once told King Bimbisāra:

"Do not permit wicked bhikṣus to cause the field of the Saṅgha to become overgrown and defiled; their sin is greater than gouging out the eyes of the entire trichiliocosm. At one time, the Lord of Rājagṛha [instructed] that for a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts, one should treat him like a withered *campaka* flower or a royal official in plain white robes, and must not subject him to corporal punishment. The *Śāsana-śeṣa-sūtra* says:
Though the campaka flower may wither,
it still surpasses all other flowers;
so too do monks who have broken their precepts.
This is still superior to the various non-Buddhist paths.
Furthermore, it says:
"If my bhikṣus should violate the laws of the king..."
They may kill or beat them;
they may strip away their monastic robes and force them to return to secular life;
or they may drive them out of the country.
To slaughter and skin three hundred oxen is a sin that is still relatively light; this is because a benevolent king exceeds in benevolence,
whereas a foolish person indulges in wickedness, and a wicked king exceeds in evil.
Fearing that people might act with partiality or excess and thus lose the middle way, two sutras were established to prevent such harm.
The *Śīlasūtra* first enjoins that one should successively exhort and admonish one another.
Throughout one's life, one should simply observe the *Śīla-sūtra*.
Regarding the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, there is the text concerning the three admonitions.
Furthermore, the *Saptabuddha-śīla* states:

"One should simply observe one's own conduct and not observe whether others act rightly or wrongly; for those who can rectify themselves but cannot rectify others, the ruler should cause them to admonish one another.
As for those who boast of their own goodness and delight in disputing over their faults—"
The regulations require that one withdraw for reflection on all that has already occurred.
When there is a matter to conceal, one speaks the truth;
as was the case with Gavāmpati.
Having dropped a few grains of millet,
he was reborn as an ox for five hundred lifetimes;
he shall yet have further karmic retribution as an ox.
Yet it illustrates but a single instance: namely, the monk Gomayapāṣi (The Cow-Chewer).
In a past life, he plucked a stalk of grain and dropped several grains of millet;
for five hundred lifetimes, he was born as a cow with hooves and a mouth.
Fearing that the people of the world would criticize him,
the Buddha then had him reside permanently in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where Anuruddha (translated here as "Unextinguished") was provided with a single meal daily;
thus, for ninety-one kalpas, he enjoyed the pleasures of gods and humans.
That foremost in the divine eye accomplished it over many kalpas by means of virtuous conditions mutually supporting one another; yet,
it originated from a single meal.
This is to conceal the derivative and emphasize the fundamental.
It is like when people in the world refer to a wealthy person who eats but a single gold coin.
He began with a single coin and subsequently became wealthy.

Now, if those who equally attain the Ten Titles differ in strength and weakness such that their prostrations vary in abundance or scarcity, it is because although they equally achieve Buddhahood through the Ten Titles, the benefits obtained from paying homage to them while one still possesses views are not the same; this is merely a matter of citing a single moment or a single practice.

Yet they demonstrate that conditions are not uniform: for instance, the Western Paradise is specialized in welcoming and guiding beings, while the Medicine Buddha is specialized in rescuing those from calamities;
thus, there is a principle behind this, and it would be an error to speak of one as superior to the other.
It is like drinking alcohol while holding a jewel;

it is certainly not something prohibited by the *Śramaṇera-śikṣāpada-sūtra*. Devadatta was recorded as entering hell for one kalpa because he committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*); Devadatta entered hell for one kalpa because he, with a heavy heart, harmed ants.
The gravity of the sin of intentionally killing an ant with a superior grade of hatred is greater than that of killing a person through negligence;
although the latter is minor in terms of the actual act.
Yet, when it comes to human sentiments, they reach their ultimate limit;
these are all words of the Sage’s most profound censure.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
I say that those who have attained the stage of Srotāpanna can achieve Buddhahood. You do not understand my intention;

when I say they do not attain Buddhahood, I am speaking based on those whose minds have not yet turned toward practice. You likewise do not understand my intention; when I speak of those with fixed natures who have extinguished their bodies without turning their minds, [it is for them that I say so]. Truly, the August Sage illuminates the capacities of beings.
The unfolding and rolling up [of the teachings] are not fixed; they are fixed only insofar as there is a purpose for instructing those who follow according to their capacities.

Thus, the human and celestial realms were explained first, and subsequently, these were diminished by means of the Truths and Conditions. "Human and celestial" refers to the five precepts, the ten wholesome paths of action, and so forth.
The "Truths" refer to the Four Noble Truths;
the "Conditions" refer to the twelvefold dependent origination. Having previously explained the Truths and Conditions, he subsequently subsumes them within the One Vehicle.

He causes [beings] to abandon the sheep and deer carts and proceed toward the great white ox cart; having reduced what is to be diminished until nothing remains to be diminished, they finally return home.
It is said that the Great Way has its own means of instruction and does not rely on others.
This is like the first assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
where lesser sages were present in the audience.
The eighth assembly was so obscured that even those of minor sagehood present in the hall could neither see nor hear.
This is because it is not their realm;
it is only upon reaching the ninth assembly that they are able to see and hear it. This is because there are those who do not follow the teaching.
It was like the first turning of the wheel of Dharma,

when twelve billion beings resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path. This refers to the Buddha’s first teaching of the Dharma to the elder Trapusa immediately after his initial attainment of enlightenment.
Twelve hundred million beings attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), subsuming the branches back into the root.
Immeasurable humans and devas attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Indeed, such as this is neither to probe the profound nor to fail to reach it.
In ancient times, when Zhongni compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals to record praise and censure,
the disciples of You and Xia did not dare to add a single word;
was this not because their wisdom did not equal his?
As for such instances as being questioned about benevolence or government and acting upon what one hears immediately— the questions asked were all the same,
yet the responses given differed; it is like the *Analects*, where although ten thousand streams all provide nourishment.
Yet one does not sully its source. Therefore it is said:
"When trustworthiness approximates righteousness, one's words can be fulfilled; where there is righteousness, trustworthiness is not necessarily required.
This means that one may examine and verify them. Formerly, the Great Śākya clan [was led by] Maudgalyāyana.
In ancient times there was an immortal who dwelt in a secluded place in the mountains;
he constantly gathered mung beans to eat.
He took this as his clan name, becoming known as the Clan of the Bean Gatherer (Cai-shu).
The mother of the Venerable One was a member of this lineage. He could predict that it would rain after seven days, and he could also predict that it would rain on the seventh day when it did not.
Thus, Maudgalyāyana observed that it was not a small matter; the white calf of the female cow would ultimately prove to be exceptional. Furthermore, he recorded:
"In the house of a brāhmaṇa, a female cow gave birth to a calf whose forehead was white and whose tail was white."
All of this was due to Maudgalyāyana’s lack of circumspection; five hundred of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) collectively used their divine eyes to examine the heavens and the earth,
yet they all arrived at two or three different accounts.
Indeed, the division between principle and phenomena may sometimes be at odds.
Now, the twelvefold teachings are like the alternating cycle of day and night.
The cold and heat have their months;
medicines have their distinct flavors.
If these are lacking, one's strength will diminish.

If there is too much, it lacks essential focus; all that has been mentioned above is a dharma that must not be omitted, and this is likewise true for the *Vibhāṣā*. It states that just as one cycles through the Four Noble Truths three times, if one were to discuss them exhaustively, it would be endless.

To cycle through the Four Truths three times means to reduce the objects of cognition (*ālambana*) and reduce the modes of practice (*ākāra*) during contemplation. Now, the Mahāyāna "I" does not obstruct the attainment of the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.
Regarding that Vatsīputrīya school, there was an ancient seer who fathered [a son] by a cow; therefore,
they are called the Vatsīputrīyas, or some maintain this view.
Yet everyone regards the nature of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) as the self;
I do not believe this.
Therefore, Vasubandhu composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*.
There are two schools of tenets;

indeed, one does not consider a single school to be the gateway to ultimate perfection. Vasubandhu originally left the household life within the Sarvāstivāda school, yet his explanations of doctrine mostly followed the Sautrāntika.
As it says in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* composed by Dharmottara:
If the arising of various afflictions is what the Noble Ones describe as "outflowing" (sāsrava),
Dharmatrāta felt that the term "arising" was too broad and overlapped with cessation and the path;
he therefore separately composed the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, stating:
If one increases various afflictions, the Noble Ones call this "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
Asanga composed the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*;
Vasubandhu composed two [treatises on it]. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Asanga composed the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Since the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu also composed [a commentary], it is said there are two.

Whether reckoned by age—elder and younger brother—or by the relationship of teacher and disciple, or by spiritual rank and position, Vasubandhu did not precede him in any of these respects. Asanga, Vasubandhu, and Siṃhabuddhi were three brothers.
He was a native of Puruṣapura in Northern India;
this is translated as "Land of Men.
It is the place where the devas battle the asuras.
Both were ordained in the Sarvāstivāda school.
Asanga first awakened to the Mahāyāna;
he traveled to Tuṣita Heaven to request Maitreya to expound the *Yogācāra*.
The claim that he later exhorted Vasubandhu to realize the Mahāyāna is not correct;
it is merely because Asaṅga’s cognitive obscurations had not yet been eliminated that his strike did not reach the horse’s belly.
A foot may be shorter than an inch; likewise, the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) is [shorter] than the obscuration of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa).
The *Zhuo zhuan* says:
"Though a whip be long, it cannot reach [the horse's tail]."
This refers to the "horse's belly," a metaphor for those who, though they have composed treatises without attachment, still fail to reach the ultimate point. Thus,
Bhāviveka and his disciples vowed to wait within the Asura cave until the attainment of Buddhahood under the Dragon Flower (Nāgapuṣpa).
Just as he was about to seek guidance therein,
it was said that Maitreya was not yet omniscient; thus, the Bodhisattva Bhāviveka struck the Asura cave with a mustard seed and waited in concealment for the descent of Maitreya Buddha.
"I am about to ask of matters that remain undecided.
Now, Maitreya Bodhisattva is not yet the Ultimate Sage; later, when Devarāja assumes the form of a dragon, he will be able to see him, though he shall not prostrate before him."

Furthermore, he sought him by means of his physical appearance; how could he have reached Tuṣita to see Maitreya? He did not prostrate because [Maitreya] manifested the form of a celestial being. Previously, the doctrine of *nirvāṇa* as eternal permanence had not yet existed in the Middle Kingdom.
He merely stated that his lifespan was exceedingly long.
Master Huiyuan sighed and said,
"The Buddha is the ultimate."
"At the ultimate limit, there is no change.
How could the principle of non-change ever come to an end?
Thereupon, Huiyuan of Mount Lu composed the *Dharmatā-śāstra*. When Kumārajīva saw it, he said:
The people of the borderlands had not yet possessed the scriptures,
yet they naturally accorded with the underlying principles; how marvelous this is!

Zhu Daosheng lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and asserted that even those of the icchantika nature could all attain Buddhahood. The scholars of the old school regarded this as heterodox teaching and banished him,
casting him out at Huqiu Mountain.
He subsequently traveled to Mount Lu;
when the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra arrived,
it was indeed in perfect accord with the teachings of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* that he had previously contemplated.
There is a class of icchantikas who lack the spiritual lineage and will never become Buddhas;
yet, when the *Nirvāṇa-parivarta-sūtra* arrives,
it states that all sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood.
The result accorded with the meaning established by Master Daosheng; thereupon, Daosheng ascended the Dharma seat.
After several rounds of debating the doctrine, his fly-whisk fell down in a flurry.

He leaned on his armrest and passed away in accordance with the transformation [of death]. This was because Śāṇakavāsin had not yet died in his former life and thus remained subject to conditions; since the *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra* had not yet arrived, he waited for it.
Now that he has arrived, he has reached his end.
People of the time called him "One Who Endures Life and Death," for he lived in the present while awaiting the completion of his death.
Had it not been for Master Wusheng’s knowledge of penetrating the ultimate meaning, [this would not have been possible].
Thus, the luminous Buddha-nature remains hidden from those who lack understanding.
At the beginning of the dynasty, Xuanzang traveled to the Western Regions.
Taking flowers, he made this request to the image of Avalokiteśvara:
"If all sentient beings truly possess Buddha-nature,
let these scattered flowers hang upon the neck of the Bodhisattva."
He then immediately granted his wish.
Now it is said:
"If only Xuanzang had possessed the insight of Master Sengzhao."
Then there ought not to be such a prayer.
If one were to pray for what is inauspicious,
would it not lead to a lack of faith?
Now, divination is for resolving matters where doubts remain;
if there is no suspicion, what need is there for divination? The *Yi* says:
"When one harbors doubt at the center, the expressions become ramified.
Am I not, Xuanzang, one who has compared and corrected these ramifications?
If Master Xuanzang were to harbor doubts regarding the Way of the Ramifications, it would mean that such things exist as external objects."
"Indeed, it is by leading beings into doubt that one carries away their minds. I, Xuanzang, originally had no doubts;
I only fear that later generations might harbor them."
Therefore, this was shown to guide them.
"To carry away" means to disperse.
It refers to the subsequent doubt that falls within and scatters [the mind]. This is from the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* composed by Tanyan.
Concerned that his thoughts did not accord with the Sage’s inner intent,
he placed the petition before the Śāriputra Stūpa,
burned incense, and requested a sign of verification.
He emitted light from his śarīra,
which shone continuously through three days and nights without ceasing;
yet, the followers of Jingying did not accept this.
The work composed by Master Chang concludes with the phrase "finally driving side by side.
Now, once the Moon-God (Wangshu) has taken the reins, there is no need for the sunstone (zaidui); "Moon-God" refers to the moonlight.
Once the moonlight has appeared, [the sun is no longer required].
The practitioner does not need to rely on holding a torch; once the name "Yi" (Curtain) is established as a clan, how could one expect to privately sprinkle it?

"Yi" refers to the thundering clouds. Once the thundering clouds are spread, the sweet rain nourishes everywhere. Yet, in a house with its doors closed, the ornate lamp-stand alone is raised; though the moonlight flows forth, the fragrant lamp still illuminates [the interior]. The old man tending the garden waters his own vegetables with a bucket and rope; he must surely irrigate the greens. This is truly because—
Distant light does not illuminate the innermost recesses,
and torrential rain does not nourish the roots;
this is because each considers what is beneficial to itself to be beautiful.
Critics held that while Huiyuan’s compositions were elegant and precise in their phrasing,
Huicheng’s works were grand and comprehensive in their thematic outlines;
thus, scholars extolled the merits of both.
To seek virtue while failing to move the spirits,
and to prolong one's life while neglecting the distant [truth], is a matter of reproach.
Bei Yuan was a contemporary of Tan Yan.
They both authored commentaries on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
Yan was extensive and erudite in his literary style,
while Yuan was concise and precise in his exposition of the essential meaning.
Later, the commentary by Daoyuan was widely transmitted rather than that by Zhiyan;
this was because [Daoyuan’s work] possessed the spiritual efficacy of the *Fàngguāng* (Prabhāsa) tradition. Thus, it is said in ancient times:
"Though one possesses the wisdom of a water-carrier, one does not lend out the vessel. Du Yu (Du Yu) commented:
"The wisdom of a water-carrier is that of a minor intelligence."
Although what is maintained by those of limited wisdom cannot be entrusted to others, in matters of Dharma and meaning, they act as craftsmen.
Now, regarding current practices,
all hold the Central Kingdom’s traditions to be the pinnacle of excellence.
In the Sanskrit language, the new translations are all considered authoritative.
To examine this in detail:
the systems of governance established by the various kings of the Five Indias differ from one another.
How much more so regarding the differences between ancient and modern eras, and the variations in customs, governance, and disorder!
To examine the origins:
the Great Sage, according to the specific conditions of each land he reached, [adapted his teachings].
Teachings are expounded according to specific circumstances;
how could they be identical in their regulations, like using the same weights and measures—*liang* (weights) and *heng* (scales)—for all?
Thus, regarding *yojana* and *krośa*, there are differing accounts concerning distance: eight *krośas* are said to constitute one *yojana*.
Some say sixteen *li*, others forty; thus the distances differ.
The summer retreat (*varṣā*) is adjusted by the intercalary month.
There are many varieties regarding the duration of the retreat, and there are seven types of *varṣā*.
The first retreat begins on the sixteenth day of the fourth month;
the middle retreat begins on the seventeenth day and ends on the fifteenth day of the fifth month.
The later retreat begins on the sixteenth day of the fifth month.
It involves four types of mental recitation (*cittotpāda*): face-to-face (*pratyakṣa*), for one who has forgotten, for the accomplishment [of the retreat], and for the boundary (*sīmā*).
Furthermore, there are four kinds of boundaries.
One foot and a boundary;
two feet and a boundary;
one foot and a monastery enclosure (ārāma).
The two-footed [human] and the blue [non-human], together with the preceding, constitute seven.
Regarding the five classes: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs.
In the preceding *anvārambhaṇa* (early retreat), there are five times seven, which is thirty-five;
in the subsequent [retreat] there are likewise thirty-five,
totaling seventy.

In the mid-summer retreat (*antarā-vassa*), there are only two types of formal procedures: the mental intimation (*cittavijñapti*) and the face-to-face (*saṃmukha*). These two, each consisting of five parts, total ten;
together with the other [eighty], they constitute eighty.
The "mental intimation" for the retreat refers to the ritual performed when one dwells alone without anyone else present.
Regarding the formal declaration (*pratideśanā*), if one forgets it as usual and only remembers it on the seventeenth day at dawn, the *varṣa* (rainy season retreat) is still valid.
This does not apply to the middle *varṣa*, as there is no such period of one month [in that case].

Regarding the boundaries and so forth—meaning those coming from outside—it is not yet clear whether entering even with one foot into the monastery constitutes [a violation]. As for those who go there, they have not yet had the opportunity to observe everything; why then do those who come lack such limited knowledge? How can one wish to establish the teachings of a Sage spanning ten thousand regions and a thousand ages based on the customs of a single era in Central India?
The Sūtra says:
"If a person lives for a hundred years without understanding the dharma of arising and ceasing,
it is not as good as living for a single day and attaining such understanding."
There was a bhikṣu who, following his teacher’s erroneous instruction, recited:
"If a person lives for a hundred years without knowing the 'water-old crane,' it is not as good as living for a single day and beholding it."
Upon hearing this, Ānanda sighed with emotion and went to correct that teacher, but in the end he could not change the reason for his adherence to that faction.
Indeed, among teachers, none is greater than the Buddha; as for those who study after him, [they must follow his path].
Each of these masters did not accept the Buddha as their teacher;
therefore, they gathered similar-sounding words to accommodate the unenlightened masses. They dismissed the scriptures and images, claiming that the true transmission lies within one's own nature.
In our school, those who concern themselves with words and phrases— namely, the masters of exegesis—
all rely upon commentaries and treatises to examine their expressions and determine their principles.
One who has never relied on the scriptures but is thoroughly practiced in their application says:
"I received this from my teacher. As for those who specialize in exegesis, one may indeed learn by taking them as one's teachers."
It is not that one merely guards what was learned, for true illumination resides with the teacher;
rather, transformative application depends upon oneself, and commentaries may be used as "fish-traps" (*quán*).
One must not, however, cling to the trap itself; for a trap is an instrument for catching fish.

To capture the rabbit while discarding the trap is to hinder learning; when the written form reaches such extremes, one must not allow the literal text to obstruct the underlying meaning. Thus, it is that subordinate ministers may be loyal to their feudal lords yet find no trust with the Son of Heaven.
Thus, the King’s transformation of the people will flourish.
The head of the household will be loyal to the Great Officer,
yet not trusted by the feudal lords.
Then the ducal house will be endangered; this is because they have abandoned the canonical texts to cling to the commentaries. Thus, those who form factions harm their sovereign.
And yet, those [commentators] claim they are not benevolent, though they know themselves to be factionalists.
One should merely maintain strict affection and protection therein;
profit and reputation reside within it.
If one harms their own faction, what they gain will not remain with themselves.

In the past, Devadatta was ensnared by the five heterodoxies and fell into blazing fires; Devadatta entered hell due to the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*). Even today in the Western Regions, there are still those who practice his teachings.
Is this not like the pungent stench under the armpits of a "K'u-ya" fish found upon the sea?
Now, even the crow, though its odor is foul, does not dwell alone;
there must indeed be those who seek its kind, for every person has their own faction. Thus, the gentleman is reverent and diligent; "reverent" (祇) here means respectful awe.
"Ordinary" means common; small people harbor enmity toward the good.
Their factionalism is indeed extreme; it is the way they envy the virtuous and align with the wicked.
They assist one another by concealing their own inadequacies while feigning competence.
When one excels at what is evil while failing to excel at what is good,
to display such prowess in that which one does not master is like boasting about the colors black and yellow to a blind man.
To dally with the musical notes of Gong and Zhi while being deaf is merely to do so in vain.
If one were to consider the vision of Li Lou and the hearing of Shi Kuang— Li Lou seeing the fine tip of an autumn hair from a hundred paces away— then [the comparison becomes clear].
When Master Kuang heard a sound and knew whether it portended rise or decline, he possessed detailed knowledge;
I have attained the ultimate.
Therefore, his lofty discussions and extraordinary discourses were surely like boring through darkness to open a window.
One will have something to perceive.
As for the praise and censure that manifest the honoring and the decline— the honoring being esteemed and the decline being abandoned—
such praise and censure do not conform to worldly trends.
One may be called a gentleman when the whole world agrees with him;
one may be called not a gentleman when the whole world disagrees with him.
Some say: "One must examine that which many detest, and one must examine that which many love;
for instance, although Duke Ling of Wei was dissolute and depraved, Zhongni considered him an excellent ruler."
By entrusting power to the wise and bestowing authority upon the capable, one does not lose the state or the altars of soil and grain.
Although Duke Ling was devoid of the Way, he did not perish because he was not dark, ignorant, or wicked.
Wangsun Jia governed the army;
Lü Zhujie governed the ancestral temple;
and Zhongshu Yu governed matters of state guests. It was because of his employment of these men that the Master praised him, for Zang Wenzhong was profound and wise.
Zhongni considered him not worthy;
he was neither benevolent nor wise, having reached two of the three [vices]. Zang Wenzhong had three instances of unbenevolence.
He demoted Guan Qin; he allowed the ancestral sacrifices to be performed in reverse order;
and his concubines wove reeds for mats.
The three [sacrifices] were not known;
the six gates were abandoned;
the sacrifice was offered to the *yu* bird.
As for the making of hollow vessels, Guan Zhong achieved merit by unifying the nine states;
yet he descended to the level of a minor vessel, assisting Duke Huan without reaching the Way of the King, and thus he was diminished because of his hegemonic arts.
When Zi Gong caused the state of Lu to destroy its jade vessels, it was considered an unfortunate misfortune for Duke Ding of Lu in the fifteenth year of his reign.
Duke Yin of Zhu came to court; he held the jade scepter high and his countenance was upturned.
Duke Ding received the ritual fan and his countenance was downturned. Zigong said:
Judging by the rites,
both of these rulers met with death.
In this year, Duke Ding passed away.
In the seventh year of Duke Ai of Lu, the Lord of Zhu fled into exile.
All these events accorded with his words; thus, he took his mouth as a garden of rhetoric and his mind as a treasury of wisdom.
The garden does not possess the virtue of being round;
it is square and angular.
One who possesses wisdom can make it round, bringing forth the radiant brilliance of profound goodness.

Only then can it be called a mirror for human relations; "pànjiàn" (鞶鑑) refers to a mirror. Now, on one hand, there are ten thousand who falsely condemn those who harmonize, while on the other, there are ten thousand who vulgarly praise those who harmonize.
Those who follow the current and chase after clods of earth are numerous; they merely acquiesce, completely ignorant of what constitutes good and evil.
As for those who harbor the door of vulgar contention and a love for victory, they do not restrain their own folly;
they charge headlong and strike out, taking what they have practiced as their spear and shield, regarding their companions as formidable enemies—like a signal-staff thrown at a stone.
The "staff" (ji) refers to the signal-staff used in archery.
Using wood to pull stones for the purpose of striking enemies,
it is like the modern-day catapult.
What is called "abandoning" means thinking one can conceal one's position on the enemy's frontier;
yet in the lands of the border regions, there is nothing that does not harbor danger for those with whom one does not associate.
Thus, they may charge, bite, kick, and trample, which is truly to be feared. Within factions and disciples, mutual destruction arises.
This is what is meant by "hating someone so much that one desires their death. Those who propagate the arts do not necessarily require admonition;
those with refined discernment are difficult to harmonize with.
When one propagates extensively, the times do not permit such priorities.
The essence of this is that people detest those who are discerning and those who possess conduct superior to others;
thus, they are reviled by the world.
Those who possess insights born of solitary knowledge are likewise censured.
One will inevitably be met with arrogance from others; yet, one must not fail to act upon what is right simply because others do so.
Now, you disciples, as small as fluttering insects, have attempted to soar in your sparse discourse on the Dharma of Chan.
Having disparaged others as inferior and exalting oneself as superior,
one claims that what one has not heard was unheard by others,
and that what one does not know was unknown to others.
He never compared his work with that of other artisans to determine his own specialty;
thus, while he practiced minor skills, he remained ignorant of those not practiced by him.

Looking at his vessel, it was full and could admit nothing more. He entangled himself among the vulgar and fanned the flames of delusion within the ranks of the mediocre and foolish. Indeed, it is only upon waking from a dream that one realizes it was a dream.
Only upon awakening does the deluded one realize they were deluded;
had they previously been situated in the midst of that very dream of delusion.
People call him one who is deluded and dreaming;
he will surely revile and scold—“reviling and scolding” meaning angry abuse. Observing what he has composed in the past, there is little that accords with correct principle and logic.
As stated in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks):
when a parrot died, it was said to have attained "nirvana.

When Dao Fa passed away, he was called one who "transformed while sitting in meditative concentration" (*dingzhong zuohua*). All states of meditative concentration are devoid of birth and death. Master Kumārajīva’s eulogy says: "The Son of Heaven has perished; the sun has set."
It was like the collapse of heaven and earth.
For feudal lords, it was called *bēng* (薨),
sounding like the crashing of mountains.
Now, some may compare Master Shi to the feudal lords. Xuanzang’s "great relinquishment" refers to the *śuddhaka-pāyattika* (懺);
this means the relinquishment of what constitutes a downfall (*pāyattika*), specifically the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.
For example, regarding the keeping of extra robes:
within ten days, one should perform a formal relinquishment (*pratikṣepa*) by means of a face-to-face exchange between two people; this is called "relinquishing.
If more than ten days pass without relinquishing them, [one incurs an offense].
One then incurs a *naiḥsargika* offense,
which is termed a "fall" (*pāta*); therefore, it is called "abandonment and fall" (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*).
To say "abandoning wealth and repenting of offenses" (*shècái chànzuì*) now is merely a vulgar and shallow error;
it is an uninhibited way of speaking that lacks restraint.

Zhongni said: "The gentleman is simply not remiss in his speech. "Remiss" means to be casual or negligent. Thus, when the Lord of Wei awaited you to administer the government for him, the Master said:
"It must be that names are rectified. This refers to Duke Ling of Wei summoning the Master.
Zilu asked, "If you,
Master, were to go to Wei, what would you have us set out with first?
The Master said:
First, one must correctly standardize the names of all things.
If names are not correct, then speech will not be orderly;
if speech is not orderly, then affairs will not succeed. Linggan lectured on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
He practiced the visualization of the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha).
As his death approached, celestial music came to welcome him;
however, Dao-gan declined, expressing no desire to go.
Suddenly, he saw a vast expanse of water and sat upon a lotus flower.
If that transmitter had not attained realization, how could the celestial palaces also reside within the Flower Treasury (Kusuma-garbha)? The intention of the commentator is as follows.
The spiritual faculty does not desire to be born in the heavens;
it seeks instead to be born in the lands of the Buddhas.
Yet, if one does not penetrate the Flower Treasury World (*Gandavyūha*) which encompasses the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), how could there not be the various heavens within it?
This is likely an error on the part of the transmitter; according to Tánróng, while Sēngháng was practicing the Way, he saw seven Buddhas within a light,
who told him,
"These are the Buddhas of Universal Radiance (Pǔmíng) of the Bhadrakalpa."
Now, though one cultivates the primary and secondary marks for a hundred kalpas,
even seeking them through the true transformation body,
they are not yet attained as they truly are until after the Vajra-samādhi at the completion of the tenth bhūmi.
For one hundred kalpas, one cultivates the primary and secondary marks;
for one thousand kalpas, one studies the Buddha’s majestic deportment;
and for ten thousand kalpas, one studies the practices of transformation and so forth.
If it were the true body (dharmakāya),
how could it be subject to ordinary perception?
If it were the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya)...
How could one possibly cultivate the marks and signs? Indeed, such matters are not worth recording, and such words do not constitute a standard for conduct;
why trouble oneself with scrolls and tablets? If the matter does not follow ancient precedent, what is there to be compiled and transmitted?
Therefore, the great eloquence is wordless;
words serve only to guide the mind,
and the mind must have its ultimate destination.
Therefore, he speaks of the essentials while penetrating the profound,
and his expressions are exhaustive while their intent remains subtle.
As stated in the preface to the *Xu zhuan* (Continued Biographies), he does not record that which is false.
Dharmavivardhana was practicing the meditation on water.
His family members went to gather firewood and saw clear, pure water upon his rope bed.
He collected twelve pebbles and placed them there;
when he returned in the evening, he felt pain in his back and other symptoms.
This was a most egregious error.
Furthermore, to claim that this visualization of a solitary shadowy tomb is merely a product of mental construction,
and that if it were seen by another person it would belong to the category of objective reality (dharmāyatana),
is the reckless talk of Master Xuan; such a statement must be recorded as it contradicts the established world order.
This is what is called the constant standard.
Is it not the same for Confucianism and Daoism?
As for evaluating the present and the past, or determining the truth and the falsehood, the right and the wrong:
It cannot be upheld by means of honor;
it cannot be discarded by means of humiliation;
it cannot be biased by means of intimacy.
One must not allow personal prejudices to interfere with the execution of the historian’s pen.
First is talent;
second is learning.
The third is called "cutting off.
Unless one belongs to the class of Dong Gu or Nan Shi, no one can shoulder this responsibility.
As for the three Huan clans of Lu—Ji Sun and Zhong Sun—[they were unable to do so].
The Shusun clan were all descendants of Duke Huan of Lu; how could they compare to the Yan and Min clans, or the seven noble houses of the Han dynasty such as the Jin and Zhang clans?
These seven houses enjoyed honor and prosperity for seven generations.

Zuo Si said: "The Jin and Zhang families have held their ancestral offices for seven generations, with their descendants wearing the pheasant-feather hairpins at the Han court; how could their talent fail to surpass that of Yang and Ma?
Yang Xiong’s courtesy name was Ziyun."
He authored the *Da xuan jing*,
the *Fayan*, the *Fangyan*, and other works.

Sima Xiangru, whose courtesy name was Changqing, authored the "Treatise on the Feng and Shan Sacrifices," the "Rhapsody on Literature" (*Wen fu*), and other works. He had a son who regarded a four-inch coffin made of paulownia wood as sufficient, knowing that the dead do not wish for their remains to decay too quickly. When Bo Shang cited the lines from the *Shi Jing* regarding the lament of the poet, Confucius sighed, saying: "The Master said..."
It was my disciple Shang who inspired me; since his golden words descended from afar,
many traditions have been compiled and recorded,
resulting in both extensive and abridged versions.
Names and meanings differ;
there are single translations and repeated translations.
Regarding the presence or absence of differences, those in the Tripiṭaka that have been translated only once are termed "single" (dan).
That which involves two or three successive translations is called "re-translation" (*chóngyì*). Therefore, the Great Sage enjoined that one should rely on the meaning and not on the words;
this is a prominent example of what has been observed previously.
The Buddha possesses eight tones and four types of eloquence. Regarding the eight tones:
First, the pure sound;
second, the gentle sound;
third, the harmonious and appropriate sound.
Fourth, the voice that clearly understands the Four Truths;
fifth, the voice that is not feminine;
sixth, the voice that is without error.
Seventh, the profound and far-reaching voice.
Eighth, the inexhaustible voice. As for the four analytical knowledges (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ):
First, the unimpeded eloquence of dharmas;
second, the unimpeded eloquence of language;
third, the unimpeded eloquence of meaning.
Possessing the four dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence that transcend all beings,
his sagely mind shines with profound illumination;
his spiritual exhortations are truly sublime and elegant.
Yet the translators, following their own inclinations, rendered the text shallow and easy;
their chapters and sentences were omissions and negligences,
which caused those of the gentry and the Confucian scholars— who carry their tablets with hands tucked between their girdles— to [be led astray].
The *shen* is a large sash;
the *fengye* is a Confucian robe with wide sleeves. They looked at one another with expressions of disapproval because the language was not elegant or classical.
Among them, however, there were those like An Shigao who had extracted and compiled materials from the ancient classics (*fen*) and bamboo slips (*su*).
He carves at the wording;
his language is excessively worldly, like the sutras translated by Zhu Fahu, Zhi Qian, and others.
His prose entirely conforms to the style of secular composition, and its principles deviate from precision and subtlety.
This is especially a failure to grasp the sage’s aphorisms.
How difficult it is! Throughout the ages, from antiquity to the present, there have been those who have proclaimed and translated [the teachings].
Everyone recommended that [the texts] be entrusted to Master Kumārajīva;
whether in substance or style, whether elaborate or concise,
he always attained the appropriate balance.
Opening the scroll and lending my ear,
the ancient style resonates with clarity;
I have often directed my attention toward the translators.
Is it based on the Sanskrit original?
Or is it based on the edited version?
For example, as in the "Dharmabhāṇaka" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Kumārajīva did not include its opening; Śikṣānanda subsequently produced its conclusion.

Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* [translated by Kumārajīva] lacks the beginning, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* [translated by Dharmarakṣa] and the *Avalokiteśvara-parivarta* [translated by Śikṣānanda] are complete.
Among these, there are also instances where errors were made in the wording.
For example, in Paramārtha’s translation of the *Abhidharmakośa*, it says:
"One sees that dharmas have non-acquisition (*aprāpti*)."
Xuanzang produced the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
adding sixteen characters [to the title] as the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
This was based solely upon the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
Adding sixteen characters to its text, one thus knows that these words,
which cannot be altered,
were not yet realized by him.
Dao’an evaluated translations in detail based on the three difficulties and five errors;
he exhaustively elucidated these subtle points because the Sanskrit texts are difficult to comprehend.
The Sage’s intention is profound and far-reaching;
the phrasing and purport are elegant and appropriate.
This is indeed what makes it unalterable.
The noble intent was not well understood;
the chapters and sentences were omitted,
and the phrasing was coarse and defiled.
This is a fault; those of later generations were unable to investigate its underlying intent.

Taking "treasure" (bao) as a standard of measurement, they composed their discourse without adhering to the central principle, staring blankly as if they had not heard it at all—"chēng" (瞠) being a term for the manner of staring straight ahead.
Because the ancient translations of the scriptures were not refined,
one was ultimately unable to investigate them thoroughly;
thus, one remained dimly ignorant, with nothing to realize or understand.
This is as translated by An Shigao; furthermore, Confucianism is the teaching of this region.

Among its scripts, the *kedou* (corncob) script was the first, followed by the two types of seal script (*zhuan*). In antiquity there was the *kedou* script, later succeeded by the large seal script (*dazhuan*) and the small seal script (*xiaozhuan*).
The Grand Scribe Shi Zhou of King Xuan of the Zhou dynasty created the Dazhuan script.
Li Si and others of the Qin dynasty created the Xiaozhuan script.
Cheng Miao created the Lishu script and others; thus, the seal scripts evolved into the clerical script.
Furthermore, during the Qin dynasty, when the texts were destroyed or became corrupted and incomplete, in the thirty-third year of the First Emperor,
various scholars each debated matters concerning the Qin state,
whereupon Chancellor Li Si submitted this memorial:
Consequently, he burned the books and buried the Confucian scholars.
He destroyed the classics of previous dynasties; regarding the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, there are differing accounts of what was selected or rejected.
Some say that the Three Sovereigns refer to the Celestial Sovereign (Tianhuang), the Earthly Sovereign (Dihuang), and the Human Sovereign (Renhuang).
Some say [the sequence refers to] Fuxi, Shennong, and Huangdi;
the Five Emperors—Shaohao, Zhuanxu, Di Ku, Yao, and Shun. As for the arrangement of the chapters in the *Lunyu* of Lu and the *Lunyu* of Qi, how were they determined?
The *Lunyu* of Lu consists of twenty chapters.
The *Qi Lun* consists of twenty-two chapters,
the sequence of which also differs [from other versions]. Regarding the *Liji* and the *Chunqiu*,
Duke Ai offered a eulogy for Kong Qiu.
As for the variations in addition and subtraction, which is correct?
When Confucius died, Duke Ai of Lu composed a eulogy (*lei*) for him.
The texts transmitted in the *Book of Rites* (*Liji*) differ from one another; the same is true of the *Jia Yu* and the *Tan Gong*.
When Zhongni [Confucius] handed over the lute, his discourse was grave and earnest;
how could its text be the same as that of the "Qin" chapter following the funeral rites?
Thus, the texts in the *Liji* and the *Jia yu* differ; this is what Meng Zhuang understood.
Meng Ke, styled Ziyu, took the meaning rather than the words.
He authored fourteen chapters of a book.
Zhuang Zhou composed ten fascicles of writings, all of which employ allegory to convey their intended meaning;
one must not cling to the literal text to grasp the underlying substance. These were annotated by Ma Rong and Zheng Xuan.
Wenzi Hugai Ma Rong, courtesy name Jichang,
was a native of Beihai.
Zheng Xuan,
courtesy name Kangcheng,
was also a native of Beihai.
Furthermore, the commentaries on the *Shi*, *Li*, and *Lunyu* all contain differing interpretations; how much more so when it comes to the diverse languages of the Five Indias?
Within the various schools, their tenets diverge, with six major sects and ten distinct sub-sects.

Furthermore, the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna is distinct; having repeatedly suffered destruction during the reigns of the Northern Zhou and Northern Wei due to unrighteous rulers, it has become difficult to distinguish between the "clear" and "turbid" streams.
When translating from Sanskrit into Chinese, how could these not be unified?
Now, if one strikes a bell with a small hammer or blows a tiny bamboo flute, they will not exhaust its resonance.
To peer at the heavens through a tube, one cannot reach its boundaries.
How much less can an ordinary person fathom the profundity of a sage?
Nevertheless, one cannot help but rely on the power of the flute to hear its harmony,
examine its boundaries by following the edges of the pipes,
and exhaust all considerations to refine its principles.
Furthermore, the reason why those who transmit the Dharma deeply loathe errors and discrepancies is that they perceive people who lack sincere devotion to the Ultimate Way;
such individuals, confronted by the vastness of the scriptures and observing the variations and contradictions among different editions, become timid and fail to investigate them thoroughly.
This is the failing of scholars. They treat the jade-encased scrolls with ribbons and cords— where "ribbons" (kun) refers to the sashes and "cords" (teng) refers to the bindings—
and thus they strike at the very scriptures themselves, claiming that what issued from the Golden Mouth has been definitively established as the written word.
Those who indulge in the carving of words consider it a fault to study the scriptures;
those who disparage critical inquiry consider it a mark of worldly wit and cleverness.
This is because those who transmit the mind regard exegesis as a fault resulting from an excessive attachment to the flavor of the scriptures.
The debater suffers from the affliction of worldly wisdom and clever eloquence. Confucius said:

"The gentleman uses what he cannot do to inspire awe in others, and because he himself is incapable, he respects those who are capable. The petty man uses what he cannot do to distrust others; since he himself has no ability," [he does not respect the capable].
Furthermore, because they do not value what others understand, the gentleman nurtures the talents of others,
whereas the petty person suppresses them to seek victory for himself;
thus, the world comes to possess hidden flaws and concealed sores.
Adorning their superficial wisdom while ensnaring the base,
they plundered the empty reputation of the profound master;
concealing their muddled emotions to deceive themselves, they were fundamentally devoid of accumulated insight.
He then addressed him as "Master," his feelings filled with excessive audacity.
He was always apprehensive about being subjected to rigorous examination; he simply did not realize that when one is at the height of thirst, one drinks much.
When doubt is deep, awakening is distant.
That man is a usurper—what is called a man who usurps ease. Someone said:
"To pick out the flaws of former sages."
Thus, would there not be no flaw in the teaching regarding things? By using directness to elucidate ultimate truth, one does not become obstructed by things.
To use this to disparage former sages is incorrect.
Shen Nong distinguished the hundred herbs.
It is not that Qibó intended to lead people into poison when he discussed acupuncture and stone therapy;
nor did the Buddha preach the sutras with the desire to cause people's downfall. How could the *Nanhua* (Zhuangzi) disparage Jī and Kǒng?
If every household lacks the Six Classics, it is not that Zhuang Zhou disparaged the Duke of Zhou and Confucius;

how could it be that the Six Classics do not circulate? When Ban Gu’s *Book of the Later Han* critiques Sima Qian’s *Records of the Grand Historian*, does this mean that every household lacks the *Records of the Grand Historian*? Just as Ban Gu’s *Book of the Han* was not the *Records of the Grand Historian* by Sima Qian, so too did Vasubandhu compose the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Saṃghabhadra composed the *Vaiśeṣika* (or *Abhidharmasamayapradīpikā*) to criticize it;
Vasubandhu then revised the title to the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Both treatises were widely propagated.

To enable those who come to investigate the truth, dispel ignorance, discern the refined from the coarse, and thereby adopt or reject [the teachings], the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*.
The Master Saṃghabhadra then composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra-ṭīkā-kṣaṇabhaṅga* (The Hailstorm against the Abhidharmakośa) to refute it.
Like rain and hail destroying young sprouts,
he went to attack Vasubandhu,
but Vasubandhu avoided him every time.
He then sent the treatise he had composed;
when Vasubandhu examined it, he found that it accorded with his own views,
and consequently changed its title to *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (The Treatise in Accordance with Correct Principle).

12. Section on the Verification of Retribution (VII). Section Twelve: The Verification of Retribution. This clarifies that the karmic retribution for good and evil deeds is never obscured. For those who do good, Heaven bestows upon them a hundred auspicious blessings.
Virtue is what Heaven assists. Great Heaven has no partiality; it assists only virtue. For those who do evil, Heaven sends down a hundred calamities.
"To rectify licentiousness" means to correct excess.
Since Heaven blesses the good and brings disaster upon the licentious, one should therefore accord with principle, for even creatures of different species will show affection toward such a person.
How much more so for sages and worthies? It would be contrary to reason for dragon-spirits to show such deference and submission, or for close relatives to engage in mutual warfare;
how much less so for ghosts and spirits?
As Zhuangzi said:
If one does evil in the light of day, men shall find and punish them;
if one does evil in the darkness of night, ghosts shall find and punish them.
As the *Shi* says:
"The misfortunes of the common people do not descend from Heaven;
they arise from oneself. Calamity has no gate of entry; it is summoned by man himself. Thus did Zhongni say to Duke Ai.
Survival and ruin, fortune and calamity, depend solely upon oneself.
The *Zhou Song* says:
"Reverence the majesty of Heaven."
At that time, Puṣyamitra,
the grandson of King Aśoka of the Western Regions,
descended from his court to deliberate, saying:
"How may I leave my name to endure imperishably?
The ministers replied,
"You should follow the example of the former kings by constructing eighty-four thousand stūpas."
Otherwise, it is the reverse.
Though their reputations may be good or bad, both shall be imperishable.
The King said:
"I lack the majestic virtue to succeed my predecessor;
we must deliberate further on this matter.
Thus, he proceeded to insult the instructions of his imperial ancestor.
The "Ordinary Ethics" (Yílún) refers to the constant and fundamental principles of human relations;

it is the principle of daily practice for emperors and kings. [The Emperor] burned the Dharma and desecrated the sounds [of the scriptures]; he prepared the stupas while ruthlessly slaughtering the assembly of Śākyas—"qínlíu" meaning to slaughter. Heaven grieved and men were resentful.
There is no way to counter its cruelty;
even sages and worthies cannot defy it.
Ascending that southern mountain,
they seek for themselves escape from harm;
such are the companions who have stilled their minds.
Blood flowed in streams as he slaughtered the practitioners; heads were displayed as rewards, and the provincial offices were never idle.
Taxation was consequently exhausted by this, for those who captured the heads of monks were granted rewards. The King’s anger increased further.
He further committed even more slaughter and cruelty;
leading his army to the Tooth Relic Stūpa,
he perished beneath a collapsing mountain.
During the reigns of Emperors Huan and Ling of the Han dynasty,
a Buddha image was cast from refined metal;
it fell into disarray during the national turmoil and was buried in a desolate wilderness.
Sun Hao of Wu dispatched his guards to tend the imperial gardens.
He ordered that anyone caught there be placed in the latrines.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, he urinated over their heads, saying: "This is the urine of a head."
He performed the consecration for him;
while the sovereign and his ministers were laughing and enjoying themselves together,
in an instant, the king's entire body became swollen with tumors.
The private parts were especially painful;
the poison spread through the five internal organs,
and cries of lamentation resounded outwardly.
He sent diviners and shamans,
all of whom declared that he had offended a great deity while seated;
Sun Hao then traveled everywhere to worship various deities, yet his condition improved not at all.
The palace attendants who were Buddhists claimed that this was indeed a Buddha.
Emperor Hao then welcomed the image and bathed it;

day and night he showed profound awe and reverence—*yinyi* meaning reverence—and prostrating himself with his forehead touching the *zai*, which refers to the wooden planks of a bed; *sang* meaning the forehead.
This refers to striking one's forehead against the bed while confessing transgressions and reproaching oneself.
When those to his left and right heard this,
they were moved with compassion and shed tears.
After a short while, his illness slightly abated; he then purified himself through fasting and ritual observances before finally participating.
He was Helián Bōbō of the "Pseudo-Xià," a Xiongnu.
Occupying the Ordos Desert,
he raised his dragon banners and imperial robes,
exalting his own virtue.
He was ignorant of the Way of the Sage.
He said, "The one called 'Bó' is Buddha; I am a Buddha."
He placed statues of the Chen emperors on the seats behind him and ordered the assembled śramaṇas to prostrate themselves before them as if to him,
thereby invoking heavenly punishment upon those who were guilty.
They die from the sudden shock of thunder.
Therefore, thunder is a numinous phenomenon;
it manifests its majesty by relying upon yang energy. As Wang Chong states in the *Lunheng*: [Thunder is the spirit of the heavens.]
Thunder is the striking and damaging of objects caused by the mutual clash and impact of the qi of yin and yang;
thus, when the yang qi reaches its extreme, light and other phenomena are produced.
Nevertheless, thunder possesses a divine spirit.
They are the messengers of Heaven;
they protect purity and loathe evil.
They move by relying on the yang qi.
They move according to the clouds and rain;
they hibernate in winter because the yang energy is withdrawn and stored. Such is the nature of the yin and yang energies.
When released, it is peaceful and still;
when stored, it steams and rages.
At times, it loathes evil and strikes with a tempest upon earth and wood.
This is to serve as a warning to the people.
If they do not exercise caution, they will proceed to inflict harm; "sì" (肆) means to let loose or abandon caution and fear.
Thus, if one has no sense of awe or restraint regarding their actions, [they will cause harm].
This will surely bring swift harm. Xie Hai of the Song dynasty was stationed at Jingzhou.
Troubled by the śramaṇa Sengchang’s construction of a stupa within the city—which was cramped and obstructed the battlements—he personally supervised the labor of his soldiers.
He treated them with generous hospitality of wine and food,
allowing them full scope for their martial prowess; then,
with the sounding of drums, he issued strict commands to inspire awe.
None dared to advance.
"Zhuangji" (撞擊) means to strike down; it refers to overturning, damaging, and collapsing.
It is also written as "chì" (褫).
The "Monstrous Sound" (Huài yīn guài) is so called because it destroys;
though there was no actual damage, it was specifically destroyed, and thus the niche and the image were ruined and collapsed.
Suddenly a violent wind arose;
clouds and mists joined the heavens in a darkening gloom, so fierce and intense that even the bold were struck with cold dread.
All was obscured and shrouded in dust.
He wiped it away with his hand;
the skin fell off following the touch of his fingers,
revealing festering sores and wounds.
Tiyu was without facial features or skin;
he was ultimately executed along with his clan for rebelling. Xie Hai, whose courtesy name was Xuanning, [was also executed].
He was a native of Yangxia in Chenjun.
He possessed a handsome appearance and was skilled in conversation and wit.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, he served as General of the Household and Governor of Jingzhou. When he rebelled, Tan Daoji was summoned to suppress him;
his troops were nearly captured, and he was sent to the capital city of Ye, where he was executed in the marketplace.
Emperor Shizong of the Zhou dynasty,
surnamed Chai,
melted down the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva statue of Zhenzhou to cast the "Zhou Tongyuan" cash coins.
Later, his limbs rotted away and he collapsed;

this case is also of that same category. Thus, for one whose transgression is great, the world will not offer *diao*—that is, compassion or relief. Having initially employed his strength to rescue others, he is now about to overflow with calamity.
