This takes up the principle of seeking blessings that does not contradict one’s ancestors;

"hui" (回) here means "to reverse. Furthermore, while the karma of past lives may be either determinate or indeterminate, the resulting nature and life-span in this present life may likewise be subject to change or remain unchanged; and regarding the timing of the retribution for such karma, it too may be determinate or indeterminate.
Life and nature possess both change and non-change.
If one follows present conditions and transforms into a snake or the like,
then the retribution of specific karma changes.
The retributive result as a whole is unchanging;
if one's karma is fixed, the life span it induces will certainly not be altered.
If, however, that karma is not fixed, [the life span may change].

However, the life span resulting from such karma can indeed be diminished or increased; for instance, through the power of goodness, heavy [karma] may be transformed into light, and the same applies to evil. Furthermore, the karma of this present life is both determinate and indeterminate.
Yet, it causes the natures and destinies experienced in past lives to either change or remain unchanged.

If one's karma were fixed, one would be unable to alter past causes; however, just as wholesome karma can transform the evils of past lives, so too does indeterminate destiny lead to the attainment of success or failure within that same state of indeterminacy.
This refers to individual retribution.
Originally, one was impoverished due to evil;
now, because one has transformed it through the power of goodness, one becomes prosperous. Such karma is indeterminate.
Thus, it is merely a matter of alternation between prosperity and adversity; it is said that one cannot change what is not fixed. Take Śāriputra and Aniruddha as examples:
though they encountered the Buddha as their physician of the Dharma and Jīvaka as their physician of the world, they were nonetheless unable to eliminate their chronic ailments.
For example, when Śāriputra suffered from bloody diarrhea,
a skilled physician said that he could eat lotus roots;
thereupon, Maudgalyāyana was sent to the Mandāraka Pond to fetch lotus roots for him to eat, and so forth.
The loss of his sight by Aniruddha and others were all due to past karma;
likewise, Yan Hui and Min Sun encountered Confucius and thereby manifested their virtuous conduct.
When meeting with the feudal lords, he focused on the worthy and the wise,
yet did not eliminate the poor or the prematurely deceased;
this was likely because the destiny shaped by his past lives was fixed.
Therefore, practicing good deeds in this present life cannot benefit him. Yan Hui, whose courtesy name was Ziyan,
[was such a person].
The disciple was a man of Lu.
He was the son of Yan Lu.
His family was poor.
[Min Ziqian] died early at the age of thirty. Min Dun,
courtesy name Ziqian, was also a native of Lu.
There was a man of filial piety whose family was poor;
he suffered at the hands of his stepmother.
For the sake of the Nanda family’s expenses, he served Baddhālambana, yet because of the abundance of his merit, he became the bhikṣu Baddhālambana.
He was immensely wealthy, possessing billions in gold and silver. King Aśoka was tyrannical and unrestrained yet possessed great power;
he slaughtered people without limit and cast them into the hells and other realms, while his majesty shook the very corners of the sea.
He encountered the śramaṇa Kūṭadanta, who converted him;

he built eighty-four thousand stūpas. When the Lord of the Ji clan died beneath his window, Ji Huanzi expelled Duke Zhao of Lu, who died at Qianhou while presiding over the ancestral sacrifices, yet ultimately met his death within the state of Lu. As for the bandit Zhi, he lived out his natural lifespan while feeding on entrails; though Zhi was a thief, he attained a full longevity.
At Dongling, he killed passersby every day,
taking their hearts and livers for his meal.
Confucius was unable to transform him.
That he ultimately met his death was surely the fixed destiny brought about by his past lives;
the unwholesome deeds of this present life could not diminish it, for it manifested as the result of wholesome karma accumulated in former times.
Evil could not conceal it. Mallikā, having offered food, became the Queen Consort of the kingdom.
Mallikā was born from a lowly official family and was extremely ugly;
the King, her father, did not wish to see her.
He then consulted Caogong about the Buddha;
as he was too busy with his recitations,
the Buddha manifested his body before him.
Through transformation, he attained a dignified appearance.
King Prasenajit took him as his queen; [another] yielded his life on a boat plank for the sake of a sea deity. The *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* states:
"There was a bhikṣu..."
While sailing at sea, they encountered a storm and their ship was damaged.
A young bhikṣu obtained a plank from the vessel and saw the elder monk drowning.
He thought to himself,
"The Buddha now honors the senior monk," and he consequently yielded his seat to him.
The Sea God beheld them and rejoiced;
together they were pushed out from the sea and thus survived. Zhao Dun took pity on the man at Yi Sang; Zhao Xuanni went out and saw the starving man at Yi Sang and questioned him.
He said, "I have not eaten for three days.
Thereupon [the dog] took food and fed him.
Later, however, at the command of Duke Ling of Jin, a fierce dog was unleashed to bite him.

In Yi-sang, Ling Che killed a dog to provide meat for Fu Lun, who rescued him and brought him out; the漂母 (Floating Mother) took pity on Han Xin, the Marquis of Huaiyin, when he was in extreme hunger before his rise to fortune.
He saw an old woman washing cotton絮 (xù) and threw it to her;
the mother gave him food.
Later, he assisted the Han dynasty and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Huaiyin.
The mother had already died;
he opened her grave and cast a thousand pieces of gold inside it. These are all the certainties of wholesome karma in this present life.
The lifespan from past lives, however, is not fixed.
Thus, one is able to transform decline into prosperity. From the time of Mallikā onwards, these are examples of wholesome karma that bears fruit in the present life.
Regarding the account of the woodcutter who pointed at a bear and had his arm fall off, the *Jinglü yìxiàng* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of the Sutras and Vinaya) states:
A woodcutter entered the mountains and encountered a great snowfall and extreme cold;
a white bear took him into its cave.
When the snow cleared and he descended the mountain,
he encountered a hunter who led him with his knife to show him the bear's location,
pointing it out with his finger.

As soon as he pointed his finger, the arm fell off. A bhikṣu was eating a sheep's tripe when his intestines were pierced. Another man, chasing a sheep into the monastery, saw the bhikṣu pointing at him and killed him; he then ate the tripe and gave some to the bhikṣu. After the bhikṣu had eaten it, the tripe spread beneath the skin, ran through his body, pierced his intestines, and he died.
In the "Discourse on Distinguishing Orthodoxy" (Bianzheng lun), Li records that the Duke of Jin was punished for murdering his lord:
Duke Xian of Jin doted upon Lady Lijun and banished his various brothers;
he killed Crown Prince Shen-sheng and installed Xi-qi.
Li Ke killed him. The people of the state then installed Zhaizi,
but Li Ke killed him as well and welcomed Yi Wu to take the throne.
This was Duke Hui.
When Duke Hui returned from Qin,
he said to Li克 (Li Ke):
Zi killed two rulers and one high official;
this refers to Xun Xi,
who then committed suicide.
This was because Duke Hui had executed him; thus, Zhang Lu— also known as Zhang Lü or Fan Sui— fulfilled his ambitions by serving as Chancellor of Wei,
and subsequently entered Qin together with Xu Jia.
Qin was pleased with him.
When Xujia returned, he slandered him to Wei Qi.
Wei Qi then hosted a drinking feast.
Next, he struck him, and his teeth were broken.
He sank into the mud, recovered, and fled to Qin,
where he changed his name to Zhang Lu.
Qin appointed him as Chancellor.
Later, he plotted to seize Wei.
Lord Qi of Wei ordered Xu Jia to serve as an envoy to Lu.
He then ordered Xu Jia to be transformed into a donkey and commanded that Wei Qi be captured;
Wei Qi fled into exile until his death.

That he ultimately perished in Wei was entirely due to the fixed ripening of unwholesome karma in his present life; these were all the retributions for unwholesome karma to be experienced in the present life. His lifespan in past lives, however, was not fixed.

Therefore, it is possible to transform existence into non-existence. This is because the lifespan of a previous life, though its merit was originally not yet exhausted, is brought to an end by the karma of this present life, causing one to undergo its manifest retribution. Devadatta harmed a saint until blood flowed from the foot, pushed a mountain to injure the Buddha’s foot, and caused a schism in the Sangha; he will certainly undergo one kalpa in the Avīci hell.
This refers to the certainty of producing unwholesome karma in the present life, as well as unwholesome determinate karma to be experienced in the present life. Ajātaśatru murdered his father,
yet upon seeing the Buddha,
he placed faith in the Dharma.
King Ajātaśatru, who had murdered his father King Bimbisāra and was thus destined for the great suffering of Avīci Hell,
saw his own body afflicted with malignant sores.
Taking refuge in the Buddha, he addressed him.
The Buddha shone his light upon him, and the wound was healed;
he then preached the Dharma for him,
thereby liberating him from the sufferings of hell.

The name "Avīci" (Unrelenting) hell signifies that there is no selection between good and evil; it is essentially the indeterminate cause for the production of unwholesome karma. Through repentance, one's offenses may be extinguished;
this is because both the time and the retribution are indeterminate. Thus, even Yan Hui and Min Ziqian suffered from poverty and premature death.
This repays the unwholesome causes of the past;
his virtuous conduct shall serve as the wholesome retribution for future lives.
As for the wealth and longevity of the likes of Ji and Zhi—
The good karma of past causes will bring its retribution;
that their rebellious violence will result in heavy suffering in future lives is truly beyond doubt.
Now, the medicinal ointment that prevents the hands from cracking is one and the same;
yet the resulting honor and meanness differ. "Gūi" refers to the peeling and fissuring of the skin.
There was one who sold medicine to treat this condition.
What was obtained was very little.
The man from the south sold his local products;
having returned, he presented them to his lord.
It coincides with what is required for military expeditions;
one thereby obtains great emolument.
This is the first instance of "cutting away the lands of the feudal lords" as mentioned in the *Zhuangzi*.
Yet their rise and fall were not the same: the First Emperor of Qin eradicated the territories of the feudal lords and ceased to enfeoff them;
when the Han army entered Qin, there was no one to offer rescue, and thus it perished.
When Li Shiqi saw the Han King, he urged him to enfeoff the various lords for their lands;
however, when Zhang Liang arrived,
he immediately stopped him.
It was improper to borrow a bone from within the tent to serve as a tally for strategic planning;
thus, it was not sealed.
That the Han dynasty indeed rose was truly due to the skillfulness or clumsiness of the timing and fortune.
Yet, within one's nature and destiny, there are things that can be changed and things that cannot.
Therefore, the gentleman knows that fortune and destiny cannot be altered;
he thus rejoices in Heaven and understands his destiny.

The petty person, being ignorant, transgresses their own limits and acts with restless agitation; lacking knowledge of the Dao, they cannot become a superior man. Thus, fortune and misfortune, safety and peril, are clearly visible.
As for those who claim that the constant principles of good and ill fortune depend on fate (ming) and not on destiny (yun): [this is incorrect].

This is insufficient for a definitive judgment. Fortunes have their cycles of decline and prosperity, misfortune and good fortune; these are matters pertaining to the "mountain man" (the individual). Just as winter grass withers but does not die, how could this ever not be due to the operation of destiny?

By employing the transformative power of destiny, one may avoid calamity. When there is that which is rooted in innate nature, then fate is realized; thus, there are those whose realization depends on destiny rather than mere fate.
This too is insufficient for severance; if one relies on expedient movements, it will not endure beyond a single night.
Furthermore, it is improper for karma to persist. Indeed, when cold wood is irrigated, it does not flourish; such nourishment merely provides moisture.
It is like watering an ancient cypress tree:
how could it immediately flourish?
This is because its strength is firm; how could this ever not be due to destiny?
Only when both forms of faith are perfected can one be said to have penetrated the profound mystery. Therefore,
when faith possesses momentum, it is the faith of karma.
If one believes in destiny, then the belief in karmic fruition is established;

for destiny is the result of karma. How is it any different from being angry upon hearing that "in the morning there are three" and "in the evening there are four," while believing in destiny yet disbelieving in karmic fruition?
As Zhuangzi says: "When they heard that there would be three in the morning and four in the evening, they were delighted;
yet when it was said that there would be three in the morning and four in the evening, all the monkeys were angry."
Yet, when it was said that there were four in the morning and three in the evening, all the monkeys were delighted;
they did not realize that while the names differed, the substance remained the same. Therefore, this school [of thought] is the former sage among Confucians.
Although it does not explicitly speak of karmic retribution,
it implicitly governs and determines it through destiny;
because destiny secretly establishes the principles of karma, the names differ while the meaning remains one and the same.
The *I Ching* says:
"To know the subtle signs—is this not divine?
Master Zhuang said:
The myriad things arise from the subtle pivot (*ji*). The *Yinfu* says:
"Life arises from the pivot, and death arises from the pivot. Fundamentally, when the mind encounters objects, the pivot is born.
How much can the mind produce?
How much can the eyes see?
The mind of birth and death resides within phenomena.
"The signs of success and failure appear before one's eyes.
Zhang Zan said: "The 'incipient' (ji) is the beginning of all that exists."
That which is honored in movement is the subtle manifestation of movement;
this refers to the operation of karma.
Some say that since karma arises from movement, the principle of its retribution is uniform.
How can there be lightness or heaviness, or determinacy and indeterminacy?
Since the karma produced is the same, why would there be differences in lightness or heaviness, or an indeterminacy in receiving retribution? It is said:
because the mind possesses joy and anger.
Matters involve both kindness and cruelty, and because the minds that give rise to them differ in their conduct, outward forms may not be commensurate with inner colors.
King Zhou’s lack of the Way led him to indulge in the "burning pillar" (pàoluò) torture; [the Duke of Zhou] subsequently abolished the punishment of the burning pillar.
To practice the cruelty of disemboweling and decapitation—such is the gravity of this karma. Yet the Book of Documents says:
"Pardon transgressions, no matter how great; punish transgressions, no matter how small. This refers to pardoning those who have been exiled.
One does not fail to pardon because a crime is great, nor does one fail to execute because an offense is small. As the Sūtra says:
"Iron formed into a ball, though small, will sink;
iron formed into a bowl, though large, can float."
There are none who do not escape [retribution] even if their karma is heavy provided they have intense remorse;

yet there are none who do not undergo it even if their karma is light provided they do not repent. Furthermore, regarding the three types of action (trikarma) across the three periods of time, their combination and separation constitute eight categories: those where body, speech, and mind are single and thus separated from the three actions; those where all three are present and thus combined; and those where two types are combined. When these are further conjoined with the three periods of time—namely, the past, present, and future—the karma becomes heavy.
If there is a discrepancy, it is light; when the three karmas arise together, it is called heavy.
When they do not arise together, it is light; being light, it is indeterminate, whereas being heavy, it is determinate.

Because of this, Bimbisāra was starved to death by his rebellious son; Bimbisāra was King Śreṇika, and the "party of Śākya" refers to his death at the hands of the cruel King Virūḍhaka. When Yao was wise and sagacious, the floods surged and overflowed, washing over the mountains and submerging the hills, leaving the common people in darkness and distress; yet when Tang possessed benevolent virtue, there was a great drought—Tang attained the throne through his benevolent virtue.

There was a great drought for seven years. [The King] prayed at Sanglin and other sites. Zhang Yi and Shan Bao both sought life through their respective modes of nourishment, yet neither could preserve it. As for Zhang Yi of Qi: [He was a man who] walked with such haste that his heels did not touch the ground; he kept his hands tucked inside his sleeves and never looked back. He lived in a house without doors and slept on a mat of straw. He ate only when hungry and drank only when thirsty. He wore coarse hemp clothing and carried a staff. He traveled by carriage drawn by a single horse. He was so focused on avoiding harm that he sought only to protect himself from external injury. However, he died young, struck down by internal heat. This was because he had neglected his inner nature while over-exerting himself externally. Thus, though he sought life, he failed to attain it. This is what is meant by "seeking life through the pursuit of life. It is like trying to avoid death by running toward it. Therefore, those who seek life by means of life are no different from those who seek death by means of death. Both fail to achieve their goal. This is why the ancients said: "Those who seek life through life lose their life; those who seek death through death lose their death. He was a man of cautious integrity.
Whenever he saw a high gate with a hanging list of names, there was nowhere he would not go.
At the age of forty, he died from a disease of internal heat.
This fault lies in being externally restless and stagnant.
Dan Bao was a man of Lu.
Dwelling in a mountain cave and drinking only water, he did not share his benefits with the people.
At the age of seventy, he possessed the complexion of an infant.
Unfortunately, he encountered a starving tiger that devoured him.
This refers to being stagnant within.
The leopard nurtures its interior;
the tiger devours its exterior.
Yi nourishes his exterior;
illness attacks his interior.
Both seek life but cannot attain it. [The story of] Boluoluo and King Zhou Houji.
Not seeking life through nourishment,
they both returned to their original state of being;
this was indeed the fixed decree of destiny, O Bāhuka.
This person, known as Shanrong (Good Appearance),
once gave a single haritaki fruit;
for ninety-one kalpas, he suffered no headaches.
He was targeted for execution by his stepmother’s stratagems;
though he encountered five perils, he did not die.
After leaving the household life, he...
The eyes do not gaze upon women;
the body does not enter a nunnery;
one does not preach even a single word of Dharma for a woman.
King Aśoka, knowing that he had few desires,
offered him a single gold coin for the stūpa;
it sprang up from the earth, and he would not accept it.
Zhou Houji was the son of Emperor Ku and was born of Jiang Yuan.
He was born with hair on his body;
he was consequently abandoned in a deep mountain, amidst cold ice, and in a humble alleyway.
Though abandoned three times, he did not die.
He was thus named Qi (Abandoner).
Good at sowing seeds, he served Yao.
In the fifteenth generation from him, King Wen obtained the empire; when a black wind blew, he was saved. There was a merchant who entered the sea.
They encountered a black wind that blew them into the land of the rākṣasa demons;

by all recollecting the Buddha together, they were spared from harm. Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu named Zhengchang (Correct-Long) who, upon seeing the majesty and power of the Wheel-Turning King, became enamored of it.
Day and night he sought it with diligent effort;
the Buddha feared that he would not attain liberation and wished to cancel his merit of a thousand wheels.
This constitutes one instance of a "correct *pura*.

As for the *pura*, the wheel-turning monarch’s karma having exhausted itself, the mulberry and grain did not flourish; this was the calamity that befell the Yin dynasty. King Taiwu of Yin appointed Yi Yin’s son, Yizhi, as his minister.
When mulberry and oak trees grew together in the court and became as large as both hands in a single day, King Wu was alarmed and cultivated virtue.
Within three years, the mulberry and oak trees died,
and sixteen states arrived from distant lands with successive translations of their scripts.
It is said that when the planet Mars (the "Middle Lord") threatened the capital of the State of Song, it appeared within the astrological division of Song.
Duke Jing was terrified and cultivated virtue;
consequently, the planet retreated by three stations. When King Wen bestowed upon King Wu a lifespan of three *ling*—where *ling* signifies years—[he extended his life].

King Wu dreamed that the Supreme Lord had granted him nine years of life; King Wen bestowed three of those years upon him, so he reached the age of ninety-three. Duke Mu of Qin pardoned Mengming, who thus died twice.
This was likely because destiny is not fixed. The Qin general Mengmeng attacked Jin on two occasions.
It was not auspicious for him to cross the river;
however, Duke Mu of Qin pardoned him.
Later, he burned his boats and marched toward Jin, which did not come out to meet him.
Thus, having cleared away former shame, one returns to examine these principles and precedents in light of human affairs;
how could it be said that there is no karma? These are all matters in which the principle of karma is clearly evident. As for those who rely on the profound mystery [of emptiness]:
They are considered to follow the sequence of the wild geese;
the young lamb kneels to suckle its mother,
the crow is black and the pheasant is white.
The thorns of the jujube are sharp and square;
the orchid is fragrant while the stinking weed is foul.
These are natural laws, for they all pertain to the doctrine of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) as conceived by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
"Could it be due to karma?
The Master of the Profound Emptiness (Zhòngkōng rén) adjusted his robes and told him: "Not so."
Now, the Sage Laozi spoke of "spontaneity" (*ziran*); this is the Way.
The Ultimate Way shares the same substance as the myriad things.
Therefore it is said: "The myriad things are spontaneous. That the myriad things and the Ultimate Way are neither identical nor separate is what is meant by this.
The alternation of one Yin and one Yang is called the Dao. The Dao is quiescent and has no substance.

two visiting bhikṣus came from afar,
wishing to offer their diligent service.

"Where are you staying now?
Dharma pointed and said,

but Dharmatrāta suddenly used his supernatural powers to return first to his original seat.

He silently took note of what he had previously seen.
Having touched his feet in respectful salutation, he asked:

why do you personally tend the firewood? 'Tend' (cān) means to burn.

The junior monk said, "Are you subjecting yourself to such menial service?

The Later Zhou was like the Ministry of Merit (Gongde Si). The Eastern Wei, Northern Qi, and Northern Zhou esteemed its governance;
the Song, Qi, Liang, and Chen esteemed its orthodoxy.
Furthermore, the three officials of the monastery— corresponding to the current Three Heads (sang)— were responsible for its governance and rectification.
When the Sui dynasty succeeded the Zhou,
the propagation of the Dharma flourished even more extensively.
The Tripitaka of the world was formerly divided and placed under ten administrative jurisdictions (shǒng).
Now, our state has abolished these jurisdictions and established two registries (lù).
As for the administration, the *Senglù* (Monastic Registrar) oversees the capital city, while the *Sengzhèng* (Monastic Rectifier) is established separately for the provinces;
these three principal offices specifically recruit their personnel based on virtue and reputation.
[There is also] the stupa in the kingdom of Rāmaṇa.
In the past, it was shared with various kingdoms, and stupas were erected for it.
Over many years, the site fell into ruin;
now only wild elephants come to carry off its fragrant flowers and offer up its fruit.
They remove chaff with their tusks and scatter water with their trunks;
yet there are wandering śramaṇas.
Moved by this event,
he subsequently renounced his precepts to apply himself with diligence;
he carefully restored the old foundations.
To subject oneself to all manner of labor is, in effect, to violate and abandon the precepts.
Why then do you urge the śrāmaṇeras to be diligent?
It is because if one possesses the precepts, such acts as digging the earth, cutting trees, and lighting fires in the open air would all constitute a violation of the precepts.
Therefore, it was not possible to carry out any work of repair or restoration. Jin Daojing, a great-grandson of the Right Army General (Wang Xizhi),
dwelt at Mount Ruoye and established the Xuanliu Vihāra,
observing the precepts as if he were at Rājagṛha.
Therefore, when the benevolent person performs good,
the whole world agrees with them; when the non-benevolent person performs evil, the whole world likewise agrees.
This is likewise true for all under heaven. The auspicious person performs good deeds as if the days were never enough;
the inauspicious person performs evil deeds in the same way.
Furthermore, Cui Huìyuán was so preoccupied with building a monastery at Wǔlíng that he felt his days were never enough.
After he passed away,
someone saw him beneath Mount Wǔdāng.
His countenance was exceedingly serene.
He entrusted the monks of the monastery with this message:
"Do not allow the affairs of the temple to fall into neglect."

From then on, there were sounds of bells in the air at their respective times. Today, at Mount Wuzhong in Qiongzhou and Jinge Temple in Pengzhou in the region of Shu, there are likewise sounds of hymns and bells in the air.
Furthermore, Faxian established a temple at Zangwei Mountain in Guangzhou.
Two youths came along, holding hands,
and sang: "The treasury of the subtle possesses the Way and its Virtue."
The joy was not yet at its end; as the song of the Qin palace concluded, he suddenly vanished.
Indeed, the spirit is moved by sincerity, and the Way is aided by the spirit.
Without sincerity, what virtue is there?
Without the divine, what can one rely upon?
Therefore, it is here that auspicious responses soar.
One should merely encourage those who have not yet taken flight.
Qi Zhou Yong established Caotang Monastery at the former residence of Lei Cizong on Mount Zhong;
some called it Shanzu.
Huiqiu requested Huiyue to take charge of the monastery.

Although Yuezhou was geographically close, it lay secluded beyond the mundane world; as Yuezhou’s profound appreciation for the transcendent and his long-standing sincerity were already in harmony with his own, he immediately entrusted himself to it as his final resting place.
Yong sighed in admiration, saying:
"The Master who restrains himself amidst the mountain thickets fills the world with purity and serenity."
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty established Guangzhai Monastery and issued an edict appointing Fayun as its abbot;
Fayun then instituted the monastic regulations.
Yayou set a model for future generations;
Yun, possessing filial virtue,
further inherited Heaven’s blessings through his religious practice and bore the imperial favor of the state.
Now, as for filial piety:
one serves the deceased as if they were alive;
one thinks of the parents as if one could not bear to live without them.
Zengzi was renowned for his service to his parents;
when he observed the mourning rites for his parents, he took no food or drink for seven days.
Gao Chai was renowned for his longing for his parents.
For three years he wept blood;
he never showed his teeth when speaking, and his weeping was soundless,
as if blood were flowing forth.
Because his smile was so subtle, his teeth were not visible; had he not possessed the humility of Sengmin, he would likely have been unable to endure the mourning.
Fayun observed the mourning for his mother until he nearly reached the point of physical destruction.
Sengmin encouraged him.
Just as he was about to take his meal, the śrāmaṇera Suītán would immerse himself in deep contemplation of the *Lotus Sūtra* and often retreat to secluded crags.
He set up stones for his listeners and,
holding a pine branch, preached the Dharma alone;
thus, he was the first thereafter to bring forth this sutra.
Although there were many masters, none could equal him.
Once, while delivering a public lecture at a temple,
he was moved by a divine response such that celestial flowers fell like snow, filling the sky and drifting into the hall.
When the sitting session concluded, he departed.
At that time, there was a monk who wished to emulate him.
A divine being appeared in a dream and admonished him, saying:
"During the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, the Dharma Master Yun already expounded this sutra.
You should quickly settle your mind; once you have completed your preparations, do not harbor any improper expectations."

Now, in this degenerate age of the Dharma-gate, people follow their own inclinations and each pursues their private interests. Regarding the legacy left by the sages of former generations, what do the younger generation care for?
They turn their backs on virtue and pursue profit.
It is easy to advance but difficult to retreat.
They constantly spy on the permanent residents;
if there is fertile land, they bribe the officials in charge to steal glances at it.
Employing wealth to seek his master was his primary duty; having obtained it, he grasped that official seal and took full advantage of his position.
Consequently, he became exclusively self-indulgent and failed to maintain solemnity even in his daily conduct, thereby disrupting the order of the six harmonies of the Sangha.
The merit of the nine-cubit well was thus ruined;
by the time the granaries were empty and the fields had turned green with weeds, it became clear that the permanent resident monk in charge of temple affairs had instead brought about ruin.
If his manors and fields fall into ruin,
he will then plot to seek retirement; he will either plot to grow old or plead illness as an excuse.
The provincial offices and monasteries have never examined their relative merits or demerits, nor scrutinized their deceitfulness or integrity.
The *Yinyi* (Phonetic and Semantic Commentary) to the *Hanshu* states:
"The highest achievement is called *zuì* (the most)."
To apply effort is called "the palace" (diàn).
It denotes the eradication of wickedness and the rectification of what is upright. To be sudden means to follow through with one's back turned toward [the enemy] and advance.
It is truly lamentable that such crafty men have gained their scheme.
Furthermore, those who are "caozhuo" (clumsy and petty) are but small fry; even when living in the secular world, they still depend on others for governance.
How could one who has donned the black robes be capable of bringing order to all things?
However, the government offices and monasteries began to select personnel based on bribes;
yet those who bore the guilt were ultimately exempted by means of bribes as well,
unless they were shielded by the multitude.
They report the crimes as they are called,
yet those who interrogate the prisoners often,
in turn, unjustly ensnare the accusers in legal proceedings by shielding them.
This is somewhat biased.
Initially, when seeking a presiding master,
he sought him by means of wealth.
Furthermore, after the envoys had been mistreated,
he used his wealth to seek their release,
or he litigated on behalf of the monks with the authorities.
The officials, acting out of personal favoritism, instead inflict punishment upon those who report them;
this is simply how public malice flourishes within the administration. This has never been understood by the district and county authorities.
Once their fields and properties have been registered and listed as assets in the official records, they must then be informed and exhorted [to rectify their conduct].
"Ji" means to borrow.
In antiquity, the tax was one-tenth;
the people cultivated ten mu of land.
The Duke lent him his strength to cultivate one mu of land as a tribute for the court;
"the courtyard is filled with a hundred offerings" refers to the presentation of tribute.
Some expected him to transcend the mundane world, while others viewed him as one capable of flight; thus, the government looked upon the monk with favor.
Some may say they are men who have left secular life to dwell beyond the boundaries of the world;
others may say they are transcendents and eminent scholars looking after one another.
In such cases, it would be appropriate to select the worthy and employ the capable, placing them outside the sphere of administrative governance.
There was no one to select the worthy or encourage the capable to repair and maintain it;

this was because the public office regarded those who dwell beyond worldly affairs as unfit for governance. Consequently, the ancestral temple fell into ruin, causing both men and spirits to sigh in lamentation.
Is it not the case that while possessing the land, one has leaked its majesty and benevolence?
It is hoped that the black-robed [monks] will be bound by the cords of law within the public offices;
for when the multitude commits a transgression, the community bears the guilt, and when the monks commit a sin, the Sangha bears the responsibility.
It was intended that the government offices would rectify this;
it is the fault of the monks that they do not prioritize this matter. It is the fault of the secular officials that powerful interests obstruct them.
That the monastic lands remain neglected without cause—this is the fault of both parties.
They cause encroachment and harassment on behalf of the state;
when officials commit transgressions, there are two offenses yet they are not punished—how can disorder ever be brought to an end?
Some even falsely assume the official titles of the Śākya school.
Provided they fall within the protective shade of the regulations for the Sangha-fields and reach the scope of their labor,
they will leap with joy and shake their heads in delight.
They believed that by remaining in comfortable dwellings and seeking ease for their own bodies,
they might preside over monasteries or manage estates,
thereby diminishing and exploiting the community of monks.
They encroach upon and damage the permanent property of the Sangha, colluding with local prefectures and counties,
and relying upon those in positions of power.
He established rigorous barriers so that litigants could find no victory; thereafter,
he meticulously prepared his saddle and mount.
The elegant attendants leaped for joy and turned their heads;
they were deeply gratified, having achieved their ambitions and fulfilled their natures.
It rests with me alone.
Whether the temple suffers loss or gain,
I shall neither drive it away nor hasten toward it.
The temple has goods and plants;
yet it does not personally attend to them nor take direct care of them.
The temple has bells and stone chimes.
To not strike [the gong] is unfilial;
to have courtyards and doors in a monastery that are neither swept nor sprinkled with water is likewise unfilial.
Regarding wealth and hardships, they are merely matters of expediency; they are simply expedient. This is a dangling tumor upon the lineage of the Dharma, a supernumerary digit among the people.
It is like a fifth finger growing from atop five fingers.
This is called having webbed fingers; it is useless.
Now, I employ this as a metaphor for those who have left the household life.
One should strive to embody the Dharma as its form and expression,
rather than embodying the pursuit of profit as its form and expression; thus,
one can rise and fall in accordance with the times.
Wherever it is, it benefits all beings:
like the southern breeze of Xun that harmonizes the myriad things,
and like the Azure Spirit (the planet Jupiter) bringing blessings to a region under the lunar mansion of Jiao.
It is called the Star of Longevity,
also known as the Star of the Elder;
it is the essence of the Azure Dragon.
To see [this truth] is itself a blessing; how could it merely be a matter of using one's breath to stop a whirling wind or using one's strength to restrain a galloping horse?
It is rather a matter of being courageous in bringing peace to oneself.
Is it because they are stingy in accepting what is good?

Thus, those of mediocre capacity admire the inferior, which gradually forms a custom; as custom becomes habit, it becomes one's nature. Consequently, those who can rectify, broaden, and govern the whole system are ultimately rare.
Now, as for the end of the Xia and Yin dynasties,
why did they reach such a state that everyone was executed and none failed to transform into evil? Yet,
during the era of Tang and Yu, it was otherwise.
How could it come to the point that all are corrupt and do not transform toward goodness? The people of Jie and Zhou were such that every household could have been executed;
the people of Tang and Yu were such that every household could have been enfeoffed. Now, the Great Dharma is about to fall.
Our school has fallen into a state of petty negligence and superficiality, even descending into mere expediency; there is none among us who has not been transformed into an unworthy person.
Yet, some are now about to return to the source of our teaching to eradicate these corruptions.
The "Syllable" (shū) guides the flow of the waves;

"creating boats for a bridge" means constructing a bridge by lashing boats together. Furthermore, [the term] "supporting the net and knot of Jia" refers to Zhi Dun and others supporting Huiyuan. "Chasing the clouds and binding the foundation" refers to the disciples of Fayun and Huiyue. Indeed, these are not what is esteemed in the present day.

There are those whose karmic conduct is meager yet who hold themselves in high esteem, their reputation slightly manifest—such as the class today who carry a single scripture or treatise, or sons who recite and savor the depths of consciousness.

When they gather what is beneficial, they offer no thanks; when it comes to worldly affairs, they say, "This hinders the Way. They abruptly abandon the intent to maintain and support, suddenly composing flowery pretexts to seek a mere evasion. This is like the butcher of the clan whose blade has become blunted.
One has not yet attained the skillful butcher’s way of throwing his blade. Zangzi said that an ordinary butcher, when first learning to dissect an ox, must inevitably blunt his blade.
A skilled butcher, however, sees no whole ox before his eyes; he speaks of "throwing the blade" as being without any damage. Thus, the gentleman is not merely a vessel for a single function.
This vessel is neither square nor round; its supreme goodness is like water.
Yet this is not like water.
This is the study of the Way by Heaven.
First comes practice, and then its preservation.
When practice encounters obstruction, one preserves it; when preservation becomes unimpeded, practice flows forth.
To act while maintaining such [pretenses] is called hypocrisy;
it is to steal the office of a high official for the sake of governance.
Know the worthy and bestow talent upon them.
To examine slander and redress grievances: when one finds the right person, slander is examined;
when there is no obstruction, grievances are redressed. Eliminate severity and devote oneself to benevolence.
These six individuals were the ultimate in saving the living people;
as teachers and models of the Dharma, they brought stability and gravity to their respective regions.
Why did he not dismiss his followers in such a manner?
As for his gathering of the worthy and capable,
and his distribution of labor and assignment of offices—
He does not seek personal enrichment nor does he oppress the multitude; rather,
he takes all hundred transgressions upon himself.
He attributed all his merits to others;
he bestowed his grace first upon those who had served him,
and only later did he extend it to the common people.
He causes his conduct to extend first to those he is close to,
and later to those who are distant; his mind remains equanimous toward both the loved and the hated.
Equalizing all matters, whether honorable or base,
they drift freely as if upon an unmoored boat;
they roam at ease as if on a leisurely excursion or a wandering journey.
How could they not have attained the Way?
The Grand Master Yin, the Archivist of Zhou, the Magistrate of Qiqian, Pengzu, Laozi, and Zhuangzi were all men of official rank and emolument.
In turbidity, one is like a pearl cast into water;
treading upon favor is like the wind passing over grass.

How could one ever allow external affairs to disturb the Way and its Virtue? One harmonizes with the light and becomes one with the dust. Formerly, when Kong Mie governed a district, he was distressed by three failures. Kong Mie—
Mie was the son of Confucius’s elder brother.
He and Ziju both served Confucius.
Once, when Confucius passed by Mie, he questioned him.
"What have you gained and what have you lost in serving me?
He replied, "I have gained nothing.
As for what I have lost, there are three things."
If one is as deaf to the affairs of state as if studying there, how can one practice?
This is a lack of clarity in learning.
When one's stipend is so meager that even congee does not reach one's relatives, [how can one serve the state?]
This means that our bonds of flesh and blood grow ever more distant.
Public affairs are many and urgent;
thus, one cannot go to offer condolences at funerals or inquire after those who are ill.
"This is a deficiency in the way of friendship.
Although Mi Zijian had these three faults, he was pleased with the Three Gains of Mi Buzhi.
Confucius went to inquire about this.
He said:
"That which has been attained is threefold.
Having first spoken of them, I have now attained them and put them into practice."
This study increases one's clarity.
The stipends provided extend to one's relatives,
making the bonds of flesh and bone even closer.
Even when there were matters of public business, he simultaneously visited the sick and offered condolences for the deceased;
this was the trust and recommendation of his friends.
Confucius sighed deeply and said:
"A noble person indeed is this man!
If Lu had no noble persons, from where would he have derived such qualities? Confucius thus praised Mi as a noble person.
It is not that existence itself is lacking;
it is a pity for this burdened physical form.
A hundred years is but a human lifetime.
Those among the commoners are registered in the official temples;
those among the sages are enrolled in the immortal temples.
As for those residing in the official temples, can they truly decline to manage them as public affairs?
There are certain hermitages where I am unable to go, such as Mount Wuzhong in Dayi County of Qiong Prefecture,
where five hundred arhats reside, and Mount Sanxue, where the Holy Lamp appears.
Such as the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra at Mount Emei,
and again, as recorded in the *Gantong zhuan*,
there was a monk of unknown name who went to Zhulin Xiansi and other locations; these were all places where Zhu Tanyou had previously established [monasteries] on Mount Tiantai.
Chigeng Yuantong traveled to Dongye, and Shigu Huibao stayed overnight in a mountain cave;
both were monasteries of the immortals, where there were invariably preceptors and masters who maintained dignified decorum.
When they wished to entrust their forms to those places, those places did not retain them.
It is often heard among people in the world that there are sounds of bells and chanting from deep forests on precipitous cliffs, as well as miraculous lamps and strange images;
this is indeed verifiable.
For this reason, whenever the monastics dwell together for the recitation of the precepts, they say:
In the summer retreat, one must not fail to purify and solemnize the Dharma-hall;
the assembly shall be orderly and reverent,
as if standing in the presence of the Sage.
The *Mahāyāna-avatāra-śāstra* states:
"Sixteen great arhats, including Piṇḍola and Rāhula,
reverently received his final instructions."

Subsequently, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the King of Kaśmīra, Jayasena, and the Venerable Nandimitra brought forth sixteen great arhats from among the people of the villages. In recent times, there was a great elder and Vinaya master of the Hu clan in Zizhou Commandery.
He was also one who participated in this current of spiritual resonance.
To the southern border of the commandery lay Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
there, the foreign master led his disciples to observe the summer retreat and recite the precepts.
The number of people at night is fixed. As the tally sticks (śalākā) exceed their count, the assembly does not understand why;
thus, the monks regularly perform [the ritual] on the fifteenth day of the month and on the final day of the month.
One person shall recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra and must certainly distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*).
First, count how many monks there are and how many śrāmaṇeras there are.
Having been informed of the number of voting tallies (śalākā), and as the summer retreat was drawing to a close,
two or three Hu śramaṇas left the mountain and reached a corner of the road, where they waved their hands in farewell to the farmers.
When the Vinaya Master heard of this, he rushed toward them.
His followers galloped in all four directions;
though they were not far away when he departed,
none of them could find him.
The mind of the sage is identical to the mind of ordinary people;

the spirit of ghosts and deities is identical to the spirit of ordinary people. Thus, it is through utmost sincerity that one moves the divine intelligences. At Huizhou, the master encountered a drought while residing there.
When they were about to move their settlement, the local mountain deity spoke to them, saying, "It will flow like a spout. This was like the case at Huoyi Temple in Zizhou, where there was no water;
there was a monk named Shenxiao who recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He set a period of seven days.
When the time arrived, the spring indeed gushed forth as expected.
It remains visible today. According to the account of Sengfan, while he was staying overnight at another temple during the night of the *śīla* recitation, [the water appeared].
Those who contemplate the meaning of verticality (the vertical axis) abandon their worldly affairs;
yet the spirits and deities grew indignant and toppled them.
This truly shows that one must not overstep the bounds of harmony and moderation.
Liang Hui-chao served as the Sangharāja; he was so fond of mountains and waters that his reputation for such excursions reached several li.
When at home, he kept a retinue of servants arrayed before him like officials attending a prince—was this truly the conduct of a Sangharāja? No, indeed.
Now, the Sangzheng (Chief Monastic Overseer) ought to rectify himself as the basis for his administration.
Without integrity, how could there be rectitude?
Daodao served as the Sangzheng of Nan-Yanzhou.
Upon his retirement from office, he left behind nothing but five bundles of old paper; how could such integrity and such turbidity possibly be compared? "Gai" (概) here means to level.
One who levels measures of grain, such as bushels and pecks, [would not do so with a biased tool]; Sengmin did not hold grand assemblies.
He said to his gatekeeper-disciples:
"Although this great assembly has the merit of being convened for a time,
I lack the necessary manpower."
Hulling rice, chopping wood, and boiling vegetables;
treading upon and trampling while pouring water over roasted meats—
these cause injury to an immense number of beings.
It is like relying on the power of borrowed officials:
though the laborers employed are numerous,
it remains difficult to ensure they give their full effort.
Therefore, I do not act upon it.
A commentator says:
"The tranquil person excels at initiating movement."
The active person excels in stillness;
this is the way of the man who provides universal succor—one whose outward form is restless yet loves stillness, and whose substance is supple yet cherishes firmness.
It is also like the principle of using leniency to remedy severity; if one is still, one acts with stillness.

This is because the common mind is desolate and virtue does not shine forth; it is due to the fact that their traces are submerged and hidden. If one dwells in movement yet moves even further, then the principles of things become increasingly manifest, while the Way and its Virtue become superficial and false.
Therefore, the worthy person treads upon the interval between movement and stillness,
finds their place beyond existence and non-existence,
and unifies all virtues within non-action.
There is no good deed that he would not perform.
Thus, the Great Yu made his palaces and chambers humble while exerting all his strength in the ditches and canals;
he made his food and drink simple yet offered the utmost filial piety to the spirits.
Is it that one desires calluses on the hands and feet and hairless shins? When Yu of Xia governed the waters, his calves were hairless and his shins were hairless.
Wei Zhao said: "Bao (胈) refers to the small hairs on the thighs. This was because he did not seek private comfort for himself.
Yet he desired to bestow his merit upon the world.
The elder’s son, Śubhavyūha,
established a great assembly for giving— as described in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra— and the Sage rejoiced and instructed him.
This demonstrates that the blessings of extensive charity and succoring the multitude transcend the mind, and their joy is inexhaustible.
Therefore, in the Western Regions, there is the *pāñcavārṣika*, which is the Great Assembly of Offerings; those of superior wisdom practice it.
Having accumulated wealth, one is able to disperse it;
returning the favor to me and returning the riches to others.

"The continuous bestowal of gifts encompasses all of Zhou; in truth, this is a celebration of universal bounty. Chen Huanzi’s measures of *dou*, *qu*, *fu*, and *zhong* were distributed extensively among the people, reaching them all.
This was precisely because he ultimately secured a lasting legacy for his descendants in Qi. Indeed, if a great person truly benefits all things, [the merit will surely endure].
Even if it were harmful to oneself, one would not avoid it;
how much less so when it is not harmful? For a Bodhisattva’s practice, the body is a mountain of flesh and a source of fish and rice.
If one wishes to traverse the Great Path,
how can one regard a narrow bypath? If the undertaking of meritorious works harms the lives of sentient beings,
then who is at fault for the pillars, stupas, clay and wood images, robes, and food that result from such efforts?
Śāriputra was begging for alms and observed insects in the air,
as numerous as a torrential rain.
It was like grain in a vessel that had not been eaten for many days;
the Great Sage said:
"What is seen with the physical eye may certainly be eaten.
This was the instruction given by Lingyu to his disciples, regardless of their status—
whether noble or humble— and regardless of their age— whether young or old.
All of them stated their own names,
addressed him as "Virtuous One," and ceased all scolding and beating.
To violate one's word is surely to incur condemnation; how could he have acted so as to reach such a state?
This may be transmitted, but it cannot be emulated.
The ode says:
"I cherish his illustrious virtue.
This means that King Wen did not manifest himself through loud voices or haughty countenances.
"It is by means of his countenance.
Furthermore, it says:
"Without conscious knowledge, he follows the pattern of the Sovereign. Zhongni said:

Sound and color are but peripheral to human nature; to manifest authority through intimidation and to display a stern countenance are the ways of the base. Now, a world that achieves order without punishment prizes such methods;
yet people today fear authority and treat virtue with contempt, allowing severity to outweigh benevolence. The Sage, therefore, regards this with great concern.
The Ode says:

"If the noble man were to show anger, the rebellion would surely be quickly quelled. This means that if the noble man were to express indignation, the rebellious masses would certainly disperse and dissolve. It further says:
The King was greatly incensed;
he then marshaled his forces,
intending to use awe to quell the disorder.
Indeed, a fine horse must rely upon its bit and whip;
a beautiful bird must await grooming and stroking;
and excellent timber must depend upon the chisel and saw.
There has never been one who could achieve personal excellence while abandoning these [virtues].
The *I Ching* says:
"The petty person feels no shame in being unbenevolent."
They do not fear unrighteousness;
they are not encouraged by the sight of profit,
nor deterred by the display of intimidation.
"A slight punishment serves as a great warning":
"punishment" refers to the censure for the crimes of injury and abandonment.

It means that by being censured for such offenses, one immediately receives a great warning regarding the benefits of cultivating merit and performing virtuous deeds. Therefore, those who lead the masses should guide people toward the realization of the Way before it becomes manifest.
To punish those who have not yet caused disorder,
causing people to look up to his majesty and benevolence with diligent reverence and fear—
this may be called a good beginning.
At the commencement, having established silence as if the five vital energies were in mutual resonance,
the eight winds opened their sequence;
all was majestic and perfectly harmonious.
His words and deeds were characterized by order and propriety.
Although there were instances of censure, flogging, and verbal abuse—
where "flogging" refers to the use of a staff— he never actually employed such punishments.
This is what is called a "good end.
Among people, few achieve such an end with composure; it is only Lingyu who is capable of this. As for others, they are rare indeed.
Observe that although he was not subjected to physical punishment or humiliation, he was nonetheless censured and cast out from the ranks of the assembly.
Or perhaps the reprimand has already been too severe.
If one now hands over the robe and bowl and leaves the hall, the Sūtra says:
"This is killing; this is the retribution for killing."
"This is hell; this is the retribution for hell.
Regarding the Vinaya provision that permits teaching [the Dharma] even while disparaging [a person], why is this so?
This is because one desires to bring about the state where there is no need for punishment by means of punishment; it is to strictly admonish offenders so that they will not commit such acts again.
Thus, praising the good encourages goodness, while exposing evil blocks evil.
Rāhula spoke with loving words,
yet he rebuked Devadatta;
was this not so, O son of the Buddha?
Devadatta was the Buddha’s enemy, yet you, O Benevolent One, held forgiveness in your heart.
The crafty hold forgiveness in their mouths; the benevolent are loyal and sincere, and thus hold forgiveness in their hearts.
The crafty are deceitful and treacherous.
Therefore, if forgiveness resides in the mouth and the heart, one ascends toward things and attains benefit;
if it resides only in the mouth, one ruins things while feigning compassion.
