"Tripamā" refers to matters such as ritual etiquette, the ten marks, music, the art of war, and so forth.
The four ātharvaṇas refer to incantations and the like;
all were spoken by Brahmā and have been transmitted entirely through oral tradition.
They do not record [the teachings] on skins or shells; at seven years of age, they approach a teacher to learn them by oral recitation.
Once their studies are complete, they become teachers of the nation. That country has handed down the tradition that there exists a method for learning intelligence.
First, "re-examination" refers to the arising of wisdom through the investigation of principles;
it means to carefully examine the meaning and flavor [of the teachings].
Second, "manifesting the phonemes" means that characters give rise to characters, and sounds give rise to sounds. Within a period of months, his contemplation flowed like a spring.
If one does not possess this method, there is no means by which to recite the multitude of words as swiftly as a whirled arrow.
In the past, Buddhayaśas and Guṇavarman were precisely such individuals.
When Yaśas first arrived in the Qin kingdom and was about to undertake the work of translation,
the people of Qin tested him.
He was granted a register of medicinal prescriptions and various texts.
Guṇavarman completed the recitation of them all in three days;
the total amount he recited amounted to over one million words.
Among the various Tripitaka masters who have come here, there are few who have not arrived at this place.
Since the time of Lord Shui-ren in China, people looked up at the North Star to determine the names of the directions;
yet, as for the simplicity and dullness of the people under Fu Xi...
He recognized only his mother,
but did not recognize his father;
he knew only to cover what was before him.
Unaware of what lies behind them,
they seek food when hungry and discard the leftovers once full.
Tàihào bowed down and transformed them;
hence it is said that Fúxī gazed upward at the celestial patterns and looked downward to examine the terrestrial principles.
This was for the purpose of distinguishing the various things of the world. Fuxi employed it to draw the Eight Trigrams and create writing and seals.
As for the *Sanfen*, *Wudian*, *Basuo*, and *Jiuchiu*, these are all ancient surviving books; the *Sanfen* are the books of the Three Sovereigns.
The Five Classics are the books of the Five Emperors;
the Eight Searches are the books of the Eight Trigrams;
and the Nine Mounds are the records of the Nine Provinces, such as those read by Yi Shi of Chu during the time of King Ling of Chu.
The Left Scribe Yixiang was able to read the Three Primordial Records, the Five Canons, the Eight Investigations, and the Nine Mounds; subsequently, Zhongni [Confucius] edited the Odes,
standardized the Rites and Music, expounded the Way of the Changes, and compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Regarding the restoration of collapsed customs: since the time of Kings You and Li of the Zhou dynasty, the capital was moved east to Luoyi;
the feudal lords usurped the right to wage war, and the rites and music fell into ruin.
In the eleventh year of Duke Ai of Lu,
the Master returned from Wei to Lu;
in the fourteenth year, he obtained the *qilin*.
He then compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals,
edited the Book of Poetry,
and codified the Rituals.
To rectify the customs that had fallen into ruin, there were the Six Classics: the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the Book of Rites,
and the Book of Changes.
The Book of Documents,
the Mao Version of the Odes,
and the musical lyrics; therefore, Confucius said:

Gentleness and profound sincerity are the teaching of the Odes (*Shi*). Without studying the Odes, one is unable to speak. Broad knowledge and far-reaching understanding are the teaching of the Documents (*Shu*). Rectifying the way of royal pronouncements, being expansive, broad, and easygoing, is the teaching of Music (*Yue*). Harmonizing the sentiments of the people, being pure, clean, subtle, and refined, is the teaching of the Changes (*Yi*). Exhausting principles and perfecting nature through reverence, frugality, and solemn respect is the teaching of Rites (*Li*). Bringing peace to superiors and governing the people by arranging phrases and comparing events is the teaching of Spring and Autumn (*Chunqiu*). This rectifies the way of praise and censure. As for the *Zuo Zhuan* and the *Guoyu*, the Master Zuo (Zuo Qiuming) [composed them] because the matters and meanings of the Spring and Autumn had not been fully exhausted.

The *Guoyu* (Discourses of the States) is set aside here so that it may be consulted in conjunction with other sources. Regarding Sima Qian’s *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian): having incurred the offense of imprisonment in the "silkworm chamber," Sima Qian composed the *Shiji*.
By the time of Emperor Wu of Han, it comprised one hundred and thirty fascicles. From the Han and Wei dynasties onwards...
There are bibliographic records for all of them, including Ban Gu’s *Book of the Former Han* in one hundred and twenty fascicles,
Sima Biao’s *Book of the Later Han* in eighty fascicles,
and Chen Shou’s *Records of the Three Kingdoms*.

The books of various states are extremely numerous, encompassing the works of a hundred masters and fully recorded in the catalogs of Jīnmǎ and Shíqú; these were all repositories for the books of the Han.
Furthermore, more recently there have been the *Jīngjízhì* (Catalogue of Classics and Writings) by Wú [Zhòngyán] of Xīqí and Mǔ [Shùlín] of Dōngqí.
In all of these, one can see their vision; for instance, from the beginning of literary composition, there were the songs of Yu and the hymns of Yin.
When the virtue of the Zhou declined, the poets flourished.
Following the age of these poets—
The *Sao* and Song styles deviated from the *Feng* and *Ya*. "Sao" refers to Qu Yuan and Song Yu; both were men of the Warring States period.

Jia, Ma, Yang, and Ban gradually transformed the *Sao* style—namely Jia Yi, Sima Xiangru, Yang Xiong, and Ban Gu. Reaching the time of Emperor An, the style changed from that of Jia and Ma; this refers to the era of Han Emperor Xian and those who followed in the Jin and Song dynasties.
The *Xian* and *Shao* music, the music of Yao and Shun, were not heard among the states of Qi and Liang.
As for the comparison of floral patterns and painted designs, Shen Yue, Liu Xie, Ren Fang, Xie An, and others [studied] the six scripts of this region, such as *xiangxing* (pictographic).
Indicative (shì),
associative (yì), and phonetic-associative (shēng).
"Transitional annotations (zhuanzhu) and phonetic loans (jiajie) establish the origins of written characters. Therefore,
by mastering the Great Seal script (Dazhuan), one will not be confused regarding written characters."
In that context, there are six types of *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive compounds):

first, those based on the identity of the activity (*karmadhāraya*); second, those derived from the dependent (*bahuvrīhi*) which further yield the possessive (*tatpuruṣa*); and third, those involving contradiction (*virodha*).
Fourth is the "possessive compound" (*bahuvrīhi*) where the members share a common substratum;
fifth is the "proximate";
sixth is the "possessor of wealth. This concludes the analysis of the causes for the application of these designations.
Therefore, by exhaustively investigating worldly terminology and canonical terminology,
one gains mastery over names and titles. All names and titles of the ultimate and conventional truths, as well as worldly conventions,
are subsumed within the six types of grammatical analysis (*ṣaḍvidha-vyākhyāna*).
There were none who failed to discern the essential tenets [of the tradition], namely: Kang Senghui, Zhi Daolin, Fotudeng, Kumārajīva, Hui'an, and Huiguan;

the "Four Sages" of Kumārajīva’s school—Sengsheng, Daosheng, Daorong, and Daorei; Sengyou of the Liang dynasty; Daohan of the Zhou dynasty; Yancong of the Sui dynasty; and Jing, Xuan, Lin, Gai, and Huijing from the beginning of our dynasty.
Daoxuan’s Dharma Forest was so profoundly familiar with the fundamental teachings that nothing remained obscure to him;
he had mastered both the Buddhist scriptures and secular histories.
He devoted himself to the study and mastery of literature and calligraphy, and engaged extensively in writing and composition;
he was one who reached the pinnacle of upholding and propagating [the Dharma]. This refers to the eminent monk Li, who participated in the translation of scriptures during the Zhenguan era.
"One who is widely learned and possesses a powerful memory yet remains humble; who is earnest in performing good deeds and never indolent—such a person is called a 'gentleman-monk' (junzi seng).
This refers to Zhi Dun’s commentary on the "Xiaoyao" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.
Xi Xuan’s guests praised his profound realization;
Huijing compiled the *Yinghuaji*, and the scholars of elegant composition admired his discernment.
Thus, he manifested the correct path for humans and devas.
In the art of military strategy and the laws of the army,
as well as in the literary arena and the garden of Dharma,
who in any age has ever lacked such capability?
Once, there was a guest who listened to Master Huiyuan’s exposition on the true nature (*tathatā*).
Although they engaged in a dialogue for several hours,
his doubts and confusion only increased further.
He drew extensively upon the meanings of Zhuangzi to provide analogies.
Those who were deluded thereby attained awakening.
From then on, during the time of Master Dao’an, Huiyuan studied the scriptures of the secular classics without ceasing while listening to [the Buddhist teachings].
During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, on the third day of the third month—a ji-si day—Emperor Wen personally visited the Qu-shui (Flowing Water) site.
He commanded Huiguan and the court officials to compose poems;
Huiguan presented his work first while still seated.
In the Jiande era of the Northern Zhou, Chen Hongzheng came as an envoy to seek counsel from scholars.
Tan Yan was the first to respond to him during the reign of Emperor Wu of Zhou. On that occasion, the Emperor personally presided over the ritual of Shi-dian (the sacrifice to the First Sage-King).
Yan presided over the assembly, modulating his voice with rhythmic intonation.

Chen Ren spread out his robes and bowed his head to listen; he adjusted his garments and performed the rites of salutation before listening. Thereupon, he composed forty poems and presented them to Yan.
He continued to employ those same rhymes in his compositions and responses as if they were familiar verses he had long been reciting.
He then commissioned a portrait of Yan and brought it back to Chang’an, the capital of the Chen and Zhou dynasties.
In the capital of Jinling, Chen paid his respects toward the north morning and evening,
regarding [Fatai] as the Bodhisattva Tanyan. Indeed,
in the world, it is difficult to find one who possesses both refined speech and virtuous conduct in their entirety.

It is difficult to describe his deficiencies; he may truly be called a majestic figure, one with whom it is hard to compete for the virtue of benevolence. As for the countenance of Zizhang and the words of Zi (Zigong), and the conduct of Yanhui, each had its own particular bias. When Lingyu first left the household life, [he was like this].
The Master ordered him to recite the scriptures;
grasping the scroll, he declared:
"Regarding the Tripitaka as well as the Confucian teachings..."
He certainly hoped for a thorough understanding;
he was not one whose resolve would ever waver or change. Consequently, his learning outshone the contemporaries of his time, and the world hailed him as "Yù Púsà" (Bodhisattva Yù).
In the final years of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
he issued an edict renouncing the Daoist teachings; as recorded in the *Hongming ji*,
it states that Emperor Wu initially venerated the Dao.
In the second year of the Tianjian era, he abandoned the Daoist path to take refuge in Buddhism;
there are extant records of this, as well as his humble critique of Confucian teachings.
Others may fear that people will become so deeply immersed [in worldly matters] that they do not return; thus, the Sage commanded the study of external classics.
Provided that one knows this, there is concern that they may become addicted and deluded, sinking into deviant paths or losing the ultimate standard of correctness;
such would be a sign of impending ruin. If one loses that correctness, one becomes confused regarding principle. Indeed, [this teaching] is beneficial to the people.
The Great Sage never sought to eliminate the teachings of Confucianism and Daoism;
both are beneficial to humanity.
For this reason, my teaching does not require their abolition; thus the Sutra says:
Without destroying conventional truth, one establishes ultimate truth.
These two teachings are practiced by those endowed with benevolence and wisdom,
and they also constitute the retribution for humans and devas— such as being pure, detached, of few desires, benevolent, filial, loyal, and trustworthy.
All are practitioners of the human and celestial realms; their retribution merely lies within those realms as gateways and steps toward the Way.
Why must one abandon them and treat them with contempt?
The Sage does not treat himself as private property.

How could he impose upon the world what he himself does not desire? One cannot command the world to reject something simply because one does not desire it oneself; thus, the weight of the Name-Teaching (mingjiao) is maintained.
He still has no distinction between kin and stranger;
he values ritual and music yet still lacks the relationship between ruler and subject;
he values the precepts.
Though they follow the calendar, they remain ignorant of the distinctions between cold and heat.
Though they impose heavy punishments, they remain confused regarding the *yidian*—*yidi* meaning the constant and *yan* meaning the law.
Though they emphasize integrity and yielding, they still follow rules of emulation, rivalry, and contention.

If those who value morality and ethics still remain superficial and hypocritical, how much more so will it be for those whom you seek to transform? The latter two teachings [Buddhism and Daoism] would then become as chaotic as birds and beasts;

if people do not study these two teachings, how are they any different from birds and beasts? Yet you wish to instruct them in non-arising (*anutpāda*). Even Confucianism and Daoism are still obscure in this regard.
By what means can the True Principle be revealed? One who desires to display the brilliance of the five colors must first purify the white silk;
one who desires to traverse the Way and its Virtue must first tread upon benevolence and righteousness.
Thus, the Dharma bequeathed by the Great Sage has endured for two thousand years.
As for the people of China, because they first encountered the teachings of emptiness, non-being, benevolence, and wisdom from Confucius and Laozi,
they subsequently came to recognize the teaching of the refined and true [Buddhism] and turned toward it with reverence and devotion.
It has been taught that every household is like the sun [reaching them]. The *Classic of Filial Piety* states:
"It is not by going to every home and seeing everyone daily that one reaches the people of the four barbarian quarters;
it is not through the extension of these two teachings [Confucianism and Buddhism] alone."
Even now they are unable to observe the fasts and precepts;

how much less can they "spiritually roam" within the principle of the eight liberations? The contemplation of the eight liberations refers to such states as "having internal contemplation but no external form," and so forth. Thus, the Buddhist scriptures take these two teachings [of fasting and contemplation] as their precursors or guides. As for what the Lao-Zhuang teachings call "spontaneity" (*ziran*), it is likely a name that resembles *tathatā* (suchness).

To say that the myriad things are spontaneous (*ziran*) means that the Way of spontaneity is one with the myriad things. The "myriad things" are phenomena characterized by conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);
"spontaneity" is the unconditioned ultimate truth (*asaṃskṛta-paramārtha*).

The phenomena of the myriad things and the truth of non-action (wuwei) are neither identical nor separate. It is not that the myriad things do not arise from causes and conditions; rather, it is said that they do not arise from causes and conditions, which is termed "spontaneity" (ziran).

Those who speak now have not yet understood the followers of divergent tenets; they thus disparage the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) within our own teachings and falsely expound the principle of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
This is identical in view to the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) of the Western Regions, such as the Svabhāvavādins, who say: [text continues].
Who drew the wild beasts with sharp thorns?
Who dug the rivers, seas, and sources of streams?
A violent wind suddenly arose.

Returning to the definitive nature of the myriad dharmas, one must know that they are all spontaneous; how could they be said to be the dual transformations of Kāśyapa? The *Qingjing faxing jing* states:

"Laozi was transformed by Kāśyapa. Yet, at the gate of the Zhu and Si [Confucius and Mencius], benevolence (*ren*) is taken as the ultimate practice; if it were not for the Way and its Power (*daode*), then benevolence would necessarily come first.
Therefore, although Yu could be employed to manage the tax levies of a thousand chariots—the tribute of a feudal lord—and Zi Lu could be employed to manage them;

Chi could be employed to stand at court wearing his sash; and Gongxi Hua could be employed as an official for diplomatic missions, standing at court and conversing with guests. As for Chu Ziwen, the Chancellor of Chu, he showed no sign of resentment even after being dismissed three times. He was the Chancellor of Chu.
His clan name was Dou;
his given name was Gu;
his courtesy name was Wutu.
Three times he served as the Chief Minister of the State of Chen without feeling joy;
three times he was dismissed from office without feeling resentment.
He invariably informed the new minister of the policies of his predecessor. Wenzi of Chen abandoned ten chariots of horses.
In seeking those who could be called benevolent, Chen Xuwu was mentioned;
yet when Cui Zhu murdered his lord,
Wenzi abandoned forty horses and fled out of abhorrence for the deed— this was something even Confucius would not approve of, as both [the former] and the latter were described by Kongzi in this way.
That it is not known whether he possessed benevolence (*ren*) illustrates how difficult the Way of benevolence is.
This benevolence permeates all hundredfold actions and harmonizes with the single virtue; there has never been a case where a specialized virtue was not made vast through benevolence.
In the Five Regions they are called Bodhisattvas;
in the Nine Provinces they are called benevolent men.
This is because such people possess compassion and wisdom.
Compassion and wisdom are the benevolence of the capable and wise;
they constitute the ultimate practice of benevolence in the bodhisattva path.
It is here that the gentleman gradually finds the gateway.
If Emperor Wu of Liang had not relied upon the two teachings [Confucianism and Buddhism],
how could he have been a "gentleman-scholar" (junzi ru) and attained the Great Way (dafang)?
As for the claim that Emperor Wu was narrow-minded and dogmatic:

How can one who merely claims to be a "gentlemanly scholar" (junzi ru) ever reach the Great Way? Those who debate today must surely rely on the strategies of Sun and Wu; Sun Wu and Wu Qi were both outstanding generals of the Warring States period.
Each is well-versed in military treatises and skilled in battle formations;
now, when debating principles, they clash like adversaries, much like the strategic maneuvers of Sun Tzu and Wu Qi.
Those who study the precepts must surely emulate the integrity of Yan Hui and Liu Zhong. When Yan Hui lived in seclusion, he had a young daughter.
During the night, the wind and rain caused the house to collapse; he threw himself inside to stay there.
His younger brother, Shuzi, would not let him stay, refusing until he was forced out of the house and made to enter the main dwelling.
Liu Xiahui’s surname was Zhan and his given name was Li.
His fief was at Liu-xia, and he was posthumously titled Hui.
On a cold night, a woman failed to reach the city gate.
Liu Xiahui covered him with his own garment;

when dawn arrived, he departed, thereby avoiding the unrighteous conduct of violating a man. Those who practice *xi-chán* (seated meditation) must surely admire the loftiness of Chao and You; Xu You and Chao Fu were both eminent scholars of the era of Yao.

When Yao was about to abdicate the throne, [Yao] disliked [the man's refusal] and washed his ears; he lived in seclusion and did not serve in office. Those who maintain the order must contemplate the transformations of Qi and Lu, for it is they who maintain the fundamental principles of governance.
One must reform and guide them, just as it is said that "if Qi undergoes one transformation, it will reach the level of Lu;
if Lu undergoes one transformation, it will reach the Way. Therefore, one employs the teachings of external schools to entice and assist them.
He peered into the inner teachings to stimulate his resolve;
yet he also feared harm—fearing that it might bring him no peace.
At first, he was enticed and led away by the external teachings.
Later, when he was instructed in the inner teachings, there was likewise no harm in this. Indeed, those who climb trees compete for height;
those who dig wells compete for depth.
If there were no one brave in front,
who would be brave behind?
Although the House of Liang was indeed possessed of ultimate sincerity, [it could not prevail].
One who does not carefully observe the movements of a carriage before it departs cannot know its fate.

To constantly attend to the details of a matter is the proper application of method; yet one who wishes to abruptly shift an object to follow the Dao, thereby exhausting the nature of that object, does not foresee the driving of Dongye Bi, which ultimately ends in failure. Yan Hui saw Dongye Bi’s carriage and knew it was certain to fail.
This was because his horse had not yet been properly broken in.
Once he took the reins, the carriage indeed overturned and the horse was injured. I have read the texts on abstaining from wine and meat;
therein, compassion exceeds even that of the Buddha.
Regarding the Dharma of Lightening the Body through Borrowing:
On three occasions, he surpassed the sovereigns in his acts of self-sacrifice by entering monasteries and becoming a slave to the assembly.
The ministers provided one hundred thousand coins to redeem him;
once the assembly of monks had given their silent consent, he returned home.
Even if one were to humble oneself by serving as a seat, it would still not surpass this [principle].
Why must it be so? Furthermore, I have issued an edict that the patterns on silk and brocade must not contain the forms of birds or beasts.

This is because I fear that cutting and tailoring them might give rise to the intent of killing and wounding, which would harm the Way of benevolence and forbearance. Although this may be seen as employing the art of feeding a tiger, [it is done for the sake of compassion].
Yet this also teaches people a murderous mind. Liang Yang, the Director of Pastures under King Xuan of Zhou, was skilled at raising tigers.
He did not provide them with living prey because he knew that killing would provoke their anger.
Do not give them whole objects;
they will become angry if you break them into pieces. Feed them at the proper times according to their hunger and satiety.
One should understand his angry mind but not oppose his will;
one should not cause him to rejoice, for if he rejoices,
he will inevitably become angry again.
Although one wishes to sever the mind of killing, one instead gives rise to the very thought of killing.
Silk and fine fabrics originally possess no characteristic of killing;
yet now, one forcibly conjures up the perception of killing toward them.
This is because [the sacrifice] originally did not exist;
even if it were to exist, its purpose would merely be to teach people the intent of killing.

When performing ancestral temple sacrifices or sacrifices at the suburban altars, one uses flour as the sacrificial victim; if one does not do so, one does nothing at all—how could this be a deception of one's ancestors?
Yet, if one were to carry [the deceased] on one's back using flour as a substitute for flesh, it would constitute a falsehood and deception;
furthermore, this would not serve as a burden for one's ancestors. If a son, having donned black robes, were to ride [in a carriage], [he would likewise fail his duty].
Failing to discern the beautiful from the ugly,
they flaunted their boastfulness and arrogance,
inscribing [their names] upon the pale walls and plain screens.
I simply do not know that this is luring the enemy and inviting invasion. Now there are those who, having donned the black robes, have attained manifest honor;
yet they fail to distinguish between good and evil, indulging only in empty arrogance.
Furthermore, by simultaneously casting aside the teachings of the Superior One and inscribing them upon plastered walls and plain screens,
one may be said to have invited upon oneself censure and interrogation. This was as stated in Zhou Dao’an’s “Treatise on the Two Teachings” (Erjiao lun).
Sui Yancong’s *Tongji lun* (Discourse on Penetrating the Ultimate) allows the mind and eyes to roam freely,
emerging from and submerging within the profound and mysterious depths.
He established the roles of guest and host;
first he posed a series of subtle challenges,
and only afterward did he provide the explanations.

To investigate the mysteries of heterodox schools and treat their thorny, deviant paths as a protective enclosure for the Dharma, one first provisionally establishes divergent doctrines to challenge and refute one's own fundamental teachings;
only then does one provide the definitive response.
Having prepared the views of rival schools, later figures such as Li Zhongqing obtained them and acted like thieves breaking through walls and climbing over fences;
they concealed what was accessible and elaborated upon what was difficult.
By composing treatises such as the *Ten Differences* and the *Nine Delusions*,
he deceived those who were ignorant; these were all followers of heterodox views from the Tang dynasty,
deceiving those of shallow learning.
That they did not see An Zong’s treatise and thus furthered his slanderous words—was this not because these two scholars, while seeking to tame [the beast], instead suffered its counter-bite?

Was it not because these two men, by composing their treatises to guard against the slightest sign of danger, were instead robbed of their vessels and used to attack one another? How could they have sought security only to bring about peril?
Yet this treatise is not yet finished;
these fallacious objections have not ceased.
Indeed, the former kings used the balance and the bushel to eliminate theft.
Yet people apply this to the case of a thief; those who place a sword [in his hand] are compared to murderers.
Now, the thief instead uses it to wage war, halting slaughter, yet people apply this to the case of murder.
Therefore, that which is to be guarded against becomes ever more numerous,
and that upon which one relies becomes ever more remote.
Alas, how difficult this is!
However, those who adhere strictly to their own teachings possess a simplicity that is more than sufficient;
yet those who study various traditions concurrently...
In competition, there is excess;
were it not for the gentleman, one would have no means to maintain the ultimate limit. If one preserves the fundamental source, one may naturally remain simple and unadorned.
Because they have studied different schools,
they consequently engage in much contention.
However, if one can be humble and prudent while also studying the doctrines of other schools and external disciplines, [they may attain such harmony].
The Master said, "A gentleman is like a monk; therefore, the sages of old remarked:
'Learning applied to the person is like bait on a hook, or like music.'"
Now, by using vinegar, soy sauce, salt, and plum,
one harmonizes them to achieve balance and supplements what is insufficient.
It drains what has been obstructed and then offers nourishment;
thus the five viscera are balanced, which constitutes "aid and benefit."
"Xie" (泄) means "to diminish.
This is the speech of Yanzi in response to the Marquis of Qi,
when the Marquis was with Liangqiu Ju at the Yuantai Terrace.
The *Zuozhuan*, fascicle twenty-four, contains slightly different wording: "Music is harmonized by means of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo. Metal refers to the *zhong* bell;
stone, the *qing* chime;
silk, the *qin* and *se* zithers.
The bamboo instruments include the *xiāo* flute and others. The gourd instruments include the *shēng* and *yú* organs.
The earthen instrument is the *xuān*.
Leather is used for the drum;
wood is used for the *zhù* and *yǔ*.
These are called the eight musical sounds (*bāyīn*), which regulate what is about to be lost.
If one were to prune away the five sounds that follow from such licentiousness,
there would be no room for plucking;
yet there still exist the profuse hand-movements and licentious sounds.
One should first prune and regulate them before allowing them to be heard.
When the five qi are rectified, if the qi of the five elements were restricted to a single flavor or a single tone,
what would there be to value therein?
In the past, Huiyuan composed the "Treatise on Why Śramaṇas Do Not Pay Homage.
He merely sought to clarify his own position,
without disparaging Confucianism or Daoism.
People to this day receive its benefits.
The "Discourse on the Security of the Zhou Way and the Two Teachings" forgets merit while pointing out faults.
They spoke of starting a fight, and the Yuwen clan observed them.
This was like Bian Zhuangzi’s method of stabbing the tigers: once, when Bian Zhuangzi saw two tigers fighting over food, he intended to slay them both.
His family members remonstrated with him, urging him to wait until their fight was over,
for the larger one would surely be wounded and the smaller one would surely die.
If one were to strike it later, both could be caught with a single blow.
It turned out exactly as he had said.
Now, Dao’an is engaged in mutual refutation with the non-Buddhist schools.
All were utterly flawed and coarse;
Emperor Wu of Zhou was able to scrutinize them and employ their schemes.
Thus, "Emperor Yong" and "Prince Yong" are names of Emperor Wu of Zhou.
He ascended the throne in the third year of the Wucheng era of Emperor Wu.
In the second year of the Jiande era, he abolished the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism.
He passed away in the first year of the Dacheng era.
From the year of Gui-si to Wu-xu, the destruction wrought by those who lacked faith was no more severe than that of Huan Xuan;
yet while Huan submitted, Zhou rejected him—Huan Xuan had intended to compel monks to prostrate and to exclude them from the category of "sands" (monastics).
Master Yuan submitted a memorial and brought the matter to a halt;
he further composed the "Treatise on Not Bowing. Is this not because one can discern the depth of their talent and insight?
It is simply that there were, at that time, those who lacked learning.
Their minds and intellects are deaf and blind;
relying on their own stubbornness and meanness,
they are like swine or sheep.
He was perverse and followed only his own whims;

"Stretching continuously" means reaching everywhere. "Jiao" (繳) is a device for shooting birds;
"zeng" (罾) is a device for catching fish.
"Ji" (蔇) means to arrive at.
The practitioner does not reach [the goal], and the Sage regards this as a malady;
all living beings lament this forever. Alas!
What can be done? There is nothing that can be done. Thus it ends.
Since the arrival of the White Horse from the West and the translation of the Sanskrit texts into Chinese during the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Later Han,
when Kāśyapa Mātanga and Zhu Falan brought the scriptures and images on white horses to Luoyang, faith and slander have alternately prevailed.

The ruler and his ministers were not of one mind; at that time, the Daoist priests of the Five Peaks, including Chu Shanxin and others, sought a contest by means of burning scriptures and images. Furthermore, as for the lands of distant regions, the Nine Provinces (Jiufu) refer to them as the "wild frontiers" (huangbiao).

Regarding the customs of the western regions (Dui-fang), the four seas regard them as "barbarians" (rong-ren). Among the nine circuits and nine provinces, the western nations of the Dui-fang further claim that the boundaries of the Central Kingdom constitute a land of Confucian scholars (ru-bang).
The eastern frontier of Mount Conglu is a remote borderland.
Generally, people cherish their own dwellings and look down upon other lands.
Yet everyone says, "Why was the Buddha not born in the Middle Kingdom? The people of China consider their own land to be the Middle Kingdom based on what they have heard.
On the summer solstice in Central India, one measures the shadow until it reaches the end of its gnomon; on the day of the summer solstice in Central India (Madhyadeśa), the same occurs.
If a pole is planted at midday, it casts no shadow;
this is because the sun is positioned directly overhead at the center of Jambudvīpa, which is why that place is called the "Center.

Although in this land, Shao Bo inspected the site for the capital while Zhou Gong went to establish the original capital of Zhou at Hao, and although Shao Gong inspected the site at Shan and Ru while Zhou Gong arrived at Chengzhou to establish it, [the true center remains there].
This is precisely what the present capital of Lu is;

yet the *Rites of Zhou* states in the duties of the Grand Minister of the Interior that "the shadow at the summer solstice measures one chi and five cun. Although the capital of Lu is the heart of Zhendan (China), [it is not the center of the world].
On the day of the summer solstice at noon, the shadow cast by a planted pole is still one chi and five cun long;
in other locations, it is even longer. This is called the "Center of the Earth," where heaven and earth converge.
It is where the four seasons intersect,
where wind and rain converge,
and where yin and yang harmonize.
When the hundred things were abundant and at peace,
he established the royal state.
It is now located in Yangcheng County, Henan.
Having reached the center of the Middle Kingdom,
the shadow still has a surplus;
were it not at Yangcheng, it would exceed one chi and five cun.
In the heavens, one spans a thousand *li*, while in the earth,
it is but one inch; thus, beyond ten thousand *li* in the Western Regions,
there exist both foreign and Chinese states.
How can antiquity and the present be fixed?
According to the *Zuozhuan*, the region of Yi and Luo was transformed into a territory of the Rong;
indeed, there were the Rong of Yi and Luo.
Furthermore, there was the expedition against the Rong of Lu-gun, all of whom were located in the Luo region. The Wu-Yue people transformed into Xia;
though the Wu-Yue were originally "barbarians," both Goujian and Fuchai became regional hegemons of the Central Kingdom. Thus, the Most Sage [the Duke of Zhou] seized the opportune moment.
This is not restricted by regional customs; rather,
taking the Jambudvīpa of this great trichiliocosm as the inner land,
one may simply take this very place as such.
That which can be is precisely that which is.
How could one be considered not the sovereign of all under heaven simply because the civil and martial virtues were not located in Luo? King Wen resided among the Western Rong.
When King Wu resided beneath Mount Qi, there was at that time no Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakravartin) in the Western Regions;
he divided the world into four domains,
with the East having Man as its presiding lord.
It is precisely because ritual and music originate from this region that benevolence and righteousness crown the eight wildernesses;
when one speaks of upholding the Mean, it does not necessarily depend on the land.
He Chengtian of the Song dynasty asked Huiyan:
"What calendar does the Buddha-land use?
Huiyan replied:
On the day of the summer solstice at midday, there is no shadow.
The Five Elements favor the virtue of Earth.
Eight *cun* constitute one *chi*.
One *liang* [of the foreign measure] corresponds to twelve *liang* in this region.

Because Huiyan personally traveled to the Western Heaven and returned, he was able to clarify this matter. Upon further investigation of the solstices and equinoxes—the spring and autumn equinoxes and the summer and winter solstices—and the subtle movements of the sun and moon across the celestial sphere, Yin and Yang, it was found to be indeed so.
However, the Tripitaka masters who came from the West crossed the sea to retranslate the scriptures,
braving hardships and risking death a hundred times to reach this one life;
yet once they arrived, they were unaware of where their own native lands lay.
This is truly lamentable.

As for his translations, when compared with the scriptures of the world at large, they already deviate from what is seen and heard and deeply contradict the desires [of the people]; they would cause those long steeped in ignorance to turn their backs on the wind like grass bending away.
It is like rolling a marble down a steep slope;
it only increases one's indignation.
This is truly difficult, as the journey for the translation of the Tripiṭaka has been so long and arduous.
Failing to master the local language,
their phrasing became plain and rustic, and their style lacked literary elegance,
as seen in the scriptures translated by An Shigao and others.
Those who do not understand will,
conversely, criticize one another,
thereby increasing their slander and abuse.
This, then, is not yet sufficient. Now, when Yongmen Zhou took up his lute for Mengchang, who was distressed and filled with sorrowful emotion,
as soon as the lute was struck once,
tears fell from his eyes and nose in profusion.
One does not know its limit; it was the state of Yongmen in the territory of Qi.
Mengchang Tian Wen was a prince of Qi.
Zhou Cheng played the lute for him, and as the music began, the strings resonated.
Yet their tears could not be restrained; thus, those who were heterodox and foolish, having inherited the doubts, vacillations, obstructions, and meanness of kings and lords, began to ply their lips.
Once their lips were parted, they slandered and incited instability.

"Enough! This passage describes those who, being light-minded and disparaging toward the religious teachings, take advantage of the uncertainty and indecision regarding our doctrine on the part of government officials to fan the flames with their lips and teeth for the sake of slander."
This caused the hearts of kings and lords to turn toward it and to place their trust in it. For this reason, they were granted high positions and great talents;
their words became the standard for all things, and their conduct became the law of the age. Thus, the Buddha-dharma was entrusted to kings and ministers.
All officials in office and scholars of talent and learning should provide protection and support; in every location,
the Three Jewels should be especially assisted and served.
He esteemed their great talents and high positions so that they might propagate and protect the religious teachings.
They served as standards and models;
by following these laws and regulations, he guided and assisted them.
If they turn their backs, one strikes them and seizes them by the armpits;
those who submit and follow will have their arms lifted and led away.
As for those who do not believe,
strike them and reprimand them so that those who have lost their way in youth may know where to turn;
let them eat the jujube fruit and cherish its sweetness.
The voice of the yellow oriole becomes beautiful when it feeds on mulberry fruits;

this is like hearing the Dharma and responding with reverence and faith. Thus, the Buddha-dharma is as secure as a golden city and a moat of boiling water, relying upon high-ranking officials as its external protectors.
Thus, if the Buddha-dharma possesses the solidity of a fortified city, those who attack it will inevitably suffer defeat.
If the Vinaya loses its teachers, yet there are external allies to provide mutual defense, it will naturally be crushed and destroyed. Such is the peril facing the Śākya school.

As for why the followers of Śākya cannot avoid this: when outsiders pose difficult questions to challenge the teachings of Śākya, they cite the very teachings of Śākya to answer them, unable to evade those challenges.
What is the reason for this? It is like being accused of a crime during the formal proceedings.
The blazing sun dries it up;
the Yang energy errs in its sequence,
and the great rain pours down— this refers to prolonged rain.
When the yin element loses its order,
it requires clear weather to resolve; this is the case for those who have suffered from a long drought.
If the yang loses its order,
sweet rain must be used to resolve it; if the yin assists the yin, or the yang assists the yang [the imbalance must likewise be corrected].
Thus, floods lasting nine years or droughts lasting seven years are not to be considered much;
yet even Yao experienced floods for nine years.
Tang experienced a seven-year drought; thus, among the worthy and virtuous of antiquity, what majesty could there be without rank?
What gratification could there be without rewards?
Without argumentation, how can there be conviction?

In their rebuttals and oppositions, they frequently cite Buddhist teachings as evidence, which conversely serves to bolster their arrogance when answering difficult challenges; yet, if they were to rely exclusively on citing their own school's teachings as evidence, [the same fault would apply].
It is like using the yin to assist the yin and the yang to assist the yang; thus, it subdues difficulties, calms violence, rectifies confusion, and eliminates chaos.
It crushes the sophistry of Gongsun Long and brings about impartiality.
"To take the chaotic and to take the victorious.
Gongsun Long was a man of Zhao.
Yu Xiang wished to request that Handan be enfeoffed as the territory of Pingyuan.
The dragon admonished him with swift eloquence and caused him to desist.
Later, the *Yuyi* says:
"The dragon possessed the eloquence of the 'White Horse' [disputation]; it cut short the slanders of Shusun [Wushu]. Shusun Wushu slandered Zhongni."
Zi Gong said, "The Master must not be disparaged.
The worthiness of others is like hills and mounds."
The virtue of our Master is like the sun and moon;
it cannot be surpassed. Even those clad in square-cut robes cannot compare to one who wears the ceremonial cap and robes.
When a Confucian scholar encounters someone who seeks to disparage our Master, he is always able to respond to them.
How can it be that these shaven-headed sons of Śākya, wearing square-cut robes, encounter such disparagement of their Master yet remain without a word in response—is this not shameful?
One must certainly rely upon learning.
"Square robes" refers to the *kāṣāya*; formerly, He Chengtian composed the "Discourse on the Attainment of Nature."
Yan Yanzhi refuted him; both were court officials of the Song dynasty.
Yan was the Viscount of Light (Yanguanglu).
He was a man of letters who frequently enjoyed drinking. Fan Zhen composed the "Treatise on the Extinction of Form and Spirit" (Xingshimieyi).
Shen Yue was a man of substance among the worthy scholars of the Liang dynasty.

His writings are found in the *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification [of Buddhism]). Thus, jackals and wolves are not subdued except by the *śarabha*, and snakes and swine are not severed except by the sword of Mohe.
Yet the sutra refers to them as "those who extend assistance to others" (zhuanyuan zhi ren); "extension" (zhan) here means "assistance" (yuan).
By taking faith as an external grant, they truly act in accordance with this title.
If it is indeed so, then they do not fail to live up to their name.
Alas! There are Heaven and Earth;
there is the process of generation and completion;
and there are those who possess sincerity.
There are those who do not believe. Since heaven and earth have created all things and human relations, within these human relations there are both those who believe and those who do not;

this is because their dispositions differ. As for those who possess faith: in the Han dynasty, there was Emperor Xianzong—the second sovereign of the Later Han, Emperor Ming—as well as Fu Wuzhong (Fu Yi), Sun Quan, the Great Emperor of Wu, Zhi with Kan (Zhi Qian and Kan Ze), and from the Eastern Jin until the end of that dynasty, figures such as Wang Meng, Xi Chao, Xu Xun, and Xie Shang.
Song Wenming; as well as the royal princes He Yan and his peers;
and Wei Zonggong.
Liu Qiu of the Southern Qi;
and the Liang dynasty ruler and his ministers, Tao Yinyu, whose courtesy name was Jingchun.
(Tao Jingchun’s courtesy name was Yinyu.)

Zhenbai (Zhengbai) was the former ruler of Northern Qi; Yan Zhitui was also among those who held deep faith. As for those who did not believe, there was Cai Mo, style name Daoming, of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The Eastern Emperor ordered him to compose a hymn in praise of the Buddha,
but Sengjian refused to comply;
the Emperor then accused him of slandering the Buddha.
Xia Tingwei was demoted to commoner status; [the others were] Wei Zhao Wang Du,
Song Zhou Lang, Yu Yuan,
Wei Zhang Pujie, Li Rang, and Yang Xuanzhi.

Liu Zhou of the Qi dynasty and Xun Ji of the Liang dynasty were truly men who disparaged the teachings with their hearts and lacked faith. For one who has faith, the mind becomes still and unified, clearly penetrating the myriad transformations;
yet some may fail to relinquish that which they cling to.
One must requite those who seek alms by honoring the principle of profound causes and conditions and maintaining a heart of sincere reverence for the precepts.
To retreat would result in the cruelty of being cast into a moat; to advance leads to the beauty of containing the light. A "moat" (huáng) is a pit.
If one were to fall into such a pit, those who do not believe would find their spirits rendered not in vain.
My humble intellect and turbid thoughts may lead me to find the stupas and towers of the Dharma either too grandly ostentatious,
or the scriptures of the Dharma too vast and profound.
The monastic community dwells in high and pure places; the followers of the Dharma are honored and great.
To vent one’s own grievances is to stretch out what is contrary to the words of Yangzi;
even four horses cannot overtake the tongue once it has spoken.
To fall into the ranks of the heterodox—
how lamentable! Yet,
there are those who go too far in their faith.
For example: Prince Wenhui of Qi and Prince Jingling;
Emperor Gaozu of Liang and Emperors Wenxuan of Chen;
and Emperors Wencheng, Xiwen, and Xiaowen of Wei, as well as Gao Yang of Northern Qi.
All these instances of faith and so forth are seen in the *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism), whether it be the expounding of the golden verses,
the relinquishing of precious thrones,
or the permitting of the people to enter the Way.

Some have exhausted their nations to erect monasteries; now the Great Song Emperor has commissioned several sets of the Tripitaka in gold and silver lettering, and carved over 130,000 woodblocks for printing the Tripitaka.
He magnificently adorned the monasteries throughout the empire.
Each year, the Ministry of Sacrifices issued official decrees to ordain over eight thousand novices.
When Emperor Taizong first ascended the throne, he permitted all boys registered in the census to leave home and become monks; however, there were some who exceeded the bounds of faith.

For instance, during the Northern Wei of Tuoba Wu and the Northern Zhou of Yuwen Wu, there were figures such as Cui Hao and the early Tang dynasty’s Fu Yi, who regarded [Buddhism] as a calamity, a pestilence, a drought-demon, or a comet.
There have also been sovereigns who proposed the discussion of purging [the monastic community].
This is truly an act of exalting purity and upholding clarity;
it is not the conduct of one who lacks faith.
Formerly, Huan Xuan issued an edict stating: "Among the śramaṇas, there are those capable of expounding and elucidating the scriptures."
He eloquently expounds the principles of meaning;
his observance of the precepts is refined and upright, sufficient to proclaim and record the Great Transformation. As for those who deviate from this:
He caused them all to disrobe.
Master Huiyuan wrote a letter to Lord Huan saying:
"The Buddha-dharma is declining."
Having been defiled and cluttered for many days, every time I approach it,
a sense of indignation fills my breast.

I have always feared that my destiny might take an unintended turn and lead to ruin; "ruin" (lunxu) implies a gradual sinking. I have observed that the teachings of the various pure and serene monastics truly accord with my own fundamental mind.
Indeed, it is like the Jing River being distinguished by the Wei River.
Thus, the clear and the turbid differ in their natures;
when the crooked is rectified by the straight,
lack of benevolence naturally recedes.
Once this mandate is implemented,
these two principles will be attained;
thereafter, those who practice hypocrisy will be cut off from the path of false ways.
Those who cherish the truth are free from the reproach of burdening the secular world;
thus, when the monastic and the secular interact, the Three Jewels flourish once more. In ancient times, there were generally two intentions behind the purging of the Sangha.
First, out of reverence for the Dharma-gate and an abhorrence of its corruption and laxity, they sought to purge the wicked and the superfluous in order to ensure its purity.

These fourteen individuals were: Emperor Wencheng of the Song dynasty, Wang Du, Yan Yanzhi, Xiao Mozhi, Zhou Lang, Yu Yuan, Zhang Puhui, Li Ran, Wei Yuansong, Gu Guan, Na Zicai, Gao Daorang, Lu Sidao, and Emperor Gaozu of the Tang dynasty.
The second [category] consists of those who, out of hatred and envy, sought to bring about their own ruin by exposing [the faith] and harboring grudges;

therefore, it was necessary to purge them in order to clear one's mind. These eleven individuals were: Emperor Taiwu of the Wei, Gaozu of the Zhou, Cai Mu, Liu Zhu, Yang Xuanzhi, Xun Ji, Zhang Chou, Yutuo, Liu Huilin, Fan Zhen, and Fu Yi. Wang Wentong is the eleventh.
In truth, [the world] was being destroyed; thus, the Mysterious Teaching (Xuanjiao) could not reach Mount Lu.
As for those who consume blood and fetuses or grains and food, does it matter whether they believe or do not believe? They are one and the same.

However, those who receive the pure vital energy (*zhèngqì*) of the five elements necessarily preserve their correct nature (*zhèngxìng*) and correct destiny (*zhèngmìng*). The worthy person receives the refined energy of the five phases (*wǔxíng*), being able to manifest flourishing conduct and clearly exert diligent practice; such a person relies upon the field of merit (*fútián*).
Therefore, this is indeed credible.
Those who receive the influence of cold qi will inevitably become perverse, licentious, and obstinate; they will suppress and destroy the principles of Heaven.
They falsely claimed that [the dynasty] would perish;
therefore, they were not believed.
If one considers the "Nine Men of Excellence" (Yuan-kai) of Tang and Yu, or Yi Yin and Fu Yue of Xia and Yin—Tang and Yu being Yao and Shun—[it is clear that such claims were groundless].
The sixteen ministers of Yuanyue were the Xia ruler Yu and the Yin ruler Tang;
they were Yi Yin and Yue Shuo. As for the "Ten Confusers" of Zhou, "luan" here means "to bring order."
Taigong, Zhougong, Shaogong, Bīgong, Rónggong, Nángōng Kuò, Sànyíshēng, Tàidiān, Yànwén, and Wǔmǔ—these ten men—and the Three Heroes of the Han, Zhāng Liáng; these are they.
Xiao He gazed upon the golden countenance with devotion and humbly listened to the jade-axled scriptures.
Thus, I have never failed to believe this.
When the five internal organs are stirred and speech and action are directed toward all beings, why is this so?
It is because practicing goodness leaves no day feeling sufficient. Although such people have not yet coincidentally encountered formal instruction, they are moved by it.
If one encounters it, the heart will revere and believe it profoundly. Were Jie, Zhou, Zhuang, Zhi, Yang Huo, Zi-zang, or even the blind to behold it, they would listen as if they were hearing;
were the deaf to behold it, they would hear as if they were not deaf—even as Jie did in the Xia dynasty.
Zhou was the tyrant of Yin;
Zhuang Qiao was a wicked robber from Chu and Shu; and Di Zhi was a violent thief from Lu.
Yang Huo was a subordinate official of Ji Huanzi who committed atrocities in Lu.
Zi-zang was the son of Zi-zang of Zheng.
A blind man hears good music but lacks the capacity for transformation; what can be done about that?
Indeed, it is because the wicked person does not do good.
This is also because one finds not enough days;
life has its limits, for the body is not made of metal or stone.
When joy is not yet fulfilled,
sorrow follows it;
the Sage of Old declared that the self is a great affliction.

Zhongni sighed that those who met face-to-face were as if already lost; how can the fleeting flow of this floating life be deemed worthy? Yet why does the Buddhist teaching harbor such animosity? To sincerely strive for self-reduction is not the beginning of seeking fortune;
rather, it is to stand at the forefront of calamity. This is truly what is called the failing of being able to dislike [the world] but unable to cultivate goodness.
If that fruit exists,
even if one wishes to cut oneself off from it,
what harm could there be to the sun and moon? This is as taught in those religious systems.
Cause and effect truly exist from the beginning;
even if you were to destroy them, how could you possibly harm their Way? Zigong said:
Even if a person wishes to sever themselves from the world,
what harm does this do to the sun and moon? If that [person] truly lacks aspiration,
they merely establish empty virtues.

It is sufficient to keep one far from harm. If the matters of cause and effect as taught in Buddhism were fundamentally non-existent, then even a hollow pursuit of a good reputation would be sufficient to keep one far from harm;
for to falsely abstain from killing is still better than being a butcher or a fisherman.
To refrain from wealth in vain is still better than theft;
to purify oneself in vain is still better than being turbid and corrupt.
If one does not maintain the curtains and screens, it is called failing to govern the inner chambers; how much more so when one does not know that their purity is not even in vain!
Furthermore, in the teachings of Śākya, "stealing" refers to the taking of wealth;
"eating meat" refers to the trading of flesh;
"harming others" refers to the pursuit of profit for one's own eyes and neck; and "selling and bartering" refers to commercial exchange.
Now that you have seized another's property,
you shall also return that property;
now that you eat their flesh, [you shall likewise repay it].
One will surely be eaten by others in the future;
today one uses the essential means of harming others, yet tomorrow one will suffer harm oneself—
this is the way of exchange.
Regarding the "Neck" (lingxiang):
if one does not engage in commerce, one's goodness will be substantial; if one can truly refrain from theft and killing, one may claim it for oneself as goodness.
The facts are real, and since their words are true,
how could these individuals be false?
Such were Fotudeng and the Great Master Sengcan of Mount Heng.
Dao'an was able to look back over many lifetimes and perceive the preliminary stages of his spiritual cultivation;
Liu Yimin and Liu Qiu were both widely learned and diligent in their studies.
Those who disregarded the bows and banners were all eminent scholars of Jin who declined worldly honors.
In antiquity, scholars were summoned with bows and banners; Xu Xun and Zong Bing were such examples.
Having completed the year’s work, one might ask:
"Is it not the case that the Buddha-dharma lacks substance, yet can cause others to establish their resolve so firmly that it cannot be uprooted? These are all matters for the wise and enlightened.
How could such sentiments be mistaken? Formerly, at the beginning of the Wude era, while the high ministers did not consider this, the subordinate officials sought to curry favor with the Emperor.
At that time, Fu Yi [argued] that because the Tang dynasty originated from the Li clan, [the state was thus of the same lineage as Laozi].
Taking Laozi as their progenitor,
they consequently slandered him and ordered his "purification and elimination" [from the state].
They claimed that the imperial lineage originated from Xuanyuan (the Mysterious Origin).
When civilization becomes vast and unified with the whole world,
it will bring harm to my teaching;
even bees and scorpions will become poisonous.

"Shell-patterned brocade has its designs"—this refers to the ornamental patterns of shell-patterned brocade. "Only the Emperor at this time was clear-sighted and intelligent," meaning that in the end there was nothing that obscured him;
*wang* (罔) means "not," and *you* (攸) means "that which"; *bi* (蔽) means "obscuration" or "darkness."

Although Fu Yi and others fanned delusions to mislead the sagely intellect of the Emperor, the Emperor remained free from any ignorance or partiality. Those who are envious and jealous are unable to overcome the sages and saints;
envy is greed, and jealousy is a destructive pest.
They were able to prevail.
As for Yan Sheng, Fali, Sengdao, Xuanshi, and others—
though the sentiments of that Fu Yi were indeed greedy and corrupt.
In the end, he could not overcome that man; thus his virtue was obscured.
Having no ground for his influence, he collapsed and lay prostrate.
Consequently, his wickedness was destroyed, and the calumnious slanders of the "moistening" type were brought to an end.
Petty grievances could not prevail; the bright sun, though about to set, was raised once more.
The dense, oily clouds gathered.
Having dispersed, they have again become a clan; as the sun of the Buddha set, it has shone forth once more.
As the clouds of wisdom scattered, they have gathered again. This truly possesses the spiritual power of the ancestral temples and altars of the Tang dynasty;
it shall surely preserve the blessings for its descendants and the common people.

Now, Heaven and Earth and the realm of the state are governed by the Great Shepherd; Heaven produces the masses of the people and establishes shepherds to rule them, using spirits and ghosts to bring them peace—“peace” meaning tranquility and security.
These spirits are intelligent, clear-sighted, upright, and just, bestowing blessings upon the good and bringing calamity upon the licentious. Should a ruler of men lose the Way...
Thus, the *Shennichuan* (Biographies of Divine Nuns) records that when the Yuwen clan destroyed the Buddha-dharma,
the divine nuns saw auspicious deities all departing toward the west.
Later, as a result, the state was destroyed.
Recently, the Chai family defaced the Great Compassionate One (Avalokiteśvara) made of copper in Zhenzhou;
consequently, they suffered from a malignant disease and perished. Thus, one cannot rely on mountains or rivers for protection.
When mountains and rivers are not at peace,
calamities and misfortunes arise; thus, Heaven reverses its regular course and Earth brings forth its portents.
People harbor disorder;
agriculture suffers; mountains collapse and rivers run dry;
and the stars lose their proper courses.
The earth quakes and mountains roar;
bandits rise up in competition,
and malevolent spirits flourish.
When floods and droughts cause calamity, what can be expected of the sacrificial grain?
In ancient times, Jie and Zhou were like King You; Jie was the Xia ruler Ao, who doted on Meixi, while Zhou was Xin of Yin, who doted on Jijiu.
King You of Zhou favored Bao Si;
both cases illustrate how one may bring state affairs into chaos through infatuation with beauty and thereby lose the empire.
There were also the "wine-pool" and the "meat-forest."
He fashioned extraordinary and decadent contrivances to gratify his women;
Zhou possessed wine-pools, forests of meat, mountains of fermented grain, and hills of dried meat,
and he employed the "burning pillar" as a form of punishment.
To cut off the shins of those wading through the morning waters,
to剖 (carve open) the hearts of the worthy,
and to disembowel and dismember pregnant women— such cruelties do not even reach the spirits and deities.
Furthermore, mountains crumbled and rivers shook;
stars fell and ghosts wailed.
How much more so when the path of goodness is cut away and destroyed!

If the myriad spirits have no refuge, how can the phoenix appear at the outskirts of the capital, the four seasons be harmonized as the "jade candle," and the steps of the Great Terrace be as level as a whetstone? During the time of Yao, the phoenix nested in the Angate Pavilion;
this harmony of the four seasons was called the "jade candle. At that time, there was the śramaṇa Huìjìng of Gāoyè Monastery.
Dharma-lin, together with the veteran scholars and eminent talents,
produced a mass of exquisite blossoms— a tapestry of five-colored patterns.
Your response was like the resonance of golden music, harmonizing in perfect accord.
Win over them with virtue;
strengthen them with righteousness;
and sharpen your spears and axes.
He completely blocked their lairs.
There was Li Shizheng, Director of Ceremonies at the Gate,
who composed three treatises titled *The Inner Virtue’s Discourse on the Rectification of Fate and the Righteous and the Unrighteous*.

Listing those points of confusion and examining them in detail to refute and eliminate [erroneous views], the text is found in the fourteenth fascicle of the *Gu Hongming ji* (Collection on the Propagation and Clarification of the Dharma). This work is both well-composed and authoritative; it is most complete and sufficient to assist and promote the True Gate.
Having elucidated the ultimate mystery,
those who observe it in future generations should maintain silence and remain profound;
they must no longer harbor doubts or slander.
